(p-١٧٨٨) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Part Six

Surah al-Ma'idah

It is so named because its story is the most wondrous of what is mentioned in it, since it contains many signs, great gentleness toward those who believe, and severe harshness toward those who disbelieve. Thus it is the greatest motivation for accepting the obligations, which produce the bond of love arising from the faith-based connection between God and His servants. This is what al-Mahayimi stated.

This surah is Medinan, and its verses number one hundred and twenty.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: The surah is Medinan, except His saying, ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] and so on, for it was revealed in Makkah. End of quotation.

I say: In his statement there are two points for consideration:

The first: This is based on the view that the Makki is what was revealed in Makkah even after the Hijrah, and the Madani is what was revealed in Madinah. This is a terminology of some of the early scholars. However, the more well-known view, as in (al-Itqan), is that the Makki is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Madani is what was revealed after it, whether it was revealed in Makkah or in Madinah, in the year of the Conquest or the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, or during one of the journeys.

The second: It remains for him, if he follows that terminology, that there are other verses.

al-Suyuti said in (al-Itqan): In the type concerning the knowledge of what was revealed while at home (al-hadari) and what was revealed while travelling (al-safari), there are examples of the latter.

Among them: the beginning of al-Ma'idah. al-Bayhaqi related in (Shu'ab al-Iman) from Asma' bint Yazid that it was revealed at Mina. He also related in (al-Dala'il) from Umm 'Amr, from her paternal uncle, that it was revealed on a journey of his. Abu 'Ubayd related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed at the Farewell Pilgrimage, between Makkah and Madinah.

(p-١٧٨٩) Among them: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. In the Sahih, from 'Umar, it is related that it was revealed on the afternoon of 'Arafah, on Friday, in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, and it has many chains. However, Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that it was revealed on the day of Ghadir Khumm. He related similarly from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and in it: it was the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage. Both of these are not authentic.

Among them: the verse of tayammum within it. In the Sahih, from 'A'ishah, it is related that it was revealed at al-Bayda' while they were entering Madinah.

(p-١٧٩٠) Among them: ﴿O you who believe, remember God's favour upon you when a people intended to stretch out their hands against you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 11] and so on. It was revealed in Batn Nakhl.

Among them: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. It was revealed at Dhat al-Riqa'. End of quotation.

These narrations will be expounded, God willing, at these verses.

Ibn Kathir said: Imam Ahmad related from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: "I was indeed holding the rein of al-'Adba', the she-camel of the Messenger of God ﷺ, when the whole of al-Ma'idah was revealed to him, and she nearly broke the foreleg of the camel from its weight."

Imam Ahmad also related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was riding his mount, and it could not bear him, so he dismounted from it." Ahmad alone related it.

al-Hakim related from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: I performed Hajj and entered upon 'A'ishah, and she said to me: "O Jubayr! Do you recite al-Ma'idah?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed, it is the last surah revealed. So whatever you find in it of lawful, consider it lawful, and whatever you find in it of unlawful, consider it unlawful." Then he said: It is sahih according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it.

(p-١٧٩١) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts. Lawful for you is the beast of cattle, except what is recited to you, not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, God decrees what He wills.﴾

﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim related that a man came to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and said: "Charge me with something!" He said: "When you hear God say, 'O you who believe,' then give it your attentive hearing, for it is either something good He commands, or something evil He forbids."

And al-wafa' (fulfilment) is the opposite of treachery, as in the Qamus. Others said: it is the persistence in the path of solidarity and the observance of the covenants of companions. It is said: he fulfilled the covenant (wafa bi-al-'ahd) and made it complete (awfa bihi).

Nasir al-Din said in al-Intisaf: The verb in the Book of God comes with the doubled form in His saying, ﴿and Abraham who fulfilled﴾ [al-Najm: 37], and comes as awfa much, and from it: "fulfil the contracts." As for wafa in the triliteral form, it occurs only in His saying, ﴿and who is more faithful to his covenant than God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], because the elative (af'al al-tafdil) is formed from wafa, since it is formed only from a triliteral root.

(p-١٧٩٢) Al-'uqud is the plural of 'aqd, which is a firm covenant. It is likened to the knotting of a rope and the like, and these are the covenants of God that He made with His servants and imposed upon them among the obligations of the commandments.

'Ali ibn Talhah related: Ibn 'Abbas said: By the covenants is meant what God has made lawful, what He has made unlawful, what He has obligated, and what He has set as limits in the whole of the Qur'an, and do not betray nor break them. Zayd ibn Aslam said: The contracts are six: the covenant of God, the alliance pact, the partnership contract, the sale contract, the marriage contract, and the oath. al-Zamakhshari said: The apparent meaning is that they are the covenants of God upon them in His religion, of making lawful what He has made lawful and unlawful what He has made unlawful, and that it is an utterance stated in summary, which is then followed by detail. That detail is His saying: Lawful for you is the beast of cattle. The beast (bahimah) is that which has no intellect at all, of the living creatures, or of the four-legged.

al-Raghib said: In common usage it is restricted to what is other than beasts of prey and birds. Its annexation to al-an'am (cattle) is for specification, like "a garment of silk." Its singular form is for the intent of the genus, that is: the eating of the beast of cattle is made lawful for you. The plural of na'am is with a vowelled 'ayn, and sometimes it is pronounced with a sukun. It means camels, cattle, sheep and goats: except what is recited, meaning: all the cattle are permitted to you, except what is forbidden to you in this surah, which is carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and other things.

That is because they used to forbid the sa'ibah and the bahirah.

So God informed that these two are lawful, except what is explained in this surah. Then He said: not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram, meaning: these things are made lawful for you without your making lawful the hunting while you are in the state of ihram. So "ghayr" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "lakum." In al-'Inayah he said: It is not disputed what is said: that it necessitates restricting the permissibility of the beast of cattle to the state in which the game is unlawful while they are in ihram. And it has been made lawful for them absolutely. Its benefit is not apparent, except if by the beast is meant the gazelles, wild asses and wild cattle, because it is known from it, with the lack of consistency in considering the concept, something else by a stronger inference. For if these are made lawful while the non-lawfulness of other things holds, while they are in ihram, to remove hardship from them, then how much more so in other than this state? So it is an explanation of God's favour upon them by what He has permitted them of that.

And an explanation that they are free from hunting and violating the sanctity of the Sanctuary. In al-Iklil: In the verse is the prohibition of hunting in ihram and in the Sanctuary, because "huruman" means "in ihram," and it is said: ahrama, meaning, with hajj and 'umrah; and ahrama: he entered the Sanctuary. End of quotation.

(p-١٧٩٣) Some of the Zaydis said: The intended forbidden game for the one in ihram is the game of the land. This is due to His saying in this surah: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travellers, but forbidden for you is the game of the land so long as you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96]. This is when "huruman" is taken as the plural of "muhrim," the one who performs ihram. If it is taken as the one who has entered the Sanctuary, the prohibition of sea game and land game becomes equal. That is where in the Sanctuary there is a river containing game, which is then forbidden, by His saying: ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], because it is said of one who enters the Sanctuary that he is muhrim, just as it is said: a'raqa and anjada when he entered Iraq and Najd. And the prohibition would apply in Makkah and the Sanctuary of Madinah, due to the reports that came concerning the prohibition of hunting in Madinah and cutting its trees, such as: "Madinah is a sanctuary from 'Ayr to Thawr." End of quotation.

Indeed God decrees what He wills, of permitting and forbidding. And He is the All-Wise in all that He commands and forbids.

(p-١٧٩٤) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾: that is, the markers of His religion, and they are the rites (al-manasik). Violating them means treating their sanctity lightly, or preventing those who observe them from doing so. Ibn Jarir reported from ʿIkrimah (p-١٧٩٥) and al-Suddi, who both said: it was revealed concerning al-Hutam, whose name was Shuraih ibn Hind al-Bakri. He came to Madinah alone, leaving his horses outside Madinah, and entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "To what do you invite the people?" He (ﷺ) said: "To the testimony that there is no god but Allah, to establishing prayer, and to giving zakat." He said: "Good. But I have chiefs whom I do not decide any matter without. Perhaps I will embrace Islam and bring them with me." He left his presence. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to his companions: "A man from Rabi'ah will enter upon you, speaking with the tongue of a devil." When Shuraih had left, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (p-١٧٩٦) "He entered with the face of a disbeliever and left with the back of a treacherous one, and this man is not a Muslim." Then he passed by a herd from the herds of Madinah, drove it off, and set out with it, while chanting and saying:

"The night has wrapped it with a driver, al-Hutam, who is neither a herdsman of camels nor of sheep,
nor a butcher upon the slaughtering-block. They spent the night sleeping, while the son of Hind did not sleep.
He spent the night driving them, a youth like the zalam, thick-calved, smooth-footed."

They pursued him but did not overtake him. When the following year came, Shuraih set out for Hajj with the pilgrims of Bakr ibn Wa'il from al-Yamamah, and with him was a great quantity of merchandise, and he had garlanded the sacrificial animal. The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah! This al-Hutam has set out for Hajj, so leave us free to deal with him." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, he has garlanded the sacrificial animal." They said: "O Messenger of Allah! This is something we used to do in the Jahiliyyah." But the Prophet (ﷺ) refused. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah.﴾" Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the rites. The polytheists used to perform Hajj and bring sacrificial animals, and the Muslims wished to raid them, so Allah forbade them from that.

And from Ibn ʿAbbas also: ﴿do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ means that you hunt while in ihram. It is also said: the rites of Allah are the laws of His religion which He set as limits for His servants, and violating them is to transgress against them. It is evident that the generality of the expression includes all of this.

(p-١٧٩٧) ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾: what is meant is the category, so it includes all the sacred months. They are four: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. That is, do not violate them by fighting in them. The Arabs used to forbid fighting in them during the Jahiliyyah, and when Islam came it did not abolish this ruling but rather affirmed it. Thus it is in "Lubab al-Ta'wil."

Ibn Kathir said: By His words ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ is meant its sanctity and acknowledging its honour, and abstaining from what Allah has forbidden in it, such as initiating fighting, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is great﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Bakrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-١٧٩٨) said in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed, time has returned to its original form of the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred..." and the hadith continues. This indicates the continuation of their sanctity until the end of time, as is the view of a group of the early scholars (al-salaf).

ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning His words ﴿nor the sacred month﴾, that it means: do not consider fighting in it lawful. Likewise said Muqatil and ʿAbd al-Karim ibn Malik al-Jazari, and Ibn Jarir also chose this view. But the majority held that this is abrogated (mansukh), and that it is permissible to initiate fighting in the sacred months. They argued with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and the intended sacred months are the four months of travel.
They said: He did not exempt one sacred month from the others. End of quotation. In Ibn Hazm's book "al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh" it is said that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword. Some of the Zaydiyyah in their "Tafsir" transmitted from al-Hasan that there is no abrogated (mansukh) matter in this surah, and from Abu Maysarah: in it are eighteen obligations, and there is nothing abrogated in it. (End of quotation.)

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAwf who said: I said to al-Hasan: Has anything been abrogated from al-Ma'idah? He said: No.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Zad al-Ma'ad," in the "Section on the Expedition of al-Khabt": its commander was Abu ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrah, and it took place in Rajab, as mentioned by the memorizer Ibn Sayyid al-Nas in "ʿUyun al-Athar."
Then he said regarding the jurisprudence of this account: it contains the permissibility of fighting in a sacred month, if the mention of the date as Rajab in it is preserved. But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is an error that is not preserved, since it is not transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he fought in a sacred month, nor raided in it, nor dispatched a expedition in it. The polytheists had reproached the Muslims for fighting in it at the beginning of Rajab, in the account of al-ʿAla' ibn al-Hadrami, and they said: Muhammad has made the sacred month lawful. Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is great﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. Nothing has been established that abrogates this by a text that must be adhered to, nor has the Ummah agreed on its abrogation. The prohibition of fighting in the sacred months has been argued from His words: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], but there is no proof in this, because the sacred months here are the months of travel in which Allah allowed the polytheists to travel in the land safely. Their first was the day of the Greater Pilgrimage, the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and their last was the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. This is the correct view regarding the verse for many reasons, which is not the place to mention. End of quotation.

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor the sacrificial animals﴾: that is, do not violate them by seizing them by force or by preventing them from reaching their place of sacrifice. The hady (sacrificial animal) is what is brought as an offering to the Ka'bah of camels, cattle, or sheep. In "al-Iklil": this is the basis for the legitimacy of offering animals to the House, the prohibition of raiding it, and slaughtering it before it reaches its place. The verse is also cited as evidence for prohibiting eating from it.

﴿nor the garlands﴾: plural of qilādah, which is what is hung around the neck of the sacrificial animal, of sandals or tree bark, so that it is known to be a sacrificial animal and is not molested. What is meant is the prohibition against molesting the garlanded animals of the hady, which are the camels. He mentioned them separately after ﴿the sacrificial animals﴾ although they are included in it, to emphasize the recommendation to them because of their superiority over others, as they are the most noble of the hady, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98], coordinated after the angels. It is as if it were said: and the garlanded ones among them, especially. Or the prohibition is against molesting the garlands themselves, as an exaggeration in prohibiting molesting (p-١٨٠٠) their owners, meaning: do not violate their garlands, let alone violate them. Just as He forbade displaying adornment in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31], as an exaggeration in prohibiting displaying its locations. Thus said Abu al-Su'ud.

The memorizer Ibn Kathir said: meaning, do not abandon offering to the Sacred House, for in it is the glorification of the rites of Allah. And do not abandon garlanding them around their necks so that they are distinguished from other livestock.

And so it is known that it is an offering to the Ka'bah, so that whoever intends it with evil avoids it, and it inspires whoever sees it to do the same. For whoever calls to guidance has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without their rewards being diminished in the least. For this reason, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed Hajj, he spent the night at Dhu al-Hulayfah, which is the valley of al-ʿAqiq. When morning came, he went round his wives, who were nine. Then he bathed, perfumed himself, and prayed two rak'ahs. Then he marked his offering and garlanded it, and he pronounced the talbiyah for Hajj and ʿUmrah. His offering was many camels, exceeding sixty, of the finest shapes and colours, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is so; and whoever honours the rites of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [al-Hajj: 32].

(p-١٨٠١) Some of the early scholars said: glorifying them is considering them good and fattening them. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to look for soundness in the eye and the ear." Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan. Muqatil said: ﴿nor the garlands﴾, so do not consider them lawful. When the people of the Jahiliyyah left their homelands outside the sacred months, they garlanded themselves with hair and wool, and the polytheists of the Haram garlanded themselves with bark from its trees, and thereby they were safe. Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim.

ʿAta' said: They used to garland themselves with the trees of the Haram and thereby they were safe. So Allah forbade cutting its trees. Likewise said Mutarrif ibn ʿAbd Allah. Their safety by this means was abrogated, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: two verses of this surah were abrogated: the verse of the garlands, and His words: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾. And with his chain to Ibn ʿAwf who said: I said to al-Hasan: Has anything been abrogated from al-Ma'idah? He said: No.

﴿nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾: that is, do not violate a people intending to visit al-Masjid al-Haram by obstructing them, fighting them, or harming them, for whoever enters it is safe. His words, exalted is He: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "ʾāmmīn" (those coming), meaning: intending to visit it while (p-١٨٠٢) seeking trade and the approval of Allah through their pilgrimage. Ibn Kathir transmitted from eight of the early exegetes that by "bounty" they meant seeking provision through trade. He said: as has preceded in His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jarir mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam ibn Hind al-Bakri, whose account has preceded. Ibn Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the believers and the polytheists used to perform Hajj, so Allah forbade the believers from preventing anyone, whether believer or disbeliever. Then Allah revealed after that: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and He said: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17], and He said: ﴿Only those maintain the mosques of Allah who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. Thus He removed the polytheists from al-Masjid al-Haram.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar narrated to us from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿nor the garlands, nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾, he said: it is abrogated. A man in the Jahiliyyah, when he left his house intending Hajj, would garland himself with tree bark, and no one would confront him. When he returned, he would garland himself with a garland of hair, and no one would confront him. The polytheist on that day was not prevented from the House, so they were commanded not to fight in the sacred month or near the House. Then His words ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5] abrogated it. Ibn Jarir chose that the meaning of His words "nor the garlands" is that whoever garlands himself with something from the Haram, grant him safety. He said: The Arabs have always reproached whoever violated that. The poet said:

"Did you not kill the two Hijrs when you two blinded them, while they tugged at the braided bark with their hands?"

(p-1804) ...the ones who need to be prohibited from violating the sanctity of the believers, and what the mention of the title "Lord" (al-Rububiyyah) with its attribution to their pronoun implies. Likewise, [the word] "good pleasure" (ridwan) honors them and indicates the attainment of their goal. So the purpose of this is to emphasize the prohibition and to intensify the condemnation of what is forbidden. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud said: They used to claim that they were upon the right course of their religion, and that the Hajj would bring them closer to Allah, the Exalted. So Allah, the Exalted, described them by their presumption. That corrupt presumption, although it is far from bringing about Allah's good pleasure, is not improbable as a means to the attainment of some of their worldly aims and their deliverance from immediate hardships, especially within the observance of the rights of Allah, the Exalted, and the glorification of His rites. Al-Razi transmitted from Abu Muslim al-Isfahani that the intended meaning of the verse is the disbelievers who were during the time of the Prophet ﷺ. When the covenant ended with Surat Bara'a (al-Tawbah), that danger disappeared, and the intended meaning became His, the Exalted, statement: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. End of quote.

﴿And when you have come out of ihram﴾, i.e., you have emerged from the state of ihram, or you have come out of the Haram into the permitted area (al-hill): then hunt, i.e., there is no blame upon you for hunting. ﴿And let not the hatred of a people﴾, i.e., let not the intense enmity toward a people lead you into transgression, ﴿because they obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, i.e., because they prevented you from visiting it and circumambulating it for the 'umrah. It is also read with a kasra on the hamza of "in" (إنْ), as a conditional particle: ﴿that you transgress﴾, i.e., against them. Abu al-Su'ud said: It was omitted, relying on its clarity, and as an indication that the primary aim of the prohibition is to prevent the transgression from proceeding from those addressed, in order to safeguard the glorification of the rites, not to prevent its occurrence against the people, out of consideration for their side. The second object of "yajrimannakum" is: i.e., let not the intensity of your hatred toward them, because of their obstruction of you from al-Masjid al-Haram, earn you transgression against them and retaliation against them for the sake of revenge.

Notes:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: Let not the hatred of a people, who had obstructed you from reaching al-Masjid al-Haram, which was in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, lead you to implement the judgment of Allah against them by taking retribution from them in injustice and aggression. Rather, judge by what Allah has commanded you of justice toward everyone. This verse, as will come in His statement: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], means: let not the hatred of nations lead you to abandon justice. Justice is obligatory upon everyone, toward everyone, in every situation.

One of the early generations (al-Salaf) said: Do not treat one who disobeys Allah regarding you with the same as obeying Allah regarding him. Justice is that by which the heavens and the earth stand. Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Sahl ibn Affan narrated to us, Abd Allah ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was at al-Hudaybiyyah with his Companions when the polytheists prevented them from the House. That weighed heavily upon them. Then some polytheists from the people of the East passed by them, intending 'umrah. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: 'We will prevent these as their companions prevented us.' So this verse was revealed concerning it."

The second: His statement ﴿and let not...﴾ is a prohibition against transgressing upon a group of those who are unrestricted (al-Amm), who were singled out for it, although they are included in the general prohibition against transgressing upon all of them, because they have distinct matters which might be imagined to justify their transgression and to motivate it.

The third: Perhaps the delay of this prohibition after His statement: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾, despite the clear connection to what precedes it, is to announce that the sanctity of transgression does not end with exiting the state of ihram, as the sanctity of hunting ends with it. Rather, it remains as long as their marks are not entirely cut off from the rites. By this, the continuation of the sanctity of harming the rest of the unrestricted people is known by a fortiori reasoning. Abu al-Su'ud transmitted this.

The fourth: The verse indicates that harm is prohibited. Similar to it is his peace and blessings be upon him statement: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm in Islam." And his peace and blessings be upon him statement: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrays you." Some of the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i school) mentioned this. In al-Iklil: In the verse is the prohibition of transgression, and that no one is taken to account for another's sin.

The fifth: (jarama) functions like (kasaba) in meaning and in its transitivity to one object and to two objects. It is said: "jarama dhanban," like "kasabahu" (he earned a sin). And "jaramtahu dhanban," like "kasabtuhu iyyahu" (I caused him to earn it). Except that "jarama" is commonly used for earning what has no good in it, and this is the reason for choosing it here over the second. The first may be transitivized from each of them with a hamza to the meaning of the second, so it is said: "ajramtuhu dhanban" and "aksabtuhu iyyahu." On this is the reading of one who read "yujrimannakum" with a damma on the ya'. Abu al-Su'ud transmitted this.

﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾. Since transgression is generally by way of joint support and cooperation, they were commanded, following what they were forbidden, to cooperate in everything that falls under righteousness and piety, and in following the command and avoiding caprice. Thus included in it, by primary entry, is what we are concerned with: cooperation in pardon and overlooking what has occurred from them. Then they were forbidden from cooperating in everything that falls under the category of injustice and disobedience. Thus included in it is the prohibition against cooperating in transgression and retaliation, by way of demonstrative proof. Abu al-Su'ud transmitted this.

Ibn Jarir said: Sin is abandoning what Allah has commanded to be done. Aggression is the transgression of what Allah has set as limits in the religion, and exceeding what Allah has enjoined regarding the self and others. Concerning the meaning of the verse there are many hadiths. Among them, from Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "One who guides to good is like one who does it." Narrated by al-Bazzar. And from Abu Mas'ud al-Badri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever guides to good has a reward like the reward of its doer." Narrated by Muslim.

And from (p-1807) Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in the least. And whoever calls to misguidance will bear a sin like the sins of those who follow him, without that diminishing their sins in the least." Narrated by Muslim.

And from Sahl ibn Sa'd: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ali, peace be upon him, on the day of Khaybar: "By Allah! If Allah guides one man through you, it is better for you than red camels." Agreed upon.

And from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah peace and blessings of Allah be upon him (p-1808) said: "Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is clear for the oppressed, but how do I help him when he is an oppressor?" He said: "You restrain him and prevent him from oppression. That is your help for him." Narrated by Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs. And from Yahya ibn Wathhab, from a man of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The believer who mixes with people and bears their harm patiently is greater in reward than the one who does not mix with people and does not bear their harm patiently." Narrated by Imam Ahmad.

Al-Tabarani and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi narrated from Aws ibn Shurahbil that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever walks with an oppressor to help him, knowing that he is an oppressor, has left Islam." And from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about righteousness and sin. He said: Righteousness is good character. Sin is that which troubles your breast and you dislike that people should become aware of it." Narrated by Muslim.

Note: on important branches.

Some of the Zaydiyya said: Among the fruits of the verse is the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. And that (p-1809) it is not permissible to assist a transgressor or a sinner. Thus entering into this is increasing the number of oppressors in any way, whether by word, deed, accepting a position of authority, or residing with them. In al-Iklil: The Malikis used the verse as evidence for the invalidity of a person hiring himself out to carry wine or the like, and for selling grapes to one who will press them into wine, and weapons to one who will disobey Allah with them, and similar things. End of quote, and it is sound. Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah said in his book al-Siyasa al-Shar'iyya: It is not lawful for a man to be a helper in oppression, for cooperation is of two kinds. One kind is cooperation in righteousness and piety, such as jihad, establishing the hudud, enforcing rights, and giving to those who deserve. This is what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. Whoever refrains from it out of fear of becoming one of the helpers of the oppressors has abandoned an obligation, individual or communal, while imagining that he is being scrupulous. How often is cowardice and failure mistaken for scrupulousness, when both are restraint and abstention.

The second is cooperation in sin and aggression, such as helping to shed a protected life, or to seize protected property, or to strike one who does not deserve to be struck, and the like. This is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. However, if property has been taken without right, and it is impossible to return it to its owners, as with much of the sultan's wealth, then helping to spend this wealth on the interests of the Muslims, such as securing the frontiers and the expenses of fighters and the like, is cooperation in righteousness and piety. For the obligation upon the sultan concerning this wealth, when it is not possible to identify its owners and return it to them or to their heirs, is to spend it, with repentance if he was the wrongdoer, on the interests of the Muslims. If someone else has taken it, then he must do the same. Likewise, if the sultan refuses to return it, then helping to spend it on the interests of its owners is better than leaving it in the hands of one who will waste it for its owners and for the Muslims. The foundation of the Shari'ah rests on His statement: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], (p-1810) which explains His statement: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102], and on the statement of the Prophet ﷺ: "If I command you with something, then do of it what you are able." Both al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it in their Sahihs.

And on the basis that the obligation is to achieve benefits and perfect them, and to nullify harms and reduce them. When they conflict, achieving the greater of two benefits by forfeiting the lesser, and averting the greater of two harms while tolerating the lesser, is what is legislated. The one who helps in sin and aggression is one who assists an oppressor in his oppression. As for one who assists the oppressed in lightening the oppression upon him, or in discharging the injustice, then he is the agent of the oppressed, not the agent of the oppressor. He is like one who lends to him, or one who undertakes to carry money to the oppressor on his behalf. An example of this: the guardian of an orphan or of an endowment, when an oppressor demands money from him, and he strives to repel it by giving less to him or to another after exerting complete effort in repelling it, then he is a doer of good, and there is no way against the doers of good. Likewise, the agent of an owner among the civil servants, scribes and others, who acts on their behalf in contracts, receipt, and paying what is demanded of them, does not act as an agent for the oppressors in taking. Likewise, if an injustice is imposed upon the people of a village, a quarter, a market, or a city, and a good man intercedes in repelling it from them to the utmost of his ability, and apportions it among them according to their capacity, without favoritism toward himself or others, and without bribery, but acts as their agent in repelling it from them and in paying it, then he is a doer of good. But generally, whoever enters into this (p-1811) is the agent of the oppressors: favoring, taking bribes, granting protection to whomever he wishes, and taking from whomever he wishes. This is among the greatest of the oppressors, who will be gathered in coffins of fire, they and their helpers and the like, then they will be cast into the Fire. End of quote.

﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., dread Him in what He has commanded and forbidden you. ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾, meaning for one who opposes His command. Therein is a great warning and threat. Then Allah, the Exalted, explained the prohibited things that were alluded to by His statement: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], and He said:

**The explanation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[3] ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than God, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what a beast of prey has eaten, except what you slaughter, and what is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek decision by arrows. That is grave disobedience. Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and approved for you Islam as a religion. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾: that is, what has departed from life without an external cause. It is impure by its departure from life without a purifier, namely the mention of God's name, whether actual or presumed, as in the case of a Muslim slaughterer. This is stated in *al-Tabsir*. Carrion has been specified by the Sunnah (prophetic tradition) as excluding fish, which is lawful whether it died by slaughter or otherwise, on the basis of what Malik narrated in his *Muwatta'*, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad in their *Musnads*, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah in their *Sunans*, and Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Hibban in their *Sahihs*, from Abu Hurayrah: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the water of the sea, and he said: "Its water is pure, and its carrion is lawful." The same applies to locusts, as will come. Al-Razi said: The prohibition of carrion accords with what is known by reason, because blood is an extremely subtle substance. When an animal dies of itself, the blood remains confined in its veins, decays and spoils, and great harms result from eating it. End of quotation.

Ibn Mandah narrated in *al-Sahabah* through the chain of Abdullah ibn Jabalah ibn Hibban ibn Hajar, from his father, from his grandfather Hibban, who said: "We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I was lighting a fire beneath a pot in which there was meat of carrion. Then the prohibition of carrion was revealed, so I overturned the pot."

﴿And blood﴾: that is, flowing blood, for His words in al-An'am: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he was asked about the spleen, and he said: "Eat it." They said: "It is blood." He said: "What is forbidden to you is only flowing blood." Likewise Hammad ibn Salamah narrated it from Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn al-Qasim, from 'A'ishah, who said: "What was forbidden is only flowing blood."

Imam Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us, from his father, from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet, who said: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood are lawful to us. As for the two kinds of carrion, they are fish and locusts. As for the two kinds of blood, they are the liver and the spleen." Likewise Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated it through Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and it is weak. The Hafiz al-Bayhaqi said: It was also narrated by Isma'il ibn Abi Idris, from Usamah, and by Abdullah and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet. The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: All three of them are weak, but some of them are sounder than others. It was narrated by Sulayman ibn Bilal, one of the trustworthy transmitters, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ibn 'Umar, but some of them stopped it at Ibn 'Umar. The Hafiz Abu Zur'ah al-Razi said: This is more sound. Ibn Kathir quoted this.

I say: Stronger than what has been mentioned as evidence is what is in the two *Sahihs* and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "We fought seven campaigns with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), eating locusts." Also in the two *Sahihs*, from the hadith of Jabir: "The sea cast up a dead whale, and the army ate from it. When they returned, they told the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Eat the provision God brought forth for you. Feed us from it if you have any with you.' Then some of them brought him some." In al-Bukhari, from 'Umar concerning God's words: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96], he said: "Its game is what is hunted, and its food is what is cast up by it." In the same book, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Its food is its carrion."

Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Umamah, who is Sudayy ibn 'Ajlan, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent me to my people to call them to God and His Messenger, and to present to them the laws of Islam. I came to them, and while we were like that, they brought a bowl of blood and gathered around it to eat it. They said: 'Come, O Sudayy, and eat.' I said: 'Woe to you! I have come to you from one who forbids you this.' Then they turned to him and said: 'And what is that?' So I recited to them this verse: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾ to the end of the verse." Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated it, and added after this context: "I began calling them to Islam, and they refused me. I said: 'Woe to you! Give me a sip of water, for I am extremely thirsty.' He said: And my cloak was upon me. They said: 'No. Rather we will leave you until you die of thirst.' He said: I grew distressed, struck my head against the cloak, and lay down on the scorching sand in intense heat. He said: Then a comer came to me in my sleep with a glass of crystal, the like of which people had never seen, and in it was a drink, sweeter than any people had ever tasted. He gave it to me, and I drank it. When I finished my drink I awoke, and by God, I was not thirsty nor 'arib (arib: one whose stomach is spoiled, according to the *Qamus*) after that drink." 

It was narrated by al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak*, from Ali ibn Hammad, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal with his chain to Abu Umamah. He added after the words "after that drink": "I heard them saying: 'A man of the nobles of your people has come to you, and you did not give him a cup of mixed milk?' They brought me a mixed drink, and I said: 'I have no need of it. God has fed me and given me drink.' And I showed them my belly, and they all embraced Islam." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to eat these prohibited things: the animal that dies of itself, and the *fasid* (fasid: the blood in the intestines), which they roasted and said: "Whoever is not given it [i.e., the animal] is not forbidden."

The discussion of this has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion and blood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173], and what follows.

Al-Mahayimi said: Blood is forbidden because it is directly connected to the soul, so it resembles what is impure in essence, and purification does not affect it. The flesh of swine is forbidden because it is impure during its life by its vile attributes, and although those attributes cease with death, it remains impure and does not accept purification. Since it was impure during life and death, it resembles what is impure in essence, as though its impurity was increased by death. He mentioned the flesh only to indicate that it, although not described in life by the attributes that make its soul impure, was impure by the impurity of its soul, and then by the departure of the soul. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: His words: ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾ mean both its domestic and wild kinds. "Flesh" encompasses all its parts, even the fat, as is understood from the language of the Arabs and from common usage. In Sahih Muslim, from Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever plays with the backgammon (nardashir) it is as if he dyed his hand with the flesh and blood of swine." If this warning is for merely touching it, how then would the threat and the firm warning be for eating it and nourishing oneself with it? This indicates that "flesh" includes all parts, including the fat and others. In the two *Sahihs*, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, swine, and idols." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what do you say about the fats of carrion, for ships are smeared with them, hides are oiled with them, and people light lamps with them?" He said: "No; it is forbidden."

﴿And that which has been dedicated to other than God﴾: that is, it was proclaimed over with a name other than God's, as in the *Sihah*. The origin of *ihlal* is raising the voice. The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to mention the names of their idols at slaughter, so God forbade that by this verse.

And by His words: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Ibn Kathir said concerning the verse: That is, what is slaughtered and over which the name of other than God is mentioned is forbidden, because God has required that His creatures be slaughtered in His mighty name. Whoever diverts them from that and mentions over them the name of another, be it an idol, a tyrant, an image, or other creatures, it is forbidden by consensus. The scholars differed only regarding what was left unnamed, whether deliberately or through forgetfulness, as will be established in Surat al-An'am, God willing. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabrah, who said: A man of the Banu Riyah called Ibn Na'il, who was a poet, competed with Ghalib, the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, over water at the outskirts of Kufa, on condition that whoever of them lost would slaughter one hundred of his camels when they came to the water. They both took up their swords and began to slash the hamstrings of the camels. He said: The people came out on donkeys and mules seeking meat, while Ali was in Kufa. He said: Ali went out on the white mule of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), crying: "O people! Do not eat of their meat, for it was dedicated to other than God." This is a strange report.

It is supported as to its soundness by what Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade *mu'aqarah* of the Bedouins." Then he traced from Ikrimah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade eating the food of the two rival competitors." Ibn Kathir cited this.

In the *Qamus* and its commentary: *Wa'aqarahu* means he boasted against him and outdid him in slaughtering camels. It is said: *Ta'aqara* when they both slaughter their camels, competing in that so that it may be seen which of them slaughters more. Among this is the *mu'aqarah* of Ghalib ibn Sa'sa'ah, the father of al-Farazdaq, and Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi when they competed at Sa'ar. Suhaym slaughtered five and then changed his mind, while Ghalib slaughtered one hundred.

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "Do not eat from the *ta'aqur* of the Bedouins, for I fear that it may be of what was dedicated to other than God."

Ibn al-Athir said: It is their slaughter of camels. Two men would compete in generosity and liberality, so one would slaughter and the other would slaughter, until one of them overcame the other. They did this for show, reputation, and boasting, not seeking the face of God. So he likened it to what is slaughtered for other than God. End of quotation.

Imam Muslim narrated from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) told me four words: 'God curses whoever slaughters for other than God. God curses whoever curses his parents. God curses whoever shelters an innovator. God curses whoever alters the boundary markers of the land.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from Tariq ibn Shihab that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A man entered Paradise because of a fly, and a man entered the Fire because of a fly." They said: "How is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Two men passed by a people who had an idol, and no one could pass it without offering something to it. They said to one of them: 'Offer.' He said: 'I have nothing to offer.' They said to him: 'Offer even a fly.' So he offered a fly, and they let him go, and he entered the Fire. They said to the other: 'Offer.' He said: 'I would not offer anything to anyone besides God, Mighty and Majestic.' So they struck his neck, and he entered Paradise."

In this story there is a warning in several respects. Among them is that he entered the Fire because of that fly, which he did not intend, but did to free himself from their evil. Among them is the recognition of the extent of *shirk* (association of partners with God) in the hearts of believers, and how that one endured being killed and did not comply with their demand, even though they only asked for an outward act. Among them is that this is a witness to the sound hadith: "Paradise is closer to any one of you than the thong of his sandal, and the Fire is likewise." Thus in the *Kitab al-Tawhid*.

﴿And the strangled﴾: that is, the one that dies by strangulation, whether intentionally or accidentally, such as when it becomes entangled in its tether and dies by it. Al-Hasan and others said: It is the one that is strangled by the hunter's rope or other things. In whatever way it was strangled, it is forbidden. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Jahiliyyah used to strangle the sheep until it died, and then they would eat it. The strangled is of the same kind as carrion, because when it dies and its blood has not flowed, it is like an animal that died of itself. Except that it differs from carrion in that it dies because of the constriction of the throat by strangling, whereas carrion dies without a cause.

Al-Mahayimi said: The strangled animal (al-munkhaniqah), even if the name of God was mentioned over it, is affected by the corruption of the strangler's impurity spreading into it, together with its being rendered impure by death. The beaten animal (al-mawqudhah) means the one killed by a piece of wood. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) used to strike a sheep with sticks until it died, and then they ate it.

In al-Qamus and its commentary: al-waqdh is intense striking. One says waqadhahu yaqidhuhu waqdhan: he struck him until he went limp and came close to death. A sheep is called waqidh or mawqudhah when it has been killed by a piece of wood. Abu Sa'id said: al-waqdh is striking on the nape of the neck, so that the force of the blow reaches the brain and the intellect is lost. One says: "a man is mawqudh." In the Sahih it is narrated that 'Adi ibn Hatim said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God! I shoot game with a mi'radh (a blunt wooden throwing stick) and I hit it.' He said: 'If you shoot with the mi'radh and it pierces, then eat it. But if it strikes with its broad side, then it is a waqidh (struck animal), so do not eat it.'"

The mutaraddiyah is the one that falls from a mountain or into a well and dies. Tardiy means falling, and it is a mihwah (a pit). These three are in the category of carrion, since they died without their blood flowing. The nationhah is the one gored by another animal and dying from it, so it is forbidden. If the horn wounded it and blood came out, even from its slaughter place, the rule is the same. If a person releases a gorer with the name of God mentioned, this does not make it lawful, because, since it was not by the legitimate method of hunting, it cannot be free of impurity.

Benefit:
Al-Tabrizi in his Tahdhib and Ibn Qutaybah in Adab al-Katib said: whatever is on the pattern fa'il, used as an adjective for a feminine noun with the meaning of maf'ul (passive), is without the feminine ending (ta' marbutah). Examples: kaff khadib (a dyed hand), and milhafah ghasil (a washed cloak). Sometimes it comes with the ending, treated as a noun. Examples: al-nattihah, al-dhabihah, al-fariisah, and akilat al-sab' ... They said: milhafah jadidah (a new cloak), because it is taken to mean majdudah, i.e. cut. When the passive meaning is not applicable, it takes the feminine ending, as in mariidah, zarifah, kabirah, and saghirah. Some irregular forms also occur: they said rih kharik (a violent wind), naqah sadis (a camel in its sixth year), and katibah khasif (a troop in disarray).

Ibn al-Sikkit said: fa'ilah may come with the feminine ending while meaning maf'ulah (passive), treated as a noun and not as a descriptive adjective. Examples: al-nattihah, al-dhabihah, al-fariisah, akilat al-sab', and "I passed by the killed one (qatilat) of the sons of so-and-so."

Al-Jawhari said: al-nattihah came with the ending only because the noun predominates over it. Likewise al-fariisah, al-akilah, and al-ramiyyah. This is because it is not that a verb "nataha-ha, fa-hiya mantuhah" (he gored it, so it is gored), but rather the thing itself is of the type that is gored, and the thing is of the type that is preyed upon and eaten.

[p. 1820] "And what the beast of prey has eaten," i.e. what a beast attacked and ate part of. Qatadah said: when the people of the Jahiliyyah saw a beast of prey wound something and kill it, or eat from it, they ate what remained of it. God forbade this.

Al-Mahayimi said: although it resembles game, when the beast ate it, it was intending itself by that, so its corruption spread into it. End of quotation.

The sab' (beast of prey) with the vowel variants damm, fath and sukun: a carnivorous animal, such as the lion, wolf, tiger, and leopard, and what resembles them of animals that have fangs, which attack people and beasts and seize them. It is called this because of the completeness of its strength. The "sab'" is among the complete numbers. In the verse there is an ellipsis, whose sense is: "and what the beast of prey ate of it (part of it)," as we mentioned, because what it ate has been lost, so it has no ruling; the ruling applies only to what remains of it.

God's words: ﴿except what you slaughter in time﴾, meaning: what you reach in time to perform its slaughter from the aforementioned: the strangled animal and what follows it, in such a way that its death is attributed to slaughtering and not to something else. Then the purifying factor is realized in it, and the earlier cause does not affect it, because the later one abrogates (naskh) it. Rather, it occurs before the earlier cause takes effect, since the effect is not complete except by death. Al-Mahayimi said this.

Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that is, except what you slaughter of these while there is life in it, then eat it, for it is dhaki (validly slaughtered). It is narrated likewise from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali, regarding the verse, that he said: if it moves its tail, or kicks with its leg, or blinks its eye, then eat it. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Harith, from Ali also, that he said: if you reach the slaughter of the mawqudhah, the mutaraddiyah, and the nattihah while it moves a hand or a leg, then eat it. The same was narrated from Tawus, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Dahhak, and others: that the slaughtered animal, whenever it moves with a movement indicating that life remains in it after slaughter, is lawful. This is the position of the majority of jurists. Ibn Kathir stated this.

In al-Muwatta: Malik was asked about a sheep that fell and broke, and its owner reached it and slaughtered it, [p. 1821] and blood flowed from it without its moving. Malik said: if he slaughtered it while its breath was flowing and it was blinking, then let him eat it.

Al-tadhkiyah means slaughter, like al-dhaka and al-dhakah. Al-Raghib said: the real meaning of tadhkiyah is the release of the innate heat, but in the Sharia it is specified for the ending of life in a particular way, which is: cutting the windpipe (hulqum) and the gullet (mari'), with something that makes the blood flow: a knife, sword, glass, stone, or reed, having an edge that cuts like a sharpened weapon, provided it is not a tooth or a nail. This is based on the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij in the Two Sahihs and others, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God! We are going to meet the enemy tomorrow, and we do not have knives. Shall we slaughter with a reed?' He said: 'What makes the blood flow and the name of God is mentioned over it, then eat it; except the tooth and the nail. I will tell you about that: as for the tooth, it is a bone; and as for the nail, it is the knife of the Abyssinians.'"

As for the hadith of Abu al-'Ushara from his father: "I said: 'O Messenger of God! Is slaughter only in the throat and the lower neck?' He said: 'If you had stabbed it in its thigh, it would have sufficed you.'" Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan narrated it, but its chain contains unknown narrators.

Abu al-'Ushara: nothing is known of who his father was, and no one narrated from him except Hammad ibn Salamah, so he is unknown. Thus in al-Rawdah.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis: Abu al-'Ushara's name and his father's name are disputed. Hammad ibn Salamah alone narrated from him, according to the correct view, and his condition is not known.

He said in al-Taqrib: "a Bedouin, unknown."

Al-Tirmidhi said in his Jami', after quoting this hadith: Ahmad ibn Mani' said: Yazid ibn Harun said: "This applies in cases of necessity." And there is a related report from Rafi' ibn Khadij. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: this hadith is sahih, but it is to be understood as applying to an animal that cannot be slaughtered in the throat and the lower neck. End of quotation.

His authentication of it, despite the unknown status of its narrator mentioned, is open to question. The definition of sahih, as in al-Taqrib, is a hadith whose chain is connected through upright and precise narrators without irregularity (shudhudh) or hidden defect ('illah). Its commentator al-Suyuti said: by the condition "upright narrators," what is transmitted by someone unknown, either in identity or in condition, is excluded; so it is not sahih but da'if (weak).

In al-Nukhbah: an individual report (khabar al-ahad) is either accepted or rejected, and the second is either due to a gap in the chain or to a defect in a narrator. The defect is either because of lying or suspicion of it, up to his saying: or because of his being unknown, in that no explicit ta'dil (praise) or jarh (criticism) is recorded for him. So reflect carefully.

On what is slaughtered at the nusub: al-Zamakhshari said: there were stones set up around the House (the Ka'bah). They would slaughter upon them and cut the meat over them, glorifying them thereby and seeking nearness to them through this. They were called al-ansab.

Ibn Kathir said: God therefore forbade the believers from this practice and forbade them to eat these slaughtered animals, even if the name of God was mentioned over them, because slaughter at the nusub contains the shirk that God and His Messenger have forbidden. End of quotation.

The prohibition has also come concerning slaughtering for God at a place where animals are slaughtered for other than Him. Abu Dawud narrated, with a chain meeting the conditions of the two Shaykhs [p. 1823], from Thabit ibn al-Dahhak, may God be pleased with him, who said: "A man vowed to sacrifice camels at Buwanah. He asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Was there in it an idol of the idols of the Jahiliyyah that was worshipped?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Was there in it a festival of theirs?' They said: 'No.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Fulfil your vow, for there is no fulfilment of a vow in disobedience to God, nor in what the son of Adam does not own.'"

In it: disobedience can affect the land, and so can obedience. In it is the prohibition of a vow if there was in that place an idol of the idols of the Jahiliyyah, even after its removal, or a festival of theirs, even after it has ceased. Fulfilling a vow made in that place is not permitted, because it is a vow of disobedience, and in it is the warning against resembling the polytheists in their festivals, even if one does not intend that. Thus in Kitab al-Tawhid.

A subtle point:
Al-nusub, with two damme or damm and sukun, is either a plural whose singular is nisab, like kitab and kutub, or a singular whose plural is ansab, like 'unuq and a'naq, and qufl and aqfal. In al-Qamus and its commentary: al-nusub is everything set up and made a sign, and everything set up and worshipped apart from God. The ansab are stones that were around the Ka'bah, set up, over which one would shed blood and slaughter for other than God. Al-Qutaybi said: the nusub is an idol or a stone, which the Jahiliyyah would set up and slaughter beside, so that it reddened with blood. From it is the hadith of Abu Dharr about his Islam, who said: [p. 1824] "I went out fainting, then I rose up as if I were a red nusub" — meaning that they beat him until they drew blood from him — "so I became like a nusub reddened with the blood of sacrifices." End of quotation.

Ibn Jurayj said: the nusub were three hundred and sixty. They would slaughter beside them and sprinkle whatever came of them toward the House with the blood of those sacrifices, and they would cut the meat and place it on the nusub.

﴿And that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: that is, God forbade you, O believers, seeking the division and judgment by them. Al-azlam is the plural of zalam (with fatha on both letters), and (like sarad) it is: three arrow-shafts with which they sought decisions in the Jahiliyyah. On one of them was written "do," on another "do not," and the third was blank, with nothing on it. They were smoothed, prepared, and placed in the Ka'bah, and the custodians of the House looked after them. When a man wanted to travel or to marry, he came to the custodian and said: "Bring out for me an arrow." He shuffled them, then drew out one. If the arrow of command came out, he proceeded with what he had resolved upon. If it was the arrow of prohibition, he refrained from what he wanted. If it was the blank one, he repeated the draw.

Al-Zuhri said (regarding the meaning of the verse): That is, you seek from the arrows what has been apportioned to you of one of the two matters. So the meaning of istiqsam (seeking the apportionment by arrows) is seeking knowledge of what has been apportioned to one of good and evil, which has not been apportioned to him, by means of casting the arrows (qidah).

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others mentioned that the greatest idol of the Quraysh was an idol called Hubal. It was set up over a well inside the Ka'bah, into which offerings were placed, and the wealth of the Ka'bah was in it. With it were seven arrows on which were written the things they would judge by in matters that were unclear to them. Whatever came out for them from these, they would return to it and not deviate from it.

In al-Lubab: Their arrows were seven smooth shafts, one of which was inscribed "My Lord commanded me," and one "My Lord forbade me," and one "From among you," and one "From other than you," and one "Attached," and one "The blood-money (aql)," and one blank (ghufl), meaning there was nothing on it. When the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah wanted to travel, or to trade, or to marry, or differed over a lineage, or the matter of a slain person, or the bearing of blood-money, or other great matters, they came to Hubal, which was the greatest idol of the Quraysh in Makkah. They would bring one hundred dirhams and give them to the keeper of the arrows so that he would shuffle them for them. If "My Lord commanded me" came out, they did that matter; if "My Lord forbade me" came out, they did not do it. If they cast lots concerning a lineage, and "From among you" came out, he was a mediator among them; if "From other than you" came out, he was an ally among them; if "Attached" came out, it remained as it was. If they differed over the blood-money, which is the debt, whoever had the arrow of blood-money on him would bear it. If the blank came out, they cast again a second time, until the one inscribed came out. So Allah forbade them from that, prohibited it, and called it fisq (transgression), as will come.

It is established in the two Sahihs that when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered the Ka'bah, he found Ibrahim and Isma'il depicted in it, with the arrows in their hands. He said: "May Allah fight them! They knew well that the two of them never sought the apportionment by them, ever."

It is also in the Sahih that Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, when he went out in pursuit of the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr while they were going to Madinah as emigrants, said: "I sought the apportionment by the arrows: Would they harm them or not? What came out was what I dislike: that they would not harm them." He said: "So I disobeyed the arrows and followed them." Then he sought the apportionment by them a second and a third time, and each time what came out was what he disliked: that they would not harm them. And it was as such. Suraqah had not yet embraced Islam at that time; he embraced it afterwards.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever practices kahanah (soothsaying), or seeks the apportionment, or returns from a journey by omen-taking (tarah), will never enter the ranks (of the Garden)."

﴿That is fisq (transgression)﴾: that is, departure from adhering to the lawful way. The reference is to istiqsam, or to consuming what has been forbidden to them, because the meaning is: "Forbidden to you is the consumption of carrion and such and such." If you say: Why was the seeking of the apportionment by arrows, for the traveller and others, to learn the state of affairs, fisq? I say: Because it is an entry into the knowledge of the unseen, which the Knower of the unseen has reserved for Himself, and He said: "Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah."

And the belief that there is a way to it and a way to deducing it. And his saying "My Lord commanded me" and "My Lord forbade me" is a fabrication against Allah. And how does he know that He commanded him or forbade him? The soothsayers (kahanah) and astrologers are in this position. And if by "the Lord" he meant the idol, then it has been narrated that they used to cast them at their idols, so its matter is evident. Thus in al-Kashshaf.

Note:
In al-Iklil: This verse was cited as proof of the prohibition of gambling, astrology, geomancy, and all that resembles them. Some extended it to prohibit drawing lots in rulings, and this is rejected. End of quote. That is, because the intention differs in them. For lots in dividing the spoils, or in determining which women go out (on a campaign) and the like, serve to content their hearts and to clear them of suspicion of favouring some over others. And if they agreed on that without lots, it would be permissible, as in al-Inayah.

Al-Hakim said: It indicates the prohibition of relying on fa'l (good omen), zajr (omen from birds' movements), tiyarah (bad omen), and astrology. As for optimism for good, it is permissible. Al-Asamm said: From this is the astrologer's saying: "When the star of such and such rises, go out; and if it does not rise, do not go out."

Al-Radi billah said: Whoever acts according to days of fortune and misfortune, believing that they have an effect, has disbelieved; and if he does not believe it, he has sinned. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban narrated from Qatan ibn Qabisah, from his father, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, 'iyafah (bird-augury by flight), tarq (line-drawing), and tiyarah (bad omen) are from al-Jibt (sorcery/idolatry)."

Awf, one of its narrators, said: 'Iyafah is the driving away of birds; and tarq is the line drawn on the earth. In the Qamus: "I 'ift the bird 'iyafah": I drove it away. It is to observe their names and places of falling, and then to judge them as auspicious or inauspicious, and this was a very common custom of the Arabs.

Abu Zayd said: Tarq is that a man draws a line in the ground with two fingers and then with one finger.

Ibn al-Athir said: Tarq is striking with pebbles, which women do. It was also said: It is drawing lines in the sand. Al-Jibt: everything worshipped besides Allah the Exalted.

Muslim narrated in his Sahih, from one of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever comes to an 'arraf (diviner) and asks him about something and believes him, his prayer will not be accepted for forty days."

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Hakim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever comes to an 'arraf or a kahin and believes what he says, has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ)." And from Imran ibn Husayn, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "He is not of us who practises tiyarah, or for whom tiyarah is practised, or who practises kahanah or for whom it is practised, or who practises sihr or for whom it is practised. And whoever comes to a kahin and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ)." Narrated by al-Bazzar with a good chain. And al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat with a fair chain from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, omitting his saying "And whoever comes to..." and so on.

Al-Baghawi said: The 'arraf is one who claims to know matters through preliminaries by which he infers the stolen item, the place of a lost animal, and the like. It was also said: he is the kahin. The kahin is one who reports the unseen in the future. It was also said: one who reports what is in the mind. Abu al-Abbas ibn Taymiyyah said: 'Arraf is a name for the kahin, the astrologer, the geomancer and the like, of those who speak about knowing matters by these methods. Ibn Abbas said (concerning people who write abjad and look into the stars): "I do not see that whoever does that has any portion with Allah." In the hadiths previously cited there is such a warning, including the explicit statement that believing a kahin cannot be combined with faith in the Qur'an, and the explicit statement that it is kufr (disbelief). And from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tiyarah is shirk; tiyarah is shirk. There is none among us but (has some of it), but Allah removes it through reliance (tawakkul)." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, and he made its end a saying of Ibn Mas'ud.

Ahmad has, from the hadith of Ibn Amr: "Whoever is turned back from his need by tiyarah has committed shirk." They said: "What is the expiation for that?" He said: "That you say: O Allah, there is no good except Your good, no omen except Your omen, and there is no god besides You." And from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no contagion (adwa) and no tiyarah, and I like fa'l." They said: "What is fa'l?" He said: "A good word." Narrated by the two Shaykhs.

Abu Dawud has, with a sahih chain, from Urwah ibn Amir, who said: "Tiyarah was mentioned in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'The best of it is fa'l, and it does not turn away a Muslim. When one of you sees what he dislikes, let him say: O Allah, none brings good things except You, none repels bad things except You, and there is no power or strength except through You.'"

Benefit:
The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Allah has commanded the believers, when they waver in their affairs, to seek His guidance (istikharah), by worshipping Him and then asking Him for choice in the matter they want. As Imam Ahmad and al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan narrated by various routes from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach us istikharah in matters, as he taught us a surah of the Qur'an, saying: 'When one of you intends a matter, let him pray two rak'ahs other than the obligatory prayer, then let him say: O Allah, I seek Your choice by Your knowledge, and I seek power by Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty. For You have power and I have no power, You know and I do not know, and You are the Knower of the unseen. O Allah, if You know that this matter (and let him name it) is good for me in my religion, my livelihood and the outcome of my affair (or he said: my immediate and deferred affair), then decree it for me, facilitate it for me, and then bless it for me. And if You know that it is bad for me in my religion, my livelihood and the outcome of my affair, then turn me away from it and turn it away from me, and decree for me the good wherever it may be, and then make me content with it.'" This is the wording of Imam Ahmad.

﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾: that is, they despaired. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas, meaning: they despaired of your returning to their religion. Likewise it was narrated from Ata ibn Abi Rabah, al-Suddi and Muqatil ibn Hayyan. On this meaning comes the established hadith in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Satan has despaired of being worshipped by the worshippers in the Arabian Peninsula, but (he is content) with inciting discord among them." Ibn Kathir related it. On this reading, "min" (from) is causal, that is: they despaired of returning to your religion because of your religion, which united the majority of the Arab nation from its lowest to its highest parts, and they entered it in multitudes.

Al-Zamakhshari has a striking interpretation, which those after him followed, and we also set it down. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: He did not mean by "today" a particular day, but rather the present time and what is connected to it and near it of past and future times, like your saying: "Yesterday you were young, and today you are gray-haired." You do not mean by "yesterday" the day before your day, nor by "today" your day. It was also said: it refers to the day of its revelation, which was revealed on Friday, the day of 'Arafah, after the afternoon prayer, in the Farewell Pilgrimage. And His saying, the Exalted: "has despaired..." etc., means: they despaired of Him annulling it, and of your returning to make lawful these abominations after they were forbidden to you. It was also said: they despaired of its overcoming your religion, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic fulfilled His promise to make it prevail over all religion.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ after the manifestation of the religion, the removal of fear from the disbelievers, and their turning into the defeated and subdued after they had been dominant: ﴿but fear Me﴾, and devote your fear sincerely to Me. End of his words.

Al-Razi clarified the first interpretation, saying: The "today" is not that very day itself, such that it could be said they had not despaired a day or two before it. Rather it is a speech in the manner of the people of the language, meaning: there is no need for you now to flatter these disbelievers, because you have now come to a state where none of your enemies hopes to weaken your affair.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 4 of 5):

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained His greatest blessing and His most important favour upon this community, which is His perfecting of their religion (dīn), so that they have no need of any religion other than it, nor of any prophet other than their own Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, made him the seal of the prophets (khātam al-anbiyā'), and sent him to humankind and the jinn. There is no lawful thing except what he made lawful, no unlawful thing except what he made unlawful, and no religion except what he legislated. When He perfected the religion for them, the blessing was completed upon them. For this reason He said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾, meaning its rulings and obligations (farā'iḍ). There is no addition after it, and no lawful or unlawful ruling was revealed after this verse. This is what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the meaning of "perfecting" (al-ikmāl) is that no polytheist performed the pilgrimage with them, and that during the season the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims were alone (in the sacred precincts).

It has also been said: its meaning is that He sufficed them against their enemy and gave them the upper hand, just as kings say: "Today our kingdom has been perfected, and what we desire has been perfected for us," when they have restrained those who contend with them.

By what we mentioned first, that the intended meaning of perfection is the absence of addition, there is dispelled what may be imagined of a deficiency having existed before. For this reason Ibn al-Anbari said regarding the verse: "Today I have perfected for you the laws of Islam without any deficiency that existed before this time." This is because Allah, exalted is He, used to make His servants worship Him with a particular thing at one time and then add to it at another time. So the first time is complete in its own time, and likewise the second time is complete in its own time. It is like one who says: "I have ten complete," and it is known that twenty is more complete than them. The laws by which Allah, exalted is He, made His servants worship Him at different times are different, and each one of them is complete at the time of worshipping by it. So Allah, exalted is He, completed the laws on the day He mentioned, which is the Day of 'Arafah, and this does not imply that the religion was deficient at any point in time.

Al-Imam al-Qaffal held something similar, which al-Razi transmitted from him and preferred. He said: the religion was never deficient at all, but was always complete. That is, the laws sent down from Allah at each time were sufficient for that time, but He, exalted is He, knew at the beginning of the time of the mission (ba'th) that what is complete on this day is not complete tomorrow and has no benefit in it. Therefore it was necessarily abrogated (yunsakh) after being established, and it was added to after being absent. At the end of the time of the mission, Allah sent down a complete law and decreed its permanence until the Day of Resurrection. So the Law was always complete, but the first was complete until a specific time, and the second is complete until the Day of Resurrection.
