For this reason He said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you﴾, meaning by perfecting the religion and the Law, because there is no favour more complete than the favour of Islam; or by the conquest of Makkah and their entering it safe and dominant, and the demolition of the minarets and rites of the Jahiliyyah, and that no polytheist performs the pilgrimage with you and no naked person circumambulates the House; or by fulfilling what He promised them with His words: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾. So the conquest of Makkah and what we have mentioned were part of the completion of the favour. ﴿And I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾, meaning: I have chosen it for you from among the religions, and I have informed you that it is the only religion that is approved, and whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will not be accepted from him. Or its meaning is: submission to My command regarding what I have legislated for you of obligations, rulings, prescribed punishments, and the markers of the religion which I have perfected for you. It is known that Islam has always been approved by the Real (al-Haqq), exalted is He, since eternity, but what is meant in the verse is the attribute in which it is today, which is the peak of perfection and its reaching its highest degree. That is: hold fast to it and do not part from it, for indeed the religion with Allah is Islam.

Al-Baghawi narrated with his chain from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Gabriel said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: This is a religion I have chosen for Myself, and nothing will make it right except generosity and good character, so honour it with them as long as you keep company with it."

Benefits (fawā'id):

First: Imam Ahmad, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and others narrated from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: A man from the Jews came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and said: "O Commander of the Believers! You recite a verse in your Book which, if it had been revealed to us, the Jewish community, we would have taken that day as a festival (ʿīd)." He said: "Which verse?" He said: "His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you﴾." 'Umar said: "By Allah! I know the day on which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hour in which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — the evening of 'Arafah, on a Friday."

Ibn Kathir said: This has been narrated through more than one route from 'Umar. Ibn Jarir narrated from Qabisah ibn Abi Dhu'ayb, who said: Ka'b said: "If this verse had been revealed to any other nation than this community, they would have observed the day on which it was revealed to them and made it a festival in which they gather." 'Umar said: "Which verse, O Ka'b?" He said: "﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾." 'Umar said: "I know the day on which it was revealed and the place in which it was revealed. It was revealed on a Friday and on the day of 'Arafah, and both of them, praise be to Allah, are festivals for us."

Ibn Jarir also narrated the story from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: it was revealed on two festival days: a day of festival and a Friday.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, from 'Ali, who said: "This verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was standing on the evening of 'Arafah: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾." He also narrated it from Samurah. Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Mu'awiyah.

It is narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "This verse was revealed on the day of 'Arafah, and no lawful or unlawful ruling was revealed after it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned and died." Asma' bint 'Umays said: "I performed the pilgrimage with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the riding-beast, and the beast could not bear the weight of the Qur'an upon it. Then it was revealed. I came to him and covered him with a cloak that I had."

Ibn Jarir and others said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died eighty-one days after the day of 'Arafah.

Ibn Jarir said: Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us from Harun ibn 'Antarah, from his father, who said: "When ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ was revealed — and that was the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage — 'Umar wept. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'It made me weep that we were in increase in our religion. But when it is perfected, nothing is perfected except that it decreases.' He said: 'You have spoken the truth.'"

Ibn Kathir said: This meaning is supported by the authentic hadith: "Islam began as a stranger and it will return as a stranger, so good tidings to the strangers." End of quote.

I say: this hadith was narrated by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, by al-Tirmidhi from Ibn Mas'ud, by Ibn Majah from both of them and also from Anas, and by al-Tabarani from Salman, Sahl and Ibn 'Abbas.

Furthermore, Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse: "That is not a day known to the people." Through the route of Abu Ja'far al-Razi from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, he said: it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his journey to the Farewell Pilgrimage. Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of Abu Harun al-'Abdi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Ghadir Khumm, when he said to 'Ali: "Whoever I am his master, 'Ali is his master." He then narrated it from Abu Hurayrah, in which it says: it was the eighteenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, meaning his return (ﷺ) from the Farewell Pilgrimage.

Ibn Kathir said: Neither this nor that is authentic. Rather, the correct position, about which there is no doubt or dispute, is that it was revealed on the day of 'Arafah, which was a Friday, as we have previously cited from 'Umar, 'Ali, Mu'awiyah, Ibn 'Abbas and Samurah, may Allah be pleased with them, and from a group of the Followers (tabi'un).

Second: Those who deny analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy) used this verse to prove that qiyas is invalid. This is because the verse shows that Allah, exalted is He, has explicitly stated the ruling for all events, since if some of them remained without a ruling explained, the religion would not be complete. And when the explicit text exists for all events, then qiyas — if it agrees with that text — is futile, and if it contradicts it, it is invalid.

Those who affirm qiyas responded to this with what al-Razi expounded, so refer to it.

Third: The author of Fath al-Bayan said: There is no meaning to completion in the verse except that the texts fulfil what the Law needs, either by explicit statement regarding each individual case, or by the inclusion of what is needed under the comprehensive general rules. What supports this is His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and His saying: ﴿and no moist thing nor dry thing but is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. It is authentically established from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I have left you upon a clear path, its night like its day." The texts of the Mighty Book have come with the completion of the religion. And with what conveys this meaning, confirms its indication, supports its proof, and suffices in repelling opinion (ra'y), and that it is not part of the religion, is the saying of Allah, exalted is He, this one. For if Allah has perfected His religion before He took His Prophet (ﷺ) to Himself, then what is this opinion that its adherents have introduced after Allah perfected His religion? For if it is part of the religion in their belief, it has not become complete for them except through their own opinion, and this entails a rejection of the Qur'an. And if it is not part of the religion, then what benefit is there in occupying oneself with what is not part of it? And whatever is not part of it is rejected by the explicit text of the pure Sunnah, as is established in the Sahih. This is an overwhelming argument and a dazzling proof that the people of opinion can never repel with any repelling. So make this noble verse the first thing with which you strike the faces of the people of opinion, and with which you humble their noses, and with which you refute their argument. For Allah has informed us in His firm Book that He perfected His religion. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until he had informed us of this report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So whoever comes with something from his own self and claims that it is from our religion, we will say to him: "Allah is more truthful than you, and who is more truthful than Allah in speech? Go away, we have no need of your opinion." Would that the imitators (muqallidah) understood this verse in its true understanding, so that they might find rest and give rest. Allah has informed us in His firm Book that the Qur'an encompasses everything. He said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and He said: ﴿an exposition of all things, and a guidance, and a mercy﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. Then He commanded His servants to judge by His Book, and He said: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49]. He said: ﴿That you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa': 105]. He said: ﴿The judgement is only for Allah; He relates the truth, and He is the best of deciders﴾ [al-An'am: 57]. He said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. In another verse: ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. In another: ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47]. He also commanded His servants in His firm Book to follow what His Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. This is the most general verse in the Qur'an, and the clearest in adopting the pure Sunnah. He said: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger." This has been repeated in several places in the Mighty Book. He said: ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, is that they say: We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Nur: 51]. He said: ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21].

[p-1837] Multiplying proofs for the obligation to obey Allah and His Messenger yields no benefit and no added value, since no Muslim disputes this, and whoever denies it has left the community of Muslims. We have cited these noble verses and great proofs only to soften the heart of the *muqallid* (one who follows blindly, practicing *taqlid*, or blind imitation) who has become hardened and like stone. When he hears such Qur'anic commands, he may comply with them and take his religion from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), out of obedience to His commands. For although this obedience is known to every Muslim, a person may be distracted from the thunderous Qur'anic warnings and the Muhammadan admonitions, but when reminded of them, he remembers. This is especially so for one who grew up in *taqlid* and saw his predecessors firmly adhering to it, not budging from it. It then enters his heart that the religion of Islam is just what he himself follows, and that whatever contradicts it is not part of Islam at all. So when he examines himself, he returns.

This is why you find that a man who grows up on one of these schools of thought, and then hears, before he rebels through knowledge and learns what people have said, a view contrary to what he is accustomed to, rejects it, his heart refuses it, and his nature recoils from it. We have seen and heard of this kind of thing in countless instances. But if the rational person weighs with his intellect the difference between one who follows one of the imams of the schools in a question from among his questions, which the *muqallid* transmits from him, where that scholar has no basis for it and merely stated it by sheer opinion because he had no knowledge of the evidence, and one who adheres to that same specific question by the proof established in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, his intellect will tell him that between the two there are distances across which the necks of camels are severed, and that there is no common ground between them. This is because the one who adheres to the proof takes what Allah obligated him to take, and follows what the Lawgiver prescribed for the whole community, the first and the last of it, and the living and the dead... [p-1839] The scholar is able to reach the proof without having to refer to anyone else. The ignorant person is able to reach the proof by asking the scholars of the Sharia and seeking the text's (*istirwa'*, seeking the text's transmission) guidance, and how Allah judged in His clear Book, or upon the tongue of His Messenger, on that question. They then convey to him the text if he is one who understands the argument when it is pointed out to him, or they convey to him the content of the text by expressing it in words he can understand. Thus they are narrators and he is one who seeks transmission; this one acts by transmission, not by opinion. The *muqallid*, however, acts by opinion, not by transmission, because he accepts another's statement without demanding proof. In his questioning, the other demands proof, not opinion; so he is receptive to another's transmission, not to his opinion. In this respect the two are opposites. Consider, then, how great the difference is between the two ranks! The discussion of this would be lengthy and would require filling many pages. It is fully expounded in its proper places, and what we have mentioned is sufficient and adequate. And success is from Allah. End of his words.

Fourth: Some of the Zaydiyyah (a Shi'i school) said: the fruit of the verse is the glorification of this mentioned day, and that it is obligatory to thank Allah, the Exalted, for holding fast to the religion of Islam.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾ is connected to the mention of the forbidden things. What lies between them is a parenthetical aside (*i'tiraḍ*, parenthetical insertion) that necessitates avoiding them. It is that consuming them is a transgression (*fusuq*), and their prohibition is part of the complete religion, the perfect blessing, and the approved Islam. Its meaning is: whoever is compelled to consume any of these forbidden things, namely carrion and what follows it, that is, is afflicted by a harm that does not allow him to refrain from carrion and what follows it, ﴿in a state of severe hunger (*makhmasah*)﴾, that is, famine by which he fears death or its onset. The word *makhmasah* is a verbal noun like *maghḍabah* and *ma'tabah*. It is said: hunger made him empty (*khamasahu al-ju'*) with *khamsan* and *makhmasah*, and the belly became empty (*khamasa al-baṭn*, the vowel of the *mīm* may be three ways), meaning it became empty. ﴿Not inclining toward sin﴾, that is, not deviating toward it by eating beyond necessity, or by disobedience through travel. Like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿neither desiring it nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ for his consuming the prohibited thing, so He does not hold him accountable for it. *Raḥīm* (Merciful) means: by granting him the concession in it, knowing the need of His compelled servant and his dependence upon that, so He overlooks it and forgives him.

In the *Musnad* and the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Ibn Hibban, from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He dislikes that His disobedience be committed." This is the wording of Ibn Hibban. In another wording of Ahmad: "Whoever does not accept the concession of Allah, upon him is sin like the mountains of Arafat." For this reason the jurists said: eating carrion may at times be obligatory, namely when one fears for his life and finds nothing else. It may also be recommended, and it may be permissible, according to circumstances.

They differed as to whether one should take from it only the amount that sustains his life, or whether he may eat to satiety and take provision. There are several opinions. It is not a condition for eating carrion that three days must pass during which he finds no food, as many of the common people and others may imagine. Rather, whenever he is compelled to it, it is permissible for him. Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Waqid al-Laythi that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are in a land where we are afflicted with famine. When is carrion lawful for us there?" He said: "When you have not had a morning drink of milk, nor an evening drink, nor have you uprooted herbs, then it is yours." Its chain is sound according to the criterion of the two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim). *Iṣṭibāḥ* is drinking milk in the morning and what is before midday, and what is in the evening is *ightibāq*. The meaning of "you have not uprooted (*lam taḥtafi'ū*)" is: you have not pulled up. There are several narrations of this word. Abu Dawud narrated from al-Fujay' al-Amiri: "He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'What is lawful for us of carrion?' He said: 'What is your food?' We said: 'We have a morning drink and an evening drink!' Abu Nu'aym said: 'Uqbah explained it to me: a bowl in the morning and a bowl in the evening.' He said: 'By my father, that is hunger!' So He made carrion lawful for them in this condition." Abu Dawud alone narrated it. It seems they used to have a morning and evening drink that was not sufficient for them, so He made carrion lawful for them to complete their sustenance. Someone who holds that it is permissible to eat from it until one reaches satiety, and that this is not restricted to merely sustaining life, may cite this as evidence. And Allah knows best.

Abu Dawud also narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah that "a man settled in al-Harrah with his family and his child. A man said: 'A she-camel of mine went astray. If you find it, hold it.' He found it, but did not find its owner, and it fell ill. His wife said to him: 'Slaughter it!' He refused, and it died. She said: 'Skin it, so that we may dry its fat and its meat and eat it.' He said: 'Until I ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' He came to him, and asked him, and he said to him: 'Do you have wealth that suffices you?' He said: 'No!' He said: 'Then eat it!' Then its owner came and informed him of the matter, and he said: 'Why did you not slaughter it?' He said: 'I was too shy before you!'" He alone narrated it.

Someone who permits eating, satiety, and taking provision from it for a period during which he strongly suspects he will need it may cite this as evidence. And Allah knows best. Ibn Kathir stated this.

His saying: (*fanafaqat*), meaning: it died (from the pattern of *naṣara* and *fariḥa*). Ibn Barri said: Tha'lab recited:

"What are these things we buy with money? If it dies, it is at its most worthless."

Note: Some exegetes said: this verse does not clarify the priority among them. The jurists say: the one that is less severely forbidden takes precedence, so the carrion of an edible animal takes precedence over the carrion of other animals. End of his words.

In *Raḥmat al-Ummah* it is stated that if the one compelled finds carrion and another person's food, and its owner is absent, he may eat the food on condition of guaranteeing compensation, but not the carrion. This is the view of Malik, most of al-Shafi'i's companions, and a group of the Hanafiyyah. According to Ahmad and others, he eats the carrion.

Ibn Kathir said: Those who hold that a sinner in his travel may not avail himself of any of the concessions of travel have used His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without inclining toward sin﴾ as evidence, because concessions are not obtained through disobedience. And Allah knows best.

[p-1843] The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[4] ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are the good things, and [the game caught by] the hunting animals you have trained, teaching them as Allah has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning."﴾

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ means: of foods. ﴿Say: Lawful for you are the good things﴾ means: that which is not foul among them. This is everything whose prohibition has not come in the Book or the Sunnah. In language, al-ṭayyib (the good) is that which is pleasant (al-mustaladhdh). Al-ḥalāl (the permitted) that is allowed is called ṭayyib by way of likening it to what is pleasant, because both share the absence of harm. ﴿And what you have trained of the hunting animals﴾ is conjoined to (al-ṭayyibāt) by supposing an omitted noun, i.e., and the game of what you have trained them to take. Or it is a new subject (mubtada'), with (mā) being conditional, and its response being (fa-kulū, "then eat").

Al-jawāriḥ (lit. "the hunters," the hunting animals) are the predatory animals of beasts and birds, such as the dog, the leopard, the eagle, the falcon, the gerfalcon, and the hawk, because they "wound" (tajraḥu) for their people, i.e., they earn for them. Its singular is jāriḥah. The Arabs say: "So-and-so wounded (jaraḥa) his family with good," meaning he earned them good. And "So-and-so has no jāriḥ," meaning he has no earner. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He knows what you have earned (jaraḥtum) by day﴾ [al-An'am: 60], i.e., you earned. It has been said that they were called (jawāriḥ) because they wound the game when they hold it.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿mukallibīn﴾ means: trainers of them, so that they go forth when sent, withdraw when called back, return when summoned, and do not run off when they wish to pursue. They become as if they were your agents, because of their training. But if they kill by their own means without training, its game is not lawful.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The mukallib (trainer) is the one who disciplines the hunting animals, instructs them to hunt for their owner, and tames them for that purpose,[p-1844] with what is known of the tricks and methods of discipline and cultivation. Its derivation is from (al-kalb, "dog"), because discipline mostly occurs with dogs, so it was derived from its word because of its prevalence among its kind. Or because the beast of prey is called a dog. From this is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "O Allah, set upon him a dog of Your dogs," and he was eaten by a lion. (The hadith is ḥasan, related by al-Ḥākim.) Or it derives from (al-kalab), which means eagerness, as one says: "He is kalib with such-and-such" if he is eager for it.

The case of (mukallibīn) is an accusative of state (ḥāl) from (ʿallamtum, "you taught"). If you ask: What is the use of this state when it is already understood from (ʿallamtum)? I answer: Its benefit is that the one who trains the hunting animals should be proficient in his knowledge, skilled in it, and described as a trainer. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿you teach them﴾ is a second state or a resumptive clause, and in it is a magnificent benefit: that whoever takes up a knowledge should take it only from the most learned of its people, the most adept in its understanding, and the deepest in its subtleties and realities, even if he must travel to it for a long distance. How many a taker of knowledge from one who is not proficient has wasted his days and bitten his fingers when meeting the masters. ﴿What Allah has taught you﴾ means: of the knowledge of training, because it is an inspiration from Allah and also acquired by reason. Or: what He has made you know that you may teach it, such as pursuing the game by sending it by its master, its withdrawal by his call, its return by his summons, holding the game for him, and that it should not eat from it. End of quotation.

Al-Nāṣir said in al-Intiṣāf: In the verse is evidence that animals have knowledge, because their being taught, linguistically, means the attainment of knowledge by its means. This is against those who deny that.

﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾ means: what they keep for you, even if they kill it, provided they have not eaten from it. ﴿And mention the name of Allah over it﴾: the pronoun refers to (what you have trained of the hunting animals), i.e., name Allah over it when you send it, as the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah and ʿAdī, to come, clarifies. It is permitted that the pronoun refer to (what they hold), in the sense: and name Allah over it when you overtake it alive to slaughter it. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ means: by eating of what lacks one of these conditions, hastening towards it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ means: swift in requital for everything, great and small.

[p-1845] Remarks:

First: Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd ibn Muhalhil al-Ṭāʾiyyayn: "Both asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Allah has forbidden carrion, so what is lawful for us from it?' Then this was revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: Lawful for you are the good things﴾." Saʿīd said: That means the lawful slaughtered animals that are good for them. Muqātil said: What is lawful for them of everything they may obtain, which is the lawful provision. Al-Zuhrī was asked about drinking urine for treatment and said: It is not among the good things. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related this.

Ibn Wahb said: Mālik was asked about selling the clay that people eat, and he said: It is not among the good things. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related another report about the occasion of its revelation, from Abū Rāfiʿ, the freedman of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the killing of dogs, and they were killed. The people came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! What is lawful for us from this community which you ordered to be killed?' He was silent. So Allah revealed: They ask you… (the verse)." The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "If a man sends his dog and names Allah, and it holds game for him, let him eat of what it did not eat."

In Ibn Jarīr from Abū Rāfiʿ, he said: "Jibrīl came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to seek permission to enter, and he was permitted. He said: 'We have permitted you, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Indeed. But we do not enter a house in which there is a dog.' Abū Rāfiʿ said: So he ordered me to kill every dog in Madinah, until I came to a woman who had a dog barking at her, so I left it out of mercy for her. Then I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He ordered me, so I returned to the dog and killed it. They came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! What is lawful for us from this community which you ordered to be killed?' He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent. He said: Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you﴾."

Al-Ḥākim related it in his Mustadrak and said: Ṣaḥīḥ, but the two (Bukhārī and Muslim) did not narrate it.

Ibn Jarīr also related from ʿIkrimah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abū Rāfiʿ to kill dogs until he reached al-ʿAwālī. Then ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, Saʿīd ibn Khaythamah, and ʿUwaymir ibn Sāʿidah came and said: 'What is lawful for us, O Messenger of Allah?' So the verse was revealed." Al-Ḥākim related this also from ʿIkrimah. Likewise Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said about its occasion of revelation that it concerned the killing of dogs. Ibn Kathīr conveyed this.

Some exegetes said: When the verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted keeping dogs that are beneficial, and forbade keeping those of no benefit among them. He ordered the killing of the vicious and harmful ones. End of quotation.

I say: Imam Aḥmad and Muslim related from Jābir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered us to kill dogs, until a woman would come from the desert with her dog and kill it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade its killing and said: 'Keep to the black, pure one with two spots, for it is a devil.'"

The two Shaykhs (Bukhārī and Muslim) related from Ibn ʿUmar: "The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the killing of dogs, except a hunting dog, a sheep-herding dog, or a livestock dog."

From ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughaffal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Were it not that dogs are a community among the communities, I would have ordered their killing entirely. So kill from them every black, pure one." Abū Dāwūd and al-Dārimī related it, and [p-1847] al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā'ī added: "No household keeps a dog except that a qīrāṭ (a measure of reward) is diminished from their deeds every day, except a hunting dog, a field-guarding dog, or a sheep-herding dog."

The apparent meaning of these hadiths is that he (ﷺ) had ordered the killing of all of them, and then permitted their retention, except the black one, which deserves to be killed.

The statement of Imam al-Ḥaramayn: Then the Sharīʿah settled on the prohibition of killing all dogs where there is no harm in them, even the black pure one, needs proof.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: In these hadiths is the permissibility of keeping a dog for hunting and for livestock.

Likewise for cultivation, because it is an added guard. And disliked is keeping it for other than these purposes. But it enters into the meaning of hunting and what is mentioned, by analogy, keeping them to bring benefits and repel harms. The bare disapproval of keeping them without need is because of the terror it causes to people and the angels' refusal to enter a house in which there are dogs.

Then he said: The meaning of the hadith, in my view, is that the acts of worship connected with dogs, such as washing the vessel seven times, are hardly performed by the one obligated, nor can he guard against them, so perhaps by keeping them something enters upon him that diminishes his reward for that.

It is related that al-Manṣūr billāh asked ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd about the cause of this hadith, and he did not know it. Al-Manṣūr said: Because it barks at the guest and frightens the beggar. End of quotation.

Al-Khaṭṭābī said: The meaning of his (ﷺ) saying: "Were it not that dogs are a community among the communities… etc." is that he (ﷺ) disliked the annihilation of a community of the communities and the destruction of a generation of creation, because there is no creature of Allah, the Exalted, except that there is in it some kind of wisdom and some sort of benefit. He says: If that is so, and there is no way to kill them all, then kill their wicked ones, which are the black, pure ones, and leave the rest for you to benefit from them in guarding.

[p-1848] Al-Ṭībī said: His saying: "a community among the communities" is an allusion to the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor bird that flies with its wings except that they are communities like you﴾ [al-An'am: 38], i.e., like you in that they indicate the Creator and glorify Him. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him with praise﴾ [al-Isrā': 44], i.e., glorifies with the tongue of speech or of state, by which it indicates the Creator and His power and wisdom and His exaltation above what is not befitting for Him. Therefore, in view of this meaning, it is not permitted to attack them by killing and annihilation. But if it is to repel harm, such as killing the five noxious creatures, or to bring a benefit, such as slaughtering edible animals, that is permitted.

Second: The majority of the Companions, the Successors, and the Imams held that the hunting animals whose game is lawful are those that accept training, from among the predators with fangs such as the dog, the leopard, and the panther, or those with talons such as the birds mentioned earlier. In al-Nihāyah it is said: Even the cat, if it is trained. They argued from the generality of the verse.

Abū Dāwūd and Aḥmad related from Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What you have trained of a dog or a falcon, then you sent it and mentioned the name of Allah over it, eat what it holds for you." I said: "Even if it kills?" He said: "Even if it kills, provided it has not eaten anything from it, for it has held it for you."

[p-1849] Al-Bayhaqī said: Mujālid alone mentioned the falcon in it, and he opposed the memorizers (ḥuffāẓ).

I say: Ibn Jarīr related, with the aforementioned chain to ʿAdī, that he said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the game of the falcon? He said: What it holds for you, eat." And from Ibn ʿUmar and Mujāhid: "Only the game of the dog is lawful, only that." Ibn Jarīr related with his chain that Ibn ʿUmar said: As for what the birds hunt (and the hawks among the birds), whatever it overtakes, it is yours; otherwise do not eat it. Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: Mujāhid disliked the game of all birds, and he recited His saying: ﴿And what you have trained of the hunting animals, trainers﴾, i.e., the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿trainers﴾ points to restricting that to the dog. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, al-Nakhaʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq said: It is lawful from every creature except the black pure dog, because he has been ordered to be killed.

Third: We have stated that the accusative of (mukallibīn) is a state from (ʿallamtum). Ibn Kathīr said: It is possible that it is a state of the object, which is (the hunting animals), i.e., and what you have trained of the hunting animals [p-1850] in the state of their being trainers for the game, and that they hunt with their claws and talons.

So it is deduced from this, in this situation, that if a trained hunting animal kills the game with its impact, its claws or its talons, the game is lawful. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i and a group of scholars. Hence He said: ﴿teach them of what Allah has taught you﴾, which means that when you send it, it runs out, and when you call it back, it returns, and when it catches the game it holds it for its master until he comes to it, and does not hold it for itself. Hence the Exalted said: ﴿So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it﴾. Thus, when the hunting animal is trained, holds the game for its master, and the name of Allah was mentioned over it at the time of sending it, the game is lawful even if it killed it, by consensus.

The Sunnah has come with the same as what this noble verse indicates. As established in the "Two Sahihs" (p-1851) from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I send trained dogs and mention the name of Allah?' He said: 'When you send your trained dog and mention the name of Allah, eat what it holds for you.' I said: 'Even if they kill?' He said: 'Even if they kill, so long as no dog that is not of them has joined it. For you only named over your dog and did not name over another.' I said to him: 'I shoot game with the mi'rad (a blunt arrow).' He said: 'When you shoot game with the mi'rad and it pierces, eat it; but if it strikes with its breadth, it is a waqidh (a beast killed by a blow), so do not eat it.'"

(p-1852) In a wording of both of them: "When you send your dog, mention the name of Allah. If it holds for you and you reach it alive, slaughter it; and if you reach it having been killed and it has not eaten from it, eat it, for the dog's taking is its slaughter." And in another narration of both: "If it eats, do not eat it, for I fear it held it for itself." This is evidence for the majority that if the dog eats from the game, it is unlawful absolutely, and they did not distinguish, as the hadith reports. It has been related from a group of the early generation that they said: it is not unlawful absolutely, whether it ate or did not eat.

(p-1853) Ibn Jarir related from Salman al-Farisi and Abu Hurayrah, who both said: "Eat, even if it ate two-thirds of it." And from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "Even if it ate two-thirds." And from him: "Even if it left only a morsel." And from Ibn 'Umar: "When you send your trained dog and mention the name of Allah, eat what it holds for you, whether it ate or did not eat." He related this from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and many of the Successors.

This has also been related as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Abu Dawud related from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "a Bedouin, called Abu Tha'labah, said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I have trained dogs, so give me a ruling concerning their game.' (p-1854) The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If you have trained dogs, eat what they hold for you.' He said: 'Slaughtered and unslaughtered?' He said: 'Yes, even if it ate from it.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Give me a ruling concerning my bow!' He said: 'Eat what your bow returns to you.' He said: 'Slaughtered and unslaughtered?' He said: 'Even if it went out of your sight, so long as it did not get lost, or you find in it a trace other than your arrow.' He said: 'Give me a ruling concerning the vessels of the Magians when we are compelled to use them.' He said: 'Wash them and eat in them.'" Thus did Abu Dawud narrate it, and al-Nasa'i has also recorded it. Likewise Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Tha'labah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you send your dog and mention the name of Allah, eat, even if it ate from it, and eat what your hand returns to you."

Those who did not make the game unlawful by the dog's eating and the like have argued with what we have mentioned. Others took a middle course, saying: if it eats immediately after it held the game, it becomes unlawful, due to the hadith of 'Adi and the reason to which the Prophet ﷺ pointed. As for if it held the game, then waited for its master, and the wait was long, and it grew hungry and ate from it out of its hunger, this does not affect the prohibition. They applied the hadith of Abu Tha'labah to this case. This is a good distinction and a sound reconciliation between the two hadiths.

Imam Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni wished in his book "al-Nihayah" that someone would make this detailed distinction. God fulfilled his wish, and a group of the companions of the school held this view and this distinction. Related by Ibn Kathir.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": People have taken various paths in reconciling the hadith of 'Adi and Abu Tha'labah. Among them, for those who hold the prohibition: (The first) the hadith of Abu Tha'labah the Bedouin is taken to mean the case where it killed the game and left it, then returned and ate from it. (The second) preference: the narration of 'Adi is in the Two Sahihs and the narration of the Bedouin is in other collections, and its weakening is disputed. Also, the narration of 'Adi is explicit and tied to an appropriate reason for prohibition, namely fear that it held the game for itself, supported by the principle that carrion is prohibited. So when (p-1855) we doubt the permitting cause, we return to the original principle and to the apparent sense of the verse mentioned, for its implication is that what it holds without being sent is not permitted. It is also strengthened by supporting evidence from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in Ahmad: "When you send the dog and it eats the game, do not eat, for it held only for itself. But when you send it and it kills and does not eat, eat, for it held for its master." Al-Bazzar related it through another route from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Shaybah from the hadith of Abu Rafi', similar in meaning. Had mere holding been sufficient, the addition of "for you" (*'alaykum*) in the verse would not have been needed. As for those who hold it permissible, they took the hadith of 'Adi to mean makruh tanzihi (reprehensible as a matter of discouragement), and the hadith of the Bedouin to explain permissibility. Some of them said: the reason for this is that 'Adi was wealthy, so the interpretation of the first was chosen for him, unlike Abu Tha'labah, who was the opposite. The weakness of this argument is not hidden, given the explicit statement of the reason in the hadith: fear that it held for itself. In a narration of Ibn Abi Shaybah: "If it drinks of its blood, do not eat, for it was not taught what you taught it." This points to the fact that if it begins to eat, that shows it is not trained to the required degree.

Fourth: the verse establishes the legislated character of saying the basmalah (tasmiyah). Ibn Kathir said: His words ﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾ mean at the time of sending it, as the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Adi ibn Hatim: (p-1856) "When you send your trained dog and mention the name of Allah, eat what it holds for you." In the hadith of Abu Tha'labah, also recorded in the "Two Sahihs": "When you send your dog, mention the name of Allah. And when you shoot with your arrow." For this reason, those imams who made it a condition, such as Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, according to the well-known position from him, required the basmalah when sending the dog and when shooting the arrow, based on this verse and this hadith. The well-known view among the majority is that the verse's meaning is the command to say the basmalah at the time of sending, as al-Suddi and others said. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse: "When you send your hunting animal, say: In the name of Allah. And if you forget, there is no blame." End of quote.

Some of the Zaydiyyah said: The basmalah here is like the basmalah over slaughter. Some say it is obligatory for one who remembers but not for the forgetful, due to the hadith: "Error and forgetfulness have been lifted from my community." Others say it is recommended. Others say it is a condition absolutely. The well-known position of Ahmad is to differentiate between hunting and slaughter; in slaughter he took the third view. Then he said: One may say that the words of the Exalted ﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾ may refer to eating; that is, say the basmalah when eating. Thus the verse's indication regarding the obligation of the basmalah is open to interpretation. End of quote. This possibility was related by Ibn Kathir, and his text is:

(p-1857) Some people said: The meaning of this verse is the command to say the basmalah at the time of eating, as is established in the "Two Sahihs" that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught his stepson 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah: "Say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is near you." In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from 'A'ishah, that "they said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Some people come to us, recently converted from disbelief, with meat, and we do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not?' He said: 'Say the name of Allah yourselves and eat.'" al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih.

Fifth: the verse permits training animals and striking them for a benefit, because training may require that. So says the "al-Iklil". What was mentioned earlier from al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasir about the verse also includes learning from the expert, and that animals have knowledge. From the verse it is also inferred that keeping a dog for hunting and for guarding is permitted, by the Sunnah, as has been mentioned.

(p-1858) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[5] ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And (lawful for you are) the chaste women from among the believers, and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you, when you have given them their bridal due, taking them in marriage, not in fornication, nor taking them as secret lovers. And whoever rejects faith, his deed has become void, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾, meaning: of the slaughtered animals and game. Its repetition is an emphasis on the favor. Abu al-Su'ud said: It has been said that by "the days" (the three days) is meant a single time, and He repeated it for emphasis; and because of the differing events occurring in it, its repetition is fine. And what is meant by "the good things" is what has already passed.

Note:
Some of the exegetes of the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i school) said: The verse indicates the permissibility of eating the finest of foods and dyes. In "al-Rawda wa al-Ghadir" he said: Although covering oneself with the inferior is the better course, as ʿAlī, peace be upon him, and other virtuous people did. It is narrated that ʿAlī, peace be upon him, would feed people the best of food, yet one of his companions saw his own food, which was unsifted barley bread and coarse salt, and it was sealed so that it would not be changed. Among his sayings, peace be upon him: "By God! I will train my soul in such a way that it will be delighted by a loaf if it finds it unseasoned, and by salt if it finds it without a relish." And this is in accordance with what is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the disliking of combining two kinds of condiment. End.

﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Umama, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and others said: it means their slaughtered animals.

Ibn Kathir said: This is a matter on which the scholars agree: that their slaughtered animals are lawful for the Muslims, because they believe in the prohibition of slaughtering for other than God, and they do not mention upon their slaughtered animals except the name of God, even if they hold beliefs about Him that are far above Him, exalted and sanctified is He. End.

Al-Mahayimi said: Even if their mention of God's name is not considered valid, yet since they did mention it, it resembles what is considered valid to mention, and so their food resembles the good things.

Discussions:

The first: What we have mentioned, that what is meant by "the food" is the slaughtered animals, is what the leading early scholars said: Companions such as Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Umama, and Successors such as Mujahid and eight others, as in Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir. In "al-Lubab": They agreed that what is meant by "the food of those who were given the Book" is specifically their slaughtered animals. Because other than slaughtered animals is lawful before it was theirs and after it became theirs, so there would be no benefit in specifying it for the People of the Book. And because what precedes this verse concerns the ruling on game and slaughtered animals, so interpreting this verse in that light is preferable, since all other food does not differ whether it is handled by a People of the Book or someone else; only the method of slaughter differs. So when the People of the Book were singled out for mention, it indicates that what is meant by their food is their slaughtered animals. End.

The second: The verse has been cited as evidence for all parts of their slaughtered animals. This is the view of the majority.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": It is reported from Malik and Ahmad that what God forbade to the People of the Book, such as fats, is forbidden. Ibn al-Qasim said: because what God permitted is their food, and fats are not part of their food, nor do they intend them at the time of slaughter. It has been objected that Ibn ʿAbbas explained "their food" as their slaughtered animals, and when their slaughtered animals are permitted, there is no need to consider their intention regarding parts of the slaughtered animal. Ritual slaughter does not apply to some parts of the slaughtered animal and not others; and if slaughter spreads to all of it, the fat necessarily enters. Also, God explicitly stated that He forbade them every animal with claws. So according to this speaker's view, it would follow that if a Jew slaughters an animal that has claws, it would not be lawful for a Muslim to eat it. Then Ibn Hajar said: His saying, "The good things have been made lawful for you" is used as evidence for permissibility, because He did not single out flesh from fat. That fats are forbidden to the People of the Book does not harm, because they are forbidden to them, not to us. At most, after it is established that their slaughtered animals are lawful for us, what was forbidden to them of them is silent in our law regarding its prohibition for us, so it remains on the原 basis of permissibility. End.

In the "Sahih" it is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Mughaffal, may God be pleased with him, who said: "We were besieging the fortress of Khaybar. A man threw a bag containing fat, so I leaped to take it, then I turned and saw the Prophet (ﷺ), and I was ashamed before him." In another narration: "A bag of fat was let down to us on the day of Khaybar, so I embraced it and said: I will not give any of this today to anyone. Then I turned, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was smiling."

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: In it is evidence against those who prohibit what was forbidden to them, such as fats, because the Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed Ibn Mughaffal in benefiting from the said bag. And in it is the permissibility of eating fat from what the People of the Book slaughtered, even if they were people of war. End.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: The majority have used this hadith as evidence against the Malikis, but there is room for examination in that, because it is a specific event, and it may be that it was fat which they believed to be lawful, such as back fat and the intestinal fat and the like. And God knows best.

More clearly in indication is what is established in the "Sahih": that the people of Khaybar presented to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a roasted sheep, and they had poisoned its foreleg, which he liked, so he took it and bit a bite from it. The foreleg informed him that it was poisoned, so he spat it out, and it affected the molars of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his aorta. Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur ate with him from it and died. He then killed the Jewish woman who had poisoned it, whose name was Zaynab. The point of evidence from it is that he resolved to eat it along with those with him, and he did not ask them whether they had removed from it what they believe to be forbidden of its fat or not. In another hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was hosted by a Jew with barley bread and rancid fat," meaning rancid grease.

The third: Ibn al-ʿArabi, one of the Maliki imams, held by this verse the permissibility of what the Franks kill, even if we see that it is done, because it is of their food. Al-Shaykh Khalil reported this from his "Tawdih" and considered it unlikely. The Imam Ibn Zikri said: Ibn al-ʿArabi wrote on the permissibility of the slaughter of a Christian not in our manner of slaughter, while the verifiers hold it to be forbidden. This was clarified by the jurist Muhammad al-Dulaymi al-Susi al-Maliki in his "Fatawa," when he was asked about the slaughter of a People of the Book: is what he slaughters lawful however it was done, whether or not it agreed with our manner of slaughter? He answered, saying: The Imam Ibn al-ʿArabi said: When a Christian cuts the neck of a chicken, it is lawful for a Muslim to eat it, because God the Exalted made lawful for us the eating of their food which they consider permissible in their religion. Whatever they slaughter according to the requirement of their religion is lawful for us to eat, and it is not a condition that their slaughter agree with ours. That is a concession from God the Exalted and an ease from Him for us. Excepted from this are only what God the Exalted forbade specifically. For that, although it is their food which they consider lawful, it is not lawful for us to eat. End.

The fourth: al-Razi said: It has been reported from some Zaydi imams that what is meant by "food" in the verse is bread, fruit, and what does not require slaughter. End.

I have looked at a fragment of a remarkable tafsir by one of the Zaydiyya in which he said: The scholars, the imams and jurists, have differed over what is meant by "food." Al-Qasim, al-Hadi, and Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, and one narration from Zayd, said: the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book and of all disbelievers are not permissible, based on His saying: ﴿except what you slaughter﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], and this is an address to the Muslims. The second narration from Zayd and the general body of jurists of the Hanafis, Shafi'is, Malikis, Ja'faris and Imamis, and it was chosen by Amir H and Amir Yahya: the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book. They interpret "food" as slaughtered animals and other things. This is reported from al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, al-Sha'bi, ʿAta', Qatada and most exegetes, and they took the generality in the unrestricted sense of "food." The first group replied that "food" is applied to grains; one says "the market of food." The judge said: The closer view is permissibility, because by their action it becomes food; and because He specified the People of the Book. It was answered: He specified them lest it be thought that their food which they did not slaughter is forbidden. Then according to al-Hadi and al-Qasim, peace be upon them both, the moistness of them is impure, based on His saying: ﴿The polytheists are only impure﴾ [al-Tawba: 28], so whatever their moisture has touched is forbidden, except what we took by force. According to al-Mu'ayyad billah and those with him: their moisture is pure. The dispute over moisture applies generally to disbelievers. End.

In "al-Rawda al-Nadiyya" its text reads: As for the slaughter of the protected people (dhimmis), the Noble Qur'an has indicated its permissibility by this verse. Whoever says that meat is not included in "food" has been negligent in research, and has not looked into the lexicons, nor considered the legal evidences explicitly stating that the Prophet (ﷺ) ate the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book, as in his eating of the sheep which a Jewish woman cooked and put poison in, and the story is too well known to need mention. There is no basis for the view of prohibiting their slaughtered animals except mere doubts and illusions to which one is subjected who has not firmly established his foot in the knowledge of the Law. If you say: they may slaughter it for other than God, or without naming God, or not in the prescribed manner of slaughter. I say: if any of this is true, the discussion concerns their slaughter, like the discussion concerning the slaughter of a Muslim if it occurs in one of these ways. The dispute is only over the mere fact that the disbelief of the People of the Book is an impediment, not over whether he has taken a valid condition into account. End.

The fifth: By "the People of the Book" are meant the Jews and Christians, and whoever entered their religion of the other nations before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for those who entered their religion after the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely the Arab Christians of the Banu Taghlib, their slaughter is not lawful. It is narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: Do not eat from the slaughtered animals of the Christians of Banu Taghlib, for they did not adhere to anything of Christianity except drinking wine. Ibn Mas'ud said likewise. Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about the slaughter of the Arab Christians, and he said: there is no harm in it, and then recited: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 51]. This is the view of al-Hasan, ʿAta', al-Sha'bi, ʿIkrima, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam and Hammad, as in "al-Lubab."

Ibn Kathir said: As for the Magians, although the jizya was taken from them by extension and assimilation to the People of the Book, their slaughter is not eaten and their women are not married. Contrary to this is Abu Thawr, Ibrahim ibn Khalid al-Kalbi (one of the jurists among the companions of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal). When he said that and it became known from him, the jurists denounced it, to the point that the Imam Ahmad said of him: Abu Thawr is like his name, meaning in this issue. He seems to have relied on the generality of a hadith narrated as a mursal report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book."

But this wording is not established. What is in the "Sahih" of al-Bukhari from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf is that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the jizya from the Magians of Hajar. Even if the authenticity of this hadith is granted, its generality is specified by the implication of this verse: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾, so by the implication of contrast it indicates that the food of others among the followers of religions is not lawful...!

The sixth point: it has been said that this verse permits the slaughter of the People of the Book without qualification, even if they mention other than the name of God, Exalted is He. It is reported from Ibn Umar that if a Jew or a Christian slaughters in the name of other than God, Exalted is He, that is not lawful. This is also the view of Rabi'ah. Al-Sha'bi and Ata' were asked about a Christian who slaughters in the name of the Messiah, and they said: it is lawful, for God, Exalted is He, has made their slaughtered animals lawful, and He knows what they say. Al-Hasan said: if a Jew or a Christian slaughters and mentions the name of God while you are hearing it, do not eat; but if it happens out of your sight, eat, for God has made it lawful for you. So it is in al-Lubab. The saying of al-Hasan on this question is the soundest.

In al-Nihayah, one of the books of the Zaydiyyah, it is stated: as for when the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah) slaughter for their festivals and their churches, Malik disliked it, Ashhab permitted it, and al-Shafi'i prohibited it. This is because of the conflict between the general wording of God's words, ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, and the general wording of His words, ﴿that over which has been invoked the name of other than God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]; so the specification of each by the other is a possibility. Then he said: the majority hold that the slaughter of an apostate is prohibited. Ishaq permitted it, and al-Thawri disliked it. The root of the disagreement is whether the term "the Scripture" (al-kitab) encompasses the apostate or not. He said: this likewise is the source of the disagreement concerning the slaughtered animals of the tribe of Banu Taghlib: does the term "the Scripture" encompass the Arabs who became Christian or Jewish, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas, or does it not encompass them, as is narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him? End of quotation.

As for God's words, ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, the meaning is: your slaughtered animals are lawful for them, so that the Jews and Christians may eat the slaughtered animals of the Muslims. So it is in the tafsir attributed to Ibn Abbas.

Some of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah relate from Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Darda', the rest of the Successors mentioned earlier, and most of the commentators and jurists, that what is meant is the slaughtered animals of the Muslims.

Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is: it is lawful for you to feed them, because the lawful and the unlawful and the rulings (al-fara'id) are established only for the people of the Shariah.

Ibn Kathir said: that is, it is lawful for you to feed them from your slaughtered animals, and it is not a report about the ruling as held by them, unless it is a report of what they were commanded regarding eating from every food over which the name of God has been mentioned, whether it comes from their own religious community or from another. The first is more apparent in meaning; that is, it is lawful for you to feed them from your slaughtered animals just as you ate from their slaughtered animals. This is of the category of reciprocity and recompense, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) put his garment on Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul when he died and buried him in it. It is said that this was because he had clothed al-Abbas with his garment when he came to Madinah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) repaid him with that. As for the hadith in which it says: "Do not keep company except with a believer, and let none eat your food except a pious person," it is to be understood as recommendation and preference. And God knows best. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: that is, it is lawful for them to feed them from your food. For there is nothing to prevent God from forbidding us to feed them from our slaughtered animals. Also, the benefit in mentioning this is that the permission of intermarriage is not established on both sides, whereas the permission of slaughtered animals was established on both sides; so God, Exalted is He, mentioned it as an admonition to distinguish between the two categories. End of quotation.

Al-Burhan al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: God's words, ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾, mean that taking it is for your need of mixing with them, due to the permission to let them remain upon their religion in exchange for the poll-tax (jizyah). Since this indicates leaving them upon what they have chosen for themselves, He reinforced it with His words: ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾; that is, there is no fault on you in giving it to them, nor on them in taking it. End of quotation.

In the Amali of the Imam al-Suhayli, may God have mercy on him: it has been asked, what is the wisdom in this sentence, when they are disbelievers who do not need our clarification? He gives two answers. The first is that the meaning is: look at what has been made lawful for you in your Shariah; if they feed you from it, eat it, and do not look at what was forbidden to them, for the flesh of camels and the like was forbidden to them, and then that was abrogated in our Shariah. The verse is an explanation for us, not for them; that is, know that what was forbidden to them, of what is lawful, has been made lawful for them also. For this reason, if they feed us pork or the like and say: "It is lawful in our Shariah, and God has permitted us to feed you," we would deny them and say: the food that is lawful for you is what is lawful for us, and nothing else. So the meaning is: their food is lawful for you, if it is the food that I have made lawful for you. This interpretation is the meaning of the saying of al-Suddi and others.

The second answer, held by al-Nahhas, al-Zajjaj, al-Naqqash and many of the later scholars, is that the meaning is: it is permissible for you to feed them from your food, not that it clarifies for them what is lawful for them in their religion, because their religion is false. However, it does not say "and your feeding" (wa-it'amukum) but "your food" (ta'amukum), and the food is what is eaten, whereas the action is the feeding. If they claim that "food" stands in the place of "feeding" by way of extension, we say: another objection remains, namely the separation of the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate of the subject. This is prohibited by consensus. They do not permit "the feeding of Zayd is good for the poor" or "your striking is severe Zayd," so how is "and your food is lawful for them" permitted? End of quotation.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: this verse may be used as evidence by one who holds that disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings of the Shariah, because permissibility is a ruling, and He has linked it to them in His words, ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, just as He linked the ruling to the believers. This verse is clearer as evidence than His words: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]; for one may say, in that verse, that negating a ruling is not itself a ruling, but he cannot say that of this verse of al-Ma'idah, because the ruling in it is affirmed. And God knows best.

Then he said: when al-Zamakhshari sensed its indication of this, and he is among those who hold that addressing disbelievers with the subsidiary rulings of the Shariah is impossible, he put forward an interpretation of it by turning the address toward the believers, meaning: there is no blame upon you, O Muslims, in feeding the People of the Scripture. End of quotation.

﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾ is conjoined to "the good things" or is a subject whose predicate has been omitted, because what precedes it indicates it; that is, it is lawful for you. By "the chaste women" (al-muhsanat) is meant those who are chaste from fornication, as He said in the other verse: ﴿chaste, not fornicators, nor taking secret lovers﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. This is what is related from al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sufyan, Ibrahim and Mujahid. Ibn Jarir related another report from Mujahid that he said: "al-muhsanat are the free women." It was said that what is meant by them is other than slave women. It was also said that what is meant is the chaste ones, as in the saying of the majority. This is because the free (hurr) is used in contrast to the slave, and for the best of anything, as in al-Qamus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: restricting them to these is an incitement to believers to choose carefully for their seed. Slave women from among Muslim women, their marriage is valid by consensus, and likewise the marriage of non-chaste women among them. End of quotation.

I say: the permissibility of marrying a slave woman is conditional upon fear of sinning and the inability to afford a free woman, due to the verse: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women...﴾ As for marrying a non-chaste woman, most scholars permit it. The Imam Ahmad held that it is prohibited for a man to marry an adulteress, whether he is an adulterer or other, until she repents and her waiting period is completed, on the basis of His words: ﴿The adulterer marries none but an adulteress or an idolatress, and that is forbidden to the believers﴾ [al-Nur: 3], and on the basis of what Ahmad related with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr: that a man from among the Muslims asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission regarding a woman called Umm Mahzul, who used to fornicate and stipulated for him that she would spend upon him. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited to him: ﴿The adulteress marries none but an adulterer or an idolater﴾ [al-Nur: 3].

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, related from the hadith of Ibn Umar: that Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi used to carry the captives in Makkah. There was a prostitute in Makkah called Anaq, and she had been his friend. He said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God! Shall I marry Anaq?" He said: so he remained silent with me. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿The adulteress marries none but an adulterer or an idolater﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. He called me and recited it to me and said: "Do not marry her."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud related with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The fornicator who has been lashed marries none but one like himself." Ibn al-Qayyim said: the Imam Ahmad and those who agreed with him took by these fatwas, against which there is no opposing evidence, and they are among the excellences of his school; for it is permissible for a man to marry a wife he loves. Twenty-odd proofs support his school, which we have mentioned in another place.

Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as sahih, related from the hadith of Amr ibn al-Ahwas, that he witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage with the Prophet (ﷺ); he praised God and extolled Him, and mentioned and admonished, then said: "Be good to women, for they are with you as captives; you possess nothing from them other than that, unless they come with a manifest immorality. If they do that, then forsake them in their beds and strike them with a stroke that is not severe; then if they obey you, do not seek a way against them." Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: my wife does not refuse the hand of one who touches her. He said: divorce her. He said: I fear my soul will follow her. He said: then enjoy her." Al-Mundhiri said: the narrators of its chain are those on whom reliance is placed in the two Sahihs.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: against this ambiguous hadith are opposed the clear decisive hadiths prohibiting permission of prostitutes. The paths of those who prohibit it differ regarding it. One group said: what is meant by "the one who touches" is one who seeks alms, not one who seeks immorality. Another group said: rather, this is in continuation, and it has no effect; what prevents it is the contract being concluded with the adulteress, and this is the prohibited act. Another group said: rather, this is adopting the lesser of two evils to avert the greater; for when he was commanded to separate from her, he feared that he would not be patient with her and would commit the prohibited act with her, so he was then commanded to keep her, since intercourse with her under a marriage contract is less corrupt than intercourse with her in fornication. Another group said: rather, the hadith is weak and not established. Another group said: there is nothing in the hadith indicating that she is an adulteress; rather it says only that she does not refuse one who touches her or places his hand upon her or the like, so she gives in to that. It does not necessarily follow that she gives him the greatest immorality. But one cannot be secure with her that she will answer one who calls to immorality. So he commanded him to separate from her, abandoning what troubles him for what does not trouble him. When he informed him that his soul would follow her, and that he had no patience with her, he judged that keeping her was the more preponderant course. And God, Exalted is He, knows best. The completion of the discussion on this will come, God willing, in Surah al-Nur.

Benefit: Jabir ibn Abdullah, Amir al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan al-Basri issued a fatwa that if a man marries a woman and she commits adultery before he has consummated the marriage with her, the two are to be separated, and she returns to him the dowry he gave her. Ibn Jarir related it from them.

﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾; that is, they too are lawful for you. The majority hold that what is meant by "the chaste women" is those chaste from fornication, as we have mentioned.

Ibn Kathir said: and this is the more likely, lest it combine in her that she is a dhimmi and at the same time not chaste, so that her state is entirely corrupted, and her husband obtains, as it is said, "a shrivelled date and a bad measure."

Ibn Jarir related from a group of the early scholars, among those who interpreted "the chaste women" as chaste ones, that the verse encompasses every chaste Christian or Jewish woman, whether she is free or a slave. But whoever interprets it as "free women" says: the marriage of a slave woman from the People of the Scripture is not valid under any circumstances, since the shame of disbelief cannot be borne together with the shame of slavery, and furthermore it would lead to the enslavement of a disbeliever who is the child of a Muslim.

Remarks:

(p-1871) The first view: the apparent meaning of the verse permits marrying a woman of the People of the Book (kitabiyyah). This is the position of most jurists and exegetes.

It is also a report from Zayd (ibn 'Ali), al-Sadiq and al-Baqir, and it was chosen by Imam Yahya, who said: it is the consensus (ijma') of the early generation of the Companions. He also said that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan married Na'ilah bint al-Farafisah while he had other wives, and she was a Christian. And Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah married a Jewish woman. The exegetes (mufassirun) transmitted this as it is. Al-Bayhaqi, 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from 'Umar that he said: "A Muslim man may marry a Christian woman, but a Christian man may not marry a Muslim woman." 'Abd al-Razzaq also reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who was in Kufah, that he had married a woman from the People of the Book, and he wrote to him: "Divorce her, for you are in the land of the Magians. I fear that the ignorant will say: the Companion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married a disbelieving woman!" and that this would make lawful the concession that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had granted, so that people would marry the women of the Magians... So he divorced her.

'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi reported from Qatadah that Hudhayfah married a Jewish woman. 'Umar said: "Divorce her, for she is a burning coal." He said: "Is she forbidden (haram)?" He said: "No, but I fear that they (the Muslim men) will take up with the prostitutes among them..."

'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Zayd ibn Wahb who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote: "A Muslim man may marry a Christian woman, but a Christian man may not marry a Muslim woman." It is also reported from Jabir who said: "The women of the People of the Book are lawful for us, and our women are forbidden to them." It is also reported from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, who said: "A man of my people married a woman of the People of the Book in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)." It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he disliked this. He argued from the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:221], and he would say: "I know of no polytheism (shirk) greater than her saying that her lord is 'Isa."

The majority answered that this is a general statement that is specified by this verse, if it is said that the women of the People of the Book are included in the general sense of "idolatresses." Otherwise, there is no conflict between the two verses, because the People of the Book have been distinguished from the polytheists in more than one place, such as the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:1], and His saying: ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:20].

The second view: those who permitted marrying women of the People of the Book who are in a state of war (harbiyyat) used the general wording of the verse as evidence. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the permission applies only to the dhimmi women (women under the protection of the Muslim state). He read: ﴿Fight those who...﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:29] to His saying: ﴿until they pay the jizyah﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:29], and he said: "Whoever pays, it is lawful; whoever does not, it is not." This argument is very subtle, so let it be pondered!

The third view: al-Mahayimi said: Since the food of the People of the Book was considered in terms of its resemblance to the good (tayyib), as we have mentioned, it was also considered in the matter of marriage, so the chaste women (muhsanat) among them were made lawful. Their disbelief was tolerated, because the disbelief of others was not tolerated, since they call to the Fire. Whereas these (the People of the Book) acknowledge the principle of prophethood, and they have no doubt about the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), let alone any proof, their call to it was weak, so it was not taken into account. Moreover, the man has authority over the woman, so she does not affect him the way a man affects her; therefore it is not valid to marry a Muslim woman to a man of the People of the Book. Moreover, it involves humiliating the Muslim woman, so this is not tolerated.

The fourth view: a number of the pure family of the Prophet ('Itrah) held that by "chaste women" (al-muhsanat) is meant the believing women among them, based on the prohibition of marrying a disbelieving woman. One of the exegetes of the Zaydiyyah (a Shi'i school), after citing the view of the majority mentioned above, said: "al-Qasim, al-Hadi, al-Nafs al-Zakiyyah, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah and most of the Qasimiyyah said, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Umar: it is not lawful for a Muslim to marry a disbelieving woman, whether she is from the People of the Book or otherwise." They argued from the saying of Allah in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:221]. They said — meaning the majority — "This applies to idolatresses, not to the women of the People of the Book." We say: the term "polytheism" (shirk) applies to the People of the Book, as evidenced by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks...﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31] to His saying: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31]. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "I know of no polytheism greater than the saying of the Christians that their lord is 'Isa." And it is narrated from 'Ata': "Allah has increased the number of Muslim women; He only granted them that concession at that time." They said: He, the Exalted, joined one of them to the other, which indicates that they are two different groups, as He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:1]. We say: this is like His saying: ﴿The bequest to parents and relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:180]. They said: The verse explicitly permits it in His saying: ﴿And the chaste women from those who were given the Scripture﴾. We say: In Surah al-Nur: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men for wicked women, and good women for good men, and good men for good women﴾ [al-Nur 24:26], and His saying in Surah al-Nisa': ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry chaste believing women, then from what your right hands possess of believing maidens﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:25]. So the condition of belief in this requires prohibition. Therefore this verse is interpreted as meaning: He intended the chaste women from among the People of the Book who have embraced Islam, because they (the Muslims) used to dislike that, so He named them by the name of what they had been (before). Similar to this occurs in the Book of Allah. Allah said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture recite it as it should be recited; they believe in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:121], and His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture know it as they know their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:146], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:199]. They said: the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) and the action of the Companions indicate permissibility. We combine the noble verses and say: His saying ﴿And do not marry idolatresses﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:221] is general, and we specify it by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾. Or we say: by "idolatresses" He meant the women who worship idols, and by ﴿the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ He meant what the apparent meaning conveys. Or His saying "and the chaste women" abrogates the prohibition of the women of the People of the Book by His saying: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:221]. We respond to what you have mentioned with what has been reported: that Ka'b ibn Malik wanted to marry a Jewish woman or a Christian woman, so he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about that, and he said: "She does not guard your water (i.e., she does not make you chaste)." It is also reported that he forbade him from that.
