And we interpret His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ by combining and saying: the specification of the idolatresses by "and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture" is delayed, and clarification (bayan) may not be delayed!

They said: Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The slaughter of the People of the Book is lawful for us, and their women are lawful for us, and it is forbidden for them to marry our women." Qadi 'Iyad said in al-Shifa: "Our scholars said: this hadith is weak in transmission." They said: His saying (ﷺ) about the Magians: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book" — the report indicates the permissibility of their slaughter and marrying their women. We say: the permissibility is abrogated by the evidence for prohibition. Moreover, we strengthen our evidence by analogy, so we say: she is a disbeliever, so she resembles the woman at war; or, since inheritance is prohibited, marriage is prohibited; or, since a disbelieving man is prohibited from marrying a Muslim woman, the reverse is also prohibited. They said: there is no ruling for analogy in the presence of textual evidence. The end of his words verbatim, and it is a strange jurisprudence.

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿when you have given them their compensation (ujur)﴾, meaning: when you have given them their dowries (muhur). The restriction of permissibility to giving them (the dowry) is to emphasize its obligation and to encourage what is better, by hastening to discharge the obligation, for occupying one's duty with the right of a human being is more serious than occupying it with the right of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Chaste﴾ (muhsinin): abstaining from unlawful intercourse (mutaʿaffifin). ﴿Not in fornication﴾ (ghayra musafihin): not openly committing adultery. ﴿Nor taking secret lovers﴾ (wa la muttakhidhi akhdan): keeping it secret. The word "khidn" means a close friend, and it applies to both male and female. Interpreting "musafahah" (fornication) as public display of adultery is because its opposite, secrecy, appears in contrast, and this is what comes to mind from "khidn," which means a friend. It has been said: the first is a prohibition of adultery, and the second is a prohibition of associating with them. Thus in al-'Inayah.

Ibn Kathir said: Just as He stipulated chastity (ihsan) in women, which is abstinence from adultery, He likewise stipulated it in men, that the man too must be chaste and abstinent. For this reason He said: ﴿not in fornication﴾, and they are the adulterers who do not refrain from sin and do not restrain themselves from those who come to them. ﴿Nor taking secret lovers﴾: i.e., those who have lovers and do not engage except with them, as was mentioned in Surah al-Nisa'. For this reason Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the marriage of a prostitute (baghiyy) is not valid until she repents, and as long as she is in that state it is not valid to marry her to a chaste man. Likewise, in his view, a contract by a dissolute man with a chaste woman is not valid until he repents and gives up what he is engaged in of adultery, based on this verse and on the hadith: "An adulterer who has been flogged marries only someone like him." (p-1876)

Ibn Jarir reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I have resolved not to leave anyone who committed a grave sin (fahishah) in Islam to marry a chaste woman." Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful! Polytheism (shirk) is greater than that, and it may be accepted from him if he repents."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become worthless, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers﴾. Here "faith" (iman) means the laws of Islam. Moreover, it is a verbal noun used in the sense of "the one believed in," like "a dirham of the ruler's minting." "Disbelief" (kufr) means turning away from it and denying it. The verse is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:5], to magnify the status of what Allah has made lawful and what He has made forbidden, and to make strict the judgement against whoever opposes that. Thus in al-'Inayah.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. And if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves. And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have contact with women and find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to place upon you any difficulty, but He intends to purify you and to complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.﴾

(p-1877) ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles﴾. Since establishing the prayer was among the covenants with which this surah opens, and since the prayer is conditioned on purity (taharah), He, glorified is He, explains in this verse how it is to be performed.

Some exegetes said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman, who was wounded. And it was said: it was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) was detained on a journey at night because of a necklace of ʿAisha's that was lost, and they awoke without water. End of quote.

The second account was narrated by al-Bukhari, as cited in Asbab al-Nuzul (Causes of Revelation) of al-Suyuti. We have already discussed this in the surah of al-Nisa', at the verse of tayammum (dry ablution with earth), so refer to it there.

This verse contains fruits, which are legal rulings.

The first: the obligation of wudu (ablution) at the time of rising to prayer, meaning the intention to perform it. His words, ﴿when you rise to prayer﴾, are like His words: ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and like your saying: "When you strike your servant, be gentle with him," in that the intended meaning is the intention to perform the act. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why is it permissible to express the intention to perform an act by the act itself? I say: Because the act comes into being by the agent's power over it and his will for it, which is his purpose toward it, his inclination, and the sincerity of his motive. Just as one expresses the power to perform an act by the act itself, as in the saying "Man does not fly" and "The blind man does not see," meaning they have no power to fly or to see. From this is His words: ﴿We shall bring it about as a promise binding upon Us; indeed We are ever doers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], meaning: "indeed We are ever able to bring it back." Thus the intention to perform an act is expressed by the act, because the act is caused by power and will. So the effect is put in the place of the cause because of the connection between them. And for brevity of speech and the like, from putting the effect in the place of the cause, is the saying: "As you do, so it will be done to you." He expressed the initiating act, which is the cause of the recompense, by the word of the recompense, which is its effect.

(p-1878) The second: the apparent meaning of the verse is the obligation of wudu upon everyone who rises to prayer, even if he is not in a state of hadath (ritual impurity), based on the generality of ﴿those who have believed﴾ without restriction to those in hadath. The majority hold otherwise, based on what Imam Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan narrated from Buraydah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform wudu for every prayer. When the day of the Conquest came, he performed wudu, wiped over his leather socks, and prayed the prayers with one wudu. ʿUmar said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have done something you did not used to do.' He said: 'I did it deliberately, O ʿUmar.'"

Al-Bukhari narrated from Suwayd ibn al-Nuʿman, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of Khaybar. When we reached al-Sahba', the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed ʿasr with us. When he had prayed, he called for food, and only sawiq (a porridge of ground grain) was brought. We ate and drank. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) stood for maghrib, rinsed his mouth, then prayed maghrib with us, and did not perform wudu."

Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, who was asked about the wudu of his father ʿAbd Allah for every prayer, whether he was in a state of purity or not, from whom he had it. He said: "Asma' bint Zayd ibn al-Khattab narrated to him that ʿAbd Allah ibn Handhalah ibn al-Ghasil narrated to her that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been commanded to perform wudu for every prayer, whether in a state of purity or not. When that became hard on him, he was commanded to use the siwak (tooth-stick) at every prayer, and wudu was removed from him except for hadath. ʿAbd Allah used to think that he had the strength for that. He kept doing it until he died." Ibn Kathir said: In the action of Ibn ʿUmar, and his constancy in perfecting wudu for every prayer, there is evidence for the recommendation of that, as is the view of the majority.

(p-1879) Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Sirin that the caliphs used to perform wudu for every prayer. And from ʿIkrimah: that ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) used to perform wudu at every prayer and would recite ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer﴾ up to the end of the verse. From al-Nazzal ibn Sabrah, who said: "I saw ʿAli pray the dhuhr, then sit with the people in the courtyard. Then he was brought water, and he washed his face and hands. Then he wiped his head and feet and said: 'This is the wudu of one who has not become impure.'" In another narration: that he performed a wudu with some leniency and said: "This is the wudu of one who has not become impure." Likewise Anas narrated from ʿUmar that he did this. All of these chains are sound.

As for what Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, that he said: "Wudu without hadath is transgression," it is strange (gharib) from him. Moreover, it is to be understood as applying to one who believes it obligatory. As for its legislation as recommended, the Sunnah has indicated it. Imam Ahmad narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform wudu for every prayer." It was said to him: "How do you do it?" He said: "We used to pray all the prayers with one wudu, as long as we had not become impure." It was also narrated by al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever performs wudu while in a state of purity, ten good deeds are written for him." Al-Tirmidhi declared it weak.

If these hadiths indicate that wudu is obligatory only upon one in hadath, then the way out of the apparent meaning of the verse is that the address in it is specific to those in hadath.

(p-1880) In al-Inayah (of al-Babarti): the consensus (ijma') turns it away from its apparent meaning. As for it being restricted, i.e., "and you are in hadath," by the indication of the situation, and because the verse made hadath a condition for the substitute, which is tayammum, so if it had no connection to wudu, while having a connection to tayammum, the substitute would not be a substitute. His words, ﴿and you find no water﴾, are explicit regarding substitution. It was also said: there is an implied condition in the speech, i.e., "when you rise to prayer, if you are in hadath," ﴿and if you are in janabah, then purify yourselves﴾. And this is very close. End of quote.

Some of them claimed that the obligation upon everyone rising to prayer was at the beginning of the legislation, then it was abrogated (naskh). This was supported by the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn Handhalah mentioned earlier. But this was examined by the hadith: "al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an in revelation." It was answered that the hafiz al-ʿIraqi said: "I have not found it traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)." Moreover, al-Zamakhshari said: It is not permissible for the command in the verse to include both those in hadath and others, for the former with the sense of obligation, and for the latter with the sense of recommendation, because the word's coverage of two different meanings belongs to the category of riddle and obfuscation. In al-Insaf (of Ibn al-Munir): whoever permits that a homonym be intended with all its meanings together, permits that in the verse. Among those who permit this is al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on him), and that is enough for the imam of the discipline and its exemplar. When it is established that the form of (af'ala, the imperative form) is shared between obligation and recommendation, it is valid for the verse to cover both groups: those in hadath and those already pure. Its coverage of those already pure is in terms of recommendation. And Allah knows best.

The third: al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari (The Opening of the Creator): Whoever holds that wudu was first prescribed in Medina has relied on this verse. As for what came before that, Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr reported the agreement of the people of biography that ghusl al-janabah (full washing from major impurity) was prescribed for the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in Mecca, just as prayer was prescribed, and that he never prayed except with wudu. He said: This is something no scholar is ignorant of.

Al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak: The People of the Sunnah need evidence to refute those who claim that wudu did not exist before the revelation of the verse of al-Ma'idah. Then he cited the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas: "Fatimah entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) weeping, and said: 'These chiefs of Quraysh have agreed together to kill you!' He said: 'Bring me water for wudu,' and he performed wudu..." the hadith.

(p-1881) Ibn Hajar said: This is suitable as a refutation of one who denies the existence of wudu before the Hijrah, not of one who denies its obligation at that time. Ibn al-Hakam al-Maliki asserted categorically that it existed before the Hijrah, not as recommended. Ibn Hazm asserted categorically that it was legislated only in Medina. Both were answered by what Ibn Lahiʿah narrated in his Maghazi (Military Campaigns), which he transmits from Abu al-Aswad, the orphan of ʿUrwah, from him: "Gabriel taught the Prophet (ﷺ) wudu when he descended to him with revelation." This is mursal (a report with a missing companion in the chain); Ahmad also connected it through Ibn Lahiʿah, but he said: "from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwah, from Usamah ibn Zayd, from his father." Ibn Majah narrated it through Rishdin ibn Saʿd, from ʿAqil, from al-Zuhri, similarly, but Zayd ibn Harithah is not mentioned in the chain. Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat through al-Layth from ʿAqil, connected (mawsul). If it were established, it would be on the condition of the Sahih, but what is known is the narration of Ibn Lahiʿah. End of quote.

That is: Ibn Lahiʿah is weak in hadith.

The fourth: It was said: the verse indicates that wudu is not obligatory for anything other than prayer. This was supported by what Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out from the toilet, and food was brought to him. They said: 'Shall we not bring you water for wudu?' He said: 'I have only been commanded to perform wudu when I rise to prayer.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan (good) hadith.

Muslim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ). He went to the toilet, then he returned and was brought food. It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you not perform wudu?' He said: 'I have not prayed, so why should I perform wudu?'"

(p-1882) As for the stipulation of wudu for tawaf (circumambulation of the Kaʿbah), for the prostration of recitation, for the funeral prayer, and for touching the mushaf (the Qur'an codex), according to those who require it, it is from other evidences established in the jurisprudence of the hadith.

The fifth: (the obligation of washing the face). Ghasl (washing) is letting water pass over the place until it flows off it. This is what is reported from most of the imams. Some added: together with rubbing (dalk). And from al-Nafs al-Zakiyyah: that mere touching suffices even if the water does not flow. The boundary of the face is from the hairline to the end of the chin in length, and from ear to ear in width. Some exegetes here cited various positions on what the face includes and what it does not include, and their place is in the books of legal disagreement.

The sixth: (the obligation of washing the hands). This is agreed upon. As for the elbows (al-mirfaqan), the dual of mirfaq (like minbar and majlis), the joint where the forearm meets the upper arm, the majority hold that they are included in what is washed. It is reported from Zufar, some Malikis and the Zahiris that they are not included. The cause of the disagreement is that what is limited by "ila" (up to, until) sometimes clearly includes the endpoint and sometimes does not, and sometimes it is ambiguous.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ila" conveys the sense of a limit absolutely. As for whether it enters the ruling or exits it, this is a matter that depends on the evidence. Among what has evidence for exclusion is His words: ﴿then a postponement until a time of ease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280], because hardship is the reason for the postponement, and when ease exists the reason is removed; if ease were included in it, one would be postponed in both states, in hardship and in ease. Likewise: ﴿then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]; if the night were included, it would make continuation obligatory. (p-1883) Among what has evidence for inclusion is your saying: "I memorized the Qur'an from its beginning to its end," because the speech is directed at memorizing the whole Qur'an. From this is His words: ﴿from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1], because it is known that he was not taken by night to Jerusalem without entering it. As for His words ﴿to the elbows﴾ and ﴿to the ankles﴾, there is no evidence in them for either matter, so all the scholars took the cautious course: they ruled that the elbows and ankles are included in the washing. Zufar and Dawud took the certain course and did not include them. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 2 of 4):

Al-Radi said: Most scholars hold that the two limits of a beginning and an end (*haddayi al-ibtida' wa al-intiha'*) are not included in what is delimited. So when you say, "I bought from this place to that place," the two places are not apparently included in the buying. Their inclusion has been permitted with a contextual indicator (*qarinah*). Some of them said: what follows "ila" (to/until) is apparently included in what precedes it, so it is not used in any other sense except metaphorically. It has also been said: if what follows it is of the same kind as what precedes it, as in "I ate the fish up to its head," then inclusion is apparent; otherwise it is not, as in "Complete the fast until the night." The preferred view is the first. Then it was said that in the verse "ila" means "with" (*ma'a*), as in His saying, ﴿And do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [An-Nisa: 2]. Al-Radi said: The correct view is that it means the limit of the end, i.e., you add them to your wealth, and they are added to the elbows. End of quote.

The author of *al-Nihayah* said: The view of those who do not include the elbows, on the basis of the verbal indication, is stronger, while the view of those who include them, on the basis of the report (*athar*), is clearer, because in the hadith of Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurairah: (p-1884) "He washed his right hand until he reached (*ashra'a*) the upper arm (*al-'adud*), then the left, then he washed his right foot until he reached the shin (*al-saq*), then the left likewise." The schools of law argued with the hadith of Jabir: "He (ﷺ) used to pour water over his elbows." They said: the indication of the verse is general (*mujmalah*), and this is an explanation of the general; and the explanation of an obligatory generality is itself obligatory. End of quote.

Majd ibn Taymiyyah said in *al-Muntaqa*: From the hadith of Abu Hurairah it follows that washing the two elbows is obligatory, because the text of the Book admits it and is general in it, and his (ﷺ) action is an explanation of the general in the Book; his going beyond the elbow is not in the place of generality, so that it would be obligatory by that. End of quote.

They replied that the hadith of Jabir was narrated by al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, and in its chain is a *matruk* (abandoned narrator). Several of the hadith masters have explicitly declared it weak. And the hadith of Abu Hurairah is an action that does not by itself establish obligation. Their statement, "it is an explanation of the general," is open to question, because "ila" is literally (*haqiqah*) used for the limit of the end, as we have mentioned, so there is no generality. And God knows best.

The seventh issue: al-Razi said: His saying, ﴿to the elbows﴾, requires the limiting of the command, not the limiting of the thing commanded. That is, His saying, ﴿Wash your faces and your hands to the elbows﴾, is a command to wash the hands up to the elbows; so the obligation of washing is limited by this limit, and what remains obligatory is only this measure. As for washing itself, it is not limited by this limit, because it is established by reports that prolonging the whiteness (*tatwil al-ghurrah*) is a strongly confirmed sunnah. End of quote.

The eighth issue: His saying, ﴿to the elbows﴾, also indicates that the washing of the hands should end at them, and begin with the fingers. Al-Hakim said: The sunnah has come with this, and it is what the jurists hold, because of the indication of the word "ila," since it denotes the limit, and the limit of a thing is its end. The Imamiyyah said: the sunnah is to begin at the elbow, and they said that "ila" here means "min" (from). Al-Hakim said: this interpretation is corrupt.

The ninth issue: The majority held that beginning with the right before the left is a sunnah; whoever opposes it misses the excellence but his ablution is complete. The 'Itrah (the Prophet's family) and the Imamiyyah, as in *al-Bahr* of al-Mahdi, held it obligatory. They were argued against (p-1885) on the ground that the verse does not indicate this; whenever one washes them in order or out of order, whether beginning with the right or the left, one has complied with the command. They replied that the proof of obligation is from the sunnah: Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurairah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you dress and when you perform ablution, begin with your right sides!" It was answered: the command is for recommendation (*nadb*), because of his saying, "when you dress and when you perform ablution," which links it with dressing. So if it indicated obligation of starting with the right in ablution, it would indicate it in dressing as well, and they do not hold that.

Also, it has been narrated from 'Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: "I do not mind whether I begin with my right or my left, once I have completed the ablution." Narrated by al-Daraqutni. Al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated something similar.

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in *al-Tuhur* that Abu Hurairah used to begin with his right side; this reached 'Ali, so he began with his left side. Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated it from 'Ali. The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: there is a break (*inqita'*) in it. These routes strengthen one another. Likewise, the hadith connecting beginning with the right to dressing, while it is agreed that it is not obligatory there, is suitable to make it an indicator turning the command to recommendation. The indication of association, though weak, is not short of sufficiency for diverting the command, especially when it is reinforced by the saying and action of 'Ali, peace be upon him.

The tenth issue: Some of the 'Itrah held that there is no wiping over splints (*al-jaba'ir*). In their books on rulings (*al-Ahkam*) it is stated: if one has a splint over a wound or a fracture, and fears harm from removing the splints, wiping is not prescribed. He said: because the verse requires washing the hand apart from what is over it. The majority among them and others held that one wipes, because of the hadith of Jabir: "It was sufficient for him to perform tayammum, bandage his wound, then wipe over it and wash the rest of his body." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni, and authenticated by Ibn al-Sakan.

(p-1886) The eleventh issue: (The obligation of wiping the head):

Wiping (*al-mash*) is making the place touched by water without letting it flow. The "ba'" in His saying, ﴿your heads﴾, indicates that the verb includes the meaning of adhesion (*al-ilsaq*), as if it were said: "and make the wiping adhere to your heads." Al-Zamakhshari said: The one who wipes part of the head and the one who wipes all of it both apply the wiping to their heads. That is, the obligation is the absolute wiping, whether all or part, and whichever is done fulfills it. The authentic sunnah came with explanation, and in it is what indicates the permissibility of confining oneself to wiping part of the head in some circumstances, as in Sahih Muslim and others, from the hadith of al-Mughirah: "He (ﷺ) put his hand under the turban and wiped the front of his head (p-1887) without removing the turban." It is also established in the authentic hadiths: "He wiped his head, moving forward and backward." This is the form which he (ﷺ) continuously maintained. This indicates the excellence of the form he constantly practised, which is wiping the head going forward and backward, and the permissibility of other forms in some circumstances. It is not hidden that the verse does not indicate applying the wiping to the entire head, as in its parallels among actions, such as: "I struck Zaid's head," and "I struck Zaid by his head," and "I struck Zaid," and "I struck Zaid's hand." The linguistic meaning is present in all of these by the striking of a part of the mentioned parts. Likewise in the verse. The dispute is not about the linguistic meaning of the name "head," so that it might be said that it is literally applied to all of it. Rather the dispute is about applying the wiping to it. Even assuming generality, the Lawgiver explained it at times by wiping the whole and at times by wiping part, unlike the face, for he never confined himself to washing part of it in any circumstance, but washed all of it. As for the hands and feet, the limit has been explicitly stated for them. If you say: wiping is not like the striking I used as an example, I reply: no one among the people of language denies that the statement of one who says, "I wiped the garment" or "with the garment," or "I wiped the wall" or "with the wall," is true of wiping a part of the garment or the wall. Denying this is obstinacy. Thus in *al-Rawdah*.

(p-1888) Shams al-Din ibn al-Qayyim said in *al-Huda*: It is not authentically reported from him (ﷺ) in any single hadith that he confined himself to wiping only part of his head, absolutely. Rather, when he wiped his forelock, he completed the wiping over the turban. As for the hadith of Anas narrated by Abu Dawud: "I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) performing ablution while he wore a Qatari turban, and he put his hand under the turban and wiped the front of his head, and did not remove the turban," the purpose of Anas in it is that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not remove his turban so that wiping of the head would cover all the hair. He did not deny completing the wiping over the turban, and al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah and others affirmed it. So Anas's silence about it does not indicate its negation. End of quote.

Al-Shawkani said: The dispute is only about obligation. The hadiths of generality, though more authentic, and containing an addition which is accepted, but where is the proof of obligation? There is only the mere action, and action does not indicate obligation. Then he said: After this, there is no doubt about the preference of covering the entire head with the wiping and the soundness of its hadiths. But short of a firm judgment of obligation, there are deserts and punishment.

Section
As for His saying, ﴿and your feet to the ankles﴾, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it in the accusative (*nasb*), and the rest read it in the genitive (*jarr*). From these two readings the schools diverged regarding the manner of purifying the feet. Some held that their purification is washing; some held it is wiping; and some allowed a choice between them. Each of these schools has arguments, interpretations, replies and debates; we will cite a sample of them. We say: The first group said: the accusative reading apparently indicates washing, and the genitive reading apparently indicates wiping. But since there is what favors washing, we interpreted what the genitive reading apparently indicates. And the factors favoring washing are several.

(p-1889) Among them is what is in the *Sahihayn* and the *Sunan*, from 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'awiyah, 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim, and al-Miqdad ibn Ma'd Yakrib: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) washed his feet in his ablution, either once, or twice, or three times," according to the variations of their reports. In the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) performed ablution and washed his feet, then said: This is an ablution with which God does not accept the prayer except with it."

In the *Sahihayn*, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lagged behind us on a journey. Then he caught up with us when the afternoon prayer was already pressing upon us. So we began to perform ablution and to wipe our feet. He said: then he called out with his loudest voice: Woe to the heels from the Fire! Twice or thrice." Likewise it is in the *Sahihayn* from Abu Hurairah. In *Sahih Muslim*, from 'A'ishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Perfect the ablution. Woe to the heels from the Fire!" Al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim narrated, with a sound chain, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Jaz', that he (p-1890) heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Woe to the heels and the soles of the feet from the Fire!" Imam Ahmad, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw on a man's foot a spot the size of a dirham that he had not washed, and said: 'Woe to the heels from the Fire!'" Ibn Kathir said: The indication of these hadiths is clear, for if the obligation for the feet were wiping them, or if it were permissible, he would not have threatened for omitting it, since wiping does not cover the whole foot, but operates as in wiping over leather socks. Imam Ahmad narrated from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from one of the Companions of the Prophet: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man praying with a spot on the top of his foot the size of a dirham that water had not reached. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded him to repeat the ablution." Abu Dawud added: "and the prayer."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: 'Amr ibn 'Abasah narrated to us, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, inform me about the ablution. He said: None of you brings near his water and then rinses his mouth, sniffs water into his nose and blows it out, but his sins fall from his mouth and nostrils with the water (p-1891) when he blows it out. Then he washes his face as God commanded him, and his facial sins fall from the edges of his beard with the water. Then he washes his hands up to the elbows, and the sins of his hands fall from the tips of his fingers. Then he wipes his head, and the sins of his head fall from the ends of his hair with the water. Then he washes his feet up to the ankles as God commanded, and the sins of his feet fall from the tips of his toes with the water. Then he stands and praises God and extols Him with what is fitting for Him, then he prays two rak'ahs, and he comes out of his sins like the day his mother bore him."

Abu Umamah said: "O 'Amr! Look at what you are saying. Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Should this man be given all of it in his station?" 'Amr ibn 'Abasah said: "O Abu Umamah! My age has grown great, my bones have grown weak, and my end has drawn near. I have no need to lie about Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). I did not hear it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except once, or twice, or three times. Indeed, I heard it seven times or more than that..."

Ibn Kathir said: Its chain of narration is sound, and it is in Sahih Muslim by another route, in which is: "Then he washes his feet as Allah commanded him." This indicates that the Qur'an commands washing.

Likewise Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i narrated from al-Harith, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: "Wash the feet up to the ankles as you have been commanded."

From here the intended meaning of the hadith of 'Abd Khayr from 'Ali becomes clear: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sprinkled water on his feet while they were in his sandals, and rubbed them. He intended only a light washing while they were in the sandals." There is no obstacle to combining washing with the foot being in its shoe. This serves as a refutation of those who go to extremes and the over-scrupulous obsessive ones.

Likewise is what Ibn Jarir narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to a people's refuse heap, urinated standing, then called for water, performed ablution, and wiped over his sandals." This is a sound hadith. Ibn Jarir answered it: the reliable, retentive narrators related it from Hudhayfah as: "he urinated standing, then performed ablution and wiped over his leather socks (khuffayn)." Ibn Kathir said: It is possible to reconcile the two, by his having leather socks on his feet and sandals over them.

Likewise is the hadith that Imam Ahmad narrated from Aws ibn Abi Aws, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) perform ablution and wipe over his sandals, then he stood to pray." It was also related by Abu Dawud from him with the wording: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) come to a people's refuse heap, urinate, perform ablution, and wipe over his sandals and his feet."

Then the majority said: the reading in the genitive (al-jarr) is governed by the proximity genitive (al-jarr al-jiwari). Its like is abundant in the Qur'an and in poetry, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ʿadhāba yawmin alīm﴾ (a painful day's punishment), and ﴿wa-ḥūrin ʿīn﴾ (and fair maidens with wide eyes), read in the genitive by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, in coordination with ﴿bi-akwābin wa-abārīq﴾ (with cups and ewers), though the meaning differs, since the meaning is not "wandering among them are youths made eternal with fair maidens." And like the Arabs' saying: "juḥru ḍabbin kharib" (the hole of a lizard, ruined). The grammarians have a chapter on this, to the point that they extended its consideration in i'rab (grammatical inflection) to dual and feminine forms and other things. Abu al-Baqa' has cited a fragment of its like and parallels here, so consult him. As for what has been said, that the conjunction particle is an obstacle to permissibility (claiming it is specific to the adjective and emphasis), it is rejected, since it occurs frequently in coordination in the speech of the Arabs. The poet said:

"There remained only a captive, neither freed, and one bound in the fetters of captivity, shackled."

Here he put "mawthaqan" in the genitive by proximity to "al-munfalit," though its proper case is the nominative, in coordination with "asir."

And he said:

"So are you, if your she-camel dies, a rider going to the family of Bisṭam ibn Qays, so address (them)?"

Here he put "fa-khatibi" in the genitive by proximity, though its proper case is the nominative, in coordination with "rahil." The reading "wa-ḥūrin" in the genitive suffices as a refutation, as we have mentioned. They said: the condition for the goodness of the proximity genitive is the absence of confusion together with the inclusion of a subtle point. Here too this holds: the end-point indicates that it is not to be wiped, since wiping has no prescribed end-point in the Shari'ah. The subtle point in it is the indication of lightening it until it is as if it were wiping. The judge Nasir said in al-Intisaf: The aspect of this is that washing and wiping are close, in that each of them is a contact with the limb. So it is easy to coordinate the washing with the wiping, as in his saying: "wearing a sword and a spear," and "I fed her straw and cold water." Its parallels are numerous, and the experts have explained it thus. Then it is said: what is the benefit of this joining on the basis of closeness? Why not attribute to each of the two its specific verb in its literal sense? It is said: its benefit is brevity, conciseness, and the confirmation of the benefit, as Zamakhshari mentioned, namely that since the feet were liable to blameworthy extravagance which is forbidden, they were coordinated with the fourth, the wiped members, not in order to be wiped, but to alert to the obligation of restraint in pouring water on them. Then Nasir said: Its verification is that the original would be to say, for example: "and wash your feet, a light washing without extravagance, as is customary," so these purposes were abbreviated by joining the feet with the wiped member. By this joining, which occurs only with a single verb or two verbs very close to each other, he alerted that the washing required for the feet is a light washing that approaches wiping. The goodness of including it with it under a single form is evident. End.

As for those who made it obligatory to combine wiping and washing, it is based on combining the two readings. What is intended by those who held that it is obligatory to combine washing the two feet and wiping them is (p-1894) that those who related it reported it this way. For this reason many jurists find it problematic, and he is excused. For there is no sense in combining wiping and washing, whether one precedes the other or follows it, since one is included in the other. He meant only what I have mentioned, and Allah knows best.

Then I considered his speech further, and found that he is attempting to combine the two readings in His saying, "and your feet" (wa-arjulikum): in the genitive, for wiping, which is rubbing, and in the accusative, for washing. So he made both obligatory, out of combining this with that. End.

As for those who said: the obligatory act is wiping, they cling to the genitive reading, and this is the doctrine of the Imamiyyah. They answered regarding the accusative reading that it also necessitates wiping. I have examined the book Sharh al-Muqni'ah among their books and found that it elaborated more on this discussion, and it explained the accusative's requirement of wiping by saying that the place of the heads is in the accusative position because of the verb's falling on it, which is wiping. He said: On this basis, there is no denying that the feet may be coordinated with the place of the heads, not their wording, so they are in the accusative; and coordination with the place is permissible and well known in the language of the Arabs. Then he cited evidence for that and said afterward: If it is said: what prevents you from holding that the accusative reading does not necessitate washing, so it cannot admit wiping, since coordinating the feet with the places of the heads in affirmation is a loose and figurative usage, and the apparent and literal sense requires coordinating it with the wording, not the place? We say: The matter is not as you suppose; rather, coordination with the place is esteemed in the language of the Arabs, and permissible, not by way of extended and figurative usage. So the speaker is free to bear the inflection upon the wording at one time, and upon the place at another.

He said: This is manifest in the Arabic language and well known among its people, and in the Qur'an and poetry it has many parallels. Then he said: Moreover, even if we grant that coordination with the wording is stronger, coordinating the feet with the place of the heads would be preferable, given the accusative reading, because the accusative of the feet can only be on one of two aspects: either it is coordinated with the hands and faces in washing, or it is coordinated with the place of the heads and so is accusative, and its ruling is wiping. Coordinating it with the place of the heads is preferable. That is because when a sentence contains two governing elements, one near and the other distant, applying the nearer is preferable to applying the more distant. The grammarians have stated this in the chapter on contention (tanazu'). End. So consider their disputation.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: It has been narrated from a group of the early generation (salaf) that it is wiping. Ibn Jarir narrated from Humayd, who said: Musa ibn Anas said, while we were with him: "O Abu Hamzah! Al-Hajjaj addressed us at al-Ahwaz while we were with him, and he mentioned purification and said: Wash your faces and your hands, and wipe over your heads and your feet. Indeed, nothing of the son of Adam is nearer to filth than his two feet; so wash their bellies, their backs, and their heels." Anas said: "Allah has spoken truly, and al-Hajjaj has lied. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and wipe over your heads and your feet﴾."

He said: And Anas, when he wiped his feet, would wet them.

Ibn Kathir said: Its chain up to him is sound.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from 'Asim, from Anas, who said: "The Qur'an was revealed with wiping, and the Sunnah with washing." Its chain is also sound.

He also related from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ablution is two washings and two wipings."

Likewise Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said of "and wipe over your heads and your feet": "It is wiping." He then said: He related the same from Ibn 'Umar, 'Alqamah, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan (in one of the narrations), Jabir ibn Yazid, and Mujahid (in one of the two narrations). Ibn Jarir narrated from Ayyub, who said: "I saw 'Ikrimah wiping over his feet." And from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Jibril descended with wiping. Do you not see that tayammum is: wiping what was washing, and cancelling what was wiping?"

As for those who went to the option (takhyir), they said: since the reading has come with what requires washing and with what requires wiping, this shows that one is free to choose. In al-Shifa it is said: The two readings do not require combining; rather, they establish choice.

It is not hidden that the apparent sense of the verse is explicit that its obligation is wiping, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. The preference for washing them in what is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) is only for adding to the obligation and expanding upon it, in keeping with the Prophet's (ﷺ) habit, for he prescribed for every obligation sunnahs that support and strengthen it: in prayer, zakah, fasting, and hajj. Likewise in the purifications, as is not hidden. Among what shows that its obligation is wiping is the legislation of wiping over the leather socks (khuffayn) and the stockings (jawrabayn). It has no basis except this verse, for every sunnah has its root in the Book of Allah, explicitly or implicitly. Understand this and keep it in mind, and Allah is the Guide.

Section

On what the Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, have said about the secrets of the purity of these members:

As for the face, its washing became obligatory because in it are most of the apparent senses through which one benefits from sensible things, so it is necessary to purify it from the traces that have arisen from them. And because perception precedes action, He put first what contains most of the apparent senses, namely other than hearing. Then He commanded the purification of the instrument that performs the actions, from which those traces come, namely the hands up to the elbows, because work with the fingers requires moving the palm, which does not move generally except by moving the elbows. Then He commanded wiping the head, because it gathers the inner senses, so it resembles the gatherer of the outer senses; He placed it after washing the hands, because it is the store of the images perceived by the outer senses from its actions and others. He did not command its washing, because it would harm the one with hair, and it is necessary for adornment, especially for women, so it was lightened by wiping. Then He made obligatory the washing of the instrument of walking, for its resemblance to the instrument of work, which is the feet. And since their movement necessitates the movement of the whole body, He limited it to the lowest extremity, namely the two ankles, lest the benefit of singling out the members be nullified. And the separation of the washed members by the wiped member is an indication of the obligation of order, and its secret is what we have pointed out. Thus in the tafsir of al-Mahayimi.

Al-Sha'rani, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned regarding the secret of this that the face is the place of facing in the presence of Allah the Exalted at the time of His address, and the Law followed custom in this. Otherwise every part of the servant's body, outer and inner, is manifest to the Real, Exalted is He, from the servant. Allah the Exalted commanded the servant to repent immediately, hastening to purify from the spiritual impurity, because water does not reach the heart. Understand.

Then the view of the majority, that the elbows are included with the hands, was given the rationale that they are the place of support and use. Movement is completed through them in performing actions. The view of Zufar and Dawud was given the rationale that they are not purely for the forearms, since they are a combination of two things: the tip of the forearm bone and the head of the bones. Then the wiping of the entire head was given the rationale of taking the precautionary course. So the entire place of leadership that is with the one performing ablution is wiped, so that it may be freed from the pride contained within it, and enabled to enter the presence of Allah Most High in prayer. For whoever has in him an atom's weight of pride will not be permitted to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, as has been reported, since it is the special presence, and the same applies to the presence of prayer. Then the washing of the two feet was given the rationale of holding the servant accountable for walking with them in disobedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and for their carrying the whole body and sustaining it with the strength to walk. When they weaken through transgression or heedlessness, that weakness spreads to what they carry, just as strength spreads from them to what is above them when they are washed. For they are like the roots of a tree which drink water and supply the branches with leaves and fruits. Thus washing is required for them rather than wiping. Then he mentioned the secret of those who held that continuity (muwala) is obligatory in purification of the limbs of ablution: the majority of those who purify themselves are weakened in their bodies by much sin, heedlessness, or desires, and if there is no continuity, all the limbs dry out before standing up to prayer, for example. When they dry out, it is as though they were not washed and did not gain revival through the water, and they have no life by which they stand before their Lord. So they address their Lord without full presence and without turning wholeheartedly to His intimate conversation. This is the ruling for the bodies of most people. As for the bodies of scholars who act upon their knowledge and of other righteous people, they do not need strictness regarding continuity for the life of their bodies by water, even if a long interval separates the washing of their limbs. Therefore the statement of the one who said that continuity is obligatory is to be understood as applying to the purification of common people, and the statement of the one who said it is recommended is to be understood as applying to the purification of their scholars and righteous ones.

(p-1898) I heard my master ʿAli al-Khawwas, may Allah have mercy on him, say: How excellent is the statement of the one who said that continuity is obligatory in this age. For whoever does not make it obligatory, his statement leads to permitting a very long interval and an increase in slowness during the time of purification, and the missing of the beginning of the time. For example, he washes his face in the ablution for Zuhr after the Subh prayer, then washes his hands at about a quarter of the day, then wipes his head after the sun has passed its zenith, then washes his feet shortly before ʿAsr, while that ablution-performer, for example, is engaged in backbiting, slander, mockery, ridicule, laughter, heedlessness, and other sins and disliked acts, or acts that are less preferable if he is one who is held accountable for them just as he is held accountable for consuming desires. Such an ablution, although it is valid in the apparent sense of the Law, in that it truly counts as a complete ablution, is of little benefit, because the limbs are not revived by it after they have died, weakened, or grown lax. Thus the wisdom of the command to continuity in ablution, whether obligatory or recommended, is lost, and it is the reviving and enlivening of the body before standing before Allah Most High for intimate conversation. Furthermore, even if we assume that this ablution-performer who did not maintain continuity was not engaged in sin or heedlessness during the interval between washing the limbs, the body is still dry, like the limbs overwhelmed by heedlessness, forgetfulness, boredom, and weariness. So there is no longer any drive within it toward full turning to Allah Most High during His intimate conversation.

The secrets of the Sunan have been fully made clear in a delightful way, so let it be consulted in "Mizanihi," may Allah Most High have mercy on him.

In the words of Allah Most High there are benefits, secrets, and subtleties that the volumes cannot contain.

As for His words, Most High: ﴿And if you are junub, then purify yourselves﴾, that is: by the emission of semen or the meeting of the two circumcised parts. ﴿Then purify yourselves﴾, that is: with water, i.e., wash with it. Al-Mahayimi said: That is, go to the utmost in purifying the body, for all of it takes pleasure in it, a pleasure that drowns it in other than Allah, and it is affected by the impurity. ﴿And if you are﴾ junub ﴿sick﴾ and fear using water, ﴿or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾, that is, returns from the place of excrement, ﴿or you have touched women and you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾, that is, intend ﴿clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾, as a humbling of the two noble limbs. The explanation of this and its rulings has already passed in Surat al-Nisa'. (p-1899) ﴿Allah does not intend﴾, that is, ﴿does not intend﴾ by the command of purification for prayer or by the command of tayammum, ﴿to place upon you any hardship﴾, that is, any constriction in obedience or in obtaining water, ﴿but He intends to purify you﴾, that is, from sins, or to place you in the status of the pure through humbling oneself in the dust. For when He removed arrogance, it is as though He removed the impurity that arises from its like. ﴿And to complete His favor upon you﴾, that is, by His Law providing what purifies your bodies, revives them from what has befallen them, and expiates your sins; or to complete His bounty upon you by His concessions, enabling you to worship Him in every state, even in a state of impurity. ﴿So that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor and concession, and He will reward you.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever performs ablution and does it well, then stands for prayer, his sins will come out from his hearing, his sight, his hands, and his feet." It was also related by Muslim and the authors of the Sunan from Abu Hurayrah in detail.

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Knowing of that within the breasts.﴾

﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ by guiding you to this upright religion, so that it reminds you of the Benefactor and encourages you to thank Him. ﴿And His covenant﴾, i.e., His firm pact. ﴿With which He bound you﴾, i.e., He affirmed it upon you by His saying ﴿when you said﴾, i.e., to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿"We hear and we obey"﴾, when you pledged allegiance to him to hear and obey in hardship and ease, in what you like and what you dislike. ﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., regarding breaking any part of His covenants, even in the heart. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, i.e., of its hidden matters.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[8] ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah﴾ That is: the requirement of your faith is steadfastness, so be exceedingly steadfast, exerting your utmost effort in it for Allah. It is only completed by considering the rights of Allah and the rights of His creation. So be ﴿witnesses in justice﴾, that is, in justice (al-'adl). Do not abandon it out of love for anyone or out of enmity toward anyone. ﴿And do not let﴾ That is, do not let it drive you: ﴿the hatred (shana'an) of a people﴾, that is, the intensity of enmity, ﴿prevent you from being just﴾ toward them. Al-Mahayimi (d. 835 AH) said: That is, we do not command you to this in terms of fulfilling the rights of enemies, but rather in terms of fulfilling the rights of your own selves in steadfastness. ﴿Be just; it﴾, that is, justice, ﴿is nearer to righteousness﴾, that is, for preserving the souls from exceeding the limit of their steadfastness. ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, lest you seek their rights or the rights of His servants even by a means you imagine to be just. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ of deeds, and He will recompense you accordingly.

It is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) (p-1901) from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he said: "My father gave me a gift. My mother said: I will not be satisfied until you have the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) witness it. So he came to him to have him witness my gift, and he said: Did you give all your children the like of this? He said: No. He said: Fear Allah and be just among your children. And he said: I will not bear witness to injustice." He said: "So my father returned and retracted that gift."

Some exegetes (mufassirun) said: The fruit of the verse is the indication of the obligation to enjoin good and forbid evil, and to stand firm for justice. This includes bearing witness to justice and judging by it. Likewise, issuing legal rulings (fatwa). And that the utterance of truth is not abandoned, its obligation not forsaken, because of an enemy or a friend. And it is not permissible to follow whims.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In this there is a great admonition that justice, if it is obligatory with the disbelievers who are the enemies of Allah, when it is with this quality of strength, then what is the presumption regarding its obligation with the believers who are His allies and beloved?

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, which include among them justice and piety, ﴿for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾, meaning abundant reward in Paradise.

The discussion of the Most High's saying:

[10] ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾ — among which are those (signs) recited concerning justice and righteousness.

﴿Those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ — the people of the Fire.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 11 (part 1 of 3)**

Then God, exalted is He, explained that among the requirements of faith is to be constant in thanking Him for recounting His blessings. So He, glorified is He, said:

[p. 1902] The discussion on the interpretation of the words of God, exalted is He:

[11] ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of God upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear God; and upon God let the believers rely.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of God upon you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], that is, in His protecting you from your enemies. ﴿When a people determined to extend their hands against you﴾, that is, to strike you with killing and destruction. ﴿But He withheld their hands from you﴾, that is, He prevented them from being extended towards you, and turned back their harm from you.

It has been said: the verse refers to what ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salama, from Jabir: "The Prophet ﷺ stopped at a place, and the people scattered among the acacia trees, seeking shade beneath them. The Prophet ﷺ hung his sword on a tree. A Bedouin came to the sword of the Messenger of God ﷺ, took it and drew it. Then he came up to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'God, mighty and majestic.' The Bedouin said, twice or three times: 'Who will protect you from me?' And the Prophet ﷺ kept saying: 'God.' He said: So the Bedouin sheathed the sword. The Prophet ﷺ called his companions and informed them of the Bedouin's affair, while he (the Bedouin) was sitting beside him, and he did not punish him."

Maʿmar said: Qatada used to mention something similar, and mention that a group of the Arabs wanted to treacherously kill the Messenger of God ﷺ, so they sent this Bedouin. And he interpreted this verse accordingly.

Abu Nuʿaym also related in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwa* (*The Proofs of Prophethood*), through the route of al-Hasan, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: "A man from Muharib called Ghawrath ibn al-Harith said to his people: 'I will kill Muhammad for you.' So he came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was sitting with his sword in his lap, and said: 'O Muhammad! May I look at this sword of yours?' He said: 'Yes.' So he took it, drew it, and began to brandish it and intend to strike with it, but God restrained him. He said: 'O Muhammad! Do you not fear me?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Do you not fear me while the sword is in my hand?' He said: 'No. God protects me from you.' Then he sheathed the sword and returned it to the Messenger of God." So God revealed the verse.

The story of this Bedouin is established in the *Sahih* (the authentic collection of al-Bukhari). Ibn Jarir also narrated, from ʿIkrima and Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, and the wording is his: "The Prophet ﷺ went out, with Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Talha, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, until they entered upon Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and the Jews of Banu al-Nadir, seeking their help regarding a blood-money (ʿaql) which had fallen upon him. They said: 'Yes. Sit down until we feed you or give you what you ask of us.' So he sat. Huyayy ibn Akhtab said to his companions: 'You will not see him closer than he is now. Throw stones at him and kill him, and you will never see evil again.' They came to a great millstone to throw it upon him, but God withheld their hands from it, until Gabriel came and raised him from that place. So God revealed the verse." Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar.

Ibn Kathir said: "Then the Messenger of God ﷺ was commanded to go out to them, and he besieged them until he brought them down and expelled them." End of quotation.

In light of these narrations, what is meant by the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿remember the favor of God upon you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 20] is a reminder of God's favor upon them in repelling evil and harm from their Prophet, for if that had happened, it would have been among the greatest of trials.

Al-Zamakhshari and those after him mentioned, among the indications of the verse, what happened at ʿUsfan of God's protection of them from their enemies, when those enemies intended to kill them while they were occupied with the ʿAsr prayer, after they had seen them praying the Zuhr prayer. They regretted that they had not attacked them at once. So God repelled the plot of their enemies when He sent down upon them the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf). End of quotation.

The wording of the verse can accommodate this, but I have not yet seen it traced to the leading authorities of transmitted reports (al-athar).

﴿And fear God﴾, that is, in observing the rights of His favor, and do not neglect its thanks. ﴿And upon God﴾ alone, to the exclusion of others, ﴿let the believers rely﴾, for He is the sufficient one in bringing good and repelling evil for whoever relies upon Him.

Abu al-Suʿud said: The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it. The choice of the imperative form of the third person, and attributing it to the believers, is to make reliance (tawakkul) obligatory upon the addressees by a demonstrative method, and to indicate that what they were described with at the time of address, the attribute of faith, calls them to what they were commanded of reliance and piety, and restrains them from neglecting these two.

**A Weighty Discussion on Reliance (Tawakkul)**

Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din ibn Taymiyya, may God sanctify his secret, said in one of his works: A group of those who have spoken about the actions of the hearts have assumed that reliance does not bring about the acquisition of benefit or the repelling of harm. Rather, whatever is decreed without reliance is decreed with reliance. But reliance is an act of worship for which one is rewarded, of the same kind as contentment with divine decree (al-rida bi al-qada'). Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn Batta mentioned this in what he wrote on this subject. The saying of these people resembles the saying of one who says that supplication does not bring about the acquisition of benefit or the repelling of harm, but is rather an act of worship for which one is rewarded, like the throwing of pebbles at the Jamarat. Others say: rather, supplication is a sign and an indicator. They say this about all acts of worship. This is the position of one who denies causes (asbab) in creation and command, and says that God acts at their occasion, not through them. This is the position of a group of the theologians (mutakallimun) of the people of affirmation of divine decree, such as al-Ash'ari and others, and it is the position of a group of jurists and Sufis. The origin of this innovation (bid'a) is the statement of Jahm. For he was extreme in negating the divine attributes and in determinism (al-jabr). He made the perfection of the unity of the Essence to consist in negating the attributes, and the perfection of the unity of actions to consist in negating causes. He went so far as to deny the effect of the power of the servant, indeed he denied that the servant was capable, and denied wisdom in reliance and mercy. He used to go out to the leper and say: "Does the Most Merciful of the merciful do such a thing?" meaning that He does it by sheer will without mercy. His saying on decree has been brought close to by al-Ash'ari and whoever agreed with him among the sects. What the early generations (al-salaf), the imams, the jurists, the majority, and many of the people of kalam (speculative theology) hold is the affirmation of causes, as the Book and the Sunna indicate, together with the evidence of the senses and reason. The discussion of these people is expounded in other places. The aim here is to speak of reliance. The majority hold that the one who relies obtains through his reliance, in bringing benefit and repelling harm, what others do not obtain. The same applies to supplication. The Qur'an indicates this in many places. Then, reliance is a cause according to most, and a sign according to those who deny causes. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever fears God—He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] ﴿And will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon God—then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. And ḥasb (sufficiency) means the one who suffices. So He made clear that He suffices whoever relies upon Him. In the supplication: "O Sufficer of those who rely!" So it cannot be said that He is sufficient for one who does not rely in the same way that He is sufficient for one who relies, because He attached this sentence to the first as a conditional clause is attached to its condition, so in such a case the existence of the condition cannot be like its non-existence. And because He (p. 1906) connected the ruling to the fitting attribute. So it is known that his reliance is the cause of His being sufficient for him. And because He mentioned this in the context of encouraging reliance, just as He encouraged piety. If the one who relies did not obtain from sufficiency what others do not obtain, that would not be an encouragement to reliance, just as He made piety a cause of escape from distress and the obtaining of provision from where one does not expect. God, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Sufficient for us is God, and [He is] the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173]. So He praised them, glorified is He, by saying that He is the best Disposer of affairs (niʿma al-wakil). A disposer of affairs does not deserve praise if he does not bring benefit to the one who relies upon him, nor repel harm from him. God is the best one in whom servants can rely, so He is the best Disposer of affairs, who brings to them every good and repels from them every evil.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 11 (part 2 of 3):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And mention the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8] ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no deity but Him, so take Him as trustee (wakil)﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]. And He says: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take anyone other than Me as a trustee (wakil)"﴾ [al-Isra': 2]. So He commanded that a wakil be taken, and forbade that a wakil be taken other than Him, because the created being cannot independently fulfill all of a servant's needs. The permissible form of wakala (delegation) is that a person relies on another in an action that the other is able to perform, so that the one who delegates obtains some of what he seeks. As for all of his aims, none is able to accomplish them except Allah. The one whom he appoints does nothing except by the will and power of Allah. Therefore he may not rely on that person in an absolute sense, even if he has appointed him. Rather, he depends on Allah for facilitating what he has entrusted to him. If what is obtained by one who relies upon Allah were obtained even if he relied on someone else, or were obtained without any tawakkul (reliance), then taking some created being as a wakil would be more beneficial than taking the Creator as a wakil. This is among the most repugnant implications of this corrupt view, because reliance upon creatures is seen to benefit only in a limited, visible way.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers who follow you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64]. That is: Allah is sufficient for you and sufficient for those believers who follow you. If His sufficiency were for the believers who follow the Messenger, whether or not they actually followed him, then faith and following the Messenger would have no effect on this sufficiency, and singling them out for it would have no meaning. This would be like saying: "He is your Creator and the Creator of those who follow you." It is known that the intended meaning is other than that. When sufficiency (hasb) is a meaning specific to some people, it is known that the words of the one who relies, "Allah is sufficient for me" (hasbi Allah), and His words, ﴿and whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3], refer to a matter that is specific, not shared. Reliance is the cause of that specificity. When Allah promises a reward for an action, or honors its people with a blessing, there must be a difference, in obtaining that blessing, between the presence and the absence of that action, even if a similar result may come about through another cause. Allah may suffice some who do not rely on Him, such as children. But reliance must have an effect in obtaining the sufficiency granted to those who rely, so that the sufficiency obtained through reliance is not the same sufficiency that would be obtained even without reliance. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best trustee (wakil)"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty, untouched by harm, and they followed the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 174]. Here He linked this reward and judgment to that attribute and action with the particle "fa" (so), which indicates causation. This shows that this reliance is the cause of that return with blessing and bounty from Allah, and that this reward is a recompense for that action. There is also the saying transmitted in a report: "Whoever wishes to be the strongest of people, let him rely upon Allah." If tawakkul did not bring benefit or repel harm, the one who relies would not be stronger than others.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1]. ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord; indeed Allah is ever Aware of what you do﴾ [al-Ahzab: 2]. ﴿And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as trustee (wakil)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 3]. He also says in the course of the same surah: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and disregard their harm, and rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as trustee (wakil)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48]. So He commanded him to fear Him, to follow what is revealed to him, and to rely upon Him. In the same way, He combined these two principles in more than one place, such as His words: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him﴾ [Hud: 123], His words: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], and ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no deity but Him, so take Him as trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9]; His words: ﴿In Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance﴾ [Hud: 88]; His words: ﴿Our Lord, in You we have put our trust, and to You we have turned in repentance﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]; His words: ﴿He is my Lord; there is no deity but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30]; and His words: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]; and His words in al-Fatihah: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5].

The knowledge of the Qur'an is gathered in al-Fatihah in these two principles: the worship of Allah and reliance upon Him. When the word "worship" ('ibadah) is mentioned alone, reliance (tawakkul) is included within it, since it is one form of the worship of Allah. An example is His words: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], and His words: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. When reliance is mentioned alongside it, the worship is then commanded in its particular sense. This is like the terms Islam and iman (faith), iman and 'amal (action), the term salah (prayer) together with worship and with following the Book, and the terms fahsha' (indecency) and baghy (oppression) together with munkar (wrongdoing). Similar examples are numerous: a term, when used alone and unqualified, includes several kinds, and sometimes some of those kinds are joined to it, so that each is commanded in its own right. It is then said that when a term is conjoined, it does not enter into the term it is conjoined to. It is also said that the command concerning it is both particular and general, as in His words: ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

Since Allah commanded him to rely upon Allah and then said, "and sufficient is Allah as trustee," it is known that Allah is the trustee who suffices for whoever relies upon Him. This is like what is said in sermons and supplications: "Praise be to Allah, who suffices whoever relies upon Him." When it is said "sufficient is He as trustee," this is specific to Him, glorified is He. None of the other existing things is sufficient as a trustee. The most that one who takes a created being as a trustee can expect is that he will do some matters, and even then he does them only with Allah's help, and he is powerless over most aims. So when Allah describes Himself as "sufficient as trustee," it is known that He does for the one who relies upon Him what requires no other, in bringing benefits and repelling harms. For if anything were left over, He would not be "sufficient as trustee." This is the opposite of the view of those who imagine that the one who relies upon Allah gains through his reliance neither the bringing of benefit nor the repelling of harm, but that what decree (qada') befalls him is the same as what would befall him had he not relied upon Him. The root of the doubt (shubha) of those who held this view is that, having affirmed that when Allah decrees something it must come to be, that whatever He wills comes to be and whatever He does not will does not come to be, and that whatever His knowledge has preceded is certainly going to occur, they came to think that what exists through a cause also exists without it, and what exists when an obstacle is absent also exists when the obstacle is present. This is a grave error, into which several groups fell. One group said: there is no need for the commanded actions. Rather, whoever is created for Paradise will enter it even if he does not believe, and whoever is created for the Fire will enter it even if he believes and does not disbelieve. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about this doubt when he said: "There is none of you but his place in Paradise or the Fire has already been known." They said: "Should we not abandon action and depend upon the Book?" He said: "No! Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. As for one who is of the people of happiness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of happiness, and as for one who is of the people of wretchedness, he will be made easy for the deeds of the people of wretchedness." This meaning is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Sahih (authentic collections) in several places, which clarify that what the Book has preceded has preceded together with the causes that lead to it. Happiness preceded with the decree that its possessor will be employed in what makes him happy, and wretchedness preceded with the decree that its possessor will be employed in what makes him wretched. Thus qadar (divine decree) includes the end and its cause; it does not include an end without a cause. It is like the decree that a child will be born to a man through his marrying and having intercourse with a woman, or that a man's land will produce crops through his planting and watering the seed, and similar matters.

[p-1911] And similarly, in the *Sunan* (of Abu Dawud and others) it is narrated that it was said to him: "O Messenger of God! What do you say about medicines we treat with, incantations we use for protection, and precautions we take? Do they ward off anything of God's decree (qadar)?" He said: "They are part of God's decree." So he made clear that the means by which hardships are averted are themselves part of the decree, and that the decree is not merely the averting of a hardship without a cause.

Similarly, the saying of one who says, "Supplication has no effect whatsoever, and trust in God (tawakkul) has no effect whatsoever," belongs to this same category. However, denying what He has commanded of deeds is a plain matter, unlike denying the effect of trust in God. Nonetheless the root is one: looking at what is decreed in isolation from its causes and necessary conditions. From this category is the view, held by the majority of Muslims, that the one who is killed dies at his appointed term (ajal). Only a group of the Qadariyya (the school that denied divine predestination) said that the killer cut short his term. Then the majority discussed: "What if he had not been killed?" Some of them said he would have died, because his term had come to its end. Others said he would not have died, because the cause was absent. Both opinions have been held by people who are attributed to the Sunnah, and both are mistaken. For the decree had already determined that he would die by this cause and not by another. If the absence of this cause is supposed, that would be the supposition of the opposite of what is decreed. If what was decreed was that he would not die by this cause, it would be possible that what was decreed was that he would die by another. And if what was decreed was that he would not die by this cause, it would be possible that the decree was that he would not die at all. So to assert either one of them is ignorance concerning a matter whose causes are many. One does not assert its non-occurrence when some of its causes are absent, nor assert its occurrence if no other cause is known for it. This is unlike what has only a single cause, such as entering the Fire, for one enters it only if one has disobeyed. So if it is supposed that he did not disobey, he will not enter it.

And God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. Then when you have resolved, put your trust in God. Indeed, God loves those who put their trust [in Him].﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159] ﴿If God helps you, none can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon God let the believers put their trust.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 160]

[p-1912] So He commanded him, when he had resolved, to put his trust in God. Had trust in God not helped him attain what he had resolved upon, there would have been no benefit in commanding him to it at the time of resolve.
