Hadiths have been related about this. Malik related from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned to him that a man and a woman among them had committed adultery. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'What do you find in the matter of stoning?' They said: 'We expose them and they are flogged.' Abdullah ibn Salam said: 'You have lied; in it is the stoning.' They brought the Torah and spread it open. One of them placed his hand upon the verse of stoning and read what came before it and what came after it. Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: 'Lift your hand.' He lifted his hand and there was the verse of stoning. They said: 'He has spoken truly, O Muhammad; in it is the verse of stoning.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that the two be stoned. Abdullah ibn Umar said: 'I saw the man bending over the woman, shielding her from the stones.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related it in the two Sahihs, and this is the wording of the Muwatta'.

Imam Ahmad related from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: "A Jew who had been blackened and flogged passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He called them and said: 'Is this how you find the penalty for the adulterer in your Book?' They said: 'Yes.' He called a man from among their scholars and said: 'I adjure you by Him who revealed the Torah to Moses! Is this how you find the penalty for the adulterer in your Book?' He said: 'No, by Allah! Had you not adjured me with this, I would not have informed you. We find the penalty for the adulterer in our Book to be stoning. But it became widespread among our nobles, so when we seized a noble we left him, and when we seized a weak person we enforced the penalty upon him. So we said: Come, let us devise something that we apply to both the noble and the lowly.' So they agreed upon tahmim and flogging." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah! I am the first to revive Your command when they had caused it to die." He said: "So he commanded that he be stoned." He said: "Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you﴾ until His saying: ﴿'If you are given this, then take it.'﴾" That is: they say: "Go to Muhammad. If he gives you a ruling of tahmim and flogging, take it; but if he gives you a ruling of stoning, beware."

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Muslim alone related it, without al-Bukhari, and Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. Likewise Abu Bakr al-Humaydi related in his Musnad something similar concerning the occasion of its revelation, from Jabir, and Abu Dawud also (related it) from Ibn Umar.

﴿And whoever Allah wills to test﴾ means: whose misguidance He wills. ﴿You will not avail him anything against Allah﴾ means: in repelling his misguidance. ﴿Those are the ones for whom Allah did not will to purify their hearts﴾ means: from the filth of temptation and the stain of disbelief, due to their immersion in them, their persistence upon them, and their turning away from directing their choice toward attaining guidance. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ means: exposure and the tearing away of their veil, by the manifestation of their hypocrisy with regard to the hypocrites, and humiliation, the jizyah (poll tax), and public exposure, by the manifestation of their lying in concealing the text of the Torah with regard to the Jews. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾, which is the Fire.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 42:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿They are listeners to falsehood, devourers of the unlawful. So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them. And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾ means: to what is false. It is a predicate of an omitted subject. It is repeated for emphasis of what precedes it and as a preparation for His saying: ﴿devourers of the unlawful﴾, i.e., the forbidden (haram). It is bribery (al-rashwa), as Ibn Mas'ud said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-suht (the unlawful gain) is everything whose earning is not permitted. It is from (sahatahu), meaning he uprooted it, because it is deprived of blessing (mash'uh al-barakah), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah destroys interest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], and usury is a form of it. It has been read as (al-suhti) with light and heavy pronunciation, and (al-sahti) with a fatha on the sin as a verbal noun from (sahatahu), and (al-sahati) with two fathas, and (al-sihti) with a kasra on the sin. They used to take bribes for rulings and for making the forbidden lawful. End of quotation.

In al-Lubab: al-suht is entirely forbidden; intense greed drives toward it. It goes back to a base forbidden gain that carries no blessing, whose taker has no dignity, and whose acquisition brings shame such that one inevitably conceals it. It is well known that the state of bribery is like this. For this reason bribery is forbidden to the judge. From Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who gives bribes and the one who takes bribes in judgment."

Al-Tirmidhi recorded it. Abu Dawud recorded it from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.

Ibn Mas'ud said: bribery is in everything. Whoever intercedes in order to return a right by it or to repel an injustice by it, and a gift is given to him for it, and he accepts, that is the suht. It was said to him: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman! We did not regard this as anything but taking payment for judgment?" He said: "Taking payment for judgment is disbelief! Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]."

﴿If they come to you﴾ means the Jews, to have you judge between them. ﴿Then judge between them﴾ because they have taken you as an arbiter. ﴿Or turn away from them﴾ because they do not intend by their seeking your judgment the following of truth, but rather what agrees with their desires; i.e., you have the choice. Whoever said that the imam has the option to judge between the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah) or to turn away from them has used this verse as evidence. It is related from some of the early generation (al-salaf) that the mentioned option was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49]. The verified view is that it is muhkam (unabrogated) and the option remains.

This is related from al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri, and Ahmad also said it, because there is no contradiction between the two verses. His saying: ﴿So judge between them or turn away from them﴾ contains the option, and His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49] contains the manner of judgment when one judges between them. ﴿And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all﴾ means they will not be able to harm you, because Allah, exalted is He, protects you from people. ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾ means with the justice you were commanded, even if they are wrongdoers who have deviated from the path of justice. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ means those who are just in what they are entrusted with and in their judgments.

Muslim recorded from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, those who act justly are with Allah on pulpits of light, at the right hand of the Most Merciful, and both His hands are right. They are those who are just in their judgment, their families, and whatever they are entrusted with."

The discussion of the words of His saying (Exalted is He):

[43] ﴿And how do they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not believers.﴾

﴿And how do they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah﴾ is an expression of astonishment at their seeking judgment from one in whom they do not believe, nor in his Book, even though the ruling is stated in their own Book, which they claim to believe in.

Some scholars said: The meaning of "in which is the judgment of Allah" is: in the matter about which they sought judgment from the Prophet ﷺ. It is the judgment of Allah according to their belief, or according to the reality. He said: The presence of this particular ruling in it does not contradict the claim that many other things in it have been distorted. They called it the Torah either by their own usage, or by considering its origin, or because it includes many things from the true Torah. Were it not so, it would not be correct to call it by that name, as with the Gospel, even though it is believed that it has been altered and changed, and that much of its parts and books are not valid... (end of quotation).

﴿Then they turn away after that﴾, meaning: after the clarification in the Torah and your judgment, which agrees with what is in their Book. ﴿And those are not believers﴾, meaning: not believers in the Torah as they claim.

Al-Hakim said: The verse indicates that it is not permissible to seek a concession by abandoning what one believes to be true in favour of what one believes to be untrue. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then they turn away after that, and those are not believers﴾, indicates that turning away from the judgment of Allah takes one out of faith.

Some of the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i sect) said: If one dislikes the ruling of the Shari'ah and seeks to prevent it, does that take him out of the judgment of faith? This should be detailed: if he believes in its validity, or sees in it merit or honour, or if he treats the ruling of Islam with contempt, there is no difficulty in his disbelief. But if none of that occurs from him, rather he believes it to be false and base, and that he honours the Shari'ah of Islam, yet he inclines to the desire of his soul, then this does not amount to disbelief on the apparent reading, since disbelief requires a decisive proof.

In al-Hakim's words cited above, there is [the view] that it takes him out of faith. If it gives the impression that it is true, or that it is better than the Shari'ah of Islam, then this admits of disbelief, because it is the disbelief of the accursed Iblis, in that he believed that Allah's command to him to prostrate to Adam was not good, because He created him from clay while Iblis was from fire. End.

Then Exalted is He pointed to the state of the Jews, who did not care for the Torah and distorted it, and killed the Prophets, in that they opposed what Allah had commanded them concerning it, namely guidance by it and safeguarding it from distortion. So He said:

(p-1995) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[44] ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted (to Allah) judged for those who were Jews, and so did the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses over it. So do not fear the people, but fear Me, and do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is those who are the disbelievers.﴾

﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance﴾ — i.e., direction to the truth. ﴿And light﴾ — i.e., clarification of what was obscure of the rulings. ﴿By it the prophets judged﴾ — from the Children of Israel. ﴿Who submitted﴾ — i.e., those who were Muslims (submitting to Allah) from the time of Moses to Jesus, peace be upon them. We will mention the secret of this attribute. ﴿For those who were Jews﴾ — and they are the Jews. And "hada" (هادَ) means to repent and return to the truth.

Al-Mahayimi said: ﴿For those who were Jews﴾ means: not for those who come after them. The judging by it was not restricted to the prophets; rather, it is judged by it: ﴿and the rabbis﴾ — i.e., the ascetics and the worshippers; ﴿and the scholars﴾ — i.e., the learned jurists; ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah﴾ — i.e., because of what they were charged with of the Book of Allah, to preserve it from alteration and change, and to judge by its rulings. The pronoun in (istuhfizu) refers to the prophets, the rabbis and the scholars all together; then the entrusting is from Allah, i.e., He charged them with its preservation. Or it refers to the rabbis and the scholars, and the entrusting is from the prophets. ﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾ — i.e., guardians who protect it from any alteration or change in any way. Or, that it is truth and sincerity from Allah. So the teachers of the Jews and their righteous scholars do not issue fatwas or judge except by what has not been abrogated from their law and what has not been distorted from it, because of its being widespread, transmitted, and continuously practiced.

A subtle point:
Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who submitted﴾ is an attribute applied to the prophets by way of (p-1996) praise, like the attributes applied to the Eternal, glorified is He. It is not for specification and clarification. Its application is intended as an insinuation against the Jews, that they are estranged from the religion of Islam, which is the religion of all the prophets, past and present, and that Judaism is far removed from it. End.

Al-Nasir said in "al-Intisaf": What led him to take this attribute as praise rather than specification and clarification is that the prophets are only characterized by it, so mentioning prophethood entails mentioning it; therefore he took it as praise. In this there is room for examination, for praise is generally through distinctive attributes by which the praised is distinguished from others, whereas submission is a general matter that encompasses the nations of the prophets and their followers just as it encompasses them. Do you not see that it is not fitting in praising the Prophet ﷺ to limit it to his being a Muslim man? For the least of his followers is like that. So the correct view, and Allah knows best, is that the attribute may be mentioned for its greatness in itself, and to draw attention to it when a great-ranked subject is described by it, just as its establishment is in proportion to its subject. The summary is that just as the attribute may be used to magnify the one described by a great attribute, it may also be used to magnify the attribute by the greatness of the one it describes. On this pattern is the description of the prophets with righteousness in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112] and similar verses, glorifying the measure of righteousness, as it is made an attribute of the prophets, and urging ordinary people to strive to attain its description. Likewise it was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who carry the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], where He informed about the near angels by faith, magnifying the rank of faith and urging mankind to enter into it, so that they might be equal to the near angels in this attribute. Otherwise, it is known that the angels are believers and nothing more. For this reason He said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], meaning from among mankind, because of the established right of brotherhood in faith between the two groups. So likewise, Allah knows best, the description of the prophets in this verse with Islam was used to glorify it. Indeed the one who said well about the attributes of the noble, and the poet in praising him ﷺ said:

"If I praise Muhammad in my poem, then I have praised my poem with Muhammad."

Islam, although it is among the most noble of attributes, since its essence is knowing Allah, the Exalted, by what is obligatory for Him, impossible for Him, and permissible regarding Him, nevertheless prophethood is more noble and exalted, because it encompasses the generality of Islam along with the special gifts that expression cannot contain. Had we not gone to the stated benefit of mentioning Islam after prophethood in the context of praise, we would have departed from the familiar rule of eloquence in the Noble Book and in the eloquent speech of the Arabs, which is ascending from the lower to the higher, not descending in reverse. Do you not see how Abu al-Tayyib deviated from this course in his saying:

"A sun whose forenoon is the crescent of its night, the pearl of its pendants is its emerald!"

He descended from the sun to the crescent, and from the pearl to the emerald, in the context of praise. So tongues chewed the edge of his eloquence and tore the fabric of his phrasing. So it is incumbent upon us to contemplate the miraculous verses, until our understanding clings to the hems of their loftiness in the eloquence known for them. And Allah is the Granter of success.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not fear the people﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a prohibition for the rulers against fearing other than Allah in their rulings, and against their leniency in them, and their enforcing them contrary to what they were commanded with regarding justice, out of fear of an oppressive ruler, or fear of harm from some relatives and friends.

(p-1998) Abu al-Su'ud said: It is an address to the leaders and scholars of the Jews by way of iltifat (shift of address). As for the rulers of the Muslims, the prohibition encompasses them by way of implication rather than explicit expression. The "fa" (فاء) is for the arrangement of the prohibition upon what has been detailed of the state of the Torah and its being given care among the prophets, peace be upon them, and those who follow them among the rabbis and scholars who came before, in practice and preservation. For that is what necessitates avoiding neglect of the duties of observing it and guarding it in any manner, let alone distortion and alteration. And since the basis of their audacity in that was fear of a holder of authority or desire for worldly portions, they were forbidden from each of these explicitly, i.e.: since its matter is as mentioned, then do not fear the people, whoever they may be, and follow in observing and preserving its rulings those before you of the prophets and their adherents: ﴿and fear Me﴾ in opposing My command and neglecting the rights of observing it. ﴿And do not exchange﴾ — i.e., do not substitute — ﴿My verses﴾ — i.e., those contained in it — by abandoning acting upon them and taking for yourselves a replacement for them: ﴿a small price﴾ — from bribery and seeking status and the approval of people, for it, however great it may be, is small and despicable in itself, especially in comparison to what they lost by abandoning acting upon it. ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ — i.e., whoever he may be, not only those addressed specifically, for they are included in it primarily. That is, whoever does not judge by it while belittling it, denying it, as the act they committed clearly implies it. ﴿Then they are the disbelievers﴾ — for their belittling of it. The sentence is a concluding statement affirming what precedes it in the most eloquent affirmation, and a warning against neglecting it in the strongest warning, since it attaches the ruling of disbelief to the mere abandonment of judging by what Allah the Exalted has revealed. How then when judging contrary to it is added to it? Especially with the direct commission of what they were forbidden from, distorting it and putting something else in its place, and claiming that it is from Allah, in order to exchange it for a small price. Said by Abu al-Su'ud.

Points of note:
The first: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear the people﴾, there is an indication that the ruler must not be deterred in Allah's cause by the blame of any blamer.
The second: In His saying, ﴿and do not exchange﴾ etc., there is an indication of the prohibition of bribery in exchange for altering and concealing the truth, and that doing so for a worldly purpose, such as seeking status or wealth, is forbidden.
(p-1999) The third: In His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ etc., there is severity regarding judging contrary to what is explicitly stated, since He attached disbelief to it here, and wrongdoing and defiance afterward.
The fourth: What Muslim transmitted from al-Bara': that His saying, exalted is He: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed" — the three verses are all about the disbelievers. Likewise what Abu Dawud transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: that they are specifically about the Jews, Qurayza and al-Nadir. This does not contradict their application to others, for the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation, and the word "man" (مَن) occurs in the context of a condition, so it is general.
The fifth: The disbelief of a ruler in judging by other than what Allah revealed, with the qualification of belittling it and denying it, is the view that many have adopted and transmitted from 'Ikrimah and Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Hatim and 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Ibn 'Abbas and Tawus that whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, regarding it, is disbelief, but it is not a disbelief that removes one from the religion, like one who disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. Similar to this al-Thawri related from 'Ata', who said: It is disbelief short of disbelief, wrongdoing short of wrongdoing, and defiance short of defiance. Ibn Jarir related it.

In "al-Lubab" it is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i that these three verses are general concerning the Jews and this Ummah, so whoever accepts bribes and alters the ruling, judging by other than the ruling of Allah, has disbelieved, wronged and transgressed. Al-Suddi also took this view, because it is the apparent sense of the address. Then he said: It was said: this applies to one who knows the text of Allah's ruling and then deliberately rejects it openly and judges by something else. As for one whose knowledge of the text is hidden, or who errs in interpretation, he does not fall under this threat. End.

(p-2000) Isma'il al-Qadi said in "Ahkam al-Qur'an": The apparent meaning of the verses indicates that whoever does the like of what they did — meaning the Jews — and invents a ruling that contradicts the ruling of Allah, making it a religion to be practiced, then the same threat mentioned that applied to them applies to him, whether he is a ruler or otherwise.

The sixth: Another cause of revelation of these noble verses has been related:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, and: those are the wrongdoers, and: those are the defiantly disobedient, concerning the two groups of the Jews. One of the two groups had dominated the other in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), until they agreed or reconciled that for every slain person whom the powerful group killed from the weak group, the blood-money would be fifty wasq (a measure of dates), and for every slain person whom the weak group killed from the powerful group, the blood-money would be one hundred wasq. They continued in this state until the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, and both groups were humbled by the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). At that time he had not prevailed over them, and they were in a treaty with him. Then the weak group killed a slain man from the powerful group. The powerful group sent to the weak group: 'Send us one hundred wasq.' The weak group said: 'Has there ever been, between two tribes whose religion is one, whose lineage is one, and whose land is one, that the blood-money of one part is half the blood-money of another part? We only gave you this out of oppression by you against us and out of fear of you. Now that Muhammad has come, we will not give you that.' War nearly erupted between them. Then they agreed to make the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) their arbiter. Then the powerful group remembered and said: 'By Allah! Muhammad will not give you from among them double what he gives them from among us. They spoke truly; they only gave us this out of oppression by us and subjugation of them.' So send to Muhammad someone who will inform you of his opinion. If he gives you what you want, you will appoint him as judge; and if he does not give you, beware, and do not appoint him as judge.' So they sent some of the hypocrites to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to inform them of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) opinion. When they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of their entire affair and what they intended. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O Messenger, do not let grieve you those who hasten into disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41] up to His saying: ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47]. Then he said: 'By Allah! They were revealed concerning these two, and it is them whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meant.'" Abu Dawud narrated it in a similar wording.

Ibn Jarir narrated through another chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The verses in al-Ma'idah, His saying: ﴿So judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42] up to: ﴿the just﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42], were only revealed concerning the blood-money among the Banu al-Nadir and Qurayzah. That is because the slain of the Banu al-Nadir, who had nobility, were paid full blood-money, while the Qurayzah were paid half blood-money. They brought their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed that concerning them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then guided them to the truth in that matter, and made the blood-money equal in that case." Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated it in a similar wording.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There were Qurayzah and al-Nadir. Al-Nadir were more noble than Qurayzah. So when a man of Qurayzah killed a man of al-Nadir, he was killed in retaliation for him. And when a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayzah, he was made to pay one hundred wasq of dates as blood-money. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayzah. They said: 'Hand him over to us.' They said: 'Between us and you is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]." Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated it in a similar wording. Thus said Qatadah, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and others besides them.

Al-'Awfi and Ali ibn Abi Talhah al-Walibi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning the two Jews who committed adultery, as the hadiths mentioned earlier. It may be that these two causes (of revelation) coincided at one time. So these verses were revealed concerning all of that, and Allah knows best. End of the words of Ibn Kathir.

We have already mentioned in the Muqaddimah (introduction), in the discussion of asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation), what removes the difficulty of there being multiple causes, so reflect on it. And among what strengthens that the cause of revelation is the matter of retaliation, as Ibn Kathir said, is His saying, exalted is He, after that:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 45 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation. But whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾, i.e., We obligated upon the Jews in the Torah: ﴿that the life is for the life﴾, i.e., the one who is killed by it (the killer) if he kills it without right; ﴿and the eye﴾ gouged out, ﴿for the eye﴾; ﴿and the nose﴾ cut off, ﴿for the nose﴾; ﴿and the ear﴾ cut off, ﴿for the ear﴾; ﴿and the tooth﴾ pulled out, ﴿for the tooth﴾; ﴿and for wounds is retaliation﴾, i.e., having retaliation, meaning retaliation is carried out in them where possible, such as the hand, the foot and the male organ, and the like. But where it is not possible, such as breaking a bone or wounding flesh where one cannot determine its limit, there is no retaliation; rather, there is a just assessment (ḥukūmah ʿadl) for it.

Notes (tanbihat):

The first: This verse is one with which the Jews were also rebuked and reproached. For they had in the text of the Torah that the life is for the life, yet they deliberately and obstinately contravened its ruling. They executed an Naḍrī (man) for a Quraẓī (man), but did not execute a Quraẓī for a Naḍrī. They turned to blood-money (diyah) just as they contravened the ruling of the Torah concerning the stoning of the married adulterer, and they turned to what they had agreed upon among themselves: flogging, blackening of the face and parading. Therefore there He said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is those who are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], because they denied the ruling of Allah intentionally, out of obstinacy and deliberate purpose. And here He said, in the continuation of the verse: ﴿it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾, because they did not give the wronged party justice against the wrongdoer in the matter (p-2003) in which Allah commanded justice and equality among all. So they contravened, wronged, and transgressed against one another. This is what Ibn Kathir conveyed.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ and what follows it are all read in the accusative and in the nominative. The nominative is for coordination (ʿaṭf) with the place (maḥall) of ﴿that the life is for the life﴾, because the meaning is: "And We prescribed for them the life for the life," either by treating "katabnā" (We prescribed) as if it were "qulnā" (We said), or because the meaning of the sentence "the life is for the life" is among the things that can be the object of "writing" just as it can be the object of "reading." You say: "I wrote: Praise be to Allah," and "I read: a surah which We sent down." Therefore al-Zajjaj said: "Had it been read as 'anna al-nafsa bi-l-nafsi' with a kasra, it would have been sound." Thus in al-Kashshaf. Al-Khafaji has expanded in al-ʿInayah on the discussion of the nominative here, in his habit regarding grammatical matters, so consult it if you wish.

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim narrated from Anas ibn Malik: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: 'And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life and the eye for the eye,' putting the life in the accusative and the eye in the nominative." Al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib." And al-Bukhari said: "Ibn al-Mubarak alone narrated this hadith."

The third: Many of the usuliyyun (jurists of legal theory) and fuqaha who hold that the law of those before us is law for us - when it is related as confirmed and not abrogated, as is well known from the majority, and as Shaykh Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini related it from the explicit text of al-Shafi'i and most of his companions - have cited this verse as evidence, since the ruling in cases of injury is in accordance with it according to all the imams. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "It is for them and for people generally." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it. Imam Abu Mansur ibn al-Sabbagh in his book "al-Shamil" related the consensus of the scholars on arguing with this verse according to what it indicates.

The fourth: Ibn Kathir said: All the imams argued that a man is killed for a woman by the general application of this noble verse. Likewise it occurs in the hadith narrated by al-Nasa'i and others: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-2004) wrote in the letter of ʿAmr ibn Hazm: that a man is killed for a woman." And in another hadith: "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafa'u dimaauhum)." This is the view of the majority of scholars. But from the Commander of the Faithful ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and it is related from al-Hasan and ʿUthman al-Busti, and a narration from Ahmad, that if a man kills a woman he is not killed for her; rather, her blood-money is due. Likewise Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, argued from the general application of this verse that a Muslim is to be killed for a dhimmi non-Muslim, and a free man for a slave. The majority disagreed with him on both. In the two Sahihs, from the Commander of the Faithful ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (p-2009) "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever." As for the slave, there are numerous reports from the early generations (salaf): they did not require retaliation of a free man for a slave, nor was a free man killed for a slave. Hadiths on this have come but are not sound. Al-Shafi'i related the consensus against the position of the Hanafis in this matter. End of quote.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: In this verse is the legislation of retaliation for life, limbs and wounds according to our law, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith of Anas: "The Book of Allah is retaliation." Those who said a Muslim is killed for a disbeliever, a free man for a slave, and a man for a woman, used the general wording "the life for the life" as evidence. Ibn al-Faras answered that the verse intends free Muslims, because the Jews for whom it was prescribed in the Torah were one religious community, not divided into Muslim and disbeliever, and they were free with no slaves among them, since the institution of the dhimma and enslavement was permitted only to the Prophet (ﷺ) among the prophets, because enslavement comes from war booty and was not lawful for anyone else, while the dhimma contract is for the continuance of disbelievers, which did not happen in the time of any prophet, rather those who denied were all destroyed by punishment. This was postponed for this nation out of mercy. This is a clear answer.

As for His saying: ﴿and for wounds is retaliation﴾, it has been cited as evidence for every wound in which retaliation is said to apply - such as the tongue, the lip, skull and face fractures, and the rest of the body - and as evidence that plucking hair and striking carry no retaliation, since they are not wounds. End of quote.

Some of the Zaydis said in their tafsir: The position of the Imams of the House (ahl al-bayt), Malik and al-Shafi'i is that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever. Abu Hanifa said: he is killed for him, but not for a harbi (combatant enemy) nor for a musta'man (one under safe-conduct) among the combatants, taking the general application of the verse. We say: it is specified by His saying in Surat al-Hashr: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal﴾ [al-Hashr: 20], and this requires negating equality in general. They said: He meant "in the Hereafter." We say: Allah said: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 141]. They said: This is not on its generality, for he has the right to collect a debt from him, and that is a way. We say: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A believer is not killed for a disbeliever," so it is general. They said: He meant by "disbeliever" a combatant enemy, by evidence that at the end of the report: "nor one who has a covenant during a covenant." The meaning: a believer is not killed, nor is one who was given a covenant, for a disbeliever who has no covenant. We say: The first sentence was complete, which is his peace be upon him saying: "A believer is not killed for a disbeliever." As for his saying: "nor one who has a covenant during a covenant," this is another sentence. He means: he is not killed while he is within the covenant. Furthermore, even if the hadith allows that it is one sentence, the intended meaning is: a believer is not killed for any of the disbelievers in general; and likewise the one under covenant is not killed for any of the disbelievers in general. Thus evidence has established that the one under covenant is killed for some of the disbelievers, and the believer remains under the general rule. What we said is related from ʿAli, peace be upon him, and Zayd. These specifications restrict the general expressions that have come in this matter. End of quote.

(p-2011) Fifth: The generality of His saying, exalted is He: "the eye for the eye" is like the generality of His saying: ﴿the life for the life﴾. Whatever specified that general term, specifies it here too. But we point out some particulars:

Among them: the left is not taken for the right, since the view is non-equality.

Among them: the eye of a one-eyed man is taken for the eye of a sound man, according to what is stated in al-Ahkam, and to this went Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, by the generality of the verse. But in al-Muntakhab and Malik said: it is not taken, because its light is greater, so equality is sought. They argued that it is related from ʿAli, peace be upon him, ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar and ʿUthman. In al-Sharh it is said: Imam Yahya did not authenticate this report from ʿAli, peace be upon him.

Among them: concerning the manner of retaliation. If the eye is extracted, retaliation is established by extraction. If it is struck until its sight is lost, retaliation is established. In al-Tahdhib it is said: It was said: by extraction. It was also said: an iron rod is heated and then brought near his eye.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the nose for the nose﴾, the discussion of its generality is as already passed. It is mentioned here as a note: retaliation applies only if the whole organ is removed at its root, because that is like the joint, not if only part of it is cut. The generality in His saying: ﴿and the ear for the ear﴾ is likewise as passed. Retaliation applies when it is cut from its root, not when part is cut. The ear of a sound man is not taken for the ear of a deaf man.

Likewise the generality of His saying: ﴿and the tooth for the tooth﴾. Retaliation applies when it is pulled from its root, and equality is necessary. Thus a sound tooth is not taken for a black one or a broken one, nor an incisor for a molar, and the like, just as the right is not taken for the left.

As for His saying: ﴿and for wounds﴾, this applies where equality is possible and safety for life is assured, given the caution of the community.

Thus in the tafsir of some of the Zaydis. The complete jurisprudence of this verse is to be sought in the extended books of Sunnah and their commentaries.

(p-2012) As for His saying: ﴿But whoever gives it as charity﴾, i.e., of those entitled: ﴿it﴾, i.e., the retaliation; that is, whoever pardons the offender. The expression of it as "charity" is for emphasis in encouraging it: ﴿it is﴾, i.e., the charity, ﴿an expiation for him﴾, i.e., for the one who gives charity, by which Allah expiates his sins. It was also said: it is an expiation for the offender; if the rightful owner overlooks him, what was due from him falls away. This second interpretation was related from many of the early generations, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated. The wording allows it, but the reports concerning the merit of pardon support the first.

Imam Ahmad narrated from al-Sha'bi that ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No man is wounded in his body and then gives it as charity, except that Allah expiates for him the like of what he gave as charity." Al-Nasa'i also narrated it.

Imam Ahmad narrated from a man of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: Whoever is afflicted with something in his body and leaves it for Allah, it will be an expiation for him.

Imam Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Safar, who said: "A man of Quraysh pushed a man of the Ansar, and his front tooth was broken. The Ansari took him up to Mu'awiyah. When the man pressed the matter, Mu'awiyah said: 'Take your companion.' Abu al-Darda' was with Mu'awiyah, and Abu al-Darda' said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'No Muslim is afflicted with something in his body and forgives it, except that Allah raises him one degree thereby and removes from him one sin thereby.' The Ansari said: Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? He said: I heard it with my ears and my heart retained it. So he released the Qurashi. Mu'awiyah said to him: Give him money."

(p-2013) Imam Ahmad also narrated it from Abu al-Safar, who said: "A man of Quraysh broke the tooth of a man of the Ansar. He sought redress against him from Mu'awiyah. The Qurashi said: This one broke my tooth. Mu'awiyah said: No, we will certainly satisfy him. When the Ansari pressed the matter, Mu'awiyah said: Take your companion - and Abu al-Darda' was sitting there. Abu al-Darda' said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'No Muslim is afflicted with something in his body, and then gives it as charity, except that Allah raises him one degree thereby and removes from him one sin thereby.' He said: The Ansari said: Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? He said: Yes, my ears heard it and my heart retained it. Meaning: so the Ansari forgave him." Likewise al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: Gharib, and I do not know that Abu al-Safar heard from Abu al-Darda'.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers﴾ — because they judged contrary to the just judgment of Allah. And the secret of expressing it here with "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun), while before it with "the disbelievers" (al-kafirun), was mentioned earlier, shortly before, in the first of the Five Admonitions (al-tanbihat al-khams), so recall it.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[46] ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah (Tawrah); and We gave him the Gospel (Injil), in which was guidance and light, and confirming what was before it of the Torah, and a guidance and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾

﴿We sent after them﴾, meaning: We caused to follow: ﴿in their footsteps﴾, meaning the prophets of the Children of Israel: ﴿Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning: We sent him after them: ﴿confirming what was before him of the Torah﴾, meaning: believing in it and ruling by what is in it: ﴿and We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance﴾, meaning: to the truth: ﴿and light﴾, meaning: a clarification of the rulings: ﴿and confirming what was before it of the Torah﴾, meaning: confirming what is in it of rulings. The repetition of this is for the sake of further affirmation.

(p-2014) Ibn Kathir said: Meaning: following it, not contradicting what is in it, except in a few matters, which were made clear to the Children of Israel, some of what they had been disputing about, as He, may He be exalted, said reporting about the Messiah, that he said to the Children of Israel: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran 3:50]. For this reason, the well-known view among the scholars is that the Gospel abrogated (nasakha) some of the rulings of the Torah. ﴿And a guidance and an admonition﴾, meaning: a deterrent from committing the forbidden acts and sins: ﴿to the God-fearing﴾, meaning: to those who fear God, dread His threat and His punishment. The specification of it being a guidance and an admonition to the God-fearing is because they are the ones guided by its guidance and the ones who benefit from its bounty.

And His saying, may He be exalted:

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[47] ﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾ is a fresh command addressed to them: that they should judge and act by what is in it, among the matters of which are the proofs of his message, peace and blessings be upon him, and the evidences of his prophethood. It has been said: it is a relating of the command that was directed at them, with a verb governed by conjunction understood as following (ātaynāhu): "and We said: let the People of the Gospel judge." It has also been read as (wa-liyaḥkuma) with the accusative, on the basis that the lām is the lām of purpose (lām kay), meaning: We gave him the Gospel so that the people of his religion would judge by it in their time.

Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) said: He specified the People of the Gospel for mention only to clarify that Allah did not send down the Gospel for all nations, and that its law does not remain for every age, because the mission of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, was specific to the Jewish nation.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient﴾ means: those who depart from obedience to their Lord, inclining towards falsehood, abandoning the truth.

(p-2015) Admonition: In this verse and the two preceding verses there is a warning whose extent cannot be measured. It has already been mentioned that these verses - although they were revealed concerning the People of the Book - are not restricted to them, but are general for everyone who does not judge by what Allah has revealed, by considering the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the cause. The cause itself is included in it by primary inclusion.

In "Fath al-Bayan" concerning the exegesis of these verses there are rare discussions of wide scope, so it should be consulted.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the Torah which He sent down to Musa, His interlocutor, praised it and commanded following it, and then mentioned the Gospel, praised it and commanded following it, He began to draw attention to the Glorious Qur'an, which He sent down to His noble Messenger, saying:

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[48] ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming that which came before it of the Book and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have made a law and a method. And had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation, but [He did that] to test you in what He has given you. So race to [all that is] good. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.ﴩ

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ — that is, the complete and singular one, deserving of being called "the Book" without qualification, because it possesses all the perfect attributes of the genus of heavenly books and surpasses the rest of its kind; this is the Noble Qur'an. The definite article here is for previous reference (lil-'ahd). This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

﴿in truth﴾ — that is, with the truthfulness about which there is no doubt that it is from Allah. ﴿confirming that which came before it of the Book﴾ — an explanation of "that which" (ma). The "al" in "al-Kitab" is for the genus. The meaning is that it confirms all the books that Allah sent down to His prophets before it. It is said "that which is before a thing" is "between its hands" because what comes after it is behind it and beyond it, while what precedes it is in front of it and between its hands. ﴿and as a guardian over it﴾ — that is, trustworthy over it, a witness, and a judge over the books that came before it.

Ibn Jurayj said: The Qur'an is a trustee over the books preceding it: whatever of them agrees with it is true, and whatever of them contradicts it is false.

﴿So judge between them﴾ — that is, between the People of the Book when they bring their disputes to you — ﴿by what Allah has revealed﴾ — that is, by what Allah has made clear to you in the Qur'an.

In al-Iklil, it is said: This abrogates the ruling of every previous law. Thus, it entails that when the dhimmis bring their disputes to us, they are judged by the rulings of Islam, not by their own beliefs. Among the instances of this is the non-liability for wine and the like. End of quote.

﴿and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you﴾ — he was forbidden to judge by what they had distorted or altered, relying on their saying. The verb is implicitly construed: "and do not follow" carries the sense of "and do not deviate," which is why it takes "from" (ʿan). It is as if it were said: "and do not deviate from the truth that has come to you, following their desires." Or the estimated sense is: "turning away from what has come to you."

﴿For each of you We have made a law﴾ — that is, a law leading to Allah — ﴿and a method﴾ — that is, a clear path in religion, which you follow. Ibn Kathir said: This is information about the nations of differing religions, in terms of the varied laws in rulings that Allah sent His noble messengers with, agreeing in monotheism. As is established in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We, the company of prophets, are half-brothers; our religion is one." He meant by this the monotheism with which Allah sent every messenger He dispatched, and which He included in every book He sent down, as He said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya: 25], and He said: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid Taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36].

Abu al-Su'ud said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ is a resumed statement brought to move the People of the Two Books, among his contemporaries (ﷺ), to submit to his judgment by what was sent down to him of the Noble Qur'an, by explaining that it is the one they were charged to act upon, rather than the other two books; and that those who were charged to act upon those two were those who lived before their abrogation among the earlier nations. The address is in the manner of variation and turning (iltifat) to mankind in general, but not only to those present; rather also to those past, by way of prevalence (taghlib). The meaning: for each nation among you — O nations present and past — We have made, that is, appointed and established, a law and a method specific to that nation. No nation may transgress its law which was appointed for it. So the nation that existed from the time of Musa to Isa, peace be upon them both, had the Torah as its law; and the one that existed from the time of Isa to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon them both, had the Gospel as its law. As for you who exist now, your law is the Qur'an alone. So believe in it and act upon what is in it.

In al-Iklil: whoever said that the law of those before us is not law for us derived evidence from this verse. And whoever said that it is law for us, unless a abrogating text comes, derived it from His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], etc. Also, whoever said that disbelief consists of religions (milal), not one single religion, and that Jews do not inherit from Christians, derived evidence from the verse. End of quote.

Al-Nasafi said: Allah mentioned the sending down of the Torah upon Musa, peace be upon him; then the sending down of the Gospel upon Isa, peace be upon him; then the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ). And He made clear that it is not merely for hearing, but for judging by it. So He said in the first: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾; in the second: ﴿and let the People of the Gospel judge﴾; and in the third: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾.

﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation﴾ — that is, a community agreed upon one law — ﴿but [He did not], that He may test you in what He has given you﴾ — this is connected to an omitted element required by the context. That is: "but He made you into different nations, that He might test you regarding what He has given you of the differing laws: would you abandon what you are accustomed to of them in favor of what has been newly introduced, submitting to it, believing that its opposition to them is by the requirement of divine will, founded on lofty wisdoms and beneficial interests for you in this life and the next? Or would you turn away from the truth, follow desire, exchange harm for benefit, and buy misguidance with guidance?" And with this it becomes clear that the basis for the non-willing mentioned is not merely testing; rather, the foundation of that is what was alluded to of the difference containing what is in their interest in this life and the next, as His saying indicates: ﴿So race to the good﴾ — that is, if the matter is as mentioned, then hasten to what is best for you in both abodes: sound beliefs and righteous deeds included in the Noble Qur'an, and seize them, grasping the opportunity and securing precedence and preeminence. In this there is, regarding the emphasis on encouragement to submit to the truth and the intensification of warning against deviation, what is not hidden. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾ — a resumed statement brought as a reason for racing to good deeds, with what it contains of promise and threat. That is: your destination and return, O people, is to Him on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾ — that is, He will inform you of what you cannot doubt regarding the decisive recompense that separates your righteous from your wrongdoers, and your doer from your negligent in action. Thus in al-Kashshaf.

So "inbaʾ" (informing) is metaphorically used for requital, and it was expressed by it because it occupies the place of removing the disagreement, which is the function of informing.

(p-٢٠١٩)The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[49] ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿And that judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf, grammatical coordination) with "the Book", meaning: We revealed to you the Book and the judgment by what is in it. Or it is coordinated with "the truth", meaning: We revealed it with the truth, and with "judge" (an-uḥkum). It may also be a separate clause (jumla), with the implied sense: "and We commanded that you judge." Mentioning the title of His revealing it (ʿunwān inzālihi) emphasizes the obligation to comply, and paves the way for what follows: ﴿and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾, meaning, they divert you from it. Stating the Majestic Name explicitly serves to stress the command by magnifying the gravity of the matter, like the repetition of "what Allah has revealed."

﴿And if they turn away﴾, meaning from the revealed judgment, and desire something other than it: ﴿then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾, meaning for the sin of turning away from the judgment of Allah and desiring its opposite. He put "for some of their sins" in place of that. And the intent is that they have many sins, numerous in count, and that this sin, despite its enormity, is one part of them and one of them. This vagueness (ibhām) serves to magnify the act of turning away and their excess in committing it. The use of "some" (al-baʿḍ) in this speech is similar to Labid's line: (p-٢٠٢٠)"Or some souls are bound by their death..!" He meant himself. He intended to exalt its status through this vagueness, as if he said: a great soul, and what a soul! Just as indefiniteness (tankīr) conveys the meaning of magnification, which is the meaning of partiality, so too when "some" is stated explicitly. Thus in the Kashshaf.

In al-Hawashi: Similar to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ [al-Anʿam: 165], meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that this is from the particular (khuṣūṣ) used to mean the general (ʿumūm). It was also said that it means the punishment in this world, whereas in the Hereafter he will be punished for all sins. The poet has been subtle:

"I say 'some of the people' about you, as a euphemism, out of fear of informers, though you are all the people."

﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning: those who are stubborn in disbelief, holding to it as a belief. This is a recording against them for opposition. That is: turning away from the judgment of Allah is a great defiance and transgression in disbelief. The clause is a concluding parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī) that confirms the content of what precedes it. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And most of the people, though you should strive, will not be believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Anʿam: 116].

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Kaʿb ibn Asad, Ibn Ṣaluma, ʿAbdullah ibn Ṣuriyya, and Shas ibn Qays said to one another: 'Come, let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion.' So they came to him and said: 'O Muhammad! You know that we are the rabbis of the Jews, their nobles and their leaders. If we follow you, the Jews will follow us and will not oppose us. There is a dispute between us and our people, so we will bring it to you to judge, and you will rule for us against them, and we will believe in you and affirm you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused that. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning them: ﴿And that judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires﴾, the verse."

The Explanation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[50] ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance (jahiliyyah)? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾

﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance?﴾ That is: do they desire it from you?

Abu al-Su'ud said: It is a denunciation, a wonderment at their state, and a rebuke for them. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction with an implied clause that the context requires. That is: do they turn away from your judgment and so seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance? The fronting of the object (taqdim al-maf'ul) serves restriction, which confirms the denunciation and wonderment, because turning away from his ﷺ judgment and seeking another judgment is a strange denunciation, and seeking the judgment of the Time of Ignorance is even more abhorrent and more wondrous. As for the "Time of Ignorance" (al-jahiliyyah), it is either the ignorant creed, which is the following of desire, which necessitates inclination and flattery in judgments, so that it is an address to the Jews that, despite being People of the Book and knowledge, they seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance, which is desire and ignorance that does not proceed from a Book and does not return to revelation; or it refers to the people of the Time of Ignorance, and their judgment was what they were upon of distinction among the slain. End of quotation.

﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment﴾ That is: in decision. ﴿for a people who are certain﴾ That is: who look with the eye of certainty upon the outcomes. The interrogation is a denial that anyone's judgment could be better than His judgment, or even equal to it.

Ibn Kathir said: He, exalted is He, denounces those who depart from the judgment of Allah, the firm (muhkam) judgment that includes every good and forbids every evil, and turn instead to other opinions, desires and conventions that men have devised without any basis in the Law of Allah, as the people of the Time of Ignorance used to judge by their errors and ignorance which they laid down by their own opinions and desires, and as the Tatars judge by the royal policies taken from Genghis Khan, who laid down for them the (Yasa), which is a collection of rulings that he borrowed from various laws, from Judaism, Christianity, the Islamic community and others. In it are many rulings he took from his mere opinion and desire, and they became a followed law among his descendants, whom they prefer over judgment by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Whoever among them does this is a disbeliever who must be fought until he returns to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, and he should not judge by anything else, in little or in much. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance?﴾ That is: they seek and desire it, and they deviate from the judgment of Allah.

﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ That is: and who is more just than Allah in His judgment for one who understands from Allah His law, believes in it and is certain, and knows that Allah, exalted is He, is the most judicious of judges and more merciful to His creation than a mother to her child? For He, exalted is He, is the All-Knowing of everything, the All-Powerful over everything, the Just in everything. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan who said: Whoever judges by other than the judgment of Allah, then it is the judgment of the Time of Ignorance. And Tawus, when a man asked him: Shall I favour between my children in gifts? he recited: ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance?﴾ the verse. And al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The most hateful of people to Allah, mighty and majestic, is one who seeks in Islam the practice of the Time of Ignorance, and one who seeks the blood of a man without right, to spill his blood." It was also narrated by al-Bukhari with an addition. End of the words of Ibn Kathir.

One of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah said: The words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48] through His words: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ comprise twenty aspects of emphasis on adhering to the law of our Prophet ﷺ which Allah, exalted is He, sent down and chose for His community, and singled out many of its secrets so that they were not disclosed. How intense is compliance with what it contains! And how can one be free of its obligation, especially for the leaders and rulers? That will not be achieved until a man blames himself with the bridle of truth, and removes from himself the looking toward creation. Regarding this sentence, it is not said that he ﷺ is infallible and does not follow their desires; so how is he forbidden from what Allah knows he will not do? Al-Hakim said: That is within his capacity, so the prohibition is valid even if it is known that he will not do it. It was also said: the address is to him, and the intent is others.

Likewise, it is not said that His words: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48] are excluded from that analogy, because that—if it is taken as an address to him, peace and blessings be upon him—then he was not charged with analogy (qiyas). And if it is an address to all, then analogy is established by evidence, and it stands in the position of what was revealed. Thus did al-Hakim mention. The majority hold that it is permissible for him, peace and blessings be upon him, to exercise independent reasoning (ijtihad), while others forbade it. His words, exalted is He: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48] may be used as evidence that obligations are for the attainment of success, and this is possible, because the intent is before death overtakes you. End of quotation.

In al-Iklil it says: It is used as evidence that hastening the acts of worship at the beginning of their time is better than delaying them. End of quotation.

Muslim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet ﷺ: "The best of deeds is prayer at its time, and kindness to the two parents."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim narrated from Umm Farwah from the Prophet ﷺ: "The best of deeds is prayer at the beginning of its time."

(p-2024) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. And whoever among you allies with them is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ That is: none of you should take any of them as a close friend (waliyy), meaning: do not be companions to them or associate with them in the intimacy of loved ones.

Al-Mahayimi said: If the affection of the People of the Book toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was aimed at seducing him away from some of what Allah had revealed, despite his utmost perfection, then what is the state of those among the believers who show affection to them? End of quote.

He described them with the title (of faith) because it impels them, from the outset, to refrain from what they were forbidden.

For reminding them of the attributes opposed to the qualities of the two groups is among the strongest deterrents from allying with them both.

﴿They are allies of one another﴾ This is an indication of the reason for the prohibition. That is: they are superior over those who oppose them; some of them ally with others because of their unity in religion and their consensus against you. So what does someone whose religion differs from theirs have to do with allying with them!

﴿And whoever among you allies with them is indeed one of them﴾ That is: one of their number. His ruling is their ruling, even if he claims that he differs from them in religion, for by the indication of his condition he is from them, since it indicates complete agreement with them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a severe warning and emphatic insistence from Allah on the obligation to keep away from and separate oneself from those who differ in religion, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Their fires should not see each other." And from this is the saying of ʿUmar (p-2025) (may Allah be pleased with him) to Abu Musa regarding his Christian scribe: "Do not honor them, since Allah has humiliated them. Do not trust them, since Allah has deemed them treacherous. Do not bring them near, since Allah has distanced them." It is related that Abu Musa said to him: "There is no stability for Basra except through him," and he said: "The Christian has died, and peace be upon you." He meant: suppose he has died; what would you do then? Do it now and dispense with him by another.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ That is: those who wronged themselves by allying with the disbelievers.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Sirin, who said: ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUtba said: "Let each of you beware lest he become a Jew or a Christian while he does not perceive it." He said: "We thought he meant this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take…﴾, the verse."

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the manner of their alliance, and indicated its cause and what its matter leads to. So He said, glorified is He:

LOCAL: The passage is a tafsir commentary, so I translate it faithfully with the required formatting conventions.

Interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[52] ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring about victory or a decision from Him, and they will become, over what they had been concealing within themselves, regretful.﴾

﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ i.e., hypocrisy and doubt regarding the promise of Allah to make His religion prevail. ﴿Hastening toward them﴾ i.e., in their affection (for the disbelievers), inwardly and outwardly, without considering the harm that would befall them to the religion of Allah and the disgrace of hypocrisy. ﴿Saying﴾ i.e., in their excuse: ﴿"We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾ i.e., one of the reversals of time and one of its vicissitudes, so that the dominion would belong to them and we would need them, and so we guard ourselves against their evil. They do not reflect that misfortune may well strike those whom they befriend. The word "dā'irah" (misfortune, lit. "circle") is one of the qualities that became predominant, so that the noun it describes is not mentioned with it. Its origin is the line that encircles a surface. It was borrowed for the calamities of time, with consideration of its encompassing and its use for what is disliked. And "al-dawlah" (dominion, turn of fortune) is its opposite, though it may occasionally come with the meaning of "dā'irah" as well, but this is rare. So said [al-Alusi] in "al-'Inayah" [al-Babarti's commentary on al-Baydawi].

(p-2026) Then Exalted is He refuted their false pretexts and cut off their empty hopes, and gave good news to the believers of victory by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿But perhaps Allah will bring about victory﴾ i.e., the conquest of Mecca, according to al-Suddi; or the conquest of the Jewish villages of Khaybar and Fadak, according to al-Dahhak. Qatadah and Muqatil said: it is the decisive judgment by His granting victory to the Prophet (ﷺ) over his enemies and the manifestation of the Muslims. ﴿Or a decision from Him﴾ that uproots the root of the Jews and expels them from their lands. ﴿And they will become﴾ i.e., the hypocrites ﴿over what they had been concealing within themselves﴾ of doubt regarding the manifestation of Islam, or of hypocrisy ﴿regretful﴾ because of their being exposed in hypocrisy before both groups. The linking of regret to what they had been concealing, rather than to what they used to display of allegiance to the disbelievers, is because it was what drove them to allegiance and incited them toward it. This indicates their regret over it, in its origin and its cause.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[5:53] ﴿Those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you? Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers."﴾

﴿Those who believe will say﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: It is read with the accusative (*naṣb*), coordinated with (*an yaʼtiya*, "that He may bring"), and with the nominative (*raf*), as a new independent sentence. That is, "Those who believe will say at that time." It is also read as *yaqūlu* without the *wāw* (and), and this is how it appears in the codices of Mecca, Medina and Syria. This reading answers a questioner who asks: "What will the believers say at that time?" So it is said: "Those who believe will say: Are these the ones who swore...?" (If you ask): To whom will they say this statement? (I answer): Either some of them will say it to others, in wonder at their condition and in gladness at what Allah has bestowed upon them of success in sincerity: ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾, that is, they swore to you with the strongest oaths: ﴿that they were with you﴾, that is, that they were your allies and supporters against the disbelievers. Or they say it to the Jews, because the hypocrites had sworn to them their support and help, as Allah related of them: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely help you﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. That is, they have distanced themselves from you. It thus becomes clear that they were neither with the believers nor with the Jews: ﴿Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers﴾, that is, in this world, since their hypocrisy became manifest to all, and in the Hereafter, since they have no reward left.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This sentence is part of the speech of the believers, that is: their deeds that they used to strain to perform for the sight of people have been nullified. It carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How void their deeds are, and how great their loss!" Or it is part of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as a testimony to them of the nullification of their deeds and as a marvel at the evil of their condition. End of quotation.

In this there is a mockery of the hypocrites and a rebuke to the addressees that is not hidden.

Notes:

The first: concerning the occasion of revelation of these noble verses:

It is narrated from al-Suddi that they were revealed concerning two men, one of whom said to his companion after the Battle of Uhud: "As for me, I am going to that Jew, so I will be his ally and become a Jew with him, so that he may benefit me if an event occurs or a calamity befalls." The other said: "As for me, I am going to such-and-such Christian in Syria, so I will be his ally and become a Christian with him." Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians [as allies]﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51] and the verses.

ʻIkrimah said: It was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah ibn ʻAbd al-Mundhir, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to the Banu Qurayzah. They asked him: "What is he going to do with us?" He gestured with his hand to his throat, meaning slaughter. Ibn Jarir narrated it.

It was also said: It was revealed concerning ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. Ibn Jarir narrated from ʻAtiyyah ibn Saʻd who said: "ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit came from the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah! I have many clients among the Jews, in great number. I disavow to Allah and His Messenger the alliance with the Jews, and I take Allah and His Messenger as my allies. ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy said: I am a man who fears the turning of fortune; I will not disavow the alliance with my clients. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy: O Abu al-Hubab! What you withheld of the alliance with the Jews from ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit, it is yours instead of him. He said: I accept. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who believe﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], the two verses."

Then Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri who said: "When the people of Badr were defeated, the Muslims said to their Jewish allies: Believe before Allah strikes you with a day like the day of Badr. Malik ibn al-Sayf said: You were deceived if you struck a group of Quraysh who have no knowledge of fighting! Had we determined to gather against you, you would have had no power to fight us. ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit said: O Messenger of Allah! My allies among the Jews have fierce souls, abundant weapons, and great might, and I disavow to Allah and to His Messenger their alliance, and I have no ally except Allah and His Messenger. ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy said: But I will not disavow the alliance with the Jews; I am a man who cannot do without them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: O Abu al-Hubab! Did you see what you withheld of the alliance with the Jews from ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit? It is yours instead of him. He said: When he comes forward! [He said]: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], to His saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "It was the first tribe of the Jews that broke what was between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, until they came down to his judgment. ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul stood up to him when Allah had enabled him over them, and said: O Muhammad! Be kind to my clients—they were the allies of the Khazraj. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ delayed in answering him. He said: O Muhammad! Be kind to my clients. He said: So he turned away from him. Then he put his hand into the collar of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ coat of mail. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Release me! And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry until they saw shadows on his face. Then he said: Woe to you! Release me! He said: No, by Allah! I will not release you until you are kind to my clients: four hundred unarmored men and three hundred mail-clad men, who have protected me from the red and the black; will you mow them down in a single morning? I am a man who fears the turning of fortune. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: They are yours."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: My father, Ishaq ibn Yasar, narrated to me from ʻUbadah ibn al-Walid ibn ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit who said: "When the Banu Qaynuqa' made war on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy clung to their cause and stood in their defence. ʻUbadah ibn al-Samit went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ—he was one of the Banu ʻAwf of the Khazraj, and they had the same alliance with him as with ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy—and he disengaged from them before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and disavowed before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and before His Messenger, their alliance, and said: O Messenger of Allah! I take Allah and His Messenger and the believers as my allies, and I disavow the alliance and the allegiance of these disbelievers... Concerning him and ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy the verses were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 56]."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Usamah ibn Zayd who said: "I entered with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ upon ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy to visit him when he was ill. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: I used to forbid you from loving the Jews. ʻAbd Allah said: Surely As'ad ibn Zurarah hated them, and he died." Abu Dawud also narrated it likewise.

Second: Some exegetes of the Zaydiyyah said: The fruits of the verse are rulings:

The first: It is not permissible to take the Jews or the Christians as allies. Al-Hakim said: What is meant is taking them as allies in religion. Al-Zamakhshari made the alliance to be in support and close friendship. He explained the obligation of separation from one who differs in religion, as has preceded. Distance and separation are recommended, since association has been permitted in some situations by consensus (*ijmaʻ*), namely where it does not imply love for them or that they are upon the truth.

The second ruling: The ruler may drop the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*) if he fears (consequences), or may postpone it. This was mentioned by Imam Yahya, al-Radi billah and al-Hakim, and this is derived from the occasion of revelation and from the Prophet's ﷺ leaving the Banu Qaynuqa' for the sake of ʻAbd Allah ibn Ubayy.

The third ruling: The validity of alliance among them for one another. ʻAli ibn Musa al-Qummi said: The verse indicates that they are one religious community, so intermarriage among them and inheritance are valid. The school (*madhhab*) holds otherwise. The indication for what was mentioned is open to interpretation, because it may mean that some of them are allies of others in opposition to the Muslims, or it may mean that some Jews are allies of some Jews.

The fourth ruling: Whoever allies with them is one of them. There is no dispute that he has become disobedient to Allah as they were disobedient. But how far does the limit of his disobedience reach? It has been disputed. It was said: The meaning of His saying "then he is one of them" is that his ruling is their ruling in disbelief, and this is a statement that approves them in their religion, so it is as if he has been content with it.
