It was said: Whoever allies with them in rejecting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was said: What is meant is that he is one of them in the obligation of hostility toward him and disavowal of him. Al-Hakim said: The indication of the verse is general; it does not show that he is a disbeliever unless it is taken to mean agreement in religion.

The fifth ruling: Al-Hakim mentioned that it is not permissible to seek help from them. We say: al-Radi billah mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ had made an alliance with the Jews against Quraysh and others until they broke it on the day of the Confederates (*al-Aḥzab*), and the Prophet ﷺ renewed the alliance between him and Khuzaʻah, until that became the cause of the conquest. Khuzaʻah were the trusted confidants of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, both its Muslims and its disbelievers. Al-Radi billah said: This is the apparent meaning of the statement of our forefathers, peace be upon them. ʻAli, peace be upon him, sought help against the killers of ʻUthman, and the Prophet ﷺ sought help from the hypocrites. Al-Radi billah said: It is permissible to seek help from sinners in fighting the wrongdoers, so this seeking of help is not allegiance.

Third note: In the preceding tafsir the following text appears: In the noble verse there are warnings against allying with the Jews and the Christians from several aspects:

The first: The prohibition by His saying: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], and all other disbelievers are included with them.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], meaning: the alliance among them is because of their unity in disbelief, while the believers are higher than them.

The third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever allies with them from among you, then indeed he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]. This is a strong threat, severity and emphasis, like his ﷺ saying: "Their fires must not see each other," and like his, peace be upon him, saying: "Do not seek light from the fire of the polytheists."

The fourth: What Allah informed, that He does not guide them.

The fifth: Describing them with wrongdoing, meaning: those who wronged themselves by allying with the disbelievers.

The sixth: That He, Exalted is He, informed that alliance with them is the custom of those in whose hearts is a sickness, that is, doubt and hypocrisy.

The seventh: What Allah, Exalted is He, informed of as the cause of those who ally with them, that it is fear of the turning of fortune, not that it is by permission from Allah or from His Messenger.

The eighth: Allah's cutting off what Satan made attractive to them of fear that the state of disbelief would return. So Exalted is He said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring the victory﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52]. The word "perhaps" (*ʻasā*), regarding Allah, Exalted is He, means the certainty of the attainment of the victory of Mecca or of the lands of polytheism.

The ninth: What Allah, Exalted is He, announced of their humiliation by His saying: ﴿Or a command from Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52]. It was said: the abasement of polytheism by the poll-tax (*jizyah*). It was said: the killing of Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir. It was said: that He would make the Muslims inherit their land and their homes.

The tenth: What Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned of the matter to which their condition leads, and that they will become regretful in the morning over what they concealed within themselves of their deceit toward the Muslims and their sincere advice to the disbelievers. It was said: over their hypocrisy. It was said: over their opposition to the disbelievers, and that is at the time of witnessing the punishment. It was said: in this world, by what they have come to of humiliation and disgrace.

The eleventh: What Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned of the wonder of the believers at the exposure of the enemies of Allah and their wickedness in their faith, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Are these..."﴾, the verse.

The twelfth: What Allah informed of their condition by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers﴾. It was said: they lost their share from their alliance with them. It was said: they destroyed themselves. It was said: they lost the reward of Allah. End.

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[54] ﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.﴾

When He, exalted is He, had earlier forbidden the taking of Jews and Christians as allies, and showed that allying with them leads to apostasy from the religion, by His words ﴿for indeed, he is of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51] and His words ﴿their deeds have become worthless﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 53], He began to explain the state of apostates in general.

He also emphasized His great power. He informed that whoever turns away from supporting His religion and establishing His law, Allah will replace him with one who is better than him in that regard, stronger in protection, and more upright in path. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people; then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away, O people, and bring others﴾ [an-Nisa': 133] (p-2033). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation﴾ [Fatir: 16] ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ [Fatir: 17], meaning: not impossible nor hard.

In this verse there are several issues:

**The first:** The scholars who investigate said: this verse is one of the unseen events that were foretold in the Qur'an before they occurred, and what was foretold came to pass accordingly. Therefore it is a miracle. It is narrated that eleven groups apostatized from Islam: three during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): (the Banu Mudlij), whose leader was Dhu al-Himar - with an unpointed (muhmalah) ḥāʾ, though some pointed it with a dotted letter - namely al-Aswad al-'Ansi - with the nūn, attributed to 'Ans, a tribe in Yemen. He had been a soothsayer, then claimed prophethood in Yemen, seized its lands, and expelled the agents of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen. Allah destroyed him at the hands of Fayrouz al-Daylami, who attacked him by night and killed him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed of his killing on the night he was killed, and the Muslims rejoiced. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away the next day, at the end of the month of Rabi' al-Awwal.

And (the Banu Hanifah), the people of Musaylimah: he claimed prophethood and wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "From Musaylimah, the Messenger of Allah, (p-2034) to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah. To proceed: the earth is half mine and half yours." He (peace be upon him) replied: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Musaylimah the liar. To proceed: the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the righteous." Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fought him with the armies of the Muslims, and he was killed at the hands of Wahshi, the killer of Hamzah. Wahshi used to say: "I killed the best of people in the Jahiliyyah and the worst of people in Islam." He meant: in my pre-Islamic time and my Islamic time.

And (the Banu Asad), the people of Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid: he claimed prophethood during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and his followers increased, and he died (p-2035) while still upon that. Abu Bakr sent Khalid, may Allah be pleased with both of them, against him, and he marched against him. Tulayhah fled to Syria after the battle. Then he embraced Islam, and his Islam was good.

Seven during the time of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him:
(Fazarah), the people of 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn.
And (the people of Ghatafan), the people of Qurrah ibn Salamah al-Shiri.
And (the Banu Sulaym), the people of al-Fuja'ah ibn 'Abd Yalil - with two yāʾs and two lāms, like Habil - an idol after which he was named.
And (the Banu Yarbu'), the people of Malik ibn Nuwayrah.
And (some of Tamim), the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir. She was a soothsayer, then claimed prophethood, and married herself to Musaylimah the liar. Then she embraced Islam, and her Islam was good.
And (Kindah), the people of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays.
And (the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il) in Bahrain, the people of al-Hutam - like Zufar - ibn Zayd. Allah sufficed them through Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

And one group during the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: (Ghassan), the people of Jabalah ibn al-Ayham. Al-Lutmah (the slap) gave him victory, and he was sent to the lands of the Romans after his Islam. The majority hold that he died upon his apostasy, though it has been said that he embraced Islam.

Al-Waqidi narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to the rabbis of Syria - when he joined them - (p-2036) a letter in which he said: Jabalah came to me with the notables of his people and embraced Islam, and I honored him. Then he went to Mecca and circumambulated, and a man from the Banu Fazarah stepped on his lower garment, so Jabalah struck him, breaking his nose and knocking out his front teeth. (It was also said: he gouged out his eye, and what will follow supports this.) The Fazari then sought redress against Jabalah before me. I ruled either for pardon or for retaliation. He said: "Will you take retaliation from me while I am a king and he is a commoner?" I said: "Islam has made you and him equal. You are not preferred over him except by well-being (i.e., by piety)."

Jabalah asked for a delay until the next day. When it was night, he rode off with his paternal cousins and joined Syria as an apostate.

It is narrated that he regretted what he had done and recited:
"I became a Christian after the truth, a shame, because of a slap, which was not harmful to me, had I endured it.
Then stubbornness of zealotry overtook me, so I sold for it my sound eye for a blind one.
Oh, would that my mother had not borne me, and would that I had endured the word which 'Umar said."

This is what is in al-Kashshaf and al-'Inayah.

Al-Khattabi said: The people of apostasy were of two kinds: a kind that apostatized from the religion, renounced the community, and turned to disbelief. This group is of two sects:
The first: the companions of Musaylimah the liar from the Banu Hanifah and others (p-2037) who affirmed his claim to prophethood, and the companions of al-Aswad al-'Ansi and those among the people of Yemen who responded to him. This group, entirely, denies the prophethood of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), claiming prophethood for another. Abu Bakr fought them until he killed Musaylimah at al-Yamamah, and al-'Ansi in Sana'a. Their hosts scattered and most of them perished.

The second sect: they apostatized from the religion. They denied the laws, abandoned the prayer, zakat, and other matters of the religion, and returned to what they had been upon in the Jahiliyyah. Thus, no one prostrated to Allah on earth except in three mosques: the Mosque of Mecca, the Mosque of Medina, and the Mosque of 'Abd al-Qays.

He said: The other kind are those who separated between the prayer and zakat, denying its obligation and the obligation of paying it to the imam. These, in reality, are the people of rebellion (ahl al-baghy). They were not called by this name specifically in that period, because they were absorbed among the people of apostasy, and the name was attributed generally to the people of apostasy, as it was the greater and more important of the two matters.

See the completion of this discussion in Nayl al-Awtar, in the Book of Zakat.

Al-Shawkani said: As for those among them who withheld zakat while remaining upon the core of the religion, they are people of rebellion. They were not named disbelievers individually, though apostasy was attributed to them because they shared with the apostates in withholding some of what they withheld of the religion's rights. Apostasy is a linguistic term: whoever turns away from a matter he was facing has apostatized from it. These people did turn away from obedience and withheld the right, and the name of praise and commendation was cut off from them, and the ugly name clung to them, because they shared with the people whose apostasy was true.

**The second:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿They love Him and He loves them﴾.

The position of the early generations (al-Salaf) regarding love attributed to Him, exalted is He, is that it is established for Him, exalted is He, without how (bila kayf) and without interpretation (bila ta'wil), and without any sharing with the created in any of its attributes, as was previously mentioned in al-Fatihah regarding ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah: 3].

So the interpretation of such a verse by al-Zamakhshari - that it means His granting them the best reward, honoring them, praising them, and being pleased with them (p-2038) - is an explanation by necessary consequence, a theological approach and not a Salafi one. Al-Zamakhshari also denied that the love of the servants for Allah is real, and explained it as obedience and seeking His pleasure. Ibn al-Munayyir, the author of al-Intisaf, refuted him, saying that this contradicts the apparent meaning. It is of the figurative speech in which the effect is named by the name of its cause, and figurative speech is not resorted to instead of the literal except when the literal is impossible. Let one examine the real meaning of love linguistically according to the rules, to see whether it is established for the servant and connected to Allah, exalted is He, or not. Love, linguistically, is the inclination of the one who has it toward something pleasurable. The pleasures that give rise to love are divided into those perceived through beauty, such as the pleasure of taste in food, the pleasure of sight and touch in beautiful forms, the pleasure of smell in fragrant scents, the pleasure of hearing in pleasant melodies, and into pleasures perceived by the intellect, such as the pleasure of status, leadership, knowledge, and what resembles them. It is thus established that among the pleasures that give rise to love are those that only the intellect perceives and not the senses. Then love necessarily varies according to the variation of its motivations. If love varies according to the variation of its motivations, then the pleasures of knowledge also vary according to the variation of the things known. There is nothing more perfect or more beautiful to know than the True Worshipped One. So the pleasure gained in knowing Him, exalted is He, and knowing His majesty and perfection, is greater. The love that arises from it is stronger, and when this love is attained, it prompts acts of obedience and conformity. From this it is concluded that the love of the servant (p-2039) is possible, indeed actual in every believer. It is one of the necessary conditions and prerequisites of faith. People vary in it according to the variation of their faith. If that is so, the love of the servant for Allah must be interpreted by its literal linguistic meaning, and obedience and acts of conformity are like a consequence of it and distinct from it. Do you not see the Bedouin who asked about the Hour, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What have you prepared for it?" He said: "I have prepared no great deed for it, but the love of Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "You will be with whom you love." This hadith clearly shows that what is understood from love for Allah is other than deeds and the commitment to acts of obedience, because the Bedouin negated the deeds and affirmed love, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) approved of that. Then, if it is established that the servant's love for Allah, exalted is He, is applied to its reality linguistically, then in language, when love is intensified, it is called ʿishq (passionate love). So whoever's love for Allah, exalted is He, is intensified, and the effects of its intensity appear upon him through devoting his times to His remembrance and obedience, his love may not be prevented from being called ʿishq, since ʿishq is nothing but extreme love. End of quote.

**The third:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾.

Ibn Kathir said: These are the attributes of the perfect believers: that one of them is humble toward his brother and ally, and firm and mighty against his opponent and enemy, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: Why was it not said "humble to the believers" (with li-, "for")? I say there are two aspects to it:
One: that humility (dhull) is made to imply tenderness and kindness, as if it were said: "inclining toward them in a manner of humbleness and modesty."
(p-2040) The second: that they, despite their nobility, high rank, and superiority over the believers, lower their wings to them. It was also read as "adhillatan wa a'izzatan" in the accusative, as circumstantial (ḥāl) constructions.

In al-Hawashi: the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ are a completion, because when He described them with humbleness, it might be imagined that they have some lowliness within themselves. So He said: "And yet they are mighty against the disbelievers," like the poet's words:
"They sit in their gatherings with dignity, and if a guest visits them, they are gentle."

The verse is used as evidence for the virtue of humility toward the believers and firmness against the disbelievers.

**The fourth:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 54 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that the *waw* (and) is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "they strive in struggle (*yujahidun*), and their condition in the striving is the opposite of the condition of the hypocrites, for they used to be allies of the Jews. When they went out with the army of the believers, they feared their Jewish allies, so they would do nothing for which they knew they would be blamed by them. As for the believers, they strove for the sake of Allah's countenance and never feared the blame of anyone who blames." It is also possible that the *waw* is for conjunction (*'atf*) upon the statement that among their attributes is striving in the way of Allah, and that they are steadfast (*silab*) in their religion. When they embark upon a matter of the religion, whether denouncing an evil (*inkar munkar*) or enjoining what is right (*amr bil-ma'ruf*), they persist in it like heated nails, and no speaker's words, no objection of an objector, and no blame of a blamer frightens them. Their earnestness in denouncing and their firmness in their affair is burdensome to the one who opposes them. The word *lawmah* (blame) denotes a single instance of blame, and in it, and in its indefiniteness (*tankir*), there are two forms of emphasis. It is as if it were said: "They never fear anything at all from the blame of any of the blamers." End of quotation.

In this there is the obligation to adhere to the truth even if a blamer blames for it. And that one who adheres to it, despite the blame, is raised to a higher station than one who adheres to it without blame, because Allah the Exalted praised the one whose condition is this. Also in it: fear of censure is not an excuse for abandoning a legislated command.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Dhar, who said: "My beloved friend (ﷺ) commanded me with seven things: he commanded me to love the poor and to be near them; he commanded me to look at one who is below me and not at one who is above me; he commanded me to uphold the ties of kinship even if they turn away from me; he commanded me not to ask anyone for anything; he commanded me to speak the truth even if it is bitter; he commanded me not to fear the blame of a blamer in the cause of Allah; and he commanded me to frequently say: 'There is no power and no strength except through Allah,' for indeed they are a treasure beneath the Throne."

Imam Ahmad also narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware! Let not the fear of people prevent any one of you from speaking the truth when he sees it or witnesses it. For it does not bring one closer to his term (of life), nor does it distance one from his provision, to speak the truth or to remind of something great."

It is also narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you belittle himself by seeing a matter in which Allah has a word to be said, and not saying it. Then on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to him: 'What prevented you from saying such and such?' He will say: 'The fear of people.' Then it will be said: 'It is I who is more deserving that you fear.'"

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took our pledge (*bay'ah*) to hear and obey in ease and in hardship, and not to dispute the affair with its people, and to speak the truth wherever we may be, not fearing in the cause of Allah the blame of a blamer."

The Fifth: His statement, exalted is He: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah﴾.

The reference is to what has been mentioned: Allah's love for them, their love for Allah, their humility toward the believers, their might against the disbelievers, their striving in the way of Allah, and their indifference to the blame of blamers. So all of what has been mentioned is the bounty of Allah, with which He favored His allies.

Al-Mahayimi said: As for the two loves, it is evident. Likewise the might against the disbelievers and the striving. As for the humility toward the believers, it is because it is a humility that necessitates elevation. As for not fearing blame, it is because of what it contains of establishing affection with Allah.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, that is, to whomever He wishes to bestow upon with increased honor, from the vastness of His generosity. And ﴿Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, that is, abundant in bounties, exalted is His majesty.

When He forbade allying with the Jews and the Christians, He pointed to those who are specifically to be taken as allies, so He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion of the Exalted's saying:

[55] ﴿Your only guardian is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who have believed — those who establish prayer and give zakah while bowing in worship.﴾

﴿Your only guardian is Allah﴾, the One who pours upon you every good. ﴿And His Messenger﴾, who is the intermediary. ﴿And those who have believed﴾, those specified for the guardianship of Allah and His Messenger through their deeds, because they are ﴿those who establish prayer﴾, which is the most comprehensive of the physical acts of worship, ﴿and give zakah﴾, which cuts off the love of wealth that draws one toward desires. ﴿And they are bowing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of both verbs, meaning: they do what was mentioned — establishing prayer and giving zakah — while they are humble and submissive before Allah, lowly and not self-admiring. For their appearance influences those who take them as allies, by aiding them in their allegiance to Allah and His Messenger.

(p-2043)The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious.﴾

﴿And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies﴾, so He aids and supports them; ﴿then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾ in the end, over His enemies.

Remarks:

First: The word (al-walī, "ally") is given in the singular and not the plural, although there are several allies, to indicate that allegiance belongs to Allah as a principle, and that allegiance to others follows from His allegiance, exalted and majestic is He. The meaning is therefore: and likewise His Messenger and those who believe.

Second: The fruit of this verse is the affirmation of allegiance to the believers and distance from allegiance to the disbelievers.

Third: Ibn Kathir said: Some people imagined that this clause, meaning His words ﴿while they bow﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 55], is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to His words ﴿and they give zakat﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 55], i.e., during their bowing. Had this been so, giving zakat during bowing would have been better than other times, since it would be praised, but no scholar among those we know of the leading imams of legal opinion holds this. Indeed, some of them mentioned in this regard a report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, that this verse was revealed concerning him: that a beggar passed by him while he was bowing, so he gave him his ring. Then Ibn Kathir narrated the aforementioned report from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Jarīr, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, and Ibn Mardawayh, and then said: None of it is authentic at all, due to the weakness of its chains and the obscurity of its narrators. End.

Al-Khafājī in the "Ḥawāshī al-Bayḍāwī" related that story at length from al-Ḥākim and others. Then he recited verses of Ḥassān ibn Thābit in it. Yet the signs of weakness, indeed fabrication, are not hidden in them, especially since the style of Ḥassān ibn Thābit, who was eminent in Arabic, is far removed from what is attributed to him. And what need is there to honour the virtue of ʿAlī, peace be upon him, with such feeble reports? His virtue is more famous than fire on a mountain.

(p-2044) al-Baghawī said: It was narrated from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Sulaymān who said: I asked Abū Jaʿfar, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Bāqir, about this verse: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 55]: who are they? He said: The believers. I said: Some people say it is ʿAlī. He said: ʿAlī is among those who believe.

Ibn Kathir said: It has already been mentioned in the reports we cited that this entire verse was revealed concerning ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, may Allah be pleased with him, when he disavowed the alliance with the Jews and was content with the allegiance of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.

Fourth: Those who held that this verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī, peace be upon him, and that he gave his ring in charity while bowing, as we have mentioned, concluded that a small action within prayer does not invalidate it, and that voluntary (nafl) charity is called zakat. This was transmitted by al-Suyūṭī in the "al-Iklīl" from Ibn al-Faras.

Some of the Zaydiyyah said: The fruit of the verse is the affirmation of allegiance to the believers, the demonstration of the virtue of the one concerning whom it was revealed, that it is permissible to pay zakat during prayer, and that it may be intended (as such). Likewise, the intention of fasting during prayer is valid, and a small action does not spoil the prayer. He said: This is derived from the occasion of its revelation, not from its wording. If it is said: Was zakat not obligatory upon ʿAlī, peace be upon him? We say: If it is established that it was revealed concerning him, it is all the more likely to be valid, and that it had become obligatory upon him.

In "al-Ghiyāḍah" it is said: If it is said: It has been narrated that it was of gold, and gold is forbidden to men; it is answered that this was in the early period of Islam and was then abrogated (naskh), or that this was among the special privileges of ʿAlī, peace be upon him. End.

al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: How can it be correct that it applies to ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, when the wording is in the plural? I say: It has been expressed in the plural form, although the occasion concerned one man only, in order to encourage people to act like him so that they may attain a reward like his, and to draw attention to the fact that the disposition of the believers must be of this degree (p-2045) of eagerness for righteousness, kindness, and seeking out the poor, to the extent that if a matter that does not admit delay pressed upon them while they were in prayer, they would not postpone it until they had finished it. End.

We have only mentioned this, despite its faults, in wonder at the strange extremes of inference. Al-Rāzī, may Allah have mercy on him, expanded considerably in debating the Shīʿah here, so let it be consulted, for it is a masterful discussion.

Fifth: His words, exalted is He, ﴿then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾, mean: then indeed they are the victorious.

He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun referring back to (man, "whoever"), to indicate the cause of the victory, which is that they are the party of Allah. It is as if it were said: Whoever takes these as allies, then they are the party of Allah, and the party of Allah are the victorious. This is also to draw attention to them, to exalt their station, to honour them with this name, and to imply a rebuke to whoever takes as allies other than them, that he is the party of Satan. The root of (ḥizb, "party") is a people who gather for the affair of their party. It has also been said: a ḥizb is a group among whom there is strength. Thus it is more specific than jamāʿah (group) and qawm (people).

Then He, exalted is He, pointed out that allegiance to others, if it is for the sake of drawing benefit, its harm is greater; and if it is for the sake of averting harm, the harm resulting from it does not match what it is meant to avert. Thus He, glorified is He, said:

[p. 2046]

The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying, exalted is He:

[57] ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and amusement, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, and the disbelievers. And fear Allah, if you are [truly] believers.﴾

﴿O you who have believed﴾, i.e., the requirement of your faith is to preserve the veneration of your religion. ﴿Do not take those who have taken your religion﴾, i.e., which is the capital of your perfections, through which your livelihood and your afterlife are ordered, which is the basis of your everlasting happiness and the cause of your nearness to your Lord, ﴿as a mockery﴾, i.e., as something made light of, ﴿and amusement﴾, i.e., as derision and laughter, in exaggerated contempt for it, to the point that they toy with the minds of its adherents. Then He clarified who these mockers were and specified them by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture before you and the disbelievers﴾. It is read in the accusative and the genitive (*al-nasb wa'l-jarr*), meaning the polytheists, as in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and from among those who associated partners." ﴿Allies﴾ in support and assistance.

He ordered the prohibition according to the description of their taking the religion as a mockery and amusement only to draw attention to the reason (*'illah*), and to make known that whoever has this character is deserving of hatred, enmity and repudiation. So how about allegiance? ﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., in this matter, by abandoning allegiance to them, or by abandoning the prohibited things in general, which includes abandoning allegiance to them in a primary way. ﴿If you are believers﴾, i.e., truly, for the requirement of faith necessarily entails fearing Allah.

Then, after their mockery of the religion in general, He clarified their mockery of a specific ruling from among the rulings of the religion, to show the completeness of their wretchedness, by His saying, glorified is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[58] ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and play. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

﴿And when you call to prayer﴾ i.e., when you summon them to it by the adhan (the call to prayer): ﴿they take it﴾ i.e., the prayer or the calling: ﴿in mockery and play﴾ by ridiculing it and laughing at it: ﴿That﴾ i.e., the taking: ﴿is because they﴾ i.e., because of the fact that they: ﴿are a people who do not reason﴾ i.e., the meanings of the worship of God. For folly leads to ignorance of the excellences of the truth and to mocking it. Had they possessed any reason at all, they would not have dared to commit such an enormity. Indeed, prayer is the most noble of acts of nearness to God, and the call contains noble meanings: the magnification of God in respect of His essence, His names, His attributes and His acts; the mention of His unity in respect of His essence and the non-differentiation of His names and attributes; the magnification of His Messenger in respect of his task of caring for the interests of this life and the Hereafter; and [the magnification of] prayer insofar as it is a link between the servant and God, and insofar as it brings the loftiest ranks, and the magnification of its aim, which is success in the outward and the inward, and what is the ultimate aim of it: nearness to God in respect of the greatness of His outward and inward [nature], and reaching His true unity. This was conveyed by al-Mahayimi.

(p-2047) Points of note:

First: concerning reports transmitted about this verse:

Abu al-Shaykh Ibn Hayyan related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had professed Islam and were hypocrites, and a man from among the Muslims used to befriend them. So God revealed: "O you who believe, do not take..." the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His words: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and play﴾, he said: There was a man from among the Christians in Medina who, when he heard the caller calling, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," would say: "May the liar be burned." One night, his servant brought fire to him while he was asleep and his family were sleeping, and a spark fell and burned the house, and he and his family were burned.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar mentioned in the "Sirah": "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the Ka'bah on the day of the Conquest, and with him was Bilal, and he commanded him to call the adhan. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, 'Attab ibn Usayd and al-Harith ibn Hisham were sitting in the courtyard of the Ka'bah. 'Attab ibn Usayd said: God has honoured Usayd by not letting him hear this, so that he would not hear from it what would anger him. Al-Harith ibn Hisham said: By God, if I knew that he was right, I would follow him. Abu Sufyan said: I will not say anything; if I spoke, these pebbles would inform on me. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) came out to them and said: 'I know what you said.' Then he related that to them. Al-Harith and 'Attab said: We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God; by God, no one who was with us had witnessed this, so we say: you were informed."

Imam Ahmad related from Abd Allah ibn Muhayriz, who was an orphan in the care of Abu Mahdhurah, who said: (p-2048) "I said to Abu Mahdhurah: O uncle! I am travelling to al-Sham, and I fear I will be asked about your call to prayer. So inform me. He told me that Abu Mahdhurah said to him: Yes! I went out with a group, and we were on part of the road to Hunayn. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from Hunayn, and we met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on part of the road. The Messenger of God's (ﷺ) muezzin called the prayer in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and we heard the voice of the muezzin while we were scattered. We shouted, imitating it and mocking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard the voice, so he sent for us, until we stood before him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Which of you is the one whose voice I heard raised?' All the people pointed to me, and they spoke the truth. He sent them all away and held me back, and said: 'Stand up and call the adhan.' I stood, and nothing was more hateful to me than the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor than what he commanded me; so I stood before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) himself taught me the call, and said: Say: 'God is greatest, God is greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but God. I bear witness that there is no god but God. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.' Then he said to me: 'Return and raise your voice.' Then he said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God. I bear witness that there is no god but God. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. Hasten to the prayer, hasten to the prayer, hasten to success, hasten to success. God is greatest, God is greatest. There is no god but God.' Then he came back to me when I had finished the call, and gave me a purse containing some silver, then he placed his hand on the forelock of Abu Mahdhurah and passed it over his face twice, then twice over his hands, then over his chest, then the hand of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reached the navel of Abu Mahdhurah. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'May God bless you.' I said: O Messenger of God! Command me to call the adhan in Mecca. He said: I have already commanded you to it. And all the aversion that I had had toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ) departed, and all of that returned as love for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So I went to 'Attab ibn Usayd, the governor of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I called the prayer with him by the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Second: the verse indicates the obligation of loyalty to the believers and enmity toward the disbelievers. What is meant by it is in matters of religion, as has preceded.

(p-2049) Third: it indicates that mockery of the religion is disbelief, and that jesting about it is like being serious about it.

In "al-Iklil" he said: The verse is a foundation for declaring takfir (excommunication) of one who mocks anything of the Shari'ah.

Fourth: it indicates that prayer has a call, which is the adhan, so it is its foundation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been said: in it is evidence for the establishment of the adhan by the text of the Book, not by dream alone. And when the Exalted forbade taking allies from among the mockers, He commanded that they be addressed by saying that the religion is exalted above what the mockery that issued from them could validly issue, and that what they committed be made manifest to them, and that they be silenced, by His saying, may He be exalted:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[59] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for nothing except that we have believed in Allah and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient."﴾

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾: they were described thus as a preliminary to rebuking them and holding them accountable for their disbelief in their own Scripture. That is: O companions of the Scripture, you who know the deficiencies and perfections, upon whose existence or absence ridicule is deserved. ﴿Do you resent us﴾, that is: what do you find fault with and disapprove of in us? ﴿except that we have believed in Allah﴾, and He is the head of all perfections, ﴿and in what was revealed to us﴾, and it is the foundation of beliefs, deeds and morals, ﴿and what was revealed before﴾, and it bears witness to what was revealed to us. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, that is: rebellious, departing from faith in what has been mentioned.

Points of benefit:

The first: The word (tanqimūn) was explained as (taʿībūn) "you find fault" and (tunkirūn) "you disapprove," because (niqmah) means disapproval by the tongue or punishment, as al-Raghib said, since one is only punished for what is disapproved of. It is thus in the sense of his saying:

"And we revile by deeds, not by speech."

Hence (intaqama minhu), its reflexive form, is good usage, in the sense of punishing him and requiting him. Otherwise, how would the reflexive differ from its root? So understand. (Naqama) occurs like (ʿalima yaʿlamu) and (ḍaraba yaḍribu), and this is the eloquent form, and it is transitive with (min) and (ʿalā). Abu Hayyan said: its original usage is to be transitive with (ʿalā). Then (iftaʿala), derived from it, is transitive with (min), because it includes the sense of befalling by something disliked, and here (faʿila) is used in the sense of (iftaʿala). Thus in "al-ʿInayah."

The second: In the verse there is a censure of the People of the Scripture for complete obstinacy and inversion, in that they made belief in what has been mentioned a cause for their resentment, although in itself it is a cause for its acceptance and approval. The meaning of the verse is: there is nothing for which the believers may be resented. Therefore there is no reason for ridicule. This is of the kind the Arabs intend in such usage: emphasizing negation and exaggerating it by affirming something which does not necessitate that affirmation, so that the negation is absolute. Scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-bayān) call such a figure "emphasis of praise through what resembles blame, and vice versa." Of the first kind is the verse:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."

Of the second kind is this verse and those like it. That is: it is not fitting for them to resent anything except this, and this does not necessitate that they resent anything; so there is nothing they may resent, and therefore they ought to believe in it and not disbelieve. In it there is also an allusion to their disbelief, and a reproach for their evil conduct in return for good.

The third: The attribution of wickedness to most of them, because whoever among them said what he said and induced others to obstinacy, seeking leadership, status, and taking bribes, is indeed most of them; and lest it be supposed that those among them who believed are included in that.

And His Exalted saying:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[60] ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and among whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the false deity (tāghūt). Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way."﴾

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that?"﴾ The addressee of the plural kāf (the "you") is the People of the Book mentioned earlier, or disbelievers in general, or believers. The one referred to by "that" is the majority of the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn). The singular demonstrative is used either because it can point to one thing or to many, or because it is interpreted as "the mentioned" and the like. In the speech there is an implied element, i.e., "something worse than the condition of these people." It is also said that the one referred to is the earlier generations who were the People of the Book, meaning that the predecessors are worse than the successors. Al-Zamakhshari took it as a reference to the object of their resentment (al-manqūm).

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud has well clarified this, saying: When he (peace be upon him) was commanded to hold them to account and rebuke them, by showing that the basis of their resentment toward the religion is only that it includes what makes its approval by them obligatory, and their disbelief in what is accepted by them, he (peace be upon him) was then commanded to rebuke them by showing that what truly deserves resentment and reproach is the distorted religion they follow.

Within the explanation he disparages their crimes and what befell them of its consequences and punishments, by way of allusion, lest explicit statement lead them to persist in stubbornness and obstinacy. Before the explanation he addresses them with what indicates the great importance of what is to be explained, and calls them to attend to receiving it, through the interrogative sentence that arouses eagerness for the one informed of, and through the word "tanbi'ah" (informing), which suggests that it is a grave matter, since "naba'" is news that has significance and weight. Since the basis of resentment is the evil of the one resented, whether in reality or in belief, and mere resentment does not at all define evil, it was said "something worse than that" and not "something more resented than that," to affirm the evil of what will be mentioned and to strengthen that affirmation. It is also said that this was said because of its occurrence in the speech of the addressees, when "a group of Jews came and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about his religion, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'We believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us...' up to His saying: '(and we are submitting to Him).' When they heard the mention of 'Isa (peace be upon him), they said: We know of no evil worse than your religion." The evil is considered in relation to the religion, though it is free of any taint of evil altogether, in accommodation to their false claim that it is entirely evil, so that it may establish that their religion is worse than every evil. That is: "Shall I inform you of what is truly worse than what you believe to be evil, even though in itself it is pure good?" End of quotation.

His saying ﴿as requital (mathūbah) from Allah﴾ means: a established reward with Allah. Al-Raghib said: "Thawab" is what returns to a person as recompense for his deeds. It is so named with the notion that what he did returns to him, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7], and He did not say "will see its recompense." "Thawab" is used of good and evil, but the more common and familiar usage is for good. Likewise "mathūbah," which is a mimi noun with the same meaning. Since it is specifically used for good, it is here used for punishment, in the manner of the poet's line:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow,"

in sarcasm. It is put in the accusative as a specifier (tamyīz) of "bi-sharr."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and among whom He made apes and swine﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "sharr," with an elided genitive, i.e., "with the worse of the people of that, those whom Allah has cursed," or "with the worse of that the religion of those whom Allah has cursed," or it is an omitted predicate, i.e., "it is those whom Allah has cursed, and they are the Jews, whom Allah has removed far from His mercy and against whom He was wrathful because of their disbelief and their immersion in sins after the clarity of the signs, and some of them were transformed into apes and swine, and they are the people of the Sabbath, as was explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah." ﴿And who worshipped the false deity (tāghūt)﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause of "man" (those who). The intended meaning of "tāghūt" is the calf, or the soothsayers, and everyone who obeyed them in disobedience to Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., the cursed and transformed ones: ﴿are worse in position (makān)﴾. Ascribing evil to the place is a metonymy for ascribing it to its people, like the saying "Peace upon the lofty assembly" and "Glory is between its two cloaks," as if their evil had affected their place, or had grown so great that it became embodied! It is also said that by "makān" is meant the abode and station to which their affair returns, as in His saying: ﴿worse in position (makān)﴾, and that is their final destination, meaning Hell.

﴿And further astray from the right way (sawā' al-sabīl)﴾, i.e., more greatly astray from the straight path.

Then He, Exalted, explained the signs of the completeness of their evil and error by His saying:

(p-2054) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," while they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it. And Allah is most knowing of what they were concealing.﴾

﴿And when they come to you﴾ means the lowly among the Jews; it is also said: the hypocrites. ﴿They say, "We believe"﴾ i.e., in you and your description, that it is in our Book. ﴿While they had entered﴾ to you, ﴿with disbelief﴾, the disbelief of secrecy (kufr al-sirr). ﴿And they had left with it﴾ i.e., from your presence, ﴿with it﴾ i.e., with the disbelief of secrecy, so they remain persistent in it. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they were concealing﴾ i.e., of the disbelief, and in it is a warning (wa'id) to them.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[62] ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin and aggression and their consumption of the illegal earnings. Wretched is what they have been doing.﴾

﴿And you see many of them﴾, i.e., of the Jews, ﴿hastening toward sin﴾, i.e., the unlawful, such as lying and disobedience, without concern before Allah or before people; ﴿and aggression﴾, i.e., oppression and transgression against people; ﴿and their consumption of the illegal earnings﴾, i.e., what is forbidden, such as bribery (al-rashā). He singled it out for mention although it is included within sin, in order to emphasize its ugliness. In this there is evidence for the prohibition of bribery (al-rishā), because it was reported concerning their leaders that they would take bribes to alter the ruling. ﴿Wretched is what they have been doing﴾ of what has been mentioned.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[63] ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their saying sin and their consuming of illicit gain? Surely evil is what they have been doing.﴾

﴿لَوْلا﴾ (*lawla*) means *halla* (why not, if only): ﴿the rabbaniyyun (the pious ascetics among them and the worshippers)﴾ and ﴿the ahbar (the scholars)﴾ [p-2055] ﴿forbid them from their saying sin﴾, meaning lying, ﴿and their consuming of illicit gain﴾, meaning bribery, which corrupts the affairs of the whole world. ﴿Surely evil is what they have been doing﴾ in their asceticism and their learning that is not for the sake of God's religion, or in their abandoning of forbidding them. This censure directed at the elite is more emphatic than what is said about the common people, for two reasons. First, when He expressed the blameworthy reality of the perpetrators of evil deeds by the word "doing" in His saying ﴿Surely evil is what they have been doing﴾, and expressed their abandoning of condemnation of them by describing it as a craft in His saying ﴿Surely evil is what they have been doing﴾, this censure became more severe. For He made the blameworthy thing a craft for them and for the leaders, and a constant profession in which they are more capable than the perpetrators of evil deeds in their actions.

This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement: "It is as if they were made more sinful than the perpetrators of evil deeds, because every doer is not called a craftsman, and not every action is called a craft, until one becomes skilled in it, trained in it, and is attributed to it. It seems the meaning in this is that those who commit sin have desire with them, which calls them to it and drives them to commit it, whereas the one who forbids has no desire in the action of another. So if he neglects condemnation, he is in a worse state than the one who commits the sin." Then al-Zamakhshari said: "By my life! This verse is one that startles the listener and reproaches the scholars for their laxity." End of quotation.

In *al-Iklil*: "In this verse is the obligation of forbidding evil upon the scholars, and that this obligation is specific to them."

al-Baydawi said: "In it is an exhortation to their scholars to forbid that, for *lawla* when it precedes the past tense conveys reproach, and when it precedes the future tense conveys exhortation."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this verse."

al-Dahhak said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more frightening to me than it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Yahya ibn Ya'mur, who said: "'Ali ibn Abi Talib delivered a sermon, praised God and extolled Him, then said: 'O people! Those before you were destroyed only because they committed sins and the rabbaniyyun and the ahbar did not forbid them. When they persisted, punishments seized them. So enjoin the good and forbid evil before there befalls you what befell them. Know that enjoining the good and forbidding evil do not cut off provision, nor do they bring near a term of life.'"

The Imam Ahmad narrated from Jarir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no people among whom there is one who does evil deeds while they are more powerful and more able to prevent him, and they do not change it, but God will afflict them with a punishment from Him."

The wording of Abu Dawud from him, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no man who is among a people in whom evil deeds are done, while they are able to change it against him, and they do not change it, but God will afflict them with a punishment before they die."

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[64] ﴿The Jews say, "Allah's hand is chained up." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills. What has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. We have placed enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it. They strive throughout the land for corruption, but Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾

﴿The Jews say, "Allah's hand is chained up."﴾ Al-Tabarani and Ibn Ishaq related from Ibn Abbas, who said: A Jewish man called Shas ibn Qays said, "Your Lord is miserly; He does not spend." So this verse was revealed.

Abu al-Shaykh related through another chain from him that it was revealed concerning Finhas, the chief of the Jews of Bani Qaynuqa. It has already been mentioned that he is the one who said, "Allah is poor and we are rich," and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) struck him.

So the verse here may refer to what was related about him through that statement. And Allah knows best.

Since his people did not denounce the one who said it and were pleased with him, that grave statement was attributed to all of them, as one says, "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the actual killer was only one of them.

The phrase "chaining the hand and extending it" is a well-known figurative usage (majaz) for stinginess and generosity. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully﴾ [al-Isra' 29]. They said: the reason for this usage is that the hand is the instrument of most actions, especially of giving and spending wealth. So they used the name of the cause for the thing caused, and attributed generosity and stinginess to the hand, the fingers, the palm, and the fingertips. Thus a generous person is called "one whose palm overflows," "one whose hand is open," "one whose fingers are smooth and whose fingertips are clean." A stingy person is called "one whose fingers are tight," "one whose palm is closed," "one whose fingertips are knotted."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their hands are chained﴾ is an invocation against them, either for stinginess, or for poverty and destitution, or for the literal chaining of their hands, meaning their hands are bound to their necks, as captives in this world and dragged to the Fire in the Hereafter.

﴿And they are cursed﴾ means they are removed from mercy, so they are not granted success in repentance.

﴿For what they said﴾ refers to the shameful word which is not valid concerning Allah, either literally or figuratively.

﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ means with various kinds of diverse gifts. He used the dual form "hands" for emphasis in refuting and negating stinginess from Him, Exalted is He, and affirming the utmost generosity, since the most a generous person gives of his wealth is to hand it over with his two hands. ﴿He spends however He wills﴾ is an emphasis on what precedes it, indicating that His spending follows His will, which is founded on wisdom, and upon which the affairs of this life and the Hereafter depend.

Here there are several discussions:

The first: What al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him claim, that affirming a hand for Allah is not valid literally, is a theological tendency of the Mu'tazilah.

The Imam Ibn Abd al-Barr said in his commentary on the Muwatta': The People of the Sunnah agree on affirming all the attributes mentioned in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, believing in them, and understanding them literally rather than figuratively, except that they do not specify the modality of any of them (ta'yif) nor define any attribute as limited. As for the people of innovation, the Jahmiyyah and all the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij, they all deny them and do not take any of them literally. They claim that whoever affirms them is a likener (mushabbih). In the view of those who affirm them, they are negators of the One Worshipped. The truth lies in what those who say what Allah's Book and His Messenger's Sunnah have stated have said, and they are the Imams of the community.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said in his book "Ibtal al-Ta'wil" (Refuting Figurative Interpretation): It is not permissible to reject these reports or to occupy oneself with interpreting them. It is obligatory to take them at their apparent meaning, that they are Allah's attributes, not to be likened to the attributes of created beings described by them, and one must not believe in any resemblance in them. Then he said: What proves the refutation of interpretation is that the Companions and those after them among the Successors took them at their apparent meaning and did not engage in interpreting them or diverting them from their apparent sense. Had interpretation been permissible, they would have been first to it, for it removes resemblance and eliminates doubt.

The Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book "al-Ibanah," in the chapter "Discussion of the Face, the Two Eyes, the Sight, and the Two Hands," and he cited the verses on this. He refuted the interpreters with a lengthy discourse that this place cannot accommodate. Such as his saying:
"If we are asked: Do you say Allah has two hands? It is said: We say that, and His saying indicates it: ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath 10], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What I have created with My two hands﴾ [Sad 75]. And it has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: (Allah wiped the back of Adam with His hand and brought forth from it his offspring)." And there has come in the transmitted report from the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah created Adam with His hand, created the Garden of Eden with His hand, wrote the Torah with His hand, and planted the tree of Tuba with His hand." It is not permissible in the language of the Arabs, nor in the custom of the people of speech, for a speaker to say, "I did such and such with my two hands," meaning the blessing. And since Allah addressed the Arabs in their language and in what is understood in their speech and intelligible in their discourse, and since it is not permissible in the discourse of the people of the language for a speaker to say, "I did it with my two hands," meaning the blessing, it is invalid that the meaning of His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, "with My two hands" is "the blessing." He mentioned a lengthy discussion establishing this and similar points.

Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani said in his book "al-Ibanah":
"If one says: What is the proof that Allah has a face and a hand? It is said to him: ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 27], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad 75]. He affirmed for Himself a face and a hand. If one says: What prevents you from saying that His face and hand are a body part, since you do not understand a face or hand except as a body part? We say: That does not follow, just as it does not follow—if we do not conceive of a living, knowing, capable being except as a body—that we and you must judge Allah, glorified is He, by that."

Shaykh Taqi al-Din said in "al-Risalah al-Madaniyyah": The position of the People of Hadith—they are the Salaf (the early generations) of the three best centuries and those who follow their path among the later generations—is that these hadiths are to be let pass as they came, believed in and affirmed, and protected from interpretation that leads to negation (ta'til) and from modality that leads to likening (tamthil). Many who have related the consensus of the Salaf, among them al-Khattabi, have stated the Salaf's position as that they are to be taken according to their apparent meaning with negation of modality and likeness from them. That is because discourse about the attributes is a branch of discourse about the Essence; it follows its pattern and is modeled after it. So when affirming the Essence is affirming its existence and not affirming its modality, likewise affirming the attributes is affirming their existence and not affirming their modality. End of quotation.

May Allah have mercy on the Imam al-Sarsari al-Ansari when he says in a qasidah:
"Speech on the basis of Mu'tazilism is a blind pit, in which the deviant and the rebellious have settled.
They rushed upon the paths of guidance with their minds, by night, and they spread corruption throughout the lands and wrought havoc.
Deaf, when the hadith is mentioned to them, they flee as if they never heard it, and they warble.
Strike for them the likeness of donkeys that saw the lions of the thicket, so they scattered, fleeing from them.
... (until he said):
He calls whoever follows the hadith a likener—far-fetched! He is not a likener who transmits with a chain.
But he narrates the hadith as it came, without interpretation and without bending it."

The second: Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related regarding the meaning of the verse from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The right hand of Allah is full; spending does not diminish it. It pours forth night and day. Have you considered what He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not diminished what is in His right hand. His Throne was over the water, and in His other hand is the gift—or the withholding—He raises and lowers." And he said: "Allah, Exalted is He, says: Spend, and I will spend upon you."

The third: In this verse is evidence for the permissibility of cursing the Jews. There is no doubt that this is permissible.

The fourth: This verse is a foundation for declaring disbelief in whoever utters from his mouth, concerning the Creator, Exalted is He, something that implies deficiency. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it will surely increase many of them﴾, that is, of the Jews: ﴿in what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, which comprises the most comprehensive goods: ﴿in transgression﴾, that is, aggression against people, or persistence in denial: ﴿and disbelief﴾, that is, within themselves, after their disbelief and transgression, through distortion and first taking bribes. This is the attribution of the act to its cause, meaning they increase in transgression and disbelief because of what was sent down, as He said: ﴿So it added to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah 125].

Ibn Kathir said: That is, what Allah has given you, O Muhammad, of blessing becomes a calamity for your enemies among the Jews and their likes. Just as the believers increase through it in faith, righteous deeds, and beneficial knowledge, the disbelieving envious ones who oppose you and your community increase through it in transgression—which is exaggeration and going beyond limits in matters—and in disbelief, meaning denial, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and healing, but for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat 44], and He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra' 82].

﴿And We have placed enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection﴾: Thus their words are always divergent and their hearts scattered; no agreement or mutual support arises among them.

Al-Shahrastani mentioned that they split into more than seventy sects. When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, the Jews were three tribes around Madinah: Bani Qaynuqa, Bani al-Nadir, and Bani Qurayzah. The details of their affairs and the Prophet's ﷺ conduct regarding them are set out at length in Ibn al-Qayyim's "Zad al-Ma'ad," so refer to it.

Al-Razi said: Know that the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He, Exalted is He, made clear that they deny his prophethood after the proofs of its truth became evident, out of envy and out of love of status, following, wealth, and leadership. Then He, Exalted is He, made clear that when they preferred this world over the Hereafter, Allah, as He deprived them of the happiness of religion, likewise deprived them of the happiness of this world, because each group among them remained persistent in its doctrine and statement, exaggerating in its support and disparaging everything else among the other doctrines and statements, in order to magnify itself and promote its doctrine. Thus that became the cause of a fierce hostility among their sects and factions, and the matter ended with some of them declaring others to be disbelievers and some of them waging war against others.

There are two interpretations of the verse:
One: that it refers to what is between the Jews and the Christians, because they were mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians [as allies]﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51]. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid, because they are the ones spoken of in His saying: ﴿And the Jews said﴾.
The second: that it refers to what is among the sects of the Jews specifically.

I say: this is the apparent meaning. If you say: this meaning also exists among the sects of the Muslims, so how can it be a fault of the People of the Book such that they are blamed for it? I say: the innovation of division that occurred among the Muslims arose only after the era of the Prophet ﷺ and the era of the Companions and the Successors.

As for the first generation, none of that existed among them. Therefore it was fitting to make it a fault of the People of the Book in that age in which the Qur'an was revealed.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 64 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.﴾ That is: every time they intend war against the Messenger (ﷺ) and the stirring up of evil against him, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, repels them by causing discord to arise among them, by which He restrains their evil from him. Or (it means): every time they intended war against anyone, they were defeated and subdued, and no victory from Allah, exalted is He, ever stood for them against anyone at all. Thus, "kindling the fire" is a metaphor (kinayah) for intending war, because that was their custom, and the fires of the Arabs are well known; this is one of them. The extinguishing of the fire, in the first sense, is an expression for repelling their evil, and in the second sense, for their defeat. And "for war" (li-l-harb) is either connected to "kindled" (awqadu), or related to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "a fire" (naran), meaning: a fire belonging to war. ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾ That is: for corruption, or as those causing corruption; that is, they exert effort in plotting against Islam and its people, hindering people from it, and stirring up strife. ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ That is: whoever has corruption as his attribute. The "al-" (of al-mufsidin) is either for the genus, and they are included in it primarily, or for a specific known group. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to give the reason and to show that they are firmly established in corruption.

(p-2064) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[65] ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed and feared Allah, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss.﴾

﴿And if the People of the Scripture﴾, i.e., despite what We have enumerated of their misdeeds, ﴿had believed﴾ in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in what he brought, ﴿and feared Allah﴾, i.e., refrained from committing major sins, ﴿We would have removed from them their misdeeds﴾, i.e., their sins, ﴿and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss﴾ in the Hereafter, along with the Muslims. This contains an announcement of the enormity of the disobedience of the Jews and Christians and the abundance of their misdeeds. It also indicates the vastness of Allah's mercy and His opening the door of repentance to every sinner, however great his sins are and however far they reach, even to the extent of the misdeeds of the Jews and Christians, and that Islam effaces what came before it, however great it may be. And that a People of the Scripture does not enter Paradise unless he embraces Islam.

Al-Zamakhshari (a famous exegete and linguist) said: In it is [the proof] that faith does not save nor bring happiness unless it is accompanied by piety, as al-Hasan [al-Basri] said: "This is the pillar, so where are the tent-ropes?" End of quote.

Nasir al-Din [Ibn al-Munayyir] said in *al-Intisaf*: He seizes the opportunity from the apparent meaning of this verse and makes it a proof for his principle, that mere faith does not save from eternal abiding in the Fire until piety is added to it, because Allah, exalted is He, made the combination in this verse a condition for expiation and for admission into Paradise. Its apparent meaning is that if the two do not come together, neither expiation nor admission into Paradise occurs. But how could he [al-Zamakhshari] do that? There is consensus and agreement between the two groups, the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah) and the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that held that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position), that mere faith effaces what came before it and wipes it out, as the text has stated. So if we suppose that someone who entered faith died immediately after entering it, he would be, by agreement, like the day his mother bore him, with his sins expiated and judged to be admitted to Paradise. This shows that the combination of the two matters is not a condition. This is if by piety is meant the deeds. But if piety, in its original sense, is the fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then this meaning is established for every believer, even if he commits major sins, and in that case the aim of al-Zamakhshari is not achieved from it.

(p-2065) This is nothing but obstinacy and stubborn insistence in opposing the belief derived from his words, peace be upon him: "Whoever says there is no god but Allah enters Paradise, even if he commits adultery or steals." He (ﷺ) repeated it several times, then said: "Even if the nose of Abu Dharr is rubbed in the dust." This was when [Abu Dharr] questioned him about it, may Allah be pleased with him. And we say: "Even if the nose of the Qadariyyah is rubbed in the dust." End of quote.

[p-2066] **On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[66] ﴿Had they truly established the Torah and the Gospel, and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do.﴾

﴿Had they truly established the Torah and the Gospel﴾ means: they would have established their rulings, their limits, and what they contain of the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The root meaning of *iqamah* (establishing) is steadiness in a place. Then the establishing of a thing was used metaphorically for fulfilling its due right. ﴿And what was revealed to them from their Lord﴾ means: they would have made clear what their Lord had made clear to them in the Torah and the Gospel. It is also said: they would have affirmed the whole of the Books and the Messengers from their Lord. It is also said: it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ means: He would have widened their provision for them, by pouring upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, increasing the fruit of the trees and the yield of the crops, or granting them gardens with ripe fruit, so that they would pick it from the top of the tree and gather what fell to the ground. To take ﴿from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ to mean the rains and rivers by which their sustenance is obtained is far from the sense of eating. The closest interpretations are the three mentioned earlier. By this, the Exalted has drawn attention to the fact that the hardship and straitness that befell them is only due to the evil of their disobedience and their disbelief, not to any deficiency in the overflowing bounty of the Generous, exalted is He. The verse indicates that acting in obedience to God, exalted is He, is a cause of abundance in provision, and it is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And had the people of the towns believed and been God-fearing, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]; ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]; ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]; ﴿So I said: Ask your Lord for forgiveness, for He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10], and the verses that follow; and ﴿And that if they had remained upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16].

[p-2067] Imam Ahmad narrated from Ziyad ibn Labid that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned something and said: 'And that is at the time of the disappearance of knowledge.' He said: We said: 'O Messenger of God! How can knowledge disappear while we recite the Qur'an and teach it to our sons, and our sons teach it to their sons until the Day of Resurrection?' He said: 'May your mother be bereaved of you, O son of Ummi Labid! I used to consider you among the most learned men of Medina. Are these Jews and Christians not reciting the Torah and the Gospel, yet they gain nothing from what is in them?'"

In the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim: "Are the Torah and the Gospel not in the hands of the Jews and the Christians? Of what benefit were they to them when they abandoned the command of God?" Then he recited: ﴿Had they truly established the Torah and the Gospel﴾, the verse.

﴿Among them is a community﴾ means: a group. ﴿Moderate﴾ means: just and upright. They are those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Abdullah ibn Salam, al-Najashi, and Salman. ﴿And many of them—evil﴾ means: wretched is ﴿what they do﴾, namely, of distorting the truth, turning away from it, and excessive enmity. The verse is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and act justly by it﴾ [al-A'raf: 159].

The discussion of the Qur'anic statement, the Almighty's words:

[67] ﴿O Messenger! Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And God will protect you from the people. Indeed, God does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

﴿O Messenger!﴾ He (ﷺ) is addressed with the title of messenger, to honour him and to signal that this title is one of the reasons for carrying out what he was commanded regarding conveyance: ﴿Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, including what details the evil deeds of the disbelievers and their fighting, and the call to Islam, without being concerned about anyone in conveying it and without fear that some harm will befall you. ﴿And if you do not﴾, that is, if you do not convey all that you are commanded to convey, concealing some of their evil deeds, ﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾, that is, any part of what you were sent with. This is because some of it is no more deserving of being delivered than some other part. So if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you have neglected to deliver all of it, just as whoever does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it.

Al-Qasimi said in al-Intisaf (a commentary by Ibn al-Munayyir): Since failing to convey the message is a matter known to people and firmly established in their minds as grave and hideous, and one for which its perpetrator is blamed, and since even a scholar's failure to spread knowledge is a dreadful thing, let alone the concealment of the message by the Messenger, [the verse] dispenses with mentioning the additional elements by which the condition and the consequence differ, because the consequence is attached to the condition in people's minds. Everyone who hears of the failure to convey the message understands the threat and warning behind it. This style is excellent in the Noble Book, in that the condition is stated in general terms with His words ﴿And if you do not﴾, and He did not say: "If you do not convey the message, then you have not conveyed the message." So that the wording varies, and this verbal variation, although the meaning is one, has greater splendour and clearer grace than the repetition of the same word in the condition and the consequence. This section is like the essence of the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan).

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ are a promise from Him, the Exalted, to guard him from any harm reaching his noble person. It motivates him to be earnest in what he was commanded regarding conveyance and not to care about their enmity and their plotting. ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a reason for His protection, that is, He does not guide them to the path of harming you, so what excuse do you have for being wary of them?

Remarks:

The first: There is no doubt that the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed the complete message, discharged it in the fullest manner, and stood firm in hardships, while he was sought after, and endured adversity and distress while he was afflicted and wronged. He met in Mecca from the Quraysh what would turn the forelocks grey and break the strongholds. Despite his weakness, he endured with the patience of one who prevails, and stood firm with the steadfastness of one who holds sway. Then he rose to strive against the enemies, though they had surrounded his sides and encircled his flanks, and by his heavy blows against the enemies he became feared, and through awe of him he was made victorious, until the lamp of religion blazed and people entered the religion of God in multitudes.
