Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her, that she said to Masruq: "Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed anything of what God sent down to him has lied, for God says: ﴿O Messenger! Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, and the verse [continues]."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also from her, she said: "If Muhammad (ﷺ) had concealed anything of the Qur'an, he would have concealed this verse: ﴿And you would conceal within yourself what God is to disclose, and you feared the people, while God has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]."

Al-Bukhari and others related from Abu Juhayfa who said: I said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "Do you have anything of revelation other than what is in the Qur'an?" He said: "No, by Him who split the grain and created the soul! Except an understanding that God gives a man concerning the Qur'an, and what is in this sheet." I said: "And what is in this sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (diya), the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever."

Al-Bukhari said: Al-Zuhri said: "From God is the message, upon the Messenger is the conveyance, and upon us is submission."

Ibn Kathir said: His community has testified that he (ﷺ) conveyed the message and discharged the trust, and he had them affirm this in the greatest of gatherings, in his sermon on the Day of the Farewell Pilgrimage, when there were some forty thousand of his Companions. As established in Sahih Muslim from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said in his sermon that day: 'O people! You will be asked about me, so what will you say?' They said: 'We testify that you conveyed, discharged, and advised.' He then began raising his head and his hand towards the sky and pointing it at them, saying: 'O God! Have I conveyed?'"

Imam Ahmad related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said on the Farewell Pilgrimage: 'O people! What day is this?' They said: 'A sacred day.' He said: 'What land is this?' They said: 'A sacred land.' He said: 'What month is this?' They said: 'A sacred month.' He said: 'Indeed your wealth, your blood, and your honour are sacred to you, like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this land of yours, in this month of yours.' He repeated it several times. Then he raised his finger to the sky and said: 'O God! Have I conveyed?' several times. (Ibn ʿAbbas said: By God, it was indeed a charge to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.) Then he said: 'Let the one present convey it to the absent. Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking one another's necks!'" Al-Bukhari related something similar.

The second: The words of the Exalted ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ contain a great miracle for His Messenger (ﷺ).

Imam al-Mawardi said in his book Aʿlam al-Nubuwwa (The Signs of Prophethood), in the eighth chapter on his miracles, his protection (ʿisma) (ﷺ). His text reads:

"After the establishment of his prophethood through the miracle of the Qur'an and its sufficiency as proof, God the Exalted manifested to His Messenger (ﷺ) some of the signs of his prophethood, as an increase in insight, by which whoever is dull of perception is confronted, and to which whoever has weak insight yields. So that the miraculousness of the Qur'an is apprehended through penetrating reflections, by contemplation and reasoning, and the miraculousness that is visible is known through the initial senses, as a precaution and a support. Thus the dull is overcome by his imagination and his sight, and the intelligent is confuted by his understanding and his clarity. For each group of people has a path that is closer to them and more attractive to them, so what unites the groups is the clearest way and the most general proof. Among his miracles is his protection from his enemies, who were a vast multitude and a great number, and who were in the fullest rage against him and the strongest pursuit of his life. Yet he was among them, unhindered and dominant, mixing with them and outnumbering them, their eyes glancing at him sideways, and their hands recoiling from him in terror. His companions had emigrated from him out of fear, until he completed his term among them thirteen years. Then he went out from them unharmed, neither in soul nor in body. This was nothing but a divine protection which God promised, and He fulfilled it when He said: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾, and He protected him from them."

Then al-Mawardi, may God have mercy on him, said: "The Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (the council house). Among them was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kalada, who was the leader of the people, and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿra, who was the poet of the people, supported him. He urged them to kill Muhammad (ﷺ) and said to them: 'Death is better for you than life.' Some of them said: 'How shall we act?' Abu Jahl said: 'Is Muhammad anything but one man? And are the Banu Hashim anything but one tribe among the tribes of Quraysh? Is there not among you one who would renounce life, kill Muhammad, and relieve his people?' He lowered his head for a while. They said: 'Whoever does this will be a leader.' Abu Jahl said: 'Muhammad is no stronger than any man among us. I will go to him and split his head with a stone. If I am killed, I will have relieved my people, and if I survive, that is what I prefer.' They set out on that plan. When they gathered at al-Hatim, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out to them. They said: 'He has come.' He advanced from the Corner and stood to pray. They looked at him prolonging his bowing and prostration. Abu Jahl said: 'I will stand and relieve you of him.' He took a large stone, approached the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was prostrating, not turning and not fearing him, though he could see him. When he came close, he trembled and let the stone fall on his own foot. He returned with his fingers crushed and trembling, and his veins dazed. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was still prostrating. Abu Jahl said to his companions: 'Take me back to you.' They held him, and he had fainted for an hour. When he recovered, his companions said to him: 'What has happened to you?' He said: 'When I drew near to him, a stallion with its mouth open came at me from his head, and bit me with its teeth. I could not restrain myself. I see Muhammad as shielded.' One of his companions said to him: 'O Abu al-Hakam! You have grown fond of life and loved it, and you have turned back.' He said: 'You do not deceive me about myself.' Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: 'If he returns tomorrow, I will be the one for him.' They said to him: 'O Abu Sahm! If you do this, you will surely lead.' When the next day came, they gathered at al-Hatim waiting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When he appeared before them, they all rose together and rushed at him. He took a handful of dust and said: 'May the faces be disfigured.' And he said: 'Ha Mim. They will not be helped,' and they dispersed from him."

This was a divine repelling in which one trusts from God, the Exalted. He endured it until God protected him, and it was among the strongest evidence of his truthfulness.

(Among his signs): Quraysh sought help from Mʿamar ibn Yazid, who was the bravest of his people, and complained to him about the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Banu Kinana would act according to his opinion and obey his command. When they complained to him, he said: "I am coming to you with three hundred men, and I will relieve you of him. I have twenty thousand armed men, and I do not see this clan of the Banu Hashim being able to fight me. If they ask me for blood-money, I will give them ten blood-moneys, for my wealth is ample." He used to carry a sword seven spans long and one span wide, and his story among the Arabs is famous for courage and valour. On the day he promised Quraysh, he put on his weapons and wore two coats of mail. He met them at al-Hatim while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was praying in the Hijr. He knew of this, yet he did not turn, was not shaken, and did not shorten the prayer. It was said to him: "This is Muhammad prostrating." He rushed towards him, having drawn his sword, and came near him. When he came close, he threw away his sword and turned back. When he reached the gate of al-Safa, he stumbled over his coat of mail and fell, then got up, with his face bleeding from the stones, running as fast as possible, until he reached al-Batha without looking back. They gathered around him, washed the blood from his face, and said: "What has befallen you?" He said: "Woe to you! The deceived is the one you deceived." They said: "What is your condition?" He said: "I have never seen the like of today. Leave me, so that I may return to myself." They left him for a while and said: "What has befallen you, O Abu al-Layth?" He said: "When I drew near to Muhammad and wanted to strike at him with my sword, two bald, horned serpents came at me from above his head, spitting fire, and their eyes flashed. So I ran. I will never return to harm Muhammad in anything."

(Among his signs): Kilda ibn Asad, Abu al-Ashadd, who was of great strength, once wagered Quraysh on killing the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They made a great stake for him if he accomplished it. He saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the road going to the mosque, between the house of ʿAqil and ʿIqal. Kilda came with his javelin, but the javelin turned back into his own chest. He returned in terror. Quraysh said to him: "What is the matter with you, O Abu al-Ashadd?" He said: "Woe to you! Do you not see the stallion behind me?" They said: "We see nothing." He said: "Woe to you! I see it." He kept running until he reached al-Ta'if. Thaqif mocked him, and he said: "I excuse you. Had you seen what I saw, you would have perished."

Among its proofs of prophethood: "Abu Lahab went out one day when the Quraysh had gathered, and they said to him: 'O Abu 'Utbah! You are our chief, and you are more entitled to Muhammad than we are. Abu Talib is the barrier between us and him. If you kill him, neither Abu Talib nor Hamzah will object to anything you do. You will be free of his blood, and we will pay the blood-money, and you will lead your people.' He said: 'I will suffice you!' They rejoiced at this, and their orators praised him. When it was that night, and he was overlooking him, Abu Lahab came down while he was praying. His wife Umm Jamil climbed the wall until she stood over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was prostrating. Abu Lahab shouted, but he did not turn to him. The two of them could not move a step or do anything until dawn broke. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished. Abu Lahab said to him: 'O Muhammad, release us!' He said: 'I will not release you unless you guarantee me that you will not harm me.' They said: 'We have done so.' So he prayed to his Lord, and they returned."

Among its proofs: "The Quraysh gathered at al-Hatim. 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah addressed them, saying: 'This son of 'Abd al-Muttalib has disturbed our life, divided our community, scattered our unity, reviled our religion, made foolish our minds, and misguided our forefathers.' Among the people were al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Munabbih and Nabih, the two sons of al-Hajjaj, and Umayyah and Ubayy, the two sons of Khalaf, along with a group of the nobles of the Quraysh. They said to him: 'Say whatever you wish, for we will obey you.' He said: 'I will stand and speak to him. If he returns from his words and from what he calls to, well and good; otherwise we will decide our course regarding him.' They said: 'The matter is yours, O Abu 'Abd Shams!' He stood, went to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting alone, and said: 'Good morning, O Muhammad!' He (ﷺ) said: 'O 'Abd Shams, Allah has replaced this greeting for us with the greeting of the people of Paradise.' He said: 'O son of my brother! I have come to you from the nobles of the Quraysh to present their matters to you. If you accept them, you will have the benefit of them, and we will have the leeway!' Then he said: 'O son of 'Abd al-Muttalib! I am the spokesman of the Quraysh regarding what they have said.' He said: 'Speak.' He said: 'O son of 'Abd al-Muttalib! You have called the Arabs to a matter they do not know, so accept from me what I say to you.' He said: 'Speak.' He said: 'If what you call to is aimed at kingship, we will make you king over us without hardship, and we will crown you; so turn back from that.' He fell silent. Then he said to him: 'And if what you call to is a matter by which you desire a beautiful woman, we will marry you to her.' He said: 'There is no power except with Allah!' Then he said to him: 'And if what you say is aimed at wealth, we will give you of the wealth until you become the richest man among the Quraysh, for that is easier for us than the dispersal of our word and the division of our community. And if what you call to is madness, we will treat you, just as the Qays of Banu Tha'labah treated their madman.'

The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent, and he said: 'O Muhammad! What do you say? With what shall I return to the Quraysh?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [Fussilat: 1] ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat: 2] ﴿A Book whose verses are detailed, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know﴾ [Fussilat: 3] ﴿Bringing good tidings and warning, yet most of them turn away, so they do not hear﴾ [Fussilat: 4] – until he reached His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13]. 'Utbah said: 'When he recited these words, it was as if the Ka'bah had tilted, until I feared it would strike my head from its sides.' He stood up in alarm, dragging his cloak, and returned to the Quraysh, trembling like a sparrow. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray. The Quraysh said: 'You left us energetic and returned alarmed and terrified. What is behind you?' He said: 'Woe to you! Leave me. He spoke to me with words I do not understand at all. A tremor seized me until I feared for myself, and I said: The thunderbolt has seized me.' So they regretted that."

Among its proofs: "When he (ﷺ) intended the Hijrah, he went out of Makkah with Abu Bakr. He entered a cave on Mount Thawr to hide from the Quraysh. They sought him and offered a hundred red camels to whoever brought him back, but Allah the Exalted helped him by concealing his trace. He caused a thorn-bush (thumamah), which is a small tree, to grow at the mouth of the cave. The spider was inspired and wove at the mouth of the cave a web of years in the blink of an eye. Abu Bakr was stung by a scorpion that night and tore his garments and stuffed them into the cracks. He blocked some of them with his foot out of concern for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He remained there for three days, then left it. Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum met him; he was among those who had set out to pursue him. Abu Bakr said to him: 'This is Suraqah, and he is close!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, suffice us against Suraqah!' The earth seized the legs of his horse up to its belly. Suraqah said: 'O Muhammad! Pray to Allah to free me, and I pledge to turn back whoever comes seeking you, and never to aid against you!' He said: 'O Allah! If he is truthful, then release his horse.' Allah released it. Then Suraqah embraced Islam, and his Islam was good."

This is what al-Mawardi cited of the proofs before the Hijrah. Then he cited what occurred after it, and we will quote it from Ibn Kathir, for he said regarding this verse:

Among Allah's protection of His Messenger is His preserving him from the people of Makkah, their chiefs, their envious ones, their opponents and their affluent ones, despite the intensity of their enmity, hatred, and open hostility toward him night and day, by means of the great causes that Allah creates according to His decree and His great wisdom. He safeguarded him at the beginning of the message through his uncle Abu Talib, who was a chief, obeyed, and great among the Quraysh. Allah placed in Abu Talib's heart a natural (tabi'iyyah) love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), not a legislated (shar'iyyah) one. Had he embraced Islam, its disbelievers and great ones would have dared against him. But since there was a shared measure of disbelief between him and them, they held him in awe and respected him. When his uncle Abu Talib died, the polytheists inflicted a minor harm upon him. Then Allah appointed for him the Ansar, who pledged allegiance to him for Islam and to be moved to their home, which is Madinah. When he arrived there, they protected him from the red and the black. Whenever any of the polytheists and People of the Book intended evil against him, Allah thwarted them and turned their scheme back upon them. Just as the Jews plotted against him with sorcery, Allah protected him from them and sent down to him the two surahs of refuge (al-Mu'awwidhatayn) as a remedy for that affliction. When the Jews poisoned him in the foreleg of a sheep at Khaybar, Allah informed him of it and protected him from it. There are very many similar instances, too lengthy to mention. Among them is what the commentators mentioned regarding this noble verse:

Ibn Jarir said: al-Harith related to us, 'Abd al-'Aziz related to us, Abu Ma'shar related to us, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others related to us, saying: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) halted at a place, his companions would choose for him a shady tree, and he would rest beneath it. A Bedouin came to him, drew his sword, and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.' The Bedouin's hand trembled and the sword fell from him. He said: 'He struck his head against the tree until his brains spilled out.' So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) campaigned against Banu Anmar, he halted at Dhat al-Riqa' beneath a palm tree. While he was sitting at the edge of a well with his legs dangling, a man from Banu al-Najjar, the heir, said: 'I will surely kill Muhammad!' His companions said to him: 'How will you kill him?' He said: 'I will say to him: Give me your sword, and when he gives it to me, I will kill him with it.' He came to him and said: 'O Muhammad! Give me your sword so I may examine it.' He gave it to him. His hand trembled until the sword fell from his hand. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has come between you and what you intend.' So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message; and Allah will protect you from the people﴾."

Ibn Kathir said: "This hadith is gharib (rare) from this route. Then he said: The story of Ghawrath ibn al-Harith is well-known in the Sahih," meaning what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Jabir, who said: "We campaigned with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward Najd. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned, the time of the midday rest overtook them in a valley thick with thorny trees. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dismounted, and the people dispersed, seeking shade under the trees. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dismounted beneath a tree and hung his sword on it, and we slept a sleep with him. Then suddenly the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was calling us, and there was a Bedouin with him. He said: 'This man drew my sword over me while I was sleeping. I woke up and he had it in his hand drawn. He said: Who will protect you from me? I said: Allah,' three times. He did not punish him and sat down."

In another narration, Jabir said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Dhat al-Riqa'. Whenever we came to a shady tree, we left it for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A man from the polytheists came, and the sword of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was hanging on the tree. He drew it and said: 'Do you fear me?' He said: 'No!' He said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'Allah.' The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then threatened him."

Al-Bukhari added in one of his narrations that the name of that man was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Whenever we accompanied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, we would leave for him the largest and shadiest tree. He would rest beneath it. One day he rested beneath a tree and hung his sword upon it. A man came, took it, and said: 'O Muhammad! Who will protect you from me?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah protects me from you. Put down the sword.' He put it down. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾." Ibn Hibban narrated it likewise in his Sahih.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ja'dah ibn Khalid ibn al-Simmah, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) see a stout man, and the Prophet (ﷺ) began pointing to his belly with his hand and saying: 'If this were in other than this, it would be better for you.' He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a man, and they said: 'This man intended to kill you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Do not be frightened, do not be frightened. Had you intended that, Allah would not have given you power over me.'"

Third: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to be guarded before the revelation of this verse, as Imam Ahmad narrated from 'A'ishah: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed awake one night while she was beside him. She said: I said: What is the matter with you, O Messenger of Allah? He said: 'I wish a righteous man from my Companions would guard me tonight!' She said: While I was like that, I heard the sound of weapons. He said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'I am Sa'd ibn Malik.' He said: 'What brought you?' He said: 'I came to guard you, O Messenger of Allah.' She said: Then I heard the snoring of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his sleep.'" Both Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated it in their Sahihs.

In another wording: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed awake one night after his arrival in Madinah, meaning following his migration after his consummation of marriage with 'A'ishah, and that was in the second year after it.

From 'A'ishah, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to be guarded at night until this was revealed: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put his head out of the tent and said to them: 'O people! Disperse, for Allah has protected me.'" Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to be guarded. Abu Talib would send to him each day men from Banu Hashim to guard him, until this verse was revealed to him: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message; and Allah will protect you from the people﴾. He said: His uncle then wished to send someone with him to guard him, but he said: 'Allah has protected me from jinn and men.'" Al-Tabarani also narrated it. Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Jabir.

Ibn Kathir said: "This hadith is gharib (rare), and it contains nakarah (an unacceptable, strange element), for this verse is Madani (revealed in Madinah); indeed, it is among the last of what was revealed there, and this hadith implies that it is Makki (revealed in Makkah). And Allah knows best." End of quotation.

I say: By referring to what we have previously set out in the "Introduction" regarding the principle of asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation), the difficulty is resolved, so reflect upon this.

(p-2085) Fourth: The Allamah Abu al-Su'ud said: The placing of this noble verse amid the verses concerning the People of the Book is because all of them are thunderbolts (qawari'), whose hearing grieves the disbelievers. It is also hard for the Messenger (ﷺ) to confront them with them, especially what follows it of the text that rebukes them for the completeness of their misguidance. For this reason the command is repeated, and it is said, addressing both groups:

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[68] ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord." And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.﴾

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything,"﴾ that is, of the religion. ﴿"Until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel,"﴾ that is, you observe them, and preserve what is in them of matters, among which are the signs of the Prophet's prophethood (ﷺ) and following him.

Some of the scholars of verification (al-muḥaqqiqīn) said:

The meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel﴾ is that you act in accordance with what is obligatory from their rulings, and revive their laws, obey their commands, and refrain from their prohibitions. For iqāmah (upholding) is the performance of an act in its best form, like upholding the prayer, for example, that is, performing it in the manner fitting to it. This does not include the narratives they contain, nor the beliefs and the like, for these are not practical matters. What is meant is that they act upon what remains with them of the rulings of the Torah and the Gospel, in their defective state and with whatever deficiency, distortion, and addition they contain. For the laws of these books, their commands and their prohibitions, are the least of their parts subject to distortion, while most of the distortion is in the narratives, the reports, the beliefs, and what resembles them, and these do not fall under the command to uphold. There is no doubt that the rulings of the Torah and the Gospel, and what they contain of laws, admonitions, counsel, and the like, still contain many things free of fault, beneficial to mankind, and in them is great guidance for people. So they are among what falls under His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 3] ﴿before, as guidance for mankind﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 4]. So when the People of the Scripture uphold their rulings in their imperfect state, they are, without doubt, upon something that is counted and may be called a religion. But if they do not uphold them, and follow contrary to them, they are stripped of everything that deserves to be called a religion, and they are contentious rebels, and not believers with their religion in complete faith. This is a correct meaning, and it is what is immediately understood from the verse. Then what in this meaning indicates that the Torah and the Gospel are not distorted and that they exist in their completeness, as those obstinate ones among their people claim, especially after His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 13]?

Then he said: You may say: the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿you are not upon anything until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel﴾ is the real (ḥaqīqiyyayn) ones. That requires investigation, searching, earnestness, and striving in critiquing what they have of them, a critique that is rational, historical, and sound, until they extract their truth from their falsehood as far as possible. The outcome of all that toil is that they would be upon something of the true religion, and this is a matter with no doubt about it. Had they followed the Qur'an, they would have eased and been at rest. But they, as He, Exalted is He, has informed about them, the Qur'an increases them only in transgression and disbelief, out of envy and obstinacy, so they do not believe in it. And most of them do not concern themselves with reforming their religion from its corruptions and purifying it from its impurities. So they have attained neither the good of this nor of that. Thus the verse shows them that if they do not follow the Qur'an, it becomes obligatory upon them to undertake a very heavy burden of investigation and scrutiny, and after that they would be upon some of the truth, not upon all of the truth, even if they upheld the real Torah and Gospel to the utmost upholding. So how much more so when that is impossible, because the two do not exist in their true reality? So they are not upon anything at all, and it is not possible for them to be upon it. For their books have become worn-out rags. For this reason, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he saw a leaf of the Torah in his hand: 'Have I not brought it to you white and pure? By Allah, if Moses were alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me.'"

(If it is said): How does Allah urge them to act upon any part of their religion, when some of it has been abrogated (nāsikh) by the Qur'an? (I say): There is no doubt for any sensible person that it is better for the People of the Scripture to act upon the original laws of their religion. For then they would avoid lying, distortion, obstinacy, harm, corruption on earth, the destruction of crops and offspring, adultery, and other things that people know. So the purpose of the Qur'an, according to the first interpretation of the verse, is to urge them, if they persist in not believing in it, to act upon their religion at least, so that the Prophet and his followers may rest from the greater part of their evils and vices. But after acting upon their religion they would not be upon the complete true religion. Rather, what is understood from the verse is that they would be upon some of the religion, and this is, without doubt, better than nothing. It is not understood that they would be upon the whole truth and the complete religion, beyond which there is no greater end. For that happens only through Islam: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 83]. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that if they upheld the Torah and the Gospel, they would believe in Muḥammad (ﷺ), because upholding them necessarily requires belief in him, since what came in them of glad tidings about him, and of honoring his name and his religion, is abundant. So upholding them in their true forms absolutely demands Islam; indeed, it is Islam itself. And Allah is the Granter of success.

﴿And what has been revealed to you from your Lord,﴾ that is, the glorious Qur'an, by believing in it. In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿you are not upon anything,﴾ there is a degree of belittling and diminishing beyond which there is no further limit, as when you say: "This is not a thing!" meaning the extreme of belittling it and diminishing its status. And among their proverbs: "Less than nothing." That is: you are not upon a religion that is counted, so as to be called something, because of its corruption and invalidity.

(p-2088) Then Exalted is He explained their extremity in obstinacy and that delivering the message would not benefit them, so He said: ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression,﴾ that is, in persistence in rebellion, ﴿and disbelief,﴾ that is, steadfastness in unbelief. ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people,﴾ that is: when you have striven hard in conveying what has been revealed to you, and you see their increase in transgression and disbelief, then do not grieve over them, because of the extremity of their wickedness in themselves. For the harm of that returns to them, not to you, and among the believers there is sufficiency without them.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[69] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds – no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds – no fear will there be concerning them﴾ regarding the punishment that awaits them. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾: that is, in the Hereafter, when those who fell short become fearful and grieve over having wasted their lives.

Subtleties (lata'if):

The first: "al-Sabi'un" (the Sabeans) is in the nominative case, as a topic (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. The intention behind it is a delay of what is within the scope of "inna" (indeed), from its subject and its predicate. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians – their judgment is such-and-such. And the Sabeans likewise." Sibawayh cited as evidence for this the verse:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are rebels, so long as we remain in discord."

That is: "Know that we are rebels, and you likewise." Then al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: Is there any purpose to the advancing and delaying except for a benefit? So what is the benefit of the advancing? I say: the benefit is to draw attention to the fact that the Sabeans are to be accepted in repentance if faith and righteous deeds are sound from them. So what is to be presumed concerning others? That is because the Sabeans are the clearest of these enumerated people in misguidance and the most extreme in error, and they were not named Sabeans except because they 'sabaʾa' (turned away) from all religions, i.e., they departed. Just as the poet advanced his saying 'and you' to draw attention to the fact that the addressees are more extreme in the description of rebels than his own people, while they are more extreme in it than them and more firmly established." End.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf:

There is a question, which may be put: If it had been conjoined and put in the accusative – as Ibn Kathir recited – it would also have conveyed their inclusion among those to whom repentance is granted, and it would have been understood from mentioning them before the Christians, what is understood from the nominative [reading]: that these Sabeans – who are the most extreme of people in disbelief – are granted repentance; so what is to be presumed concerning the Christians? The speech would have been one eloquent, concise sentence, and the conjunction would have been of single words. Why did he turn to the nominative and make the speech two sentences? And it is distinguished by a benefit over the accusative and the single-word conjunction? This question may be answered by saying that if he had put it in the accusative and conjoined it, there would not have been in it an indication of the particularity of this category, because all the categories are conjoined to one another in the manner of single words, and this category is one of them, and the predicate concerning them is one. But with the nominative it is cut off from single-word conjunction, and the rest of the categories remain specified by the conjoined predicate, and the predicate of this separate category stands alone. Its estimated form might be, for example, "and the Sabeans likewise," and it has come as if it were analogized to the rest of the categories and attached to them. And it stands in this position, because after the categories, acceptance of repentance has been established for them, so they were worthy of being made followers and branches, likened to those who are more fundamental than them, by this predicate. And the benefit of mentioning it before the omitted predicate, after the speech has concluded and completed, [is as stated]. And God knows best.

The second: If you ask: how can His saying, "whoever of them believes," be a predicate of "those who believed," or a substitute (badal), when it implies a division of believers into believers and non-believers?

I answer you: the intended meaning of "those who believed" is those who believed only with the tongue, and they are the hypocrites. So the meaning is: those who believed with the tongue, and those with them – whoever among them newly acquires sincere faith. Or it is interpreted as: "whoever believes" refers to one who remains steadfast in faith, and it is then valid with regard to the sincere believers. In this there is an appearance of combining the literal and the metaphorical, and a response that steadfastness in faith is not other than faith, but rather it and its initiation are two individual instances of its absolute form. The first aspect is preferable, since joining believers with disbelievers involves a diminishing of their honor. So said al-Khafaji.

Abu al-Su'ud said: As for the case where "those who believed" refers to the absolute category of those adhering to the religion of Islam, both the sincere among them and the hypocrites, then "whoever believes" refers to whoever among them is characterized by sincere faith in the absolute sense, whether that is by way of steadfastness and persistence in it – as is the condition of the sincere – or by way of its initiation and creation – as is the state of others among the hypocrites and the rest of the groups. And the benefit of generalizing to include the sincere is the emphasis on encouraging the rest toward faith, by showing that their lateness in attaining it does not detract from their being a model for those foremost and distinguished ones. End.

The third: al-Razi said: When He, exalted is He, made clear that the People of the Book are not upon anything until they believe, He made clear that this ruling is general for all, and that no one attains any virtue or excellence unless he believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds. That is because man has two powers: the theoretical power and the practical power. As for the perfection of the theoretical power, it is only by knowing the truth. And as for the perfection of the practical power, it is only by doing good. The most noble of knowledge is knowledge of the most noble of existent things, which is Allah, glorified and exalted. And the perfection of knowing Him is attained only by His being capable of gathering and resurrection, so without doubt the best knowledge is faith in Allah and the Last Day. And the best of good deeds are two things: persistence in deeds that indicate the exaltation of the Worshipped, and striving to bring benefit to creation. Then He, exalted is He, made clear that everyone who comes with this faith and this deed will arrive on the Day of Resurrection without fear or grief. The benefit in mentioning both is that fear relates to the future and grief to the past. So He said: "no fear will there be concerning them," because of what they witness of the terrors of the Resurrection; "nor will they grieve," because of what has escaped them of the good things of this world, since they found matters greater, more noble, and better. (If it is said): how is it possible for a responsible person, who is not infallible, to be free of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection? The answer is in two respects:

The first: He, exalted is He, made that conditional upon righteous deeds, and one does not bring righteous deeds unless he has abandoned all sins.

The second: that if fear arises, it is a minor, passing matter that is not counted. End.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear another part of their crimes, which call for regarding faith from them as unlikely, by His saying:

(p-2092) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group [of them] they denied and a group they killed.﴾

﴿Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., to believe in Allah and His messengers. ﴿And We sent to them messengers﴾ to make them aware of what they should do and what they should leave off in their religion. ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire﴾, i.e., with what opposes their desires and runs counter to their appetites of the true rulings. Although the nature of the message is a call to oppose desire. ﴿A group﴾ of them ﴿they denied﴾ despite the clear evidences of their truthfulness, ﴿and a group they killed﴾ after denying them, to block their call to what contradicts their inclinations.

Two subtle points:

The first: Al-Zamakhshari said: The answer to the conditional is omitted, indicated by His saying: "a group they denied and a group they killed," as if it were said: "Every time a messenger came to them from among them, they opposed him."

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: Among what indicates the omission of the answer is that it appeared explicitly in the other verse which is its twin, His exalted saying: ﴿Is it that every time a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you waxed proud? So a group you denied and a group you kill?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87], where He placed His saying "you waxed proud" as the answer, and then explained their arrogance and their treatment of the prophets as killing some and denying others. So if al-Zamakhshari had supplied the omitted answer here in the same form as the stated one in its sister verse, saying: "And We sent to them messengers; every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, they waxed proud," it would have been better, due to the indication of its like.

(p-2093) The second: Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: Why is one of the two verbs brought in the past tense and the other in the present? I say: "They kill" is used to narrate a past state, to express horror at the killing and to bring that shameful state vividly to mind, in order to express wonder at it.

In al-Intisaf he said: Or it may be a present state in its literal sense, since they were circling around the killing of Muhammad ﷺ. This view has been given regarding the sister verse in al-Baqarah; and the reason the present verb form requires bringing the state to mind rather than the past has already passed, with the example of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green? Indeed Allah is Subtle and Aware﴾ [al-Hajj: 63], where He shifted from "fa-asbahat" to "fa-tusbihu" to depict the state and bring it before the hearer's mind, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"That I have met the ghoul, as she goes through a wide desert plain smooth as a page, [...]
So I struck her without dismay, and she fell prone upon her hands and her neck."

And its like is abundant. End of quote.

(p-2094) Al-Khafaji said: The Allamah here limited himself to narrating the state of their forefathers, due to the indication of the third-person pronouns, and left that verse, i.e., the verse of al-Baqarah, open to both possibilities, due to the indication of the second-person pronouns, so that it would be a rebuke and an address to those present regarding the deeds of their fathers. For this reason this verse is followed by the story of Jesus, peace be upon him. So reflect.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[71] ﴿They thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf again. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾

﴿They thought there would be no trial﴾ — i.e., the Children of Israel supposed that they would not be struck by a punishment from Allah for killing the prophets and denying the messengers. ﴿So they became blind and deaf﴾ — this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "thought," and the fāʾ (fa, "so") indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes; that is: they felt safe from the might of Allah, so they indulged in every kind of error and corruption, and became blind to the religion after the messengers had guided them to its clear landmarks, and deaf to hearing the truth that had been delivered to them. Therefore they did what they did. ﴿Then Allah turned to them﴾ — i.e., from what they were in.

The scholar Abu al-Suʿud said: He did not attribute the turning (tawba) to them, as with their other states of thinking, blindness and deafness, shying away from explicitly attributing good to them. It is only alluded to within the explanation of His turning toward them, as a preparation for explaining their breaking of it by His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Then they became blind and deaf again⁠— many of them.﴾ The phrase "many of them" is either a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the two verbs, or a deleted predicate, i.e., "those, many of them." ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ — i.e., of what they did. The present-tense form is for narrating a past state, to bring its dreadful image before the mind and to keep the rhyme (fawāṣil). The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyīl), by which the invalidity of their aforementioned supposition is indicated, and the occurrence of punishment from a direction they did not expect is a general indication, which he was satisfied with, relying on what was explained in some detail in Surah (Banī Isrāʾīl), as Abu al-Suʿud noted. This is taken from the words of al-Qaffal, as will come:

Note: In this verse there is an allusion to the trial and the punishment of Allah that befell the Children of Israel, both before ʿIsā and after him. That is because their prophets before ʿIsā used to rebuke their wicked leaders and their people for their sins, especially their worship of idols, and advise them to return to Allah, warning them of His severe punishment and their destruction if they did not repent. Just as Irmiya (Jeremiah), peace be upon him, foretold the ruin of their land and the terrible decree of Allah upon them if they persisted in their rebellion, yet they did not heed him, to the point that it is narrated that he was granted martyrdom, when the Jews stoned him in Egypt out of arrogance and haughtiness. Then Allah set Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon, over them, who took their people captive and whose armies destroyed their city Jerusalem and its Temple, and it became mounds of ruin. This was to root out their disbelief and evils and to purify their Temple from the impurity of their idols. Thus misery and woe came upon them from the Babylonians, and they were taken captive beyond the Euphrates, and nothing was left of them except the poor alone. With that their kingdom ended, and that was about five hundred and eighty-eight years before the birth of ʿIsā, peace be upon him. Then Allah turned to them and had mercy on them in their captivity, and returned them by His mercy to their city, Bayt al-Maqdis, after they had remained in Babylon seventy years. They began rebuilding their Temple a second time and restored worship to it. Ḥizqīl (Ezekiel), peace be upon him, stood to admonish them, refine them, call them to repentance, and remind them of the past so they might take heed. Thus every prophet among them continued to warn them and call them to Allah until Allah sent ʿIsā, peace be upon him. They became blind to being guided by him and deaf to his admonition, and what happened of their intent to kill him occurred. So Allah destroyed them after that and annihilated their kingdom. They were expelled from their land after the raising of ʿIsā, peace be upon him, by about forty years, and the Romans took their city and destroyed it along with the Temple, and Allah's vengeance descended upon them, and they were scattered in every direction.

Furthermore, what has been said — that His saying, exalted is He, "they became blind and deaf" refers to their worship of the calf — is far-fetched, because although it was a great sin arising from complete blindness and deafness, it occurred in the time of Musa, peace be upon him, and has no connection with what is related of them regarding what they did to the messengers who came after him, peace be upon him, by many centuries. Likewise, what has been said — that His saying, exalted is He, "then they became blind and deaf again" refers to their request to see Allah — is also far-fetched, for the reason we mentioned. The kinds of crimes issuing from them are almost innumerable. However, the restriction of what is related of them here to these two instances, and its being connected to the narration of what they did to the messengers, peace be upon them, requires that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned. And Allah has the knowledge of the Book. Thus Abu al-Suʿud stated.

We agree with him on what he has seen. Yet what we have presented in the Note is clearer regarding their affairs and more closely matching what is in their histories than what he presented here. So let it be established.

May Allah have mercy on the Imam al-Qaffal, for he said: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in Surah (Banī Isrāʾīl) what may be an explanation of this verse, so He said: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption on the earth twice and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾ [al-Isra: 4] ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they ransacked the homes, and it was a promise fulfilled﴾ [al-Isra: 5] ﴿Then We gave back to you the return over them and provided you with wealth and sons and made you more numerous in manpower﴾ [al-Isra: 6]

So this is the meaning of: ﴿they became blind and deaf﴾. Then He said: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to disfigure your faces and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra: 7]. So this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿then many of them became blind and deaf again﴾. End of quotation.

(p-2097) Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear the disbelief of the Christians and the corrupt belief they held, which contradicts the essence of ʿIsā's call, namely pure monotheism, by His saying, glorified is He:

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[72] ﴿Certainly those have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah – Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾

﴿Certainly those have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾

Al-Razi said: This is the saying of the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites) among them. They say: Mary gave birth to a god. He said: Perhaps the meaning of this doctrine is that they say Allah, Exalted is He, indwelt the person of Jesus and united with it. Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation.

The discussion of a verse like this has already preceded in this surah in detail, so recall it.

Then He, Exalted, made clear that they were deaf to the statements of Jesus calling to monotheism (tawhid, the oneness of God), just as they were blind to the signs of createdness (hudath) in him, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah"﴾, and He did not say "worship me." Then He declared explicitly, ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾, uprooting the source of the false imagination of union (ittihad). ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah – Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire.﴾ How (could it be otherwise), since shirk is the greatest form of wrongdoing (zulm)? ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ That is: they have no one who will help them by rescuing them from the Fire, either by way of emphasis (mubalagha) or by way of intercession (shafa'a).

The plural is used in observance of the correspondence with **al-zalimin** (the wrongdoers). The **al-** (the definite article) may be for specification (al-'ahd), and the plural is in consideration of the meaning of **man** (whoever), just as the singular in the three pronouns is in consideration of its wording. Or it may be for the category (al-jins), and they are included in it by primary inclusion. He placed it in the first sense in the position of a pronoun, to record against them that they wronged by associating partners and turned away from the path of truth.

The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyil, an appended summary) confirming what preceded it. It is either part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, or it comes from Allah, Exalted, as an emphasis of the statement of Jesus, peace be upon him, and a confirmation of its content. Abu al-Su'ud conveyed this.

(p-2098) Then He, Exalted, made clear the disbelief of another group among them by His saying, glorified is He:

**On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[73] ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three," while there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾ means: one of three gods, in the sense that He is one of them, namely Allah, Mary and Jesus.

Some of them said: a sect among them called (*Kollyridians*) said: the gods are three: the Father, the Son and Mary.

In the book *ʿIlm al-Yaqin* it is mentioned that a sect among them called (the *Maryamiyyun*, Mariamites) said: they believe that Mary and the Messiah are two gods. He said: and likewise the *Barbaraniyyun* and others. End of quotation.

We have previously cited from Ibn Ishaq that the Christians of Najran included some who held this view as well.

Or the meaning is: one of three *aqānīm* (hypostases), as is well known of them. That is, He is one substance with three hypostases: Father, Son and the Holy Spirit. They claim that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, and all of them are one God. As we have already mentioned about them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾ (al-Nisa’ 4:171).

Al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Know that this is known to be false by the immediate judgment of reason, for three cannot be one, and one cannot be three. And there is no doctrine in this world more corrupt or more manifestly false than the doctrine of the Christians. End of quotation.

I have composed a number of works refuting this belief of theirs; they are famous and widely circulated, and praise be to Allah.

**A subtle point:**

The grammarians and lexicographers agree that the meaning of their saying (*thālithu thalāthatin* and *rābiʿu arbaʿatin*, "third of three" and "fourth of four") and the like is one of these numbers in an unrestricted sense, not the attribute of being third or fourth.

In *al-Tawdih wa Sharhuhu* (a grammar work with its commentary): For the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) formed from the words for two and ten and what lies between them, you may use it in seven ways:

The first: that you use it unannexed (*mufradan ʿan al-idāfa*), to convey the attribution of its meaning. So you say: *thālithun* and *rābiʿun*. Its meaning then is one thing described by this attribute, namely being third or fourth.

The second way: that you use it together with its root from which it was formed, to convey that the one described by it is only a part of that specific number and nothing more. So you say: *khāmisu khamsatin*, that is, one of five, not exceeding them. In this case it must be annexed to its root, just as a part must be annexed to its whole, like *yadu Zaydin* ("the hand of Zayd"). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:40), and He said: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾. Al-Akhfash, Qutrub, al-Kisa’i and Tha‘lab claimed that it is permissible to annex the first to the second and also to put it in the accusative (*naṣb*) governing it. On this view, *thālithu thalāthatin* may be read with the genitive on *thalāthatin* or with the accusative, just as in *ḍāribu Zaydin* ("striker of Zayd").

The third way: that you use it with a number that is one rank below its root from which it was formed, to convey the sense of making (*tasyīr*). So you say: *hādhā rābiʿu thalāthatin*, that is, one who makes the three into four by himself. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth﴾ (al-Mujadilah 58:7), that is, He is one who makes them four and makes them six. In this case it is permissible both to annex it and to make it govern (in the accusative), just as both are permissible with *jāʿilun* ("one who makes") and *muṣayyirun* ("one who renders") and the like.

Consult the remainder of the ways.

By what we have mentioned, the rejection of what al-Jami held in his *Sharh al-Kafiyah* becomes known, namely his consideration of the attribute in examples like *thālithu thālithatin* ("third of a third"), where he said in explaining the words of Ibn al-Hajib, "*thālithu thalāthatin*, that is, one of them." But not unrestrictedly; rather, with regard to its occupying the third rank. He said: otherwise it would entail the permissibility of intending the first one from the tenth of ten, and that is extremely far-fetched. End of quotation.

Some of the verifiers (*muḥaqqiqīn*) wrote upon this the following text: The apparent meaning from the expression of *al-Tawdih* and from the words of its author is that the occupying of the second or third rank is not considered, and so on. For in the two verses it is far-fetched that what is meant by *thānī ithnayn* ("second of two") and *thālithu thalāthatin* ("third of three") is occupying the second or third rank; rather, what is meant is that he is a part of that number, without regard to whether he occupies the second or third rank. Unless this is understood with respect to the lexical formation (*al-waḍʿ*), although usage is contrary to it. For this reason the scholar ʿAbd al-Hakim wrote upon his statement "and that is extremely far-fetched": that is, according to reason; otherwise usage is contrary to it. End of quotation.

﴿And there is no god except one God﴾: in the text of the Gospel and the Torah and all the heavenly books, and in the proofs of reason, there is no god but one God, who is not multiplied in individuals or in parts.

﴿And if they do not desist from what they say﴾ of this fabrication and lie, after the definitive proof has become manifest, holding fast to the ambiguous passages of the Gospel whose clear passages have made them plain: ﴿there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, of the punishment of the Fire, the shackles and the torment.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not say "it will afflict them," because placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun has a benefit: it is the repetition of the testimony against them of disbelief in His saying, ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say﴾. And in the explanation there is another benefit, which is the informing, in the explanation of "those who disbelieved among them," that they are in a state of disbelief.

(p-٢١٠١)The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿Will they not repent to God and seek His forgiveness? And God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿Will they not repent to God and seek His forgiveness?﴾ That is, by affirming *tawhid* (the oneness of God) and *tanzih* (declaring Him free of imperfection), and by denying what they attributed to Him of *ittihad* (union with God) and *hulul* (God's indwelling in a creature). Then they would turn away from clinging to the *mutashabihat* (ambiguous verses) and return to the *qat'iyyat* (definitive matters). The interrogative is for denying and deeming unlikely what has occurred, and it contains an expression of wonder at their persistence. The basis of the denial and wonder is that they neither desist nor repent. Or its meaning is: Will they not repent, after this repeated testimony against them of disbelief and this severe warning, from what they are upon? Thus the basis of both is their failure to repent after the realization of what requires repentance, namely hearing those awesome calamities.

Ibn Kathir said: This is from His generosity, bounty, kindness and mercy toward His creation. Despite this great sin, this slander, falsehood and lie, He calls them to repentance and forgiveness. Whoever turns to Him, He turns to him in forgiveness, as He said: ﴿And God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, so He will forgive these people if they repent, and others too.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The clause is circumstantial (*hali*), relating to the subject of "they seek His forgiveness," and it emphasizes the denial and wonder at their persistence in disbelief and their failure to hasten to seeking forgiveness. That is: while the state is that He, exalted is He, is abundant in forgiveness, He will forgive them when they seek His forgiveness and will bestow upon them of His grace.

Then God, exalted is He, pointed out the invalidity of clinging to the miracles of Jesus and the marvels (*karamat*) of his mother as proof of their divinity, by stating that their ultimate significance is only to indicate his prophethood and her sainthood (*wilaya*). This is to bring them down from their persistence in what they fabricated about the two of them, and to guide them to repentance and seeking forgiveness. So He said:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[75] ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. And his mother was a truthful woman. They both used to eat food. Look how We make the signs clear to them; then look how they are turned away.﴾

﴿The Messiah﴾, i.e., whose origination is known from the fact that he was ﴿son of Mary﴾ through the manifest marvels that appeared at his hands. ﴿No more than a messenger; messengers had passed away﴾, i.e., had gone by, ﴿before him﴾, ﴿the messengers﴾, who were possessors of striking marvels. So he has precedents like them, as Exalted God said: ﴿He is only a servant on whom We bestowed favour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59], i.e., he is only a messenger of the same kind as the messengers who passed before him, who came with signs from God just as they came with their like. If God cured the leper and raised the dead at his hand, He had already given life to the staff, turning it into a moving serpent, and split the sea by it at the hand of Moses. And that is more wondrous. If He created him without a father, He created Adam without father or mother, and that is stranger still. There is also another reading of the verse: i.e., messengers had passed away before him, so he too passes away like them. The sentence, in any case, indicates that he is characterised by what is incompatible with divinity. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾, i.e., exceedingly truthful. The name "truthful woman" (ṣiddīqah) was applied to her on account of His words, Exalted Is He: ﴿and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. Describing her thus implies immersion in servanthood and the performance of its rites. So from where do they get the right to attribute to her what contradicts her description?

Note:

Ibn Kathir said:

The verse indicates that Mary was not a prophetess, as claimed by Ibn Hazm and others, who held that Sarah the mother of Isaac, the mother of Moses and the mother of Jesus were prophetesses, arguing from the angels' address to Sarah and Mary and from His words: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: suckle him﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], and this is the meaning of prophethood. What the majority hold is that God sent no prophet except from among men. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We sent none before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, may God have mercy on him, related the consensus on this. End.

Benefit (on the reality of the ṣiddīq and ṣidq):

The gnostic al-Qashani, may God sanctify his secret, said in "Lata'if al-A'lam":

The ṣiddīq is one who is much truthful, as one says "sikkīt" and "ṣirrīʿ" when this is abundant in a person.

The ṣiddīq among people is one who is perfect in affirming what the messengers of God brought, in knowledge and action, in speech and deed. Nothing rises above the station of ṣiddīqiyyah except the station of prophethood, such that whoever transcends the station of ṣiddīqiyyah attains the station of prophethood. God the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones on whom God has bestowed favour﴾ [Maryam: 58], and so forth. God, exalted is He, did not place between the two ranks of prophethood and ṣiddīqiyyah any other rank intervening between them. He then explained, may his secret be sanctified, the truthfulness of words, the truthfulness of deeds, and the truthfulness of states.

The first is the agreement of the inner heart with the outward utterance. Al-Junayd said: The reality of truthfulness is that you be truthful in situations where only lying would save you. The truthfulness of deeds is fulfilling what is due to God through action without flattery. Al-Muhasibi said: The truthful one is he who does not mind if all esteem he has in the hearts of creatures is lost for the sake of setting right his heart, and does not love that people should know of the weight of the dust-particles of his good deeds, and does not dislike that people should know of the bad of his state; for his disliking that is a sign that he wants more of it in their eyes, and this is not among the characteristics of the ṣiddīqīn.

The truthfulness of states is the gathering of resolve upon the truth, such that no wavering from the truth in any respect stirs in the heart.

His words, Exalted Is He: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ are a resumptive clause explaining what precedes it, namely that they were like all human beings in their need for nourishment. It also serves to distance them from what was attributed to them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Because whoever needs to be nourished by food, and what follows from it of digestion and elimination, is nothing but a composite body of bone, flesh, veins, nerves, humours and temperaments, along with appetite and desire and other things... which indicates that he is made, composed and governed like other bodies.

Subtle point:

The reason why the argument against the Christian doctrine places the two's need for food after their equality with the messengers, peace be upon them, is a progression in argumentation from the evident to the more evident, following the established method in marshalling proofs to constrain the opponent: if he does not accept the evident point because it is obscure to him, one brings the more evident point, reproaching his dullness, so that he is compelled to concede, unless he is obstinate or arrogant.

This is what has become apparent to me regarding the secret of the order of presentation.

As for the statement of al-Khafaji, summarizing al-Baydawi, concerning the secret of this: that He first explained the highest degrees of their perfection, and that this does not entail divinity, and placed it first so that He would not confront them with mention of human deficiencies which necessitate the invalidity of what they claimed about them, in the manner of His words: ﴿God pardon you! Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], where He placed the pardon before the reproach addressed to him, peace be upon him. End. It is far-fetched.

Its analogy with the verse is an analogy with a difference, because the two contexts differ. What we have mentioned is the more apparent, and God knows best the secrets of His Book.

﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾, i.e., regarding the oneness of God, and the invalidity of incarnation, and the divinity of Jesus and his mother, and the invalidity of their doubts! ﴿Then look how they are turned away﴾, i.e., how they are diverted from reflecting upon them to persistence in clinging to doubts that are manifestly invalid!

Abu al-Su'ud said: The repetition of the command to look is for emphasis in marvelling at the state of those who claim lordship for the two, and do not desist from that, after He has made clear to them the reality of their condition with a clarity that no shadow of doubt can approach. The "then" indicates the disparity between the two wonders. That is: Our clarifying of the signs is a matter wondrous in its kind, reaching the furthest extremes of verification and elucidation. And their turning away from them, when nothing that could validate it at all is present and what necessitates acceptance of them is united, is more wondrous and more marvelous.

(p-٢١٠٥)The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[76] ﴿Say: "Do you worship besides God what possesses neither harm nor benefit for you? And God is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾

﴿Say: "Do you worship besides God what possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?"﴾ This is another proof of the invalidity of the Christians' statement. The relative pronoun (ma, "what") is used as a metaphor for Jesus and his mother, meaning: they are not able to harm you with the like of what God harms you with, by way of calamities and misfortunes in your persons and your property, nor to benefit you with the like of what He benefits you with, such as health of body, abundance, and fertility. Moreover, whatever harm and benefit a human being is able to bring about is by God's empowerment and enablement, so it is as though they possess nothing of it at all. The choice of (ma) over (man, "who") serves to establish what is intended: that they are entirely outside of divinity, by showing that they are included in the category of things that have no power over anything whatsoever. That is, the attribute of the Lord is that He is capable of everything, and nothing that is within the scope of power escapes His power. He mentioned (al-durr, "harm") first because guarding against it is more important than seeking benefit. ﴿And God is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ of words and beliefs. So He will recompense for them: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil. This is both a promise and a warning.

Remarks:

First: Ibn Kathir made the address in His saying "Do you worship" general, encompassing the Christians and others. That is, "Say to these worshippers of other than God from among all the groups of the children of Adam."

In "Tanwir al-Miqbas" it is stated that (ma) refers specifically to the idols.

Both of these are rejected by the context of the preceding passage and by the immediate context (siyaq).

Second: In "Fath al-Bayan" it is said: If this applies to Jesus, the Prophet, then what do you think about one of the saints? For he is more deserving of this.

Third: Most exegetes made (ma) refer to Jesus, peace be upon him, alone. The context, however, indicates that it refers to him and to his mother, peace be upon them both, as al-Mahayimi clarified and as we have adopted.

(p-٢١٠٦)Fourth: The verse indicates the permissibility of debate (hijaj) in religion. If it is with unbelievers and people of innovation, then its permissibility is evident. If it is with a believer, it is permissible on condition that the aim is to guide him to the truth; but if the aim is to gain superiority, it is forbidden. It is related from al-Shafi'i that whenever he debated with anyone he would say: "O God, place the truth upon his tongue." This was conveyed by some of the Zaydiyya.

When the Exalted had established the decisive proofs against what the Christians were saying, He guided them to follow the truth and to avoid false exaggeration (ghuluww), by His, glorified is He, saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray, and strayed from the right way."﴾

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾, meaning, the one who is the standard of justice: ﴿do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth﴾, meaning, do not go beyond the bounds in exalting Jesus and his mother, and do not raise them above their rank to what you have invented about them of greatness. Thus you have introduced into your religion a belief that is not true, with no proof for it, while the proofs against it are manifest. The word (ghayr, "beyond") is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: exaggeration beyond the truth, that is, false exaggeration. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject pronoun, meaning: transgressing the truth. (Ghuluww, "exaggeration") is the opposite of negligence (taqsir), and its meaning is going beyond the limit. This is because the truth lies between the two extremes of excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit), and the religion of God lies between exaggeration and negligence.

Notice:

The verse indicates that exaggeration in religion is of two kinds: (true exaggeration), such as examining its realities, probing its remote meanings, and striving to obtain its proofs; and (false exaggeration), which is to go beyond the truth and overstep it by turning away from the evidences and following doubtful arguments.

(p-2107) Some of the Zaydis said: The verse indicates that exaggeration in religion is impermissible, which is transgressing the truth into falsehood. From this is the exaggeration in purity practised by many people, by adding to what the Law has prescribed without any obligation. End of quote.

From this same category is exaggeration in honouring the righteous and their graves, to the point of making them like the idols that were worshipped.

Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware of exaggeration in religion, for those before you were destroyed only by exaggeration in religion."

And from 'Umar, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not overpraise me as the Christians overpraised the son of Mary. I am only a servant, so say: 'the servant of God and His Messenger.'" Both of them (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated it.

In Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The over-zealous (al-mutanatti'un) are destroyed!" He said it three times. Then He, exalted is He, forbade them from following their predecessors and their misguided leaders, by His words, glorified is He:

﴿And do not follow﴾. Al-Mahayimi said: That is, by blind imitation (taqlid), the desires of a people who clung to the extraordinary things (of their two figures) in support of their divinity. If they look at their precedence, their ultimate claim is that they "had gone astray before", (p-2108) and, as to the multitude of their followers, their ultimate claim is that they "led many astray" among those who agreed with them on the Trinity; and as to their clinging to the ambiguous passages of the Gospel, their ultimate claim is that they "strayed from the right way", since they did not refer them back to the clear verses (muhkamat).

Notices:

The first: Al-Razi said:

Desires (ahwa') here means the doctrines to which lust calls without proof. Al-Sha'bi said: God has not mentioned the word "desire" (hawa) in the Qur'an except to condemn it. He said: ﴿And do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the path of God﴾, ﴿and he followed his desire, so he fell﴾, ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾, ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: We have not found "desire" used except in the context of evil. One does not say, "So-and-so desires good"; one says, "he wants good and loves it." Some of them said: Desire is a god worshipped besides God. It was said: desire was called hawa because it casts its owner (yahwi) into the Fire.

And he recited in condemnation of desire:

Indeed desire is itself humiliation in its very essence,
so when you yield to it, you have met with humiliation.

And a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Praise be to God who made my desire to be above yours." Ibn 'Abbas said: "All desire is misguidance."

(p-2109) The second: Al-Razi also said: He, exalted is He, described them with three degrees of misguidance. He made clear that they were astray before, then mentioned that they were leading others astray, then mentioned that they continued in that state until they are now astray just as they were. We know of no state closer to distance from God and nearer to the punishment of God, exalted is He, than this state. We seek refuge in God from it. It is possible that what is meant is that they went astray and led others astray, then went astray again because of their belief, in that misleading, that it was guidance to the truth. It is also possible that what is meant by misguidance is misguidance concerning the religion, and misguidance concerning the path to Paradise. End of quote.

All these aspects, together with what we have previously mentioned from al-Mahayimi, are all of them possible meanings of the verse, since they all apply to them.

The third: The verse indicates that what these disbelievers possess of falsehoods, despite their contradiction to reason and their conflict with the fundamental principles, has no basis or reliance for them except the blind imitation of their misguided predecessors, who introduced the doctrine of the Trinity about three hundred years after the raising of the Messiah, peace be upon him. They established it in their teachings after dispute and confusion. They held to it by the outward meanings of expressions whose knowledge they do not comprehend, things that have no basis in the law of the Gospel, nor are they derived from the words of the Messiah or from the sayings of his disciples. Moreover, it is confused, contradictory and incoherent, some of it refuting and contradicting the rest, as is clear from the books written in refutation of them.

The fourth: It is stated in Tanwir al-Miqbas:

The intended meaning of "People of the Scripture" here is the Christians of Najran who came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. By His words, "do not follow the desires of a people," are meant al-'Aqib and al-Sayyid. The first, as Ibn Ishaq said, was the leader of the people and their man of opinion; the second was the companion of their caravan and their gathering.

The more evident view is that what is meant by "People of the Scripture" is the Christians in general, and those mentioned enter into it in the first place.

(p-2110) The fifth: Many exegetes mentioned that what is meant by "People of the Scripture" here is the Jews and Christians, and that both exaggerated regarding Jesus, peace be upon him: as for the exaggeration of the Jews, it is the negligence regarding him to the extent that they attributed him to an illegitimate birth; as for the exaggeration of the Christians, it is well known. And that the address in His words, ﴿and do not follow the desires of a people﴾, is to the Jews and Christians who were in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. They were forbidden to follow their predecessors in the misguidance they innovated by their desires. End of quote.

It is evident that what is ascribed to both groups, of exaggeration and innovation, is established. Nevertheless, the closer reading in view of the context refuting the doubts of the Christians is that this verse is directed at them as a rebuke for what they had pursued, following its refutation by decisive proofs.
