The crier of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he said "Hasten to prayer," would call out: "No intoxicated person should approach prayer." Umar was called and it was recited to him. He said: "O Allah! Make clear to us a decisive explanation regarding wine." So the verse in al-Ma'idah was revealed. When it reached His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], Umar said: "We have desisted! We have desisted!" Narrated by Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The prohibition of wine was revealed concerning two tribes from the tribes of the Ansar. They drank, and when the people became intoxicated, some of them played with others. When they became sober, each man saw the effect on his face, head, and beard, and said: "My brother so-and-so did this to me." They had been brothers with no rancor in their hearts, but he would say: "By Allah! If he had been kind and merciful to me, he would not have done this to me." Until rancor entered their hearts. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿Indeed, wine﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], to His words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91].

Some of the over-zealous people said: "It is an abomination, and it is in the belly of so-and-so, who was killed at Uhud." So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who﴾, the verse. Al-Nasa'i narrated it in his "Tafsir."

Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) drank wine in the morning and then were killed as martyrs on the day of Uhud. The Jews said: "Some of those who were killed died while it was in their bellies." So it was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who﴾, the verse. Al-Bazzar said: Its chain is sahih.

Ibn Kathir said: It is as he said.

Ibn Kathir has cited many hadiths on the prohibition of wine, from what was narrated by the authors of the Sahih collections, the Sunan, and the Musnads, so whoever wishes may refer to it. And it is not hidden that its prohibition is known as a matter of the religion by necessity.

(p-2152) Al-Suyuti narrated in "al-Jami' al-Kabir," from Ibn Asakir with his chain to Sayf ibn Umar, from al-Rabi', Abu Uthman, and Abu Harithah, who said: Abu Ubaydah wrote to Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Some Muslims have drunk wine, among them Dirar and Abu Jandal. We questioned them, and they interpreted (the verse) and said: 'We were given a choice, so we chose.'" He said: "Will you not then desist?" and he did not decide. Umar wrote to him: "That is between us and them: 'Will you not then desist?' meaning: So desist." He gathered the people, and they agreed that they should be lashed eighty times and that they should be liable for the lives (of those who died from it), and whoever interprets it in this manner, if he refuses, should be killed. They said: "Whoever interprets it in the manner from which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fled, should be restrained by action and killing." Umar wrote to Abu Ubaydah: "Summon them. If they claim it is permissible, then kill them. If they claim it is forbidden, then flog them eighty times." He sent to them and asked them before the eyes of the witnesses, and they said: "It is forbidden." So he flogged them eighty times. He applied the hadd punishment to the people, and they regretted their obstinacy. And he said: "There will surely arise among you, O people of Syria, a calamity," and then the Ramadah (plague) occurred.

Sayf ibn Umar also narrated it from al-Sha'bi and al-Hakam ibn Utaybah.

(p-2153) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[94] ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and your spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game﴾, i.e., He sends it to you while you are in the state of ihram, ﴿that your hands can reach﴾, to take it, and that is the weak and young of the game; ﴿and your spears﴾, to thrust at it, and that is the large game. ﴿That Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾, so that he refrains from hunting because of the strength of his faith.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: This verse was revealed concerning the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah. The wild animals and birds and game would come upon them in their camps, the like of which they had never seen before; so Allah forbade them to kill it while they were in the state of ihram.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, He, exalted is He, tests them with game that comes upon them in their camps, and they are able to take it with their hands and spears, secretly and openly, so that the obedience of whoever obeys among them is made manifest, in private or in public, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord in the unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Mulk: 12].

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever transgresses﴾, i.e., by hunting: ﴿after that﴾, meaning after the notification and warning: ﴿he will have a painful punishment﴾ for opposing the command of Allah and His law.

A subtle point:

al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of the diminution and belittling in His saying: "with something of game"? I say: He diminished and belittled it so that it would be known that it is not one of the great trials that make the feet of the steadfast slip, such as being tested by giving up lives and wealth; rather it is similar to what the people of Ayla were tested with, the catching of fish, and if they did not stand firm before that, how would their state be before what is greater than it...?

(p-2154) al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: This very expression has come in the case of great trials in His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits. But give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155]. There is no doubt in the greatness of these afflictions and tribulations for which the patient one deserves to be given good tidings, because it is great patience. So al-Zamakhshari's statement that He diminished and belittled it as a warning that this trial is not one of the great trials is refuted by its being used alongside trials agreed upon to be great. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that what the wording implies of diminution and belittling is a warning that all that these afflictions befall with is a part of a whole, relative to the power of Allah, exalted is He. He is able to make what He tests them with of that greater and more terrible than what occurs. And whatever is averted from them of what is greater in what is decreed, He averts only to what is lighter and easier, out of kindness and mercy toward them, so that this warning serves as a motive for them to be patient and as a bearer to endurance. What indicates that this is intended is that the prior warning of this was only so that they would prepare themselves for it when it occurs, and so it is also a motive to bear it, because the sudden arrival of what is hated is harder. And warning of it before its occurrence eases its coming. The outcome of this is kindness in the decree... So glory be to the Kind toward His servants. When the sensible person reflects on the kinds of afflictions with which he is tested, he finds that what is averted from him of them is more, without end. So we ask Allah for pardon, well-being and kindness in what is decreed... End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari may answer that the verse ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ is evidence for him, not against him, because what is intended there too is relative to what Allah averted from them, as al-Nasir stated, though averting it is complete by the verse only if ﴿and loss﴾ is conjoined to the genitive noun after ﴿of﴾; if it were conjoined to ﴿something﴾, it would be exactly like this verse with no difference. Thus in al-Inayah.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[95] ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever among you kills it intentionally - then the penalty is an equivalent from the livestock as judged by two just men among you as an offering to be delivered to the Kaaba, or an expiation: feeding needy people, or the equivalent of that in fasting, that he may taste the bad consequence of his deed. Allah has pardoned what is past. But whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ i.e., those who are in ihram for hajj or 'umrah.

Al-Mahayimi said: "Because killing it is an act of tyranny, whereas the one in ihram is in the utmost state of humility." End of quotation.

He mentioned killing rather than slaughtering and dhakat (ritual slaughter), for generality; or to indicate that it is in the ruling of carrion. Game (al-sayd) is that which is hunted, whether edible or otherwise. The only exception is what is established in the "Two Sahihs" from ʿĀʾishah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Five are wicked creatures who may be killed in the state of non-ihram and in ihram: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the rat, and the rabid dog." In another narration, "the snake" replaces "the scorpion."

Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn ʿUyaynah said: the rabid dog (al-kalb al-ʿaqur) includes all attacking predators. This is supported by what is narrated: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab, he said: 'O Allah, set your dog upon him.' So a predator ate him at al-Zarqa'."

﴿And whoever among you﴾ O those in ihram: ﴿kills it intentionally﴾, remembering (p-٢١٥٦) his state of ihram: ﴿then the penalty﴾ (read with tanwin and the following word in the nominative), i.e., upon him is a penalty which is: ﴿an equivalent from the livestock﴾, i.e., its likeness in form. In another reading, "penalty" is in the construct form (idafah). ﴿As judged by two﴾ mujtahids: ﴿just men among you﴾ who have the discernment by which they distinguish what is most similar to it. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUmar and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, judged for the ostrich a camel. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu ʿUbaydah judged for the wild cow and its donkey a cow. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAwf judged for the gazelle a sheep. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUmar and others judged for the pigeon [a sheep], because it resembles it in gulping water. ﴿As an offering﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (penalty): ﴿to be delivered to the Kaaba﴾, i.e., it is brought to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), where it is slaughtered and given in charity to its needy. It is not permissible to slaughter it wherever one is. ﴿Or﴾ upon him: ﴿an expiation﴾ other than the penalty, even if he finds it, is: ﴿feeding needy people﴾ from the staple food of the land, an amount equal in value to the penalty, for each needy person a mudd. In another reading, "expiation" is in the construct form with what follows, and it is explanatory. ﴿Or﴾ upon him: ﴿the equivalent of﴾ that food: ﴿fasting﴾, he fasts one day for every mudd. ﴿That he may taste﴾, i.e., the violator of Allah's sanctity: ﴿the bad consequence of his deed﴾, i.e., the severity and burden of his violation of the sanctity of ihram. The phrase "that he may taste" is connected to the stable adverbial element within the prepositional phrase; i.e., upon him is a penalty so that he may taste, or by a verb indicated by the context, i.e., this was prescribed for him so that he may taste. ﴿Allah has pardoned what is past﴾ of killing game before its prohibition. ﴿But whoever returns﴾ to it: ﴿Allah will take retribution from him﴾ by exacting the penalty in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. How could He leave that? ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might﴾, dominant over His command. The requirement of His might is retribution against the violator of His sanctity, so He is without doubt ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾ against whoever disobeys Him.

Remarks:

First: Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Tawus that he said: "No one is judged for having hit game by mistake; judgment is only on one who hits it intentionally."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is a strange position, adhering to the apparent wording of the verse."

I saw in some Zaydi tafsirs that this view is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', Mujahid, Salim, Abu Thawr, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan (in one of two narrations), al-Qasim, al-Hadi, al-Nasir and others. End of quotation.

(p-٢١٥٧) The majority hold that the intentional and the forgetful are equal in the obligation of the penalty.

Al-Zuhri said: the Book indicates the intentional, and the Sunnah established the forgetful.

Second: If the game has no equivalent, Ibn ʿAbbas judged by its value, to be brought to Makkah. Narrated by al-Bayhaqi.

Third: Most of the imams held that in this context there is choice (takhyir) among the penalty, feeding, and fasting, because the wording is (aw, "or"), and its literal meaning is choice.

Some of the early scholars held that it is in graded order (tartib). They said: "Aw" entered only to clarify that the penalty does not exceed one of these things, and because we found that the expiations for zihar and for killing are in graded order. We say: this is countered by the expiation for oaths and by the blood-payment for harm (dam al-adha), so it does not depart from the literal meaning of the word, which is choice.

Fourth: Whoever relies on the apparent words of His saying ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ says: there is no expiation upon the one who returns, because He did not mention it. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Shurayh. The majority hold that it is obligatory upon him, because the threat against the one who returns does not contradict the obligation of the penalty upon him. He did not state it explicitly because it was known from what came before. Moreover, the verse may mean: whoever returns, after the prohibition, to what he did before it.

Fifth: Al-Hakim said: Just as the verse indicates referring to just men in determining equivalence, so there is in that an indication of the permissibility of ijtihad and of the correctness of the mujtahids, the permissibility of basing rulings on preponderant opinion, the permissibility of a layman referring to a scholar, and that in disputes over matters it is obligatory to refer to people of insight... End of quotation.

And the Lord's words:

The explanation of His words, exalted is He:

[96] ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear God, to whom you will be gathered.﴾

﴿Lawful for you﴾ is addressed to those in the state of ihram. ﴿The game of the sea and its food﴾. Al-Mahayimi said: because there is not in it the arrogance that contradicts the humility required by ihram. And "the game of the sea" is what is caught from it fresh, and "its food" is what is taken as provision from it salted and dried, as related in a narration from Ibn 'Abbas. The well-known position from him is that its game is what is taken from it alive, and its food is what it casts up dead. Ibn Kathir said: this is what has been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may God be pleased with them, and from more than one of the Followers (tabi'un).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Bakr, who said: "Its food is everything in it."

And from Ibn al-Musayyab: "Its food is what it casts up alive, or what recedes from it and it dies."

﴿As a provision for you﴾, meaning: an enjoyment for those of you who are resident, who eat it fresh; ﴿and for the travelers﴾ among you, who take it as provision dried.

And (al-sayyara) means a people who travel. It is feminine because it refers to a company and a group.

Two points of note:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: The majority of scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of its carrion, together with what Imam Malik related from Ibn Wahb and Ibn Kaysan from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a detachment toward the coast, and he appointed over them Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, and they were three hundred—he said: and I was among them—he said: We went out until, when we were in part of the way, the provisions ran out. Abu 'Ubayda ordered the provisions of that army to be gathered, and it came to two bags of dates. He said: He would feed us a little each day, until it ran out and we had nothing but a single date each. I said: What can a date do? He said: We found its loss when it was lost. He said: Then we reached the sea, and there was a fish like a mound of sand. That army ate from it for eighteen nights. Then Abu 'Ubayda ordered two of its ribs to be taken and they were set up. Then he ordered a riding camel to be brought, and it was saddled, and then it passed beneath them without touching them."

This hadith is recorded in the "Two Sahihs," and it has chains from Jabir. In "Sahih Muslim," from Jabir: "We took provisions of its meat in strips. When we came to Madina, we came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and he said: It is a provision that God brought out for you. Do you have any of its meat with you so that you may feed us? He said: We sent some of it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he ate it."

In some narrations of Muslim: that they were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when they found this fish. Some of them said: it was a separate incident. Others said: it was one event, but they were first with the Prophet (ﷺ), then he sent them as a detachment with Abu 'Ubayda, and they found this in that detachment with Abu 'Ubayda. And God knows best.

And from Abu Hurayrah: "A man asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God! We ride the sea and carry with us a little water. If we perform ablution with it we become thirsty. Shall we perform ablution with seawater? The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Its water is pure, its carrion is lawful.'" Related by Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and the compilers of the Sunan. Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Hibban and others authenticated it.

And from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us: as for the two carrions, fish and locusts; as for the two bloods, liver and spleen." Related by al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, and it has corroborating reports. It has also been related as a statement of Ibn 'Umar (mawquf). These are the arguments of the majority.

The second: Some jurists who held that the animals of the sea may be eaten also used this verse, and they did not exclude anything from that. It has preceded from al-Siddiq that he said: "Its food is everything in it." Some of them excepted frogs and permitted what is other than them, on the basis of what Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Taymi, that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog." And al-Nasa'i related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: its croaking is glorification."

﴿And the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾, meaning: while you are in the state of ihram. So if the one in ihram hunts game deliberately, he has sinned and must make compensation; or if by mistake, he must make compensation, and eating it is forbidden to him, because for him it is like carrion. ﴿And fear God﴾ regarding hunting in the Sacred Precinct (haram) or during ihram. Then He warned them with His words, glorified is He: ﴿to whom you will be gathered﴾, meaning: you will be raised, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

(A subtle point)

Al-Mahayimi said: Game was forbidden to the one in ihram only because he intends the Ka'ba, whose sacred precinct's game is forbidden, so he is treated as one who has arrived at it. And the game of its precinct is forbidden because it is like the house of a king, into which one is not to be intruded upon, nor anything in it or in its precinct. End of quote.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[97] ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind, and the Sacred Month, and the offerings and the garlanded animals. That is so that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind﴾ i.e., a foundation for the establishment of their religious affairs through pilgrimage to it, and their worldly affairs through the security within it, the non-violation of it, and the gathering of the fruits of everything to it.

Al-Mahayimi said: Allah made it a station of turning towards it in worship for mankind dispersed throughout the world, so that there might be achieved for them the gathering that necessitates mutual affection, which they need in their civilization, through which the perfection of their livelihoods and their institutions is realized, due to their need for mutual assistance in both.

﴿And the Sacred Month﴾ meaning the Sacred Months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram and Rajab, [made] a means of establishment for them through their security from fighting therein, because fighting was prohibited therein so that mutual harmony might be achieved therein. ﴿And the offerings﴾ which are what is brought as an offering to Makkah. ﴿And the garlanded animals﴾ is the plural of qiladah, which is what is placed on the neck of the camel brought as an offering and on others. The intended meaning of "the garlanded animals" is the animals bearing garlands, which are the camels. They are singled out for mention because the reward in them is greater and the splendour of the Hajj is most manifest through them. The second object is omitted, relying on what has passed, i.e., He made the offerings and the garlanded animals also a means of establishment for them; for they used to feel secure by driving the offerings to the Sacred House for themselves, and in this there is sustenance for the poor there. Likewise, they used to feel secure when they garlanded them, or garlanded themselves upon entering the state of ihram, with the bark of the trees of the Haram, so that no one would encroach upon them.

﴿That﴾ i.e., the aforementioned making: ﴿so that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, for His making that for the sake of bringing benefits to you and warding off harms from you before they occur is evidence of His knowledge of what exists and what will come to be.

Al-Razi has excellently elaborated the exposition of this station, so let it be consulted.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ are a generalization following a specification, for emphasis.

His words, exalted is He:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[98] ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is a warning to whoever violates His sacred prohibitions or persists in that, and ﴿that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a promise to whoever guards the observance of His sacred limits.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[99] ﴿Upon the Messenger is only the conveyance (of the message), and Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾

﴿Upon the Messenger is only the conveyance (of the message)﴾ meaning: there is nothing upon Our Messenger whom We have sent to you except conveying what he was sent with, of the warning with that which cuts off every proof. In the verse there is emphasis on the obligation of carrying out what he was commanded, and that the Messenger has already completed what was incumbent upon him of conveyance. The proof has been established against you, obedience has become binding upon you, so there is no excuse for you in negligence: ﴿and Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ of good and evil, and He will recompense you for that.

(p-2163)

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[100] ﴿Say: "The bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the bad impresses you. So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you may succeed."﴾

﴿Say: The bad and the good are not equal﴾ is a general ruling denying equality in the sight of Allah, glorified and exalted, between the inferior among persons, deeds and wealth and their excellent counterparts. It is intended to encourage righteous action and lawful wealth. ﴿Even if the abundance of the bad impresses you﴾: the criterion is quality and inferiority, not scarcity and abundance, for the praiseworthy few is better than the blameworthy many. The address is general to every person who takes heed (i.e., who looks with the eye of consideration, i'tibar), and for this reason He said: ﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding﴾, meaning: fear Him in seeking out the bad even if it is abundant, and prefer the good even if it is scarce. ﴿That you may succeed﴾, meaning: attain the stations of nearness to Him, which are prepared for the good.

Two remarks:

The first: al-Razi said: Know that when He, exalted, warned against disobedience and encouraged obedience by His words, "Know that Allah is severe in punishment" (the verse), and then by what follows it, He followed this with another kind of encouragement and warning by His words, "Say: The bad and the good are not equal" (the verse). That is because the bad and the good are of two kinds. One is the bodily kind, which is evident to everyone. The second is the spiritual kind. The worst of spiritual evils is ignorance and disobedience, and the best of spiritual goods is the knowledge of Allah, exalted, and obedience to Him. This is because a body to which some impurity clings becomes repugnant to those of sound natures. Likewise, souls characterized by ignorance of Allah and turning away from His obedience become repugnant to perfect and sanctified souls. As for souls that know Allah, exalted, and persist in serving Him, they become illuminated by the lights of divine knowledge and delighted by nearness to pure and sanctified souls. Just as the bad and the good (p-2164) in the world of bodily things are not equal, so in the world of spiritual things they are not equal. Rather, the separation between them in the world of spiritual things is greater, because the harm of the bodily bad is a small thing and its benefit of the good is brief. But the badness of the spiritually bad is great, lasting and everlasting, and the goodness of the spiritually good is great, lasting and everlasting: it is nearness to the neighborhood of the Lord of the worlds, joining the company of the angels brought near, and companionship with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. So this is among the greatest aspects of encouragement to obedience and warning against disobedience.

The second: Some exegetes said: among the fruits of the verse is that the righteous should be honored and distinguished above the wicked. And that when a ruler is asked to judge between a disbeliever and a believer, he should distinguish the believer in the assembly. End of quotation.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[101] ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned them, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask﴾, i.e., your Prophet, ﴿about things which, if they were disclosed﴾, i.e., if they were made manifest, ﴿to you would distress you﴾ because of the hardship in them. ﴿But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾. That is: if you ask about things concerning which the Qur'an was revealed in a general form, and you seek their explanation, they will be explained to you at that time, because of your need for them. This is one interpretation of the verse. On this reading, ﴿while﴾ (ḥīn) is an adverbial complement of ﴿ask﴾.

There is another interpretation: that ﴿while﴾ (ḥīn) is an adverbial complement of ﴿disclosed﴾, and the meaning is: "if you ask about them, they will be disclosed to you at the time the Qur'an is revealed."

Ibn al-Qayyim said: What is meant by "the time of revelation" (ḥīn al-nuzūl) is the period connected to it, not the moment coinciding with the revelation. It seems that in this there is a permission for them to ask about the details of what was revealed and to seek knowledge of it after it was sent down. Thus there is a removal of the misapprehension that asking about things is prohibited absolutely. He then said: There is a second opinion regarding His saying, ﴿But if you ask about them﴾, etc., namely that it is in the mode of threat and warning. That is: if you ask about them at the time the revelation descends, the explanation of what you asked about will come to you in a way that distresses you. The meaning is: do not expose yourselves to asking about what its explanation would distress you, and if you do expose yourselves to it during the time of revelation, it will be made manifest to you. End of quotation.

Some of them said: Exalted is He first made clear that those things about which they asked, if they were disclosed to them, would distress them. Then He made clear, secondly, that if they asked about them, they would be disclosed to them. The upshot of the statement is: if they ask about them, they will be disclosed to them, and if they are disclosed to them, they will distress them. Thus from the combination of the two premises it follows that, if they ask about them, there will become manifest to them what distresses them and does not gladden them.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: His saying, ﴿if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾, is a qualifier of ﴿things﴾, serving as a call to refrain from asking about them. Since the distress in this conditional clause is linked to their being disclosed, not to asking about them, it is followed by another conditional clause stating that asking about them necessarily leads to their being disclosed, which decisively entails the feared outcome. Thus it is said: ﴿But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾, i.e., those things that cause distress will be disclosed by revelation, as indicated by restricting the asking to the time of the revelation's descent. What is meant by this is: the difficult burdens that are hard for them and grieve them, which they cannot bear, and the hidden secrets by whose disclosure they would be exposed, and the like, all of which contain no good. Just as asking about events that have occurred entails their being made manifest, so asking about those burdens entails their being imposed upon them as a strictness, because of their discourtesy and their boldness in questioning and in seeking clarification, and their overstepping what befits their station, which is submission to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without inquiring into it or probing its manner and quantity. That is: do not multiply questioning the Messenger of Allah ﴿ﷺ﴾ about what does not concern you, of burdens heavy upon you, which, if he gives you a ruling on them and imposes them upon you as they were revealed to him, you would not be able to bear, and about some hidden matters the disclosure of which you would dislike.

﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾, i.e., those things, at the time when the Qur'an had not been revealed concerning them, and He did not make them obligatory upon you, as a relief for you. Or: Allah has pardoned their explanation, so that their explanation would not distress you. Then the clause is in the place of a genitive, a second qualifier of ﴿things﴾. Or the meaning is: Allah has pardoned your previous questions and overlooked your otherworldly punishment for your questions, so do not return to the like of them. The clause in that case is a new, explanatory sentence, because their prohibition was not merely for the sake of protecting them from distress, but because asking itself is a disobedience entailing accountability, and He has pardoned it. In this there is, for urging them to earnestness in refraining from it, what is not hidden. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause affirming His pardon, exalted is He, i.e., He is emphatic in forgiving sins. For this reason He pardoned you and did not hold you accountable for what had passed from you.

al-Qasimi's commentary (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 5, verse 102 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
[102] ﴿Certainly a people before you asked such questions, and then became disbelievers because of them.﴾

﴿Certainly a people before you asked such questions⦆ — that is, they asked this same kind of question, but not the very same one; rather, one like it in that it was forbidden and entailed ruin. The failure to state "like it" explicitly is for the sake of emphasis in the warning. ﴿and then became disbelievers because of them﴾ — that is, because of these questions, in that they did not comply with what they were answered with and did it. The Children of Israel used to ask their prophets about things, and when they were commanded to do them, they abandoned them and perished. The meaning is: beware of resembling them and of exposing yourselves to what they were exposed to.

Remarks:

The first: al-Bukhari narrated in his "Tafsir", regarding the occasion of its revelation, from Abu al-Juwayriyah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There were people who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in mockery. One man would say: 'Who is my father?' and another, whose she-camel had strayed, would say: 'Where is my camel?' So Allah revealed concerning them this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101], until He finished the whole verse."

He also narrated from Musa ibn Anas, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon the like of which I had never heard. He said: 'If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much...' He said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) covered their faces, and they had sobbing sounds. A man said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'So-and-so.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Do not ask about things which, if they are shown to you, will trouble you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101]."

Al-Bukhari also narrated in the Book of "Afflictions", from Qatadah, that Anas narrated to them, saying: "They questioned the Prophet (ﷺ) until they pressed him with questions. The Prophet (ﷺ) ascended the pulpit one day and said: 'Do not ask me about anything except that I will make it clear to you.' I began looking to the right and to the left, and every man had his head in his garment, weeping. Then a man, who when quarrelling would be called by other than his father's name, rose and said: 'O Prophet of Allah! Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafah.' Then Umar rose and said: 'We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger. We seek refuge in Allah from the evil of trials.'

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I have never seen in good and evil the like of today. Paradise and Hellfire were displayed to me until I saw them beyond the wall.'

Qatadah used to mention this hadith at this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101]."

In another narration: Qatadah said, it is mentioned (in the passive voice) — this hadith... etc.

Al-Bukhari also narrated in the Book of "I'tisam bil-Kitab was-Sunnah", in the chapter on what is disliked of excessive questioning, from al-Zuhri, who said: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) informed me that "the Prophet (ﷺ) went out when the sun had passed its zenith, prayed Dhuhr, and when he had given the salam he stood on the pulpit and mentioned the Hour, and mentioned that before it there were great matters. Then he said: 'Whoever wishes to ask about anything, let him ask about it. By Allah, you will not ask me about anything except that I will inform you of it as long as I remain in this place of mine.'" Anas said: "The Ansar wept greatly, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept saying..." Anas said: "A man stood and said: 'Where is my entrance, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The Fire.' Then 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah stood and said: 'Who is my father, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafah.' He then kept saying: 'Ask me.' Umar knelt on his knees and said: 'We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (ﷺ) as Messenger.'"

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell silent when Umar said that.

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul! Paradise and the Fire were just now displayed to me in the breadth of this wall while I was praying. I have never seen the like of today in good and evil."

In Muslim: Ibn Shihab said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah informed me, saying: The mother of 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah said to 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah: "I have never heard of a son more undutiful than you. Are you sure that your mother has not committed some of what the women of the Jahiliyyah committed, so that you would expose her before the eyes of the people?"

'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah said: "By Allah! If he had attributed me to a black slave, I would have been attached to him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry one day, rose to deliver a sermon, and said: 'Ask me...' — similar to what has preceded — and added: 'Then Umar came to him, kissed his foot, and said: "We are content with Allah as Lord..."' etc.

And he added: 'and with the Qur'an as imam. Pardon us, may Allah pardon you.' He did not cease with him until he was pleased."

He also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, angry, his face reddened, until he sat on the pulpit. A man rose to him and said: 'Where am I?' He said: 'In the Fire.' — similar to what passed — and in it: Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101]..." the verse.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": "With this addition — beyond what is in al-Bukhari, the man's saying to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Where am I?' He said: 'In the Fire' — it becomes clear that this incident is the occasion of revelation of: ﴿Do not ask about things...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101], for the offence against this man came explicitly, unlike the case of Hudhafah, which was by way of supposition — i.e., if it were assumed that in reality he was not his father's son, and he had declared his true father, his mother would have been exposed, as his mother herself stated when she rebuked him for this question. End of quote."

Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu al-Bukhtari, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], they said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Is it every year?' He was silent. They said: 'Every year?' He was silent. Then they said: 'Every year?' He said: 'No. And if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory, you would not have been able to do it.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101], the verse."

al-Tirmidhi said: "Gharib. I heard al-Bukhari say: Abu al-Bukhtari did not meet 'Ali."

Ibn Jarir narrated, and similar, from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Umamah, and likewise from Ibn 'Abbas (p-2170), who said regarding the verse: ﴿Do not ask about things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101] — if the Qur'an were revealed concerning them with severity, that would trouble you; but wait, for if the Qur'an is revealed, you will not ask about anything except that you will find its explanation.

Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": The sum is that it was revealed because of the abundance of questions: either by way of mockery or testing, or by way of hair-splitting about a matter which, had it not been asked about, would have remained permissible.

Second: Ibn Kathir said: The apparent meaning of the verse is a prohibition against asking about things which, if the person learned of them, would distress him. Therefore it is better to turn away from them and leave them. How excellent is the hadith which Imam Ahmad narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his Companions: "Let no one convey to me anything about anyone, for I wish to come out to you with a sound heart." Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it.

Third: Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in":
The ruling of this verse has not ceased. Rather, it is not fitting for the servant to expose himself to asking about what, if it became apparent to him, would distress him. Rather he should seek to be spared as much as he can, and take up Allah's pardon. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O owner of the spout! Do not inform us," when his companion asked him about his water: "Is it pure or not?"

Likewise, it is not fitting for the servant to ask his Lord to reveal to him any of his states or his final outcome which He has concealed from him and veiled, for perhaps it would distress him if it were revealed to him. So asking about all of that is an exposure to what Allah dislikes. For He, glory be to Him, dislikes its disclosure, and that is why He was silent about it.

(p-2171) What he mentioned of generality is according to the apparent wording. As for the primary and essential purpose — as its continuation indicates — it is the prohibition of asking about what would be distressing to disclose during the time of revelation.

Supporting this is what al-Bukhari narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The greatest of the Muslims in crime is the one who asks about something that was not forbidden, and so it became forbidden because of his asking."

Such a thing has been secured against occurring.

And from Abu Hurayrah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed by the abundance of their questions and their disputes with their prophets. So when I command you with something, do of it what you are able; and when I forbid you from something, leave it." Narrated by Imam Ahmad, Muslim and al-Nasa'i.

And from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them. He has set limits, so do not transgress them. He has forbidden things, so do not approach them. And He has left some things, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search after them." Narrated by al-Daraqutni and Abu Nu'aym.

And from Salman al-Farisi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about things, and he said: (p-2172) 'The lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book. The unlawful is what Allah has made unlawful in His Book. And what He has been silent about, it is among what He has pardoned, so do not burden yourselves.'" Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim and Ibn Majah.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Anas: "We were forbidden to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about anything. And it pleased us that a heedless man from the people of the desert would come and ask him while we listened."

In the story of the li'an from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked questions and disparaged them."

(p-2173) In Muslim, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: "I stayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a year in Madinah, and what prevented me from emigrating was only the question. Whenever one of us emigrated, he would not ask the Prophet (ﷺ)."

His meaning is: that he came as a delegate, and remained in that condition in order to gather questions, fearing that he would leave the status of a delegate for continued residence and thus become a muhajir, and then asking would be forbidden to him.

In this is an indication that the one addressed by the prohibition of asking is not only the Bedouins, whether delegates or others.

Abu Umamah said, as narrated by Ahmad: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101], we were careful not to ask him (ﷺ). So we went to a Bedouin, bribed him with a cloak, and said: 'Ask the Prophet (ﷺ).'"

And in Abu Ya'la, from al-Bara': "A year would pass over me, and I wished to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about something, but I would be too awed. And we used to wish for the Bedouins — i.e., their coming — so that they would ask him, and we would hear the answers to the Bedouins' questions, and benefit from them."

As for what is established in the hadiths of the questions of the Companions, it is possible that it was before the revelation of the verse, (p-2174) and it is possible that the prohibition in the verse does not cover what is needed of matters whose ruling has been established, or what they have a present need to know: such as asking about slaughter with a reed, asking about the obligation to obey rulers when they command disobedience, asking about the conditions of the Day of Resurrection and what precedes it of great battles and trials, and the questions in the Qur'an, such as their asking about kalalah, wine, gambling, fighting in the sacred month, orphans, menstruation, women, hunting, and other things.

However, those who relied on the verse to dislike multiplying questions about what has not occurred took it by way of analogy: since the abundance of questioning, when it was a cause of obligation to what is burdensome, its due is to be avoided.

Imam al-Darimi, in the beginning of his "Musnad", composed a chapter for this, and included in it many reports from a group of Companions and Successors. Among them: from Ibn 'Umar: "Do not ask about what has not happened, for I heard 'Umar curse the one who asks about what has not happened."

From 'Umar: "I adjure you not to ask about what has not happened, for for us there is enough of what has been."

From Zayd ibn Thabit: that when he was asked about a matter, he would say: "Has this happened?" If it was said, "No," he would say: "Leave it until it happens."

And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and from 'Ammar, something similar.

Abu Dawud related in "al-Marasil", from Abu Salama and Mu'adh, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ): "Do not hasten toward a calamity before it descends; for if you do so, there will always remain among the Muslims one who, when he speaks, is guided aright (or given success), but if you hasten, the paths will scatter you."

And from the shaykhs of al-Zubayr ibn Sa'id, as a marfu' report: "There will not cease to be in my community one who, when asked, is guided aright, until they ask about what has not yet occurred."

Some of the imams said: The correct position on this matter is that inquiry into matters for which there is no explicit text falls into two categories:

The first: inquiry into whether a matter enters the indication (dalalah) of a text according to its various modes of indication. This is desirable, not disliked; indeed, it may even be an obligation upon those among the mujtahids on whom it is incumbent.

The second: scrutinizing the aspects of difference so finely that one distinguishes between two alike matters by a difference that has no effect in the Shari'ah despite the presence of the shared attribute, or the reverse, by bringing together two dissimilar matters on the basis of an incidental attribute (wasf tardi, i.e., an attribute with no effect on the ruling), for example. This is what the salaf (early scholars) censured. It is to this that the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, as a marfu' report, applies: "Destroyed are the over-scrupulous (al-mutanatti'un)..." Related by Muslim. They regarded it as involving the squandering of time on matters of no benefit.

Similar to this is the excessive elaboration on a question that has no basis in the Book, the Sunnah, or the consensus, and which is extremely rare in occurrence, so that one spends time on it which would be better spent on other matters, especially if this leads to neglecting the thorough explanation of what occurs frequently. And more severe than this, in the multiplicity of questioning, is searching into hidden matters about which the Shari'ah has commanded belief while leaving their modality unspecified, and among them are matters that have no witness in the sensible world, such as asking about the time of the Hour, about the soul (ruh), about the lifespan of this ummah... and similar matters that are known only through pure transmission. Much of this has not been established by any report, so belief without investigation is obligatory. And more severe than that is what excessive investigation into it causes of doubt and confusion.

Some of them said: An example of over-scrupulousness in questioning, to the point that it leads the one asked to answer with prohibition after having given a permissive fatwa, is to ask about goods found in the markets: is it disliked to buy them from the one who holds them, before inquiring about how they reached him, or not? The mufti answers him that it is permissible. If he then returns and says, "I fear that it may be from plunder or usurpation, and at that time something of that sort has indeed occurred in general," he would then need to answer him with prohibition. And it is to be qualified: if something of that is established, it is unlawful; if it is doubtful, it is disliked or contrary to what is better. And if the questioner had remained silent about this over-scrupulousness, the mufti would not have added to his answer of permissibility. Having established this, whoever closes the door of questions so that he misses knowing many of the rulings that frequently occur, his understanding and knowledge become scant; and whoever expands excessively in deriving and generating (p-2176) questions, especially concerning what rarely or seldom occurs, and especially if the motive for that is vainglory and contention, his action is blameworthy, and it is precisely what the salaf disliked. Whoever delves deeply into seeking the meanings of the Book of Allah, adhering to what has come in its explanation from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and from his Companions who witnessed the revelation, and obtains the rulings that are derived from its explicit and implicit meanings, and into the meanings of the Sunnah and what it indicates likewise, limiting himself to what is fit to serve as proof from them, such a person is the one who is praised and benefited. And upon this is to be understood the practice of the jurists of the regions, from the Tabi'un and those after them. Thus far in "Fath al-Bari".

Then I saw, in the "Muwafaqat" of the Imam al-Shatibi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, at its end, on this subject, a magnificent discussion. He said at its beginning:

Excessive questioning is blameworthy. The evidence for this is the widespread transmission from the Book, the Sunnah, and the words of the righteous predecessors. Among that is the saying of the Exalted... He cited this verse and the reports we have mentioned above, and added further to what we quoted. Then he said: The conclusion is that excessive questioning and pursuing matters with rational investigations and speculative possibilities is blameworthy. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been admonished against excessive questioning until they refrained from it. They would love that the Bedouins would come and ask, so that they could hear his words and memorize knowledge from him... Then he said: It becomes clear from this that the disliking of questioning has several occasions, of which we mention ten:

The first: asking about what does not benefit in religion, such as the question of Abdullah ibn Hudhafa: "Who is my father?" And it is related in the "Tafsir" that he ﷺ was asked: "What is the matter with the crescent moon, that it appears thin like a thread, then continues to grow until it becomes full, then diminishes until it returns as it was?" So Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you about the crescents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], the verse. He was answered only with what contains benefits for religion.

The second: asking after one has reached the knowledge he needs, as when a man asked about Hajj: "Is it every year?" although the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And due to Allah from mankind is a pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 97] indicates by its apparent meaning that it is for ever, due to its absolute wording. Similar to this is the question of the Children of Israel after the saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67].

The third: asking without need of it at the time. This, and Allah knows best, is specific to what no ruling has been revealed concerning, and to this the saying of the Prophet ﷺ points: "Leave me as I have left you," and his saying: "He was silent about things out of mercy for you, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search after them."

The fourth: asking about the most difficult and worst of questions, as came in the prohibition against "al-Ughlutat" (riddling, perplexing questions).

The fifth: asking about the reason of a ruling where it is among the matters of ritual observance (ta'abbudat), or where the questioner is one for whom such a question is not appropriate, as in the hadith about making up fasts but not prayers.

The sixth: pushing the question to the point of artificiality and excessive depth; to this the saying of the Exalted points: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any wage for it, and I am not of those who burden themselves﴾ [Sad: 86]. When a man was asked: "O owner of the pool! Do predators come to your pool?" 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O owner of the pool! Do not tell us, for we come upon predators and they come upon us."

The seventh: that the question manifests an opposition of the Book and the Sunnah by opinion; for this reason Sa'id said: "Are you an Iraqi?" It was said to Malik ibn Anas: "A man who is knowledgeable in the Sunnah, may he argue on its behalf?" He said: "No, but he informs with the Sunnah. If it is accepted from him, well; otherwise he remains silent."

The eighth: asking about the ambiguous matters (mutashabihat), to which the saying of the Exalted points: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7], the verse. And from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz: "Whoever makes his religion a target for disputes will quickly shift about." Among this is the question of one who asked Malik about the Istiwa' (the Divine Establishment): he said: "The Istiwa' is known, the modality is unknown, and asking about it is an innovation."

The ninth: asking about what occurred among the righteous predecessors. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was asked about the fighting of the people of Siffin, and he said: "Those are blood which Allah has withheld my hand from, so I do not wish to stain my tongue with it."

The tenth: asking for the purpose of challenge, confounding, and seeking victory in dispute. The Qur'an, in censure of this kind: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life impresses you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], and He said: ﴿Rather, they are a people given to dispute﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58]. And in a hadith: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious disputer."

This is a collection of the occasions in which questioning is disliked, by which other cases are measured. The prohibition therein is not uniform: among them are those whose disliking is severe, some that are light, some that are forbidden, and some that are matters of ijtihad. And in summary, from them comes the prohibition of disputation in religion, as came: "Indeed, argumentation about the Qur'an is disbelief." And the Exalted said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68], the verse... and the like of that among the verses and hadiths... So questioning in such matters is forbidden, and the answer is according to it. End of his words.

Fourth caution:

Some of the exegetes said: It is necessary to restrict the prohibition in this verse to "what need does not call for" (bima la tad'u ilayhi hajah). For the matter to which need calls in religious affairs, Allah has permitted asking about it, saying: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah fight them! Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is asking..." End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the verse, with its own qualification, namely "if they are shown to you..." etc., is sufficient without being restricted by another qualification as this one mentioned; because what is intended by it is what burdens them of difficult obligations and what would expose them, as we have explained, which is plunging into superfluities and undertaking what is not needed, and in which there is the danger of harm. A thing one does not need, and which carries the danger of harm, the intelligent person must avoid.

As for what need calls for, the verse does not include it, as is evident from its noble structure, together with what the Sunnah has clarified concerning the occasion of revelation; and the Companions' scrupulous avoidance of the questions previously explained is known to be about what is not necessary. Otherwise, their questions concerning the essentials and the needs were abundant in the books of Sunnah, which shows that this verse concerns a specific subject.

The Prophet ﷺ himself disliked opening the door to a multiplicity of questions, lest it lead to hardship, distress, or contention.

Al-Shaykhan related from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba that he wrote to Mu'awiya: "The Prophet ﷺ used to forbid qil and qal (idle talk), the squandering of property, and excessive questioning."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud related: "The Prophet ﷺ forbade al-Ughlutat," which are the difficult questions; and the reports on this are numerous.

Then Allah the Exalted explained the falsity of what the people of the Jahiliyyah had innovated, namely the prohibition of some of the cattle, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[103] ﴿God did not ordain any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham. But those who disbelieve invent lies against God, and most of them do not reason.﴾

﴿God did not ordain any bahira﴾, meaning He did not legislate or establish it. The ﴿مِن﴾ (min) is redundant, serving to emphasize the negation. The bahira (بَحِيرَة), on the pattern of safina, is a form in the sense of the passive participle, from al-bahr (البَحْر), which means slitting the ear. It is said: baḥara al-naqa wa'l-shāt, yabḥuruhā, meaning he slit her ear. There are many opinions on the bahira, which the author of the Qamus (al-Qamus, the dictionary) and others have cited.

Abu Ishaq al-Nahwi said: The most established of what we have related from the people of language about the bahira is that it was the she-camel which, when she had given birth to five offspring, the last of which was a male, they slit her ear (i.e., they split it) and left her back free from riding, carrying and slaughter, and she was not prevented from water she came to or pasture. And if one who was exhausted and cut off met her, he would not ride her.

﴿Nor sa'iba﴾, and it is the she-camel that was let loose (yusayyab) in the Jahiliyya for a vow or for their idols (ṭawāghīt). That is, she is left free and is not ridden, nor is anything carried on her, like the bahira. Or, if she gave birth to ten offspring, all of them females with no male among them, she was let loose, her back was not ridden, her wool was not shorn, and none drank her milk except her young or a guest. Or a man, when he returned from a long journey, or recovered from an illness, or his mount was saved from hardship or war, would say: "She (i.e., my camel) is a sa'iba."

﴿Nor wasila﴾. When a she-goat gave birth to six offspring in succession, two females at a time, and in the seventh she gave birth to a female kid and a male kid, they said: "She has joined her brother (wasalat akhāhā)." So they did not slaughter her brother on her account. They made her milk lawful for men and forbade it for women. The ʿanāq (عَنَاق, on the pattern of saḥāb) is the female of the young goats.

It was also said: the wasila was specific to the she-goat. If she gave birth to a female, it was for them; if she gave birth to a male, they dedicated it to their gods. And if she gave birth to a male and a female, they said: "She has joined her brother," so they did not slaughter the male for their gods.

﴿Nor ham﴾, and it is the stallion camel that services the counted number of mares. When his servicing was over, they placed on him the feathers of peacocks and let him loose for the ṭawāghīt. It was also said: it is the stallion whose offspring from his loins numbered ten. Then he is a ḥām, who protects (ḥamā) the protected pasture of his back. He is left so that nothing is benefited from him, and he is not prevented from water or pasture. Abu Muslim related: when the she-camel gave birth to ten offspring, they said: "She has protected her back (ḥamat ẓahrahā)."

Other explanations of these four have been related, and there is no contradiction in that, because the people of Jahiliyya had, in their fabrications, strange varieties (tafannunāt).

Moreover, Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Ahwas ʿAwf ibn Malik ibn Naḍla, from his father Malik ibn Naḍla, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in worn-out clothes. He said to me: 'Do you have any wealth?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'From what kind of wealth?' I said: 'From all kinds of wealth: camels, sheep, horses and slaves.' He said: 'When God gives you much wealth, then increase it for yourself.' Then he said: 'Does your camel give birth with her ears intact?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do camels give birth except like that?' He said: 'Perhaps you take the blade and slit the ears of some of them, saying: "This is forbidden (ḥaram)"?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do not do that. Indeed, everything God gives you is lawful (ḥill) for you.' Then he recited: ﴿God did not ordain any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham.﴾"

As for the bahira, it is the one whose ears they cut, so that his wife, his daughters and no one of his household benefit from her wool, her hair, her fur or her milk. When she dies, they share in her. As for the sa'iba, it is the one they let loose for their gods; they go to their gods and let her loose. As for the wasila, the she-goat gives birth to six offspring; when she gives birth to the seventh, it is slit and its horn is cut, and they say: "She has joined," so they do not slaughter her, nor is she struck, nor is she prevented, however much she comes to a pool.

Ibn Kathir said: This is how the explanation of that has been mentioned, inserted into the hadith. It has also been related by another route from Abu al-Ahwas, from his own statement, and that is more likely. Imam Ahmad also related this hadith from Malik ibn Naḍla, and it does not contain the explanation of these. And God knows best.

﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God﴾. That is, God did not legislate these things, nor are they with Him a means of drawing near to Him. But the polytheists invented that and made it a law for themselves and a means of drawing near, by which they seek nearness, and that is not achieved for them; rather it is a burden upon them.

In al-Bukhari it is stated that the tabhir (تَبْحِير), the taswib (تَسْيِيب) and what follows them, all of it was for the sake of the ṭawāghīt, meaning their idols.

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayra, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir al-Khuzaʿi dragging his intestines in the Fire. He was the first to let loose the sawaʾib, slit the bahira, and change the religion of Ismaʿil." This is the wording of Muslim.

Ibn Jarir added: "And he protected the protector (wa-ḥamā al-ḥāmī)."

Imam Ahmad related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the first to let loose the sawaʾib and worship idols was Abu Khuzaʿa, ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir, and I saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire."

Ibn Kathir said: This ʿAmr is Ibn Luhayy ibn Qamaʿa, one of the leaders of Khuzaʿa who held the House after Jurhum. He was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil). He brought idols into the Hijaz and called the herdsmen among the people to worship them and draw near by them. He legislated for them these Jahili laws concerning livestock and other things, as God mentioned in Surat al-Anʿam at His saying: ﴿And they assigned to God a share of what He created of the tilth and the livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136] and the verses that follow. End of quote.

A subtle point:

Al-Razi said: If it is said: if the freeing of male and female slaves is permissible, why is it not permissible to free these animals from slaughter, exhaustion and pain? We say: the human being is created for the service of God, exalted is He, and for His worship. When slavery is removed from him, he is free to worship Him, exalted is He, and that is a praiseworthy means of drawing near. As for these animals, they are created for the benefits of people. Neglecting them entails the loss of a benefit for their owner and for others; that is, it contradicts the wisdom for which they were created. Moreover, when a slave is freed, he is able to attain his own welfare, unlike the beast. So letting it loose subjects it to kinds of ordeal and hardship.

Al-Mahayimi said: They analogized the tabhir (i.e., slitting) to the freeing of a human being, though the difference is evident, because freeing a human confers upon him ownership of his own dispositions, while mute animals have no disposition.

Then he said: The first is like freeing without a vow. The second is like freeing by a vow. The third is like what resembles freeing. The fourth is ownership of the self without conferring ownership. There is no sense of conferring ownership on mute animals. So these matters are unintelligible outwardly and inwardly, and the wise would not do them.

(p-2188) Note:

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse indicates the prohibition of these matters. From it has been deduced the prohibition of all idleness of benefits. Among the forms of sa'iba is the release of a bird and the like. Ibn al-Majishun used the verse to prohibit one from saying to his slave: "You are a sa'iba," and he said: "He is not freed." End of quote.

Some of the commentators of the Zaydiyya said: Al-Hakim said: Some of them argued from the noble verse for the invalidity of the waqf (endowment), because ownership does not leave the possession of its owner to another owner, or because it is an act of nearness to God, like the freeing of necks. Al-Hakim said: This is not correct, because waqf is an act of nearness like manumission. Someone may say: the verse can be used as evidence for something similar to that, which is throwing eggs and chicks into rivers, roads and near trees. Doing so is not permissible, and the owner's ownership does not cease. It may be said that he has become disinterested in it and has made it permissible (mubah). As for breaking eggs for construction, roads and doors, the apparent view is that it is not permissible, because that involves wasting property, and there is no evidence permitting that act. End of quote.

When He, exalted is He, made clear that most of them do not reason, that the prohibition of these things was an empty fabrication, and that they only follow their forefathers without understanding, rather than contradict them and be guided to the truth, He pointed to their obstinacy and defiance when they were guided to the truth, and to their misguidance in remaining captive to imitation, with His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[104] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers." Even though their fathers knew nothing, nor were they guided?﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down"﴾ — from the Book that makes clear the lawful and the unlawful; ﴿and to the Messenger﴾, i.e., the one upon whom it was sent down, so that you may stand upon the reality of the matter and distinguish between the unlawful and the lawful, (p-2189) and thereby abandon the imitation of the ancients who fabricated lies against Allah with misguidance. ﴿They say﴾, i.e., due to the excess of their ignorance and their absorption in imitation: ﴿Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers﴾, i.e., that suffices us. "Sufficient for us" (ḥasbunā) is a subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate is "that upon which we found" (mā wajadnā), with "mā" meaning "that which" (alladhī). The waw in His Exalted saying ﴿Even though (awa-law) their fathers﴾ is for the circumstantial (ḥāl), and the interrogative hamza of denial has entered upon it. That is: Do they suppose this, even though their fathers ﴿knew nothing﴾, i.e., did not recognize the truth nor comprehend it, ﴿nor were they guided﴾, i.e., to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that following is valid only with a learned and guided person, and his guidance is known only through proof. End.

And al-Razi said: Know that following is permissible only with a learned, guided person. He is learned and guided only when he founds his speech upon proof and evidence. So if he is not such, he is not learned and guided, and it is therefore obligatory that following him is not permissible. End.

And some of the commentators of the Zaydiyya said: The fruit of the verse is the ugliness of imitation (taqlīd) and the obligation of reflection and following proof. Then he said: Imitation has been defined as accepting the statement of another without proof. End.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[105] ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves﴾: that is, commit yourselves to reforming them by following the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger. ﴿The one who is astray cannot harm you﴾: that is, of those who say, "What we found our fathers upon is enough for us," or who adhere to a doubt (shubha), or who are obstinate in word or deed. ﴿Once you are guided﴾: that is, to faith. It seems that the believers were distressed by the persistence of the disbelievers in their disbelief and misguidance, so they were told: take care of yourselves and of what you are charged with reforming, and of walking with them on the path of guidance. The misguidance of the misguided and the ignorance of the ignorant will not harm you, (p-٢١٩٠) when you are guided. Just as the Mighty and Majestic said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿So let not your soul expire in grief over them﴾ [Fatir: 8].

Al-Zamakhshari said: Likewise, whoever grieves over the immorality and sins of the corrupt, and constantly mentions their faults and abominations, is addressed by this verse. ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ after death, ﴿all of you﴾, ﴿and He will inform you﴾, that is, He will tell you ﴿of what you used to do﴾, that is, in the world, of deeds of guidance and of misguidance. This is a promise and a warning to both groups, and a reminder that no one is held accountable for the deeds of another. End of quotation.

Caution (tanbih):

The verse should not be cited as evidence for dropping the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil (al-amr bil-ma'ruf wal-nahy 'an al-munkar), because the apparent meaning of the verse is that the misguidance of others does not harm, and that one who obeys his Lord is not held accountable for the sins of the disobedient. But whoever abandons them while able to do them is not rightly guided; rather, he is among the misguided that the verse distinguishes between them and him.

Al-Hakim said: If its obligation were derived from His saying, ﴿take care of yourselves﴾, it would be better, because it includes every obligatory duty. That is, as al-Mahayimi did in his tafsir, where he said: "Take care of yourselves": that is, commit yourselves to reforming them by following the proofs from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the rational matters supported by them, and calling one's brethren to that, by establishing arguments, removing doubts, and enjoining the good and forbidding the evil by whatever means are possible, by word and deed. Do not fall short in this, for ﴿the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾, by calling them to what was revealed and to the Messenger, establishing proofs against them, removing doubts from them, and enjoining the good and forbidding the evil by whatever means are possible, by word and deed. Do not fall short in this, for ﴿to Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, of falling short or fulfilling, in word and deed, with respect to yourselves or others. End.

(p-٢١٩١) Al-Razi transmitted from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak that he said: This is the most emphatic verse concerning the obligation of enjoining the good and forbidding the evil. He said: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ means "take care of the people of your religion," and ﴿the one who is astray cannot harm you﴾ refers to the disbelievers who go astray. This is like His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾, meaning the people of your religion. So His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ means that some of you should admonish others, encourage others toward good deeds, and deter them from ugly and evil deeds. What confirms this is what we have explained: that His saying ﴿take care of yourselves﴾ means: protect yourselves from involvement in sins and persistence in transgressions. So this is a command that we protect ourselves. If that protection cannot be achieved except by enjoining the good and forbidding the evil, then it is obligatory. End.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: O people! You recite this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾ to the end of the verse. And you place it in other than its proper place. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, when people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah the Mighty and Majestic is about to encompass them with His punishment."

It was also narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and by others.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Umayya al-Sha'bani, who said: "I came to Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani and said to him: (p-٢١٩٢) How do you deal with this verse?" He said: "Which verse?" I said: "His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾." He said: "By Allah! You have asked about it someone well informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Rather, enjoin one another to good and forbid one another from evil, until you see stinginess obeyed, desire followed, worldliness preferred, and every person of opinion admiring his own opinion. Then you must attend to your own self and leave the common people. Behind you are days in which patience is like grasping a live coal. The one who acts in them will have the reward of fifty men who do deeds like yours.'"

"Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Someone other than Utba added to me: It was said: O Messenger of Allah! The reward of fifty men from among us or from among them? He said: No, rather the reward of fifty from among you."

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan gharib hadith.

Likewise it was narrated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, that a man asked Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, about the saying of Allah: ﴿take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾. He said: This is not its time. It is accepted today, but it is about to come to its time. You will command, and then such-and-such will be done to you. Or he said: then nothing you say will be accepted from you. At that time, ﴿take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you﴾.

Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated it from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya, who said: They were sitting with Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and there was some dispute between two men, of the kind that occurs among people, until each of them rose toward his companion. A man among Abdullah's companions said: Shall I not rise and command them to good and forbid them from evil? Another beside him said: Attend to yourself, for Allah says: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾, and so on. Ibn Mas'ud heard it and said: Enough! The interpretation of this has not yet come. The Qur'an was revealed where it was revealed. Among it are verses whose interpretation had already passed before they were revealed. Among it are verses whose interpretation came during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Among it are verses (p-٢١٩٣) whose interpretation came shortly after the Prophet (ﷺ). Among it are verses whose interpretation will come on the Day of Reckoning, such as what is mentioned of reckoning, Paradise, and Hellfire. As long as your hearts are united, your desires are one, you have not been divided into factions, and some of you have not tasted the violence of others, then command and forbid. But when hearts and desires differ, you are divided into factions, and some of you taste the violence of others, then attend to your own self. At that time the interpretation of this verse will come. Narrated by Ibn Jarir.

And I also narrate that it was said to Ibn Umar: "If you sat during these days and did not command or forbid, for Allah says: ﴿take care of yourselves; the one who is astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾." Ibn Umar said: It does not apply to me or to my companions, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let the one who is present convey to the one who is absent." We were the present, and you are the absent. But this verse is for peoples who will come after us. If they speak, it will not be accepted from them.

Al-Razi has weakened what was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Umar that we have cited. He said: Because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, is a general address, and it is also an address to those present. How then would the present be excluded and only the absent be meant? End.

I say: The intention of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, is not to exclude those present from the address, or that only the absent were meant by it. Rather, their intention is to refute those who interpreted it as leaving off enjoining the good and forbidding the evil.
