They informed him that it is not permissible to cite it as evidence for abandoning that, nor to take comfort in its apparent meaning, except in the time that they have explained. Its summary is: enjoining the good and forbidding the evil are obligatory so long as they are accepted. If they are rejected in such a time, then let him recite: ﴿take care of yourselves﴾. This is their intention. And Allah knows best.

(p-2194) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[106] ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [the] testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two just men from among you or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land and the disaster of death strikes you. You shall detain them after the prayer, and they will swear by Allah, if you doubt, "We will not sell it for any price, even if it were [to] a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed, we would then be among the sinners."﴾

﴿O you who have believed, let there be [the] testimony between you when death approaches one of you﴾, meaning: its signs have appeared. ﴿At the time of bequest﴾ is a substitute for the adverbial phrase. It is an adverb of time for "death," not for its approach. Indeed, substitution here indicates that the bequest is among the important matters about which one should not be lax. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿two﴾, is the predicate. "Testimony" is taken as having an omitted modifier, meaning: the testimony between you at that time is the testimony of two. Or it may be the subject of "testimony," with its predicate omitted, meaning: concerning what has been revealed to you, that two of you bear witness between you. ﴿Two just men from among you﴾, meaning: from among the Muslims. ﴿Or two others from other than you﴾, meaning: from among the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah, protected non-Muslim subjects). ﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, meaning: you journey in it. ﴿And the disaster of death strikes you, you shall detain them﴾, meaning: you hold them back for the oath. ﴿After the prayer﴾, meaning: the afternoon prayer, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Successors (tabi'un, the generation that followed the Companions). Its not being specified is because it is specified for them by the oath taken after it, since it is the time when people gather and the time when the angels of the night and the angels of the day meet. The gathering of the two groups of angels involves a multiplication of witnesses from them concerning his truthfulness or falsehood, so it is stronger than other [times] and more frightening.

It is reported from al-Zuhri (a Successor and transmitter): "After whichever prayer of the Muslims it was." That is because prayer calls to speaking the truth and forbids lying and falsehood, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. (p-2195) The definiteness in "the prayer" is either for a previously known reference or for the genus. ﴿They will swear﴾, meaning: they will take an oath. ﴿By Allah, if you doubt﴾, meaning: if you suspect them of treachery and of taking something from the estate of the deceased. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will not sell it for any price﴾ is the answer to the oath, meaning: they say: "We will not take for ourselves a substitute from Allah," that is, from His sanctity, a worldly possession, by violating it and removing it through a false oath. That is, "We will not swear by Allah falsely for the sake of wealth." ﴿Even if it were﴾, meaning: the one for whom we swear and bear witness, which is implied by the sense of the speech, ﴿a near relative﴾, meaning: close to us. This is an emphasis on their disavowal of swearing falsely and an exaggeration in keeping far from it. It is as if they both said: "We will not take for ourselves a substitute for the sanctity of His name in wealth. Even if we were to add to that the protection of the relatives' side, how much more so when it is not like that?" ﴿And we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, meaning: the testimony which Allah, exalted is He, commanded us to uphold. Its attribution to the noble Name is to honour it and to magnify its matter. ﴿Indeed, we would then﴾, if we concealed it, ﴿be among the sinners﴾, meaning: those counted among those who persist in sin.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[107] ﴿And if it is discovered that the two have incurred sin, then two others from among those who have the prior claim against them shall take their place, and they shall swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed, we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾

﴿And if it is discovered﴾, i.e., it becomes known after the oath has been administered, ﴿that the two﴾, i.e., the two witnesses who were appointed as executors, ﴿have incurred sin﴾, i.e., have done what requires it, such as betrayal or misappropriation of some of the property bequeathed to them. ﴿Then two others shall take their place﴾, i.e., two other men shall stand in the place of those two who were discovered to have betrayed, namely by being subject to the oath against them, in order to establish the truth and expose their lie regarding their claim to what is in their possession. ﴿From among those who have the prior claim against them﴾, i.e., from among the heirs of the deceased, from among whom the two who have the prior claim, i.e., the two nearest relatives of the deceased who inherit from him and who are most entitled to testify, that is, to swear. The word ﴿the two who have the prior claim﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of ﴿has the prior claim﴾ (istahagga). The object of ﴿has the prior claim﴾ is omitted. Some scholars estimated it as ﴿their bequest﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it as ﴿their wealth and their estate﴾, and al-Zamakhshari estimated that it means that they should appoint these two for the task of testifying, because it is their right, and they should show through them the lie of the liars. It has also been read in the passive voice, meaning ﴿from among those against whom sin was committed﴾, i.e., those who were wronged. They are the family of the deceased and his kinsmen. In that case ﴿the two who have the prior claim﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "And who are they?" and it was answered: "The two who have the prior claim." Or it is an apposition to the pronoun in ﴿shall stand﴾ or to ﴿two others﴾. Its nominative case has also been permitted, with the verb ﴿has the prior claim﴾, by omitting a modifier, meaning: ﴿the recommendation of the two closest of them to testify has the prior claim against them﴾. It has also been read as ﴿the first two﴾, the plural of ﴿first﴾, as an adjective of ﴿those﴾, in the genitive or accusative case by way of praise. The meaning of priority is precedence over strangers in testimony, because they are more entitled to it. It has also been read as ﴿the two first﴾ in the dual. Its case is accusative by way of praise. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud.

It has also been read: ﴿al-awwalayn﴾, the dual of ﴿awwal﴾, in the accusative, as mentioned, as in al-Baydawi.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It may be read ﴿al-ulayyayn﴾, which is the plural of ﴿ula﴾, and its i'rab (grammatical parsing) is like the i'rab of ﴿al-awwalayn﴾. It may also be read ﴿al-awwalan﴾, the dual of ﴿al-awwal﴾, and its i'rab is like the i'rab of ﴿al-ulayyan﴾.

﴿And they shall swear by Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿shall stand﴾. ﴿Our testimony is more worthy﴾, i.e., to be accepted, ﴿than their testimony﴾, i.e., our statement that they betrayed and lied regarding their claim to entitlement, is more worthy than their earlier testimony, because it has become apparent to people that they are liable for sin. ﴿And we have not transgressed﴾, i.e., we have not exceeded the truth in it or in what we have said about them concerning betrayal. ﴿Indeed, we would then be﴾, i.e., if we had transgressed, ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who wrong themselves by exposing themselves to the displeasure and punishment of Allah, exalted is He, because of violating the sanctity of the name of Allah, exalted is He. Or: among those who place the truth in other than its proper place.

The meaning of the noble verse is: when death approaches a man while traveling, he should call upon two men from among the Muslims as witnesses.

[p. 2197] If he does not find them, then two men from among the People of the Book. He appoints them as executors and entrusts to them his inheritance. When they arrive with his estate, if the heirs confirm them and know what belongs to their companion, their word is accepted and they are left alone. If the heirs accuse them, they bring them before the authority, and the two swear after the afternoon prayer by Allah: "We did not conceal, nor lie, nor betray, nor alter." If the two heirs (al-awliyan) discover that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, two men from among the heirs stand and swear by Allah that the testimony of the two unbelievers is false, and that "we did not transgress." Thus the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected and the testimony of the heirs is permitted. This is how Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and others.

Imam Ibn Kathir said: This oath administered to the heirs and the reliance upon their word in this situation is like the oath sworn by the relatives of a murder victim when circumstantial evidence (lawth) appears against the killer. The entitled persons then swear against the killer, and he is handed over to them in full. This is established in the chapter on qasama (the oath procedure in cases of homicide). The Sunnah has also come with the same as what this noble verse indicates.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari concerning this verse: ﴿O you who believe, let there be testimony between you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] to the end. He said: "People were absolved of it except me and 'Adi ibn Bada', and the two were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They went to Syria for their trade. A freedman of Banu Sahm called Budayl (with a dal or zay, diminutive; Ibn Makula vocalized it with the second) ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, and with him was a silver cup (jam) which he intended to present to the king, and it was the most valuable of his goods. He fell ill and appointed the two as executors and ordered them to deliver what he left to his family. Tamim said: When he died we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, and 'Adi and I divided it. When we came to his family we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the cup and asked about it. We said: 'He left nothing other than this, and he did not give us anything else.'"

Tamim said: "When I became Muslim, after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, I felt guilty about that, so I went to his family and informed them of the news, and I handed over to them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had a similar amount. They then rushed at him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to have him swear by what is binding upon the people of his religion. He swore, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, let there be testimony between you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106], to His saying: ﴿they shall swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony"﴾. Then 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man from among them stood and swore, and the five hundred were taken from 'Adi ibn Bada'."

Thus al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ishaq with the same chain, and he mentioned it. In his version: "They brought him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he asked them for evidence, but they did not find any. So he ordered them to have him swear by what is greatest among the people of his religion, and he swore. Then Allah revealed this verse. 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man stood and swore, and the five hundred were taken from 'Adi ibn Bada'."

Then al-Tirmidhi commented on its chain of transmission. After that he narrated this story in abbreviated form from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man from Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada'. The Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. When they brought his estate, they missed a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had them swear. Then the cup was found in Mecca, and it was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and 'Adi.' Two men from the Sahmi's heirs stood and swore by Allah: 'Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion.' And this verse was revealed concerning them." Abu Dawud also narrated it like this. Then al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan gharib hadith."

I say: al-Bukhari also narrated it in the Book of Bequests (al-Wasaya), under a chapter he devoted specifically to this verse.

[p. 2199] The jam is a vessel, and its khawkh (decoration) is that golden plates are placed upon it like the palm-fronds of a date palm.

Ibn Kathir said: This story has been related in mursal form (without the Companion) by more than one of the Successors, among them 'Ikrimah, Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah. They mentioned that the oath was after the afternoon prayer. Ibn Jarir narrated it. Likewise, Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak related it in mursal form. This indicates its fame among the early generations and its authenticity.

Among the evidences for the soundness of this story is what Ibn Jarir narrated through two sound chains, and Abu Dawud through a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, from al-Sha'bi: that a man from among the Muslims was present at Daquqa when death approached him, and he did not find anyone among those present to witness his bequest, so he called upon two men from the People of the Book as witnesses. He said: They came to Kufa and went to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him) and informed him, and they came to Kufa with his estate and his bequest. Al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not occur after what happened in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: He had them swear after the afternoon prayer by Allah: "We did not betray, nor lie, nor substitute, nor conceal, nor alter, and this is the bequest of the man and his estate." He said: So he upheld their testimony. His saying "This is a matter that did not occur after what happened in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" most apparently refers, and Allah knows best, to the story of Tamim and 'Adi ibn Bada'.

(p-2200) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
[108] ﴿That is more suitable for them to bring the testimony in its proper form, or to fear that oaths will be rejected after their oaths. And fear God and listen. And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾
Then He explained the aspect of the wisdom and the benefit whose detail was previously mentioned, with His words:
﴿That﴾, i.e., the ruling mentioned: ﴿is more suitable for them to bring the testimony in its proper form﴾, i.e., nearer to the witnesses – or the executors – rendering the testimony in such an incident in its true form without altering it, out of fear of the punishment of the Hereafter. Thus, ﴿al-wajh﴾ (the form) means the essence and the reality.
Abu al-Su'ud said: "This, as you see, is the legislative wisdom of the oath with the aforementioned emphasis!"
His words, exalted is He: ﴿or to fear that oaths will be rejected after their oaths﴾ are an explanation of the legislative wisdom of returning the oath to the heirs, joined to an implied clause indicated by the context; as if it were said: "That is more suitable for them to bring the testimony in its proper form, and to fear the punishment of the Hereafter because of a false oath. Or to fear that the oath will be returned to the claimants after their oaths, so that they will be exposed by the manifestation of treachery and a false oath, and will be made to pay, and thus refrain from that."
﴿And fear God﴾, i.e., in opposing His rulings, of which this ruling is one, which is abandoning treachery and lying. ﴿And listen﴾, i.e., to what you are commanded, listening with acceptance. ﴿And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾, i.e., those who depart from His obedience and from following His law, i.e., to the path of Paradise or to what benefits them.
Several rulings have been derived from the verse:
First: The obligation of bequest at the time of fear of death and the presence of its signs, because He, exalted is He, said: "when death approaches" (ḥīna al-waṣiyyah), i.e., at the time when the bequest becomes due and binding.
Second: Some of them said: His words, exalted is He: ﴿two just men from among you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] indicate that the condition of a ruling is that two just witnesses testify to it. This is an unrestricted statement that does not distinguish between the right of God and the right of others, (p-2201) nor between the hudud and other matters, except for the testimony of adultery. For His words in al-Nur: "then they do not bring four witnesses," and this is agreed upon.
Ibn al-Qayyim said in *I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in*: He, glorified is He, mentioned what preserves rights through witnesses, and did not mention that judges may not rule except by that. Thus there is nothing in the Qur'an negating a ruling by one witness and an oath, nor by refusal (nukul), nor by the returned oath, nor by the oaths of qasama, nor by the oaths of li'an, and other things that clarify and manifest the truth and indicate it. The Lawgiver, in all places, intends the manifestation of the truth by what can manifest it of evidences which are proofs for it and witnesses to it.
He never rejects a right that has appeared by its proof, so that He would waste the rights of God and the rights of His servants and render them inoperative. The manifestation of truth does not depend on a specific matter, when there is no benefit in specifying it, while others are equal to it in manifesting the truth or in preponderance over it, a preponderance that cannot be denied or repelled. He elaborated on this at length, to the extent that one cannot dispense with consulting it.
Third: His words, exalted is He: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] indicate the validity of the testimony of a dhimmi against a Muslim in general. However, its permissibility is excluded in matters other than the bequest of a Muslim on a journey, by consensus.
Some exegetes said: Most scholars held that the testimony of dhimmis has been abrogated (nusikhat). It is reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Awza'i, Shurayh, al-Radi billah and his grandfather the Imam 'Abd Allah ibn al-Husayn that it is valid and established. Likewise, most held that the oath-taking of witnesses is abrogated, while Tawus, al-Hasan and al-Hadi said it is established. End.
I say: Those who claimed abrogation have not brought an argument worth mentioning or that calls for addressing its refutation.
Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in *I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in*:
He commanded, in testimony concerning a bequest on a journey, to call upon two just men from among the Muslims, or two others from (p-2202) other than them. "Other than them" means the disbelievers. The verse is explicit in accepting the testimony of disbelievers concerning a bequest on a journey when two Muslim witnesses are absent. The Prophet ﷺ ruled by it, and the Companions after him did so, and nothing came after it to abrogate it, for al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an in revelation, and there is nothing abrogated in it, and there is absolutely no contradicting evidence to this verse. It is not valid that the meaning of "from other than you" is "from other than your tribe," for God, glorified is He, addressed the believers in general with His words: "O you who believe" [al-Ma'idah: 106] and so on. He did not address a specific tribe with it, so that His words "from other than you" would mean "O tribe." The Prophet ﷺ did not understand this from the verse; rather he understood from it what it is explicit about, and likewise his Companions after him.
Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: The verse was cited as evidence for the permissibility of the testimony of disbelievers, on the basis that "other than" refers to disbelievers. A group restricted acceptance to People of the Book, to bequest, and to the absence of a Muslim at that time. Among them: Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Sirin, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ahmad – these took the apparent meaning of the verse – and the hadith of the chapter strengthened this, meaning the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier, for its context accords with the apparent meaning of the verse. It was said: "other than" means the clan; the meaning of "from among you" is "from among your clan," and "or two others from other than you" means "from other than your clan." This is the view of al-Hasan. al-Nahhas argued for it, saying that the word "other" (ākhar) must share the attribute of the preceding one, so that one cannot say: "I passed by a generous man and another miser." So in this case the two were described as just, and therefore the other two must be likewise.
This was objected to: though this may be acceptable in the noble verse, the hadith indicates otherwise. When a Companion relates the occasion of revelation, it is by consensus in the status of a raised (marfu') hadith. Also, in what was said there is a return of the disputed by the disputed, because the disbeliever's attribute of justice is disputed, and it is a branch of accepting his testimony: whoever accepts it describes him with it, and whoever does not, does not. Abu Hayyan objected to the example given by al-Nahhas, saying it does not correspond. If you say: "A Muslim man came to me and another (p-2203) disbeliever," it is correct; but if you say: "A Muslim man came to me and another disbeliever," it is not. The verse belongs to the first type, not the second; for His words "or two others" are of the same kind as His words "two," since both are an attribute of "men": it is as if He said: "then two men, two and two other men."
Some imams held that this verse is abrogated, and that its abrogator is His words: "from among those whom you approve of as witnesses" [al-Baqarah: 282]. They argued by consensus on rejecting the testimony of a sinner, and a disbeliever is worse than a sinner. The earlier scholars replied: abrogation is not established by possibility; combining the two evidences is preferable to dismissing one of them; and Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so much so that it is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, 'Amr ibn Shurahbil and a group of the early generation that Surat al-Ma'idah is muhkam (unabrogated). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning one who died while travelling with no Muslim present; then if the two (witnesses) are suspected, they are made to swear an oath. Al-Tabari transmitted it with a chain whose transmitters are trustworthy.
Ahmad denounced whoever said that this verse is abrogated.
It is authentically reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that he acted upon this after the Prophet ﷺ, as mentioned earlier.
Al-Fakhr al-Razi – and al-Tabari preceded him – preferred this view, because His words "O you who believe" address the believers; so when He said "or two others" it became clear that He meant other than those addressed, and thus they must be from among non-believers. Also, a Muslim's testimony is not conditioned on travel, and Abu Musa ruled by this and no Companion objected, so it was a proof. End of the words of the Hafiz.
In *Fath al-Bayan*: The truth is that the verse is muhkam, since there is no sound evidence indicating abrogation. As for His words: "from among those whom you approve of as witnesses" [al-Baqarah: 282] and His words: "and call to witness two just men from among you" [al-Talaq: 2], these are general in persons, times and circumstances, whereas this verse is specific to the situation of travelling on earth, to the bequest, and to the absence of Muslim witnesses. There is no contradiction between a specific and a general. End.
Al-Razi, in his *Tafsir*, extensively argued against its abrogation with many arguments, and he excellently elaborated on the meaning of "from other than you," i.e., from other than your religion, with outstanding refinement.

(p-2204) Fourth: Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*:
al-Karabisi, then al-Tabari, and others held that the word "testimony" in the verse means oath. He said: God called the oath a testimony in the verse of li'an. They supported this by consensus that a witness is not required to say "I testify by God," and that a witness is not obliged to swear that he testified truthfully. They said: so the meaning of "testimony" is oath, by His words: "they both swear by God," i.e., they both take an oath. If it becomes known that they both swore to a sin, the oath is returned to the guardians. It was objected that an oath has no required number or justice, unlike testimony; and since these were stipulated in this story, it is stronger to interpret it as testimony. As for the objection of those who rejected its ruling on the grounds that it contradicts analogy and principles – because it involves accepting the testimony of a disbeliever, detaining a witness and making him swear, the testimony of a claimant for himself, and his entitlement by mere oath – those who held it replied that it is a ruling in itself, independent of its like. The testimony of a disbeliever has been accepted in some cases, as in medicine. "Detention" does not mean imprisonment; rather it means holding him for the oath so that he swears after the prayer. As for making a witness swear, it is restricted to this case when suspicion arises. As for the testimony of a claimant for himself and his entitlement by mere oath, the verse includes the transfer of oaths to them when there is a presumption (lawth) of treachery by the two executors. Thus it is legislated for them to swear and be entitled, just as it is legislated for the claimant of blood in qasama to swear and be entitled. It is therefore not the testimony of a claimant for himself, but a ruling in his favour by his oath, which stands in place of testimony because his side is stronger. What difference is there between the presumption (lawth) establishing a valid claim for blood and its establishing a valid claim for property? Al-Tabari related that some said: the meaning of "two just men from among you" is the two executors; and the meaning of "testimony between you" is the sense of presence for what the bequeather charges them with. Then this was rejected. End of the words of *al-Fath*.
It is not hidden from you that the verse itself – together with what has been reported concerning its revelation – is independent of the burden of forcing it under analogy and principles and of far-fetched contrivances to interpret it.

(p-2205) Fifth: In His words: ﴿after the prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] there is an indication of the intensification (taghlīz) of the oath.
Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*, and some exegetes:
The majority held that intensification of the oath by time and place is obligatory. As for time, it is after the 'asr prayer. As for place: in Medina, at the minbar; in Mecca, between the Corner and the Maqam; in Jerusalem, at the Rock; and elsewhere, in the congregational mosque. They agreed that this applies to matters of blood and to large property, not to small amounts. End.
The Zaydis, the Hanafis and the Hanbalis held that the oath is not intensified by time or place. They relied on the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies," without distinction. They said: His words in this verse, "after the prayer" [al-Ma'idah: 106], may be understood as mentioning it because they were not accustomed to rule except at that time.

Among the Zaydis, some said: "Is the aggravation (taghlīẓ) regarding the place and time (of the oath) obligatory or recommended?" The Imam al-Mu'ayyad bi-Llah Yahya ibn Hamza said: "The preferred view is the aggravation in oaths, because of the corruption of the people of the age. This is related from Amir al-Mu'minin al-Murtada (ʿAlī), Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, Ibn ʿAbbas, Malik and al-Shafiʿi." He said: "The preferred view is that it is recommended (mustaḥabb), not obligatory." End of quotation.

In the Book of Testimonies (Kitab al-Shahadat) of Sahih al-Bukhari (the collection of hadith compiled by al-Bukhari), there are two chapters on this question. It should be consulted together with its commentaries.

Sixth: Ibn Abi al-Faras said: In the words of the Most High, ﴿Then the two swear by Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:107], there is evidence that "I swear by Allah" is an oath, not merely "I swear."

Seventh: Regarding the words of the Most High, ﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:106] and the rest of the verse: this is evidence for the prohibition of concealing testimony. There is no difficulty in this.

Eighth: al-Suyuti said: The restriction of the oath in the verse to two of the nearest heirs [meaning according to the reading "al-awliyan" (the two nearest)] is due to the specific incident for which it was revealed. Then he cited the earlier narration from al-Bukhari. That is: it also indicates the sufficiency of two of the nearest heirs, even if there are many among them.

[p. 2206] Rare points:
Makki said in his book named "al-Kashf":
These three verses, according to the scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani), are among the most difficult in the Qur'an in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), meaning, ruling and tafsir (exegesis). The scholars have continued to find them problematic and have refrained from them.

He said: Their sciences could be expanded to thirty folios or more. We have explained them in a separate book.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is the statement of one who has not reached the conclusion in their interpretation, and this is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him, meaning the book of Makki.

al-Qurtubi said: What Makki mentioned, Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas had also mentioned before him.

al-Sa'd said in his gloss on the Kashshaf: They agreed that they are the most difficult in the Qur'an in i'rab, composition and ruling... End of quotation.

I say: This noble verse is itself sufficient, together with what is reported about the occasion of its revelation and what the scholar of the Community and interpreter of the Qur'an (Ibn ʿAbbas) said about its meaning, to be free of doubt about it, of forced efforts to bring it under general rules, and of far-fetched interpretations. So take what we have transmitted of its excellent interpretations, and be among the grateful.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[109] ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers and say, "What response did you receive?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾

﴿On the Day﴾ is in the accusative, governed by (remember) or (beware): ﴿Allah gathers the Messengers﴾, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The mention of the Messengers specifically does not mean that gathering is restricted to them rather than the nations. How could it be, when that is a day on which all people are gathered? Rather, it is to display their nobility and eminence, and to indicate that there is no need to state explicitly the gathering of others. This is based on the evident fact that they are the ones followed by others. ﴿Then He will say﴾, i.e., to the Messengers: ﴿What response did you receive?﴾, i.e., what did those to whom you were sent answer you? In this there is an indication that they have departed from the covenant of messengerhood, since He did not say, "Did you convey My messages?" In directing the question to them, and in turning away from attributing the answer to their peoples by saying, "What did they answer?", there is an indication of the intensity of divine wrath, which is not hidden. And in the authentic collection, in the hadith of intercession: "Indeed, my Lord has become angry today with an anger the like of which He had not been angry before, and He will not be angry after it with the like of it."

﴿They will say﴾, out of awe of Him, exalted is He, entrusting the matter to the knowledge of His dominion, and displaying eloquent good manners in that majestic station: ﴿We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.﴾, i.e., and of the hidden matters; the apparent matters, among them the response of their nations to them, were not hidden from Him.

Remarks:

The first: al-Razi said: Know that it is the custom of Allah, exalted is He, in this Noble Book, that when He mentions many kinds of laws, obligations and rulings, He follows them either with matters of divinity, or with a description of the states of the prophets, or with a description of the states of the Resurrection, so that this serves as a confirmation of what was mentioned before of obligations and laws. Thus, when He mentioned earlier many kinds of laws, He followed them with a description of the states of the Resurrection.

The second: al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of their being questioned? I say: it is a rebuke to their peoples, just as the question put to the buried infant was a rebuke to the one who buried her. If you ask, how can they say, "We have no knowledge," when they knew how they were answered? I say: they know that the purpose of the question is to rebuke their enemies, so they entrust the matter to His knowledge and His encompassing of what they suffered from them and endured from their evil response, displaying complaint and seeking refuge with their Lord in taking vengeance upon them. That is more grievous to the disbelievers, more weakening to their resolve, more conducive to their regret and their helplessness, when the rebuke of Allah and the complaint of His prophets against them are combined. An example of this: one of the rebels falls upon a close associate of the ruler with a calamity, the nature of which the ruler knows and whose reality he has been informed of, and he resolves to avenge him against him. So he brings them together and says to him, "What did this rebel do to you?" [while he knows what was done to him], intending to rebuke him and humiliate him. The other replies, "You know best what he did to me," entrusting the matter to the knowledge of his ruler, relying upon him, displaying grievance, and magnifying what befell him at his hands. End of quotation.

Al-Razi favoured that the negation of knowledge for them is in its literal sense, in accordance with what is established, that knowledge is other than conjecture. He said: Because what is attained concerning the state of others by anyone is only conjecture, not knowledge. And in the hadith: "We judge by the apparent, and Allah takes charge of the hidden matters," and he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You bring disputes before me, and perhaps some of you are more eloquent in his argument than others. So whoever I decide for him something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for I am only cutting for him a piece of the Fire." So the prophets said, "We have absolutely no knowledge of their states"; what we have of their states is only conjecture, and conjecture was relied upon in this world, but in the Hereafter no attention is paid to conjecture, because the rulings in the Hereafter are based upon the realities of things and the inner truths of matters. For this reason they said, "We have no knowledge," and they did not mention what they had of conjecture, since conjecture has no weight on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah knows best.

The third: The verse indicates the permissibility of applying the name al-'Allam (the All-Knowing) to Him, just as the name al-Khallaq (the Creator) may be applied to Him. As for al-'Allamah (the Exceedingly Knowing), they have unanimously agreed that it may not be applied to Him. Perhaps the reason is the feminine form it contains. Al-Razi stated this.

Moreover, the preferred view is that His names, exalted is He, are tawqifi (determined only by revelation).

**The commentary on His words, exalted is He:**

[110] ﴿When God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit, so that you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book and wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel; and when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission; and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission; and when you brought the dead forth by My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with clear proofs, and those of them who disbelieved said: 'This is nothing but manifest magic.'"﴾

﴿When God said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾: this begins an explanation, in detail, of what passed between Him, exalted is He, and one of the gathered Messengers, in the course of the dialogue. It follows what passed between Him and all of them in summary, since this serves as a model for the detailed circumstances of the rest. The specific mention of the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, in explanation, distinguishes him from the affairs of the other Messengers, peace be upon them, while also indicating the full severity of that Day and the ultimate wretchedness of the state of those who denied the Messengers. This is because his matter is connected to both groups of the People of the Book, whose crimes are censured in this noble surah. Therefore, detailing it is greater for them, more productive of their regret and remorse, and more effective in turning them away from their error and obstinacy. This is related from Abu al-Su'ud.

﴿Remember My blessing upon you﴾: that is, My favour upon you. ﴿And upon your mother﴾: by His purifying her and choosing her above the women of the worlds. ﴿When I strengthened you﴾: that is, I empowered you. ﴿With the Holy Spirit﴾: that is, with Gabriel, peace be upon him, (p-٢٢١٠) to confirm the proof. Or by making your spirit pure from dark attachments, such that it is known that it was not through the agency of a human being, and so it bears witness to your innocence and the innocence of your mother. From that strengthening your rational soul was empowered. Therefore: ﴿You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾: that is, in the weakest and the strongest states, with one speech, without it varying between the time of childhood and the time of old age, which is the time of full intellect and the attainment of maturity.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, I made you a prophet calling to God in your youth and in your age. I made you speak in the cradle as an infant, so you bore witness to the innocence of your mother from every defect. You acknowledged to Me servitude, and you reported My sending of you and your call to worship Me. For this He said: ﴿You speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, that is, you call people to God in your youth and in your age. The phrase "you speak" is taken to imply "you call," because his speaking to people in his maturity is not a remarkable matter. End.

﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾: that is, the writing and the outward knowledge that is written down. ﴿And wisdom﴾: that is, understanding and the inward knowledge that is not written down, but is restricted to its people. ﴿And the Torah﴾: which was revealed to Moses, the one who spoke with God (al-Kalim), peace be upon him. ﴿And the Gospel﴾: which He revealed to him (ﷺ). ﴿And when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird﴾: that is, you determined and fashioned from it a form resembling the shape of a bird. ﴿By My permission﴾: that is, by My leave for you in that. ﴿Then you breathed into it﴾: that is, into that fashioned form. ﴿Then it became﴾: that is, that form became ﴿a bird﴾, through the coming of the spirit by your breathing into it. ﴿By My permission﴾. ﴿And you heal the blind﴾: that is, the one born blind with eyes obliterated. ﴿And the leper, by My permission. And when you bring forth the dead﴾: that is, from the graves, living. ﴿By My permission﴾. This is among what He did through him of bringing benefits. Then He pointed to what He warded off from him of harm, and so He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾: that is, I prevented the Jews who intended evil against you and strove to kill you and crucify you, so I saved you from them, raised you to Me, and purified you from their filth. ﴿When you came to them with clear proofs﴾: that is, the miracles that necessitate their submission to you, since they transcend human powers, so that magic cannot be imagined in them. ﴿Then those of them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but manifest magic"﴾: that is, what is this that shows us anything but evident sorcery?

(p-٢٢١١) **A subtle point:**

If it is said: the context is enumerating His blessings upon Jesus, peace be upon him, and the saying of the disbelievers concerning him, "This is nothing but manifest magic," does not, outwardly, belong among the blessings. So what is the secret in mentioning it? The answer: among the well-known proverbs is that every possessor of a blessing is envied. Thus the Jews' slander of him with this statement indicates that God's blessings upon him were great. Therefore, mentioning it is fitting when enumerating the blessings, for the reason we have mentioned. This is related from al-Razi.

Since God, exalted is He, has explained the blessings that are intrinsic (al-ni'am al-lazimah), He followed them with His blessings that are transitive upon him (al-ni'am al-muta'addiyah), and so He, glorified is He, said: [the commentary continues]

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted, Words:

[111] ﴿And when I inspired the disciples, saying: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger," they said: "We believe; and bear witness that we are submitting ones."﴾

﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾ — that is, by way of inspiration (al-ilham) and casting into the heart. ﴿Saying: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger"﴾ — that is, in his call. ﴿They said: "We believe"﴾, and they affirmed their belief by their saying: ﴿and bear witness﴾ — that is, so that you may deliver it before your Lord — ﴿that we are submitting ones﴾ — that is, compliant with everything to which you call us.

Here are some subtleties:

The first: They mentioned belief first because it is an attribute of the heart, while Islam (islam) is an expression of compliance and submission in the outward sense. The meaning is: "We believed with our hearts, and we submitted with our outward forms."

The second: Exalted is He, mentioned this in the context of enumerating the blessings, because the person's word becoming accepted among people and beloved in their hearts is among the greatest of God's blessings upon a human being. Thus al-Razi said so.

Al-Mahayimi said: so that he may attain the rank of perfection and the reward of their guidance.

The third: Al-Razi said: If it is said: He, Exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse: "Remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother" (p-2212), then all the blessings He mentioned are specific to Jesus, peace be upon him, and his mother has no connection to any of them. We say: Every blessing and every lofty rank that a child attains is attained by way of inclusion and following of the mother, and for this reason Exalted is He said: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], making them together one sign because of the intense connection of each of them with the other. End of quote.

Some of them said: It was said that the remembrance in His words, Exalted is He, "Remember My blessing," means gratitude (shukr). In this is evidence of the obligation of thanking for a blessing, and that a blessing upon the mother is a blessing upon the child. Gratitude is by speech, by action, and by belief.

[112] "When the disciples said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?' He said, 'Fear Allah, if you are believers.'" (Qur'an 5:112)

The commentary on the words of His Exalted saying:

﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾: they named him by his name and attributed him to his mother, lest it be supposed that they believed in his divinity or his sonship, so that the sending down of the table would be attributed to him alone: ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ This is the story of the table, and the surah is named after it, so it is called Surat al-Ma'idah (the Table Spread). Here there are two readings. The first: "yastaṭīʿu rabbuka" (يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ) with the yā' (ي), as a verb and subject, with "an yunazzila" (أنْ يُنَزِّلَ) as its object. The second: with the tā' (ت), and "rabbaka" (رَبَّكَ) in the accusative; that is, "the request of your Lord" (سُؤالَ رَبِّكَ), the noun being elided. The meaning is: "Do you ask Him for that without any obstacle preventing you from it?" This is the reading of ʿAlī, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Muʿādh, may Allah be pleased with them, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Kisāʾī, among others.

Most of the exegetes said: the interrogative in the first reading is to be understood figuratively, since it is not permissible for anyone to suppose of the disciples that they doubted the power of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, it is like a man saying to his companion: "(p-2213) Are you able to stand with me?" while knowing that he is capable of standing, out of emphasis in the request. He only intended by his words "Are you able" to ask: "Would it be easy for you, and light, to stand with me?" So likewise is the meaning of the verse, since the disciples were believers who knew Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and acknowledged the perfection of His power. Their question was not to remove a doubt, but so that greater tranquillity might be attained, as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: "But that my heart may be at rest" (Qur'an 2:260). There is no doubt that witnessing this great sign produces greater tranquillity in the heart. For this reason they said: "and our hearts may be at rest" (Qur'an 5:113). The upshot is that "Can your Lord...?" is a question about the act without the capacity for it, expressed by its necessary concomitant, or about the effect by its cause. It was also said that the meaning is: "Will your Lord obey?" That is: "Will He respond to your supplication if you call upon Him?" So "yastaṭīʿu" (يَسْتَطِيعُ) is in the sense of "yuṭīʿu" (يُطِيعُ), and both have one meaning; the sīn is extra, as in "istajāba" and "ajāba," and "istajib" and "ajib." "Yuṭīʿu" in the sense of "yujību" (responds) is figurative, because the one who responds is obedient.

Abu Shamah mentioned: "The Prophet (ﷺ) visited Abu Ṭālib during an illness. He said to him: 'O nephew! Call upon your Lord to heal me.' He said: 'O Allah, cure my uncle.' He rose as though he had been released from a shackle. He said: 'O nephew! Indeed your Lord whom you worship obeys you (li-yuṭīʿaka).' He said: 'O uncle! And if you were to obey Him, He would obey you,' meaning: He would respond to you regarding your aim."

The figurative usage is made good by the parallelism (mushākalah) in the hadith, so it is clear that the Arabs used it in this sense.

Al-Khazin said: Some of them said: it is on its apparent meaning. He said: "The people erred, and they said that before faith and knowledge had become firmly established in their hearts. They were human, so they uttered this statement." He refuted their error with His saying: ﴿He said: Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, meaning: fear Allah lest you doubt His power.

The first view is more correct. End of quotation.

(p-2214) Upon it, the meaning of "Fear Allah" is: beware of such questions, and of making your faith depend on seeing the table, if you are believers in Him and in my message, for faith is among the things that require taqwa and abstaining from such demands.

A NOTE:

Concerning the table (al-māʾidah) there are two views. The first: that it is the food itself, from (māda) meaning to be bountiful, as in "Lisān al-ʿArab." This view was affirmed by al-Akhfash and Abu Ḥātim, that is, even if there is no tray (khiwān) with it, as in "al-Taqrīb" and "Lisān al-ʿArab," and Ibn Sīdah explicitly stated it in "al-Muḥkam."

Al-Fāsī said: The verse is explicit in this, as stated by the people of tafsir and of rare vocabulary.

The second: that it is the tray (khiwān) on which the food is placed. Al-Fārisī said: it is not called "māʾidah" until there is food on it; otherwise it is a khiwān, and the jurists of language stated this explicitly. al-Tha'ālibī and Ibn Fāris affirmed it, and al-Ḥarīrī restricted himself to it in "Durrat al-Ghawwāṣ," claiming that other views are the errors of the elite. Al-Fāsī mentioned in his commentary on it that it is permissible to apply "māʾidah" to the tray alone, without food, in consideration that it has been set out or will be set out. Ibn Ẓafar said: the name "māʾidah" remains for it after the food is removed, just as one says "luqḥah" after giving birth. Abu ʿUbayd said: "māʾidah" in meaning is passive, while its form is active, like "ʿīshah rāḍiyah." It was also said: from (māda) meaning to give; one says "māda Zayd ʿAmran" when he gives him. Abu Isḥaq said: the origin in my view of māʾidah is that it is active, from (māda yamīdu) meaning to move, as though it sways with what is on it, that is, moves. Abu ʿUbaydah said: it was named māʾidah because its owner was made to give (mīda bihā) with it, that is, he was given it and was favoured with it. In "al-ʿInayah": "as though it gives to those around it of what is present upon it." In "al-Miṣbāḥ": "because the owner gives it to the people," that is, gives it to them. Its like is in "al-Abniyah" of Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ: it is said of al-māʾidah also "maydah," as stated by al-Jirmi, who recited:

"And a maydah of many colours, prepared for brothers and neighbours."

Thus in "al-Qāmūs and its commentary." The khiwān, with dammah or kasrah on the kh, is that upon which food is eaten, as in "al-Qāmūs." It is arabicised (muʿarrab), as in "al-Ṣiḥāḥ" and "al-ʿAyn." It was also said that it is Arabic, taken from (takhawwanahu), that is, diminished his right, because food is eaten upon it and it diminishes. Thus in "al-ʿInayah."

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 5, verse 113:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[113] ﴿They said: "We desire to eat from it, and that our hearts may be assured, and that we may know that you have indeed told us the truth, and that we may be of those who witness to it."﴾

﴿They said: "We desire to eat from it"﴾ meaning: we believe. But we desire to eat from it without hardship that would occupy us from the worship of Allah, exalted is He. ﴿"And that our hearts may be assured"﴾ meaning: that no doubt may afflict them that cannot be safe from its arrival, were it not for the likes of this verse. For the joining of the knowledge of direct observation to the knowledge derived by inference is among what necessitates the strength of certainty. ﴿"And that we may know that you have indeed told us the truth"﴾ meaning: regarding the claim of prophethood, and regarding what you promise us of the bliss of Paradise, although it is from heaven. ﴿"And that we may be of those who witness to it"﴾ meaning: that we may bear witness to it before those among the Children of Israel who were not present, so that the believers among them may increase in tranquility and certainty through our testimony, and that their disbelievers may believe because of it. Or [it means]: "of those who witness" with the eye, not merely those who hear the report.

Then, when he saw that they had a sound purpose in this and would not desist from it, he resolved to call for it to be sent down and to bring it down. (p-٢٢١٦) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that he performed ablution, bathed, and entered his place of prayer, and prayed as much as Allah willed. When he had finished his prayer, he stood facing the qiblah (the direction of prayer), aligned his feet, placed his right hand upon his left above his chest, lowered his gaze, and bowed his head in humility. Then he let his eyes weep, and his tears continued to flow down his cheeks and drip from the edges of his beard, until the ground opposite his face was wet from his humility. At that point he called upon Allah, exalted is He, saying: "O Allah, our Lord," as Allah, exalted is He, said:

The discussion on the exegesis (*ta'wil*, interpretation) of His, the Exalted, saying:

[114] ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down upon us a table from heaven, to be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers."﴾

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord"﴾ That is: O Allah, the One sought in every matter, the One who combines all perfections, who nurtures us with them. He, glorified and exalted, is addressed twice by His attributes of divinity and lordship, to show the utmost humility and to intensify the request. ﴿Send down upon us a table from heaven﴾ That is, one containing what You promise us of the bliss of Paradise. ﴿To be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ That is, the day of its descent will be a festival that we honor and rejoice in, we who witness it, and those after us who hear of it, so that they will be strengthened in their religion. The word *al-'id* (festival) comes from *al-'awd* (return), because it returns every year with joy and happiness. Whatever returns to you at a time is a *'id*. Al-A'sha said:

*"Oh, my liver, from the burning of love and passion,*
*when my heart has become accustomed to her festival from Umaymah."*

Thus it is stated in *al-'Inaya*.

In *al-Qamus* (the dictionary): *al-'id*, with a kasra, is whatever returns to you of worry, sickness, sorrow, or the like. (p-٢٢١٧) Every day in which there is a gathering is also a *'id*. ﴿And a sign from You﴾ That is, a proof of Your complete power, the truth of Your promise, and Your confirmation of me. ﴿And provide for us﴾ That is, give us what we have asked of You. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾ That is, the best of those who provide, because He is the Creator of provision and its giver without compensation.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 115:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[115] ﴿God said, "Indeed, I will send it down to you. But whoever disbelieves after that among you, I will surely punish him with a punishment I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds."﴾

﴿God said, "Indeed, I will send it down to you"﴾ in response to your request. ﴿But whoever disbelieves﴾ i.e., in Me and My Messenger ﴿after that﴾ i.e., after its descent, which provides necessary knowledge of Me and My Messenger ﴿among you﴾, O you who are favored with it: ﴿I will surely punish him with a punishment I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds﴾ i.e., among the worlds of their time. Or, among the worlds in their entirety.

Ibn Jarir narrated with his chain to Qatadah, who said: al-Hasan used to say: When it was said to them, ﴿Whoever disbelieves after that among you﴾, etc., they said, "We have no need for it," and so it was not sent down.

Mansur ibn Zadan narrated from al-Hasan as well that he said concerning al-Ma'idah: that it was not sent down.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Mujahid, who said: It is a parable which God struck, and nothing was sent down. That is, a parable which God struck for His creation, forbidding them from asking the prophets for signs.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: These chains to Mujahid and al-Hasan are sound. This may be strengthened by the fact that the story of al-Ma'idah is unknown to the Christians, and it is not in their scripture. Had it been sent down, its transmission would have been among the matters that motivate many to relay it, and it would have been found in their books as mass-transmitted (mutawatir), and at least as solitary reports (ahad). And God knows best.

Then he said: However, the majority hold that it was sent down, and this is what Ibn Jarir chose. He said: Because God, Exalted is He, informed of its descent in His saying, ﴿Indeed, I will send it down to you﴾, and the promise and warning of God are true and sincere.

This view is, and God knows best, the correct one, as the reports and transmitted narrations from the early generations and others indicate.

Among the transmitted reports is what al-Tirmidhi recorded from Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The table (al-Ma'idah) was sent down from heaven with bread and meat, and they were commanded not to betray and not to store up for the morrow. But they betrayed and stored up and saved for the morrow, so they were transformed into apes and swine." Al-Tirmidhi said: It has also been transmitted from Ammar, through another route, as a statement of his own (mawquf), and this is more sound.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Shihab, from Ibn Abbas, that the people said to Jesus son of Mary: "Ask God to send down to us a table from heaven." He said: So the angels descended with the table carrying it; upon it were seven loaves and seven fish. The last of the people ate from it just as the first of them did.

Ibn Kathir has cited reports about its descent that are not free from strangeness and oddity in their context, as is not hidden.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Ask your Lord to make Safa into gold for us, and we will believe in you.' He said: 'Will you really do that?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: So he prayed, and Gabriel came to him and said: 'Your Lord sends you His greeting and says to you: If you wish, Safa will become gold for them; but whoever disbelieves after that among them, I will punish him with a punishment I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds. And if you wish, I will open for them the door of repentance and mercy.' He said: 'Rather, the door of repentance and mercy.'"

Al-Hakim recorded it in his Mustadrak, and Ibn Mardawayh as well.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 5, verse 116:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[116] ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'" He will say, "Exalted are You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"﴾ Know that we have explained that the purpose of His saying, exalted is He, to the Messengers, "What was your response?" is to rebuke those among their nations who rebelled. The nation most in need of rebuke and reproach is the Christians, who claim to be the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him, because the insolence of the other nations was confined to the prophets, whereas the insolence of these heretics extended to the majesty and grandeur of Allah, in that they attributed to Him what is not fitting for His station to be described with, namely taking a wife and a son. Therefore, He, exalted is He, mentioned that He enumerates the kinds of His blessings upon Jesus in the presence of the Messengers, one by one, as an indication of his servitude, for each of those enumerated blessings upon him indicates that he is a servant and not a god. Then He followed that with His question to him, so that he would affirm, peace be upon him, before the witnesses, his servitude, and with His command to them to worship Allah, mighty and majestic. This is to refute them in their slander against him, and to establish the proof against his people. This is the secret of His question to him, exalted is He, despite His knowledge that he did not say that. All of this is to alert the Christians who were at the time of the revelation of the verse, and those who were influenced by them, to the ugliness of their statement and the feebleness of their doctrine and belief.

(p-2220) Admonitions:

The first: It was narrated from Qatadah that this statement will be made on the Day of Resurrection, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. As-Suddi said: this address and response are in this world, and Ibn Jarir endorsed this, saying: that was when he was raised to the heaven. Ibn Jarir argued for this on two grounds: the first being that the speech is in the past tense.

The second is His saying: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants, and if You forgive them...﴾

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: these two proofs are open to scrutiny, because many matters of the Day of Resurrection are mentioned in the past tense to indicate certainty and occurrence. The meaning of His saying: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118] and so on is: disavowal of them and referring the matter of their fate to Allah, exalted is He. Making that conditional does not imply that it occurs, as in similar verses. So what Qatadah and others said is the more apparent. Allah knows best that this will take place on the Day of Resurrection, to threaten the Christians, rebuke them and reprove them before the witnesses. A hadith with a raised chain has been narrated to this effect, which al-Hafiz Ibn Asakir related in the biography of Abu 'Abd Allah, the client of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who was trustworthy. He said: I heard Abu Burdah narrating to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz from his father, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the prophets and their nations will be summoned. Then Jesus will be summoned, and Allah will remind him of His blessing upon him, and he will acknowledge it, and He will say: 'O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you and upon your mother,' and so on. Then He will say: 'Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"' He will deny that he said it. Then the Christians will be brought and questioned, and they will say: 'Yes, He commanded us to do that!' He said: Then the hair of Jesus, peace be upon him, will grow long, and every angel will take a strand of hair from his head and body, and he will kneel before them in the presence of Allah, mighty and majestic, for a period of a thousand years, until the proof is established against them, and the cross is raised over them, and they are taken away to the Fire!"

Ibn Kathir said: This is a strange and rare hadith!

(p-2221) The second: The choice of His saying "my mother" rather than "Maryam" is a rebuke to those who took them as gods, as if to say: although you are a human who gives birth and is born before this.

The third: Some have imagined that the phrase "besides Allah" (min dun Allah) indicates that the Christians believe Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, to be independently deserving of worship, in place of Allah, exalted is He, just as one says: "You took so-and-so as a friend besides me," which means he substituted him for me, not that he made him a friend alongside me. They did not say this; rather, they affirmed a trinity. He answered: whoever associates another with Allah has, in meaning, negated Him, since He alone has no partner and is far exalted above that; thus their affirmation of Allah is as if no affirmation at all. So "besides Allah" would be a metaphor for "along with Allah." It is not hidden that this is a forced interpretation, since their rebuke is only achieved by what they themselves believe and openly acknowledge, not by what it implies through some form of interpretation. The correct view is that the intended meaning is taking them by way of associating them with Him, glorified is He, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], and His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 18], up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate﴾ [Yunus: 18], for it is through this that the rebuke comes about, and the reproach and reprimand are made possible. This is what they have verified here.

I say: The word "dun" (besides) in this verse and its like means "ghayr" (other than), as the linguists have verified. It does not indicate by its own designation (p-2222) independence or substitution, as was imagined; its purpose in mentioning it is to convey partnership, for without it one would imagine a claim that divinity is restricted to other than Him, even though they do not believe that. Nor is substitution understood from a phrase like "You took a friend besides me." That comes from an external indication; otherwise the example does not necessarily mean it, since it is possible that he intended taking him along with him, as is not hidden. So reflect.

﴿He said, "Exalted are You"﴾ That is: I declare You far above, in a manner fitting for You, from that being said or uttered: ﴿It is not for me﴾ that is: it is not conceivable from me, after You sent me to guide creation: ﴿to say﴾ that is: concerning myself: ﴿what I have no right to say﴾ that is: what is established in the hearts of the wise, that I have no entitlement to it, of what would mislead them: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ This is a resumptive clause establishing, by way of demonstrative proof, that the aforementioned statement did not proceed from him, peace be upon him. For its proceeding from him necessarily entails His knowledge of it, with certainty. So where His knowledge of it is absent, its proceeding from him is decisively absent, since the absence of the consequent necessarily entails the absence of the antecedent. Thus said Abu al-Su'ud.

﴿You know what is within myself﴾ is a resumptive clause functioning as a reason for what precedes it. As if it were said: because You know what I conceal within myself, so how much more so what I make public? His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and I do not know what is within Yourself﴾ is an explanation of the reality and a demonstration of its deficiency. That is: I do not know what You conceal of Your knowledge. Abu al-Su'ud stated this: ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 117:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[117] ﴿I said to them nothing except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are, over all things, Witness.﴾

﴿I said to them nothing except what You commanded me﴾ That is: I did not command them except with what You commanded me. The phrase "I said to them" was used out of regard for good manners, and in observance of what came in the interrogation. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾, is an explanation of what was commanded. ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them﴾ (p-2223) That is: a watcher who oversaw their conditions and brought them to act in accordance with the requirement of Your command, and whose forbidding them from what I witnessed in them that was not fitting was made possible. ﴿But when You caused me to die﴾ That is: by raising me up to the heaven, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I will cause you to die and raise you to Myself﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55]. And al-tawaffi (causing to die / taking in full) means taking a thing in full. Death is a type of it. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾ [az-Zumar: 42]. It was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Jesus, indeed I will cause you to die﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], with further clarification beyond what is here, so reflect.

﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾ That is: the one observing their deeds. Thus You prevented from uttering that whom You willed to preserve, and You forsook those among the misguided whom You forsook, so they said what they said. ﴿And You are, over all things, Witness﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it. In it is an indication that He, Exalted is He, was the Witness over all, at the time when he, peace be upon him, was among them.

Note of caution:

The verse indicates that the prophets, after completing their worldly term and being transferred to the barzakh, do not know the deeds of their communities. Al-Bukhari has narrated here from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon and said: 'O people! You will be gathered to Allah barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.' Then he recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise upon Us. Indeed, We will do it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104] to the end of the verse. Then he said: (p-2224) 'Verily, the first of creation to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrahim. Verily, men from my community will be brought, and they will be taken to the left side, and I will say: O Lord, my companions! It will be said: Indeed, you do not know what they innovated after you. So I will say as the righteous servant said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them﴾. It will be said: Indeed, these have not ceased to turn back on their heels since you parted from them.'"

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[118] ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This statement contains the referral of the will to Allah, mighty and majestic. He is the Doer of what He wills; He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned. It also contains a disavowal of the Christians, who lied against Allah and His Messenger and made for Allah equals, a consort and a son. Exalted is Allah above what they say, a great exaltation. End of quotation.

That is: If You punish them, then You are punishing Your servants, and there is no objection to the absolute Owner regarding what He does with His possession. This contains an indication that they deserved that because they are Your servants and they worshipped other than You. And if You forgive them, there is no incapacity and no reproach, because You are the Powerful, the Mighty, able to reward and to punish, who does not reward or punish except for wisdom and rightness. Forgiveness is praiseworthy for every criminal. If You punish, it is justice; if You forgive, it is grace. The non-forgiveness of shirk is the requirement of the threat, so there is no impossibility in it in itself, that would prevent the conditional and the use of (in, "if"). This was related by al-Baydawi.

It means: forgiveness, although its non-occurrence is definite in terms of existence, is, since it is in terms of reason, admitting of occurrence and non-occurrence. So the word (in, "if") was used for it, and what is imagined is dispelled, namely how (in) could be used for their punishment when its existence is definite, while the non-occurrence of pardon is by the ruling of the text and consensus.

(p-2225) In the books of kalam (theology): forgiveness of shirk is rationally permissible according to us and according to the majority of the Basrans among the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), because punishment is the right of Allah over the sinner, and there is no harm in waiving it.

In sum: the saying of His, exalted is He, "if You forgive them," is not an implicit request for their pardon. Rather, it is to show His power over what He wills, and according to the requirement of His judgment and wisdom. Therefore He said: indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise, indicating that no one can prevent Him from His might, so there is no objection to His judgment and wisdom.

Al-Razi said: Some people said: had He said, "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," that would have implied that He is an intercessor for them. When He said, "indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise," that indicates that His aim is the complete entrusting of the matter to Allah, exalted is He, and leaving any engagement with this matter from all aspects.

In al-Inayah (a commentary on al-Kashshaf) there is what summarizes: that what some of them supposed, that the apparent requirement is "the Forgiving, the Merciful" in place of "the Mighty, the Wise," as occurred in the Mushaf (codex) of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, has missed the secret of the context, because he thought it is connected to the second condition alone, as its answer. It is not as he imagined. Rather, it is connected to both. Whoever has the power to act and to refrain is Mighty and Wise. This is more fitting, more precise, and more suitable to the context. Or it is connected to the second, and that is a precaution, because leaving off punishing the offender may be due to an incapacity that contradicts power, or to negligence that contradicts wisdom. So He made clear that His reward and His punishment are with complete power and perfect wisdom.

Note:

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This verse has a great status and a wondrous report. It has been reported in a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up with it throughout the night until morning, repeating it.

Imam Ahmad related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed one night and recited a single verse until morning, bowing with it and prostrating with it: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ When it was morning I said: O Messenger of Allah, you did not stop reciting this verse until morning, bowing with it and prostrating with it? He said: 'I asked my Lord, mighty and majestic, for intercession for my Ummah, and He gave it to me. It will be attained, if Allah wills, by whoever does not associate anything with Allah.'" It was also recorded by al-Nasa'i.

Imam Ahmad also related from Abu Dharr who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood one night for the 'Isha prayer. He led the people in prayer, then some of his companions lagged behind, praying. When he saw their standing and their lagging, he turned to his dwelling. When he saw that the people had vacated the place, he returned to his place and prayed. I came and stood behind him, and he gestured to me with his right hand, so I stood on his right. Then Ibn Mas'ud came and stood behind me, and he gestured to him with his left hand, so he stood on his left. So the three of us stood, each one praying by himself, and we recited from the Qur'an what Allah willed for us to recite. He stood with one verse of the Qur'an, repeating it, until he prayed the dawn prayer. When we reached morning, I gestured to Abdullah ibn Mas'ud to ask him what he intended by what he did last night. Ibn Mas'ud said: I will not ask him about anything until he speaks to me. I said: May my father and mother be your ransom! You stood with one verse of the Qur'an while the Qur'an is with you! If one of us had done this, we would have been blamed for it. He said: I supplicated for my Ummah. I said: And what was your answer? Or what was returned to you? He said: I was answered with what, if many of them had seen a glimpse of it, they would have abandoned the prayer. I said: Shall I not give the good news to the people? He said: Yes. So I set off hurrying, close to a stone's throw. Then Umar said: O Messenger of Allah, if you send this out, they will shrink from worship. So he called out to him: Return. And he returned."

That verse is: if ﴿You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾"

Muslim related from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, about Abraham: ﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many people astray. So whoever follows me, indeed he is of me﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], and the saying of Jesus: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ (p-2227) Then he raised his hands and said: O Allah, my Ummah, my Ummah! And he wept. Allah, exalted is He, said: O Gabriel! Go to Muhammad—and your Lord knows best—and ask him: what makes him weep? So Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and asked him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed him of what he had said, though He knows best. Allah said: O Gabriel! Go to Muhammad and say to him: Indeed We will please you regarding your Ummah, and We will not grieve you."

Then, exalted is He, concluded the account of what He related of what occurs on the day when Allah gathers the Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, with an indication to the outcome and final result of that, by His saying, exalted is He:

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[119] ﴿Allah said: "This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the supreme triumph."﴾

﴿Allah said, "This is﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection: ﴿a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾, because it is the Day of Recompense. By "the truthful" (al-sadiqin) is meant those who persist in truthfulness in matters of religion, the greatest of which is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), which is the subject of this verse. In this there is a testimony to the truthfulness of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, in what he said, in answer to the words: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and so on.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For them are gardens﴾, is an explanation of the benefit mentioned, and for this reason it is not joined to it by a conjunction. That is: for them are orchards planted by their truthfulness. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., beneath their trees and their couches: ﴿the rivers﴾, the rivers of water, milk, wine and honey: ﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining, neither dying nor being removed: ﴿forever. Allah is pleased with them﴾ because of their truthfulness: ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾, confirming their truthfulness, for they did not feel resentment at His decree in the world. ﴿That﴾, i.e., the abiding and the good pleasure: ﴿is the supreme triumph﴾, i.e., the great one than which there is nothing greater. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾ [al-Saffat: 61], and as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for this let the competitors compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 5, verse 120:

And His saying (exalted is He):

(p-2228) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying (exalted is He):

[120] ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾ is a affirmation of the truth and an alert to the falsehood of the Christians and the corruption of what they claimed about the Messiah and his mother. This comes from the placing of the adverbial phrase first (taqdim al-zarf), because He is the Owner and no other. Therefore there is no partner to Him. ﴿And He is over all things competent﴾, i.e., exceedingly capable. All things are His possession, under His subjugation, power and will. There is no equal to Him nor minister. There is no god other than Him and no lord besides Him.

Ibn Wahb narrated it from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "The last surah to be revealed was Surat al-Ma'idah." Al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim recorded it. Al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim also recorded from Aisha, who said: "The last surahs to be revealed were al-Ma'idah and al-Fath," as cited in al-Itqan.

The completion of what Allah, exalted is He, decreed for His servants of the excellent interpretations of this noble surah

after the afternoon prayer on Friday, the 19th of Ramadan, in the year 1320,

in the upper right portico of the Sananiyya Mosque.

And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
